messages.content: Tell me a story about a lost puppy.

Biscuit was a brown puppy who belonged to a boy named Arjun. One afternoon the gate was left open, and Biscuit trotted out to chase a butterfly. By the time he looked up, he was in a street he had never seen. Every house looked the same. He sat down by a lamp post and whimpered.

A flower seller named Meera noticed him. She gave him a little water and saw the tag on his collar. It had a phone number scratched into it. She called it from the shop next door.

Ten minutes later Arjun came running, out of breath. Biscuit leapt into his arms and licked his chin until he laughed. They walked home together, and the gate stayed shut after that.
Can you write a short story about a clever crow?

It was a hot May afternoon, and a crow named Kaalu was very thirsty. Every pond in the village had dried up. At last he found a tall clay pot behind a tea stall, with a little water at the very bottom. His beak could not reach it.

Kaalu hopped around the pot, thinking. Then he saw a pile of small stones by the wall. He picked one up and dropped it into the pot. Plink. The water rose a little. He dropped another, and another, until the water came up to the rim.

He drank until he was full. The tea stall owner, Raghav, had watched the whole thing with his mouth open. After that he left a bowl of water out for Kaalu every day.
Write about the first day of the monsoon in a small village, as a story.

For three months the fields around Pipli had been cracked and brown. Old Sunita stood at her door each evening, staring at the empty sky. Her grandson Dev kept asking when the rain would come, and she kept saying soon.

One morning the air turned heavy and the crows went quiet. Then a cool wind came, and the first drops hit the dust with a sound like tiny drums. Dev ran outside with his arms spread wide. Within minutes the whole lane was a brown stream, and children were splashing in it.

Sunita laughed and held out her palms. The smell of wet earth filled the village. By evening, farmers were already out in the fields, planting.
My little sister wants a bedtime story about a sleepy bear.

Bruno the bear was very, very sleepy. The sun was going down in the pine forest, and he wanted his cave. But when he got there, a family of squirrels had made a nest right in the doorway.

"Please may I come in?" Bruno yawned. "I am so tired."

The smallest squirrel, Nutmeg, thought for a moment. "You can sleep in the back," she said, "if you keep your snoring soft."

Bruno tiptoed past the nest, one slow paw at a time. He curled up in the warm dark corner. The squirrels snuggled close to his big fur, and the cave filled with quiet breathing.

Outside, the stars came out one by one. Bruno did not snore even once.
I would like a story set by a river where a boy loses his paper boat.

Imran had spent all Sunday folding a paper boat from a page of his old drawing book. He painted a red sail on it and wrote its name on the side: Tara. When he set it on the river, it sailed away beautifully, then caught in the current and shot out of sight.

He ran along the bank, jumping over roots, until he saw a fisherman named Haridas mending a net. "Have you seen a red boat?" Imran panted.

Haridas pointed to a bend where reeds grew thick. There was Tara, stuck gently among the green stems, still upright.

Imran waded in up to his knees and lifted her out. The sail was a little wet, but it was still red.
Story please: a snail wins a race, and keep it happy.

The garden held a race every spring, and this year a snail named Gopal signed up. The other runners laughed. A grasshopper, a beetle and a fat earthworm stood at the line, stretching.

Then the judge, an old toad, explained the course. The race went up the side of the big glass jar by the tap, and the first one to reach the rim would win.

The grasshopper leapt at the glass and slid straight down. The beetle scrabbled and toppled onto his back. The earthworm took one look and went home.

Gopal just kept going, one slow inch at a time, his sticky foot holding tight to the smooth glass. Nobody could slide him off.

When he reached the rim, everyone cheered, even the grasshopper, who was still rubbing his knees.
Could you make up a story for a six-year-old about a cow who would not give milk?

Lakshmi the cow stood in the shed and would not give any milk. Farmer Prakash tried everything. He sang to her. He brushed her. He gave her fresh grass. Still, nothing.

His daughter Anu came and sat beside the cow. "Lakshmi looks sad," she said. "Maybe she misses her friend."

Prakash blinked. Then he remembered. The old goat, Moti, had been sold last week, and Lakshmi had always shared her corner with him.

That evening Prakash went to the neighbour's farm and brought Moti back for a visit. Lakshmi mooed so loudly that the hens jumped. She nuzzled Moti's head, and the next morning the pail was full of warm milk.
Give me a tale of a little sparrow who learned to fly.

Chinki was the smallest sparrow in the nest under the school roof. Her brothers had already flown. Every morning they zipped past her, chirping, while she gripped the edge with her tiny claws.

"It is too high," she told her mother.

"Then look at one thing only," her mother said. "That red flower in the courtyard."

Chinki stared at the flower. She took a breath and let go. For a second she dropped like a stone. Then her wings caught the air, and she was carried forward, wobbling, until she landed right on the red petals.

A little girl in a blue uniform saw her and pointed. Chinki puffed out her chest and hopped proudly in a circle.
Please write a short story about two friends caught in a thunderstorm on a hill.

Neha and Tobias had climbed to the top of the hill just to see the sunset. They were eating their sandwiches when the sky behind them went dark. A cold wind rolled over the grass, and thunder rumbled far away.

"We should go down," Neha said.

They started to run, but the rain was faster. It poured so hard they could barely see the path. Tobias slipped and scraped his hand. Neha pulled him up, and together they ducked into a stone shelter that a shepherd had built long ago.

They sat there, soaked and shivering, listening to the storm. When it finally passed, a rainbow stretched over the valley, and they both started laughing.
What would a story about a cat who adopts a family look like? Write it for me.

Nobody in the Fernandes house had asked for a cat. But one rainy evening, a thin grey cat walked in through the kitchen door, sat on the mat and refused to leave.

Mrs. Fernandes tried to shoo her out. Her son Carlos tried to shoo her out. The cat simply blinked at them and climbed onto the best chair.

They put out a saucer of milk, thinking she would go in the morning. She did not. She followed Carlos to the school gate. She waited on the wall when Mrs. Fernandes came home from work. By the end of the week she had a name, Smoky, and a cushion of her own.

Nobody remembered who had decided that. Smoky purred as if she had known all along.
Make up a tale about a deer who gets lost in the forest and finds her way home.

Hiran was a young deer who loved to wander. One morning she followed a bright butterfly deeper into the forest than she had ever gone. When the butterfly flew away, Hiran looked around and found only tall trees on every side.

She walked until her legs ached. Then she heard a faint, familiar sound: the tinkle of the stream near her home. She stood very still and listened. The sound came from her left.

She followed it, step by careful step, and soon the trees opened onto the meadow where her mother was calling her name.

Hiran ran to her and pressed her nose into her mother's neck. After that, she still wandered, but she always listened for the stream first.
How about a story with a talking frog who loves the rain?

A green frog named Pappu lived in a ditch behind the bus stand. While other creatures hid when the clouds came, Pappu sat on his rock and shouted, "Rain, rain, hurry up!"

One afternoon a girl named Kavya heard him. She was waiting for a bus, grumpy because her umbrella was broken. "Why are you so happy?" she asked.

"Because everything is better when it is wet!" said Pappu. "Listen!"

Kavya listened. The rain drummed on the tin roof. Puddles sang little songs. The leaves sparkled. She took off her shoes, stepped into a puddle and laughed out loud.

When the bus came, she did not want to get on. Pappu waved a webbed foot, and she waved back.
Write a gentle story about a girl and an old turtle by the river.

Every afternoon after school, Mira walked down to the river to sit on a flat rock. And every afternoon an old turtle slid out of the water to share it with her.

One day the turtle did not come. Mira waited until the light turned orange. The next day, still nothing. She felt a heavy ache in her chest.

On the third day, she saw a small, round shape far out in the water, swimming slowly. It was the turtle, and behind him paddled three tiny ones, no bigger than coins.

The turtle climbed onto the rock and the babies tumbled after him. Mira held her breath and did not move. The sun went down, and the river glowed gold around them all.
A story about a rooster who forgot how to crow, please.

Every morning, Rooster Bholu crowed to wake the whole village. But one day he opened his beak and only a small squeak came out. The hens stared. The goats stared. The sun rose anyway, and everyone slept late.

Bholu was ashamed. He hid behind the haystack. A boy named Sameer found him there and sat down. "Maybe you are thinking too hard," he said.

"I just forgot," said Bholu.

Sameer began to hum a tune. Bholu felt something tickle in his throat. He tilted his head back and, before he could worry, a loud crow rolled across the fields.

The hens clucked, the goats bleated, and in the houses lamps were lit. Bholu strutted proudly the whole day.
Can I get a story where an elephant and a tiny mouse help each other?

A big elephant named Gajraj was walking through the jungle when he stepped on a thorn. It was so deep he could not pull it out, however hard he tried with his trunk. He sat down under a banyan tree and groaned.

A small mouse named Chuhi had been watching from a hole. "Hold still," she called, and she scurried up his foot. With her sharp little teeth, she tugged at the thorn until it popped out.

Gajraj sighed with relief. "Thank you, little one. How can I repay you?"

"Just do not step on my hole," Chuhi laughed.

From then on, Gajraj walked carefully whenever he passed the banyan, and Chuhi often rode on his head to see the whole jungle.
Tell a story about a seed that did not want to grow.

Under the soil of a school garden, a tiny seed named Pinto lay curled up. The other seeds had already pushed out green shoots. Pinto stayed where he was.

"It is dark up there and scary," he said. "The wind is strong. What if I break?"

A worm named Wriggles slid by. "I have been in the dark all my life," he said. "But I can feel the sun warm the ground from here. Something lovely is waiting."

Pinto thought about the warmth. Slowly, he stretched one tiny root down and one little leaf up. It was hard work. After many days, his head popped into the light.

A girl named Rosa knelt beside him. "Look, this one is late!" she said, and gave him a drop of water.
Write one paragraph only, a story about a boy and his goldfish.

Samir's goldfish, Chotu, had lived in the same round bowl for two years, and Samir talked to him every night before bed. One Tuesday Samir came home from school and found the bowl empty. His heart dropped. He searched the floor, the shelf, under the sofa, and then he heard a soft splash from the bathroom, where his little sister Pari was holding Chotu in a mug of water. "He looked bored," she explained, "so I gave him a trip." Samir was so relieved that he forgot to be angry. Together they carried Chotu back to his bowl, and Samir made Pari promise to ask first next time, which she did, with a very serious face.
I want to hear about a parrot who could say only one word.

Mintu the parrot lived in the house of Mr. and Mrs. D'Souza, and he knew only one word: "Namaste." He said it to the milkman, to the neighbours, to the cat, and sometimes to the ceiling fan.

One evening Mrs. D'Souza felt dizzy and sat down on the floor of the kitchen. Her husband was out. Nobody was home but Mintu.

The parrot flapped his wings and squawked, "Namaste! Namaste!" louder than ever. The neighbour, Mrs. Pillai, heard the strange noise through the wall and came to check.

She found Mrs. D'Souza, helped her to a chair and gave her water. Later, everyone said Mintu was the cleverest bird in the street, and Mrs. D'Souza gave him an extra mango slice.
Could a baby owl found by a girl in the forest near her grandmother's house be the heart of a short story?

Whenever Ananya visited her grandmother in the hills, she walked in the oak forest behind the house. One morning she heard a thin, strange cry under a tree. A baby owl, fluffy and grey, sat on the ground, blinking up at her.

She ran back to get her grandmother. "Do not touch him yet," Ajji said. "His mother may be near."

They sat quietly behind a bush and waited. After a long time, a large owl glided down and landed on a low branch. She made a soft hooting sound, and the baby hopped after her, flapping, until he scrambled up the trunk.

Ananya smiled all the way home. That night she heard the owls calling from the forest, and she knew which one was his.
Share a story about a boy and his grandfather on a rainy morning, and use the word umbrella.

The rain would not stop, and Kabir was bored. School was closed, his cricket ball was wet, and his phone had no battery. His grandfather, Dada, looked up from his newspaper.

"Come," he said, taking down an old black umbrella. "I will show you something."

They walked out together, the umbrella drumming over their heads. Dada led him to a small pond, where hundreds of tiny frogs were hopping in the grass. Kabir had never seen so many.

"They only come out when it rains like this," said Dada. "Most people miss them."

Kabir crouched down and watched. His shoes were soaked, and he did not mind at all. On the walk home he asked if they could come again tomorrow.
Write a funny short story where a fisherman catches a fish that talks.

Fisherman Rustam had caught nothing all morning. Then, just before noon, his line jerked hard, and he pulled up a big silver fish.

"Excuse me," said the fish. "I have a meeting."

Rustam nearly fell into the river. "A meeting?"

"With the other fish. We are discussing the new reeds. Please put me back."

Rustam scratched his head. "But my wife will ask where the dinner is."

"Tell her a fish had better plans," said the fish.

Rustam laughed so hard he dropped his hat in the water. He let the fish go and went home with only the story. His wife, Zainab, laughed too, and they ate lentils and rice that night. The next day the fish waved from the water.
Set a story in a village where a goat saves the day.

In the village of Sonpur, a goat named Chandni belonged to a widow called Ramabai. Everyone thought Chandni was a nuisance because she ate their flowers and chewed their washing.

One night, a fire started in the haystack by the school. Everyone was asleep. Chandni, tied in her shed, smelled the smoke first. She bleated and kicked at the wooden door until it broke, and then she ran through the lanes, bleating at every window.

Lights came on. Men grabbed buckets from the well and put the fire out before it reached the school.

The next morning, the headman brought Chandni a garland of marigolds. She ate half of it, and no one minded.
A monkey stole a boy's cap; can you turn that into a story?

Ravi was walking to the temple with a new red cap on his head when a monkey leapt from a wall and snatched it. The monkey scrambled up a neem tree and sat there, grinning, with the cap on his own head.

"Give it back!" Ravi shouted. The monkey only scratched his belly.

Ravi thought for a minute. Then he took a banana from his bag and held it up. The monkey's eyes lit up. He climbed down slowly, dropped the cap in front of Ravi and grabbed the banana.

Ravi put the cap back on, still warm from the monkey's head. As he walked on, he heard a rustle above him. The monkey was following, hoping for another banana.
In under 120 words, tell a story about a mountain path and a lost hiker.

Priya had been hiking alone for three hours when the fog rolled in. The path vanished. She stopped and took a slow breath. Her father had always told her, "If you are lost, stay still."

She sat on a rock and waited. After a while, she heard a bell, then another. A herd of mountain goats came out of the mist, led by an old shepherd named Tashi.

"You are far from the trail," he said kindly. "Come, we are going down."

Priya followed the goats and the sound of their bells. An hour later, the fog thinned and she saw the village roofs below. She thanked Tashi, who only nodded and whistled his herd on.
Describe, as a story, a dog who waits for a boy at the bus stop every day.

Every afternoon at four, a yellow dog named Sheru sat at the school bus stop. He wagged his tail when the bus doors opened and ran to a boy named Vihaan.

One day, Vihaan did not get off. Sheru waited until the bus drove away, then sat there until dark. The next day he waited again.

The bus driver, Mr. Khan, noticed. On the third day he told Sheru, "Vihaan has a fever. He is at home."

Sheru could not understand the words, but he heard the name. He trotted straight down the lane and stopped outside Vihaan's gate, where he barked once.

Vihaan's mother let him in. The dog jumped up on the bed, and Vihaan, weak but grinning, scratched his ears.
Let me have a story about a peacock that is shy about dancing.

In a village field lived a young peacock named Mayur who had the most beautiful tail in the flock. But when the clouds gathered and the others began to dance, Mayur hid behind a bush.

"What if I get it wrong?" he whispered to a passing hen.

"Wrong?" she said. "It is only dancing."

As the first thunder rolled, Mayur felt a tingle in his feathers. He stepped out slowly. He spread his tail. A drop fell on it, then another, and before he knew it, he was turning in circles, tail shimmering with blue and green.

The flock gathered around and watched. A little girl at the fence clapped her hands. Mayur kept dancing until the rain stopped.
Create a story where a fox tries to trick a rabbit but fails.

A hungry fox named Reynard saw a rabbit called Clover nibbling grass by the old oak. He smiled his widest smile and strolled over.

"Good morning, Clover! I just found a field of carrots over the hill. Come, I will show you."

Clover twitched her nose. "That is kind. Why not go first, so I can see the way?"

The fox frowned. He had planned to walk behind her. But he went ahead, and the moment his back was turned, Clover bolted into a thick patch of brambles where no fox could follow.

Reynard waited an hour outside the thorns. When he finally gave up, Clover was already in the next meadow, eating real carrots she had found herself.
Tell me about a paper umbrella and a stray kitten, as a little story.

On a wet Saturday, Leela was making a paper umbrella for her school project when she heard a mew outside. A tiny, wet kitten sat shivering on the step.

Leela had no real umbrella, so she held up her paper one. It was too small, and soon it was soaked and drooping. She laughed and picked up the kitten instead, wrapping it in her dupatta.

She carried it inside and dried it with a towel. Her mother brought a saucer of warm milk. The kitten drank, yawned and fell asleep in Leela's lap.

The paper umbrella dried on the windowsill, a little crinkled. Leela named the kitten Mittens. She put a small paw-print stamp on the umbrella, wrote "For Mittens" on it and hung it above the basket.
Compose a story involving a bridge, a river and two stubborn goats.

A narrow log bridge crossed the river near the village of Dhara. One morning, a white goat called Gori started across from the east. At the same moment, a black goat called Kali started from the west.

They met in the middle. Neither would step back. "I was here first," said Gori. "No, I was," said Kali. They lowered their horns and glared.

Below them, the river rushed fast. A boy named Hamid, who was washing his bullock nearby, watched with worry. "Someone will fall!" he called.

Gori looked down at the water and gulped. "Maybe," she said, "you could lie down and I could step over you." Kali agreed. Soon both goats were safely across, and Hamid laughed so hard he nearly dropped his soap.
Could you write about a scarecrow who makes a friend?

In a wheat field outside Karnal stood a scarecrow named Bhola, dressed in an old kurta and a torn hat. Crows kept away from him, which was his job, but it made him lonely.

One evening a small crow with a hurt wing fell onto his shoulder. Bhola could not move his arms to help. He could only stand still and hold her.

The crow, named Tinku, stayed through the night, warm against his straw. In the morning, her wing felt better, but she did not fly off. She hopped up to his hat and built a small nest there.

The farmer, Mr. Gill, saw the nest and shook his head. But he left it, and the wheat grew tall.
Please tell a story about a baby elephant afraid of water.

Little Nandi, a baby elephant, was afraid of water. When the herd went to the river each evening, he stood at the top of the bank with his trunk curled tight.

"It is only wet," said his mother.

Nandi shook his head. The river looked deep and loud.

Then a heron named Bagula landed beside him. "Try it with your toes," she suggested. "Only your toes."

Nandi crept forward and dipped one foot in. It was cool, and it tickled. He dipped another. Soon, he was standing in the shallows, and his mother sprayed a little water over his back. He squealed with surprise.

By the end of the week, he was the first to charge into the river, splashing the whole herd.
Write a tale about a girl who plants a mango seed.

After eating a sweet mango, eight-year-old Zoya did not throw away the seed. She washed it, dug a hole in the corner of her grandfather's yard and planted it. Every morning she watered the spot and looked for green.

Nothing came up. After a month, her cousins teased her. "There is nothing there," they said.

Zoya kept watering. One morning in the second month, a thin red shoot pushed out of the soil. She screamed so loudly that her grandfather dropped his tea.

The little tree grew slowly, year after year. When Zoya was fourteen, it gave its first mangoes. She picked one, split it in half and gave the bigger piece to her grandfather, who smiled and said nothing at all.
Include a small problem in a story about a flock of geese flying south for winter.

The geese of Lake Vana were leaving for the south. They formed a great V in the sky, with old Gander leading. Behind him flew a young goose named Pip, who had never made such a long journey.

By the second day Pip was tired. His wings burned. He fell behind, and the wind pushed him down toward the dark hills.

"Pip!" called Gander. "Fly into my air!"

Pip swerved into the space behind a stronger goose, and at once the flying felt easier. The wind carried him along. He saw that every goose rested in turn at the front.

When it was his turn to lead, many days later, he did it for only a short while, but the others honked kindly all the same.
Dreamy story needed: the moon and a firefly.

One summer night the moon felt lonely. He hung high above the quiet fields with nobody to talk to.

Down in the grass a small firefly named Jugnu looked up. "You are very far away," she said, flashing her tiny light.

"I am," said the moon. "I wish I could be small like you, to sit among the leaves."

Jugnu thought. Then she called all her friends. One by one, hundreds of fireflies rose from the field and floated up in a glowing cloud. They danced in the dark air, blinking in gold.

The moon looked down and saw a hundred little lights shining back at him, as if the stars had come to visit. He smiled so brightly that the whole field shone silver until morning.
Write an exciting story about a rabbit who escapes from a pet shop.

The pet shop on Park Road was closing when a small white rabbit named Snowy saw the cage door swing open. Quick as a flash, he leapt out and darted between the shelves.

"Stop him!" cried the owner, Mr. Banerjee, dropping a bag of seeds.

Snowy raced through the door and into the street. A rickshaw bell rang. A dog barked. He zigzagged between legs and baskets until he reached the park, where a girl named Tanvi was sitting on a bench.

She saw the rabbit tremble at her feet and gently scooped him up. "You poor thing," she whispered.

Mr. Banerjee arrived, puffing. Tanvi handed over Snowy, and the shopkeeper smiled and fixed the cage latch the next morning.
Can you do a story about a monsoon flood in which a family and their buffalo are rescued?

The river rose faster than anyone expected. By midnight, water had crept into the courtyard of Ganesh's house, and by morning it was at the doorstep. Ganesh, his wife Sarita and their two children climbed onto the roof. Their buffalo, Kajri, stood in the water below, bellowing.

"We cannot leave her," said Ganesh.

A boat appeared around noon, rowed by two men from the next village. They took the children first, then Sarita. Then they looked at Kajri.

"Tie a rope to the boat," said Ganesh. "She can swim."

Kajri paddled steadily behind them for an hour. When they reached the high ground by the temple, she shook herself and gave a long, happy moo, and the children ran to hug her wet neck.
Story idea: a hen hatches an unusual egg. Write it up in short.

Hen Gulabo sat on her nest for three weeks. Her farmer, Mrs. Thomas, had slipped in a big pale egg she had found by the pond, and Gulabo was too polite to complain.

One morning the egg cracked. Out wobbled a fluffy yellow duckling. Gulabo stared. The duckling peeped. She clucked uncertainly.

The chicks laughed at him because he waddled. The duckling, whom Gulabo named Paddu, hung his head. But one hot afternoon, he waddled straight to the pond and floated, and the chicks stopped laughing.

They stood at the edge, watching him glide. Gulabo clucked loudly from the bank. "That is my son," she told the other hens. Paddu paddled in circles, quite happy with himself.
A tiger who is not scary at all: tell me his story.

Deep in the Sundarbans lived a tiger named Raja, who was big and striped and very gentle. The other animals ran whenever they saw him, though he never chased anyone.

Raja was lonely. One day he sat down at the edge of the water and sighed. A monkey named Chintu, hiding in a tree, was surprised. "You are sad?" he said.

"I only want someone to talk to," Raja said.

Chintu slowly came down. "Well, I like talking," he said, and began to tell Raja a long tale about a banana. Raja listened with his chin on his paws and laughed in a low rumble.

Soon more animals crept closer. By sunset, Raja had a circle of friends, all still a bit careful, but happy.
Write about a bee that gets lost in a classroom.

A bee named Bindu flew in through the window of Class 4B and could not find the way out. Thirty children shrieked. The teacher, Mrs. Das, tried to stay calm.

"Everyone sit still," she said. "Do not wave your arms."

Bhim buzzed in circles, bumping into the glass. A boy named Aarav, who sat by the window, quietly slid it wider. Then he took a flower from the vase on his desk and held it near the opening.

The bee noticed the scent. She zigzagged over, landed on the petals for a moment, and then, finding open sky, flew out into the playground.

The class clapped. Mrs. Das thanked Aarav, who turned pink and looked at his shoes.
Imagine a school day cancelled by heavy rain and tell it as a story.

On Monday morning, the rain was pouring so hard that the school ground looked like a lake. Tara's father checked the phone and read the message aloud: school was closed.

Tara cheered. Then she remembered that her best friend Jaya lived across the road and had no one to play with. She put on her yellow raincoat and splashed over.

Jaya's mother let them in. They made a boat from a plastic tray and sailed it in the big bucket on the balcony. They built a fort out of cushions. At lunch, Jaya's mother fried hot pakoras, and they ate them watching the rain slide down the window.

By evening, the sun peeked out. Tara walked home with wet socks and a very full stomach.
Write a story for me where a woodpecker helps a village.

The old neem tree at the edge of Kheda was dying, and nobody knew why. Its leaves were yellow and its branches drooped. The elders shook their heads.

A woodpecker named Tuk-Tuk landed on its trunk and began to tap. Tap, tap, tap. A boy named Omar noticed that she kept pecking one spot. Curious, he fetched his father.

Behind the bark, the two of them found a nest of beetles chewing through the wood. His father pulled them out and cleaned the hole.

Within a month the neem sprouted green again. Tuk-Tuk stayed on the highest branch, drumming each morning, and the villagers learned to look for her when a tree seemed unwell.
My five-year-old would like a story about a hedgehog who cannot find his house.

Hedgehog Hugo woke up from his nap and could not find his house. He looked under the log. It was not there. He looked behind the big rock. It was not there either.

"Oh dear," said Hugo, and his little nose twitched.

A robin named Rosie hopped over. "What are you looking for?"

"My round, leafy house!"

Rosie tilted her head. "Hugo, you are standing in it."

Hugo looked down. He was standing on a big pile of leaves, and under it was his own front door. He had walked right past it in his sleepy state!

Hugo laughed and laughed. He thanked Rosie, tidied his leaves and went inside for a warm cup of acorn tea.
Tell the story of a girl who follows a stream to its start.

Aditi's village had a stream that gurgled behind the school. One summer day she decided to find where it began. She packed a boiled egg, a bottle of water and a notebook.

She walked upstream through ferns and over rocks. The water grew thinner and colder. She crossed a log, scraped her knee and kept going. After two hours, the trees opened onto a rocky hollow, and there it was: a small spring bubbling from a crack in the stone.

Aditi sat beside it and ate her egg. She wrote, "The stream begins here," and drew a little map.

On the way home she felt she knew the stream like a friend. She pointed it out to her little brother and said, "I know its secret."
Something warm, please: a puppy's first day at a new home.

The puppy was named Mochi, and he was frightened. The car ride had been loud, and now he stood on a cold kitchen floor in a house that smelled strange.

A girl named Rhea knelt down. "Hello," she whispered. "This is your home."

Mochi crept under the table and stayed there. Rhea did not push. She lay down on the floor a short distance away with her chin on her arms and simply waited.

After a long while, a damp nose touched her hand. Then a small tongue licked her finger. Soon Mochi was in her lap, nibbling her sleeve.

That night, he slept in a basket beside her bed. Whenever he whimpered, Rhea put her hand down, and he stopped.
Narrate a story about a ferry boatman and a nervous passenger.

Boatman Chacko had crossed the river ten thousand times. That morning his only passenger was a young woman named Ishita, who gripped the sides of the boat so tightly her knuckles turned pale.

"I cannot swim," she admitted.

"Neither can my boat," Chacko joked, then saw her face and grew serious. "Look at the far bank," he said. "Not at the water. Watch that banyan tree."

Ishita stared at the banyan. The oars creaked and splashed. Little by little, her grip loosened, and the tree grew bigger.

When the boat bumped the other side, she let out a long breath. She had an interview in the town, and as she stepped off, she thanked Chacko and promised she would take the ferry back that evening.
I am after a story about an old bullock who still wants to work.

Moti the bullock had pulled the plough for fifteen years, but now his legs were stiff, and the farmer, Bhairav, had bought a young pair to replace him. Moti stood in the shed, watching them go out each morning.

One day, the new bullocks stopped in the middle of a muddy field. They would not budge. Bhairav shouted and pulled, and they only stamped.

Moti, hearing the noise, walked slowly out of the shed, still wearing his bell. He lumbered up beside them and leaned into the yoke. The young ones looked at him, then pulled.

Together, they finished the row. After that, Moti worked half-days, walking beside the young pair and teaching them where the mud was soft.
Put together a story about a camel in the desert who finds water for a traveller.

The traveller, a young trader named Yusuf, had been crossing the desert for two days when his water ran out. The sun was fierce. His lips were cracked. His camel, a calm tan beast named Rani, walked on without complaint.

On the third morning, Rani suddenly stopped and sniffed the air. Then she turned north, away from the trail.

"Rani, no," Yusuf croaked. "That is wrong."

But she kept going, and he was too weak to argue. After an hour, he saw a few green palms ahead and a small, hidden pool.

He fell to his knees and drank. Rani drank beside him, long and slow.

That evening, Yusuf gave her the last of his dates and promised never to doubt her again.
Keep it light: a story about a caterpillar impatient to become a butterfly.

A fat green caterpillar named Kiki sat on a cabbage leaf, sighing. "I want wings," she told the ladybird. "I am tired of crawling."

"You must wait," said the ladybird.

"I do not like waiting."

The next day she tried flapping her legs. She fell off the leaf. The day after, she climbed the highest twig and jumped, landing in the mud. The ladybird laughed so hard she toppled over.

Finally, tired and muddy, Kiki spun herself into a cosy bundle and slept. She slept a long time.

One warm morning, the bundle split, and out crept something wet and wrinkled. It unfolded two orange wings. Kiki flapped them, rose into the air and shrieked with joy.
Under 130 words, write a story about a duck family crossing a busy road.

Mother Duck led her seven ducklings out of the pond and up the grassy bank. The road was on the other side. Beyond it lay the lake where she wanted to take them.

Trucks roared past. A cycle bell rang. The ducklings huddled behind her, peeping.

A traffic policeman named Mr. Singh saw them from the crossing. He blew his whistle and held up one white-gloved hand. The cars slowed and stopped. A bus waited, then a tempo.

Mother Duck waddled out, head high, and the seven small ducklings followed in a perfect line. The policeman counted them aloud: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.

When they reached the grass, Mr. Singh lowered his hand, and traffic moved again.
Pen a story about a girl who dances in the first rain after a drought.

Banu was seven, and she had never seen the pond in her village full. For two years the rains had failed. The cattle were thin, her mother was tired and her father had gone to the city to find work.

One afternoon the clouds darkened. Banu stood in the yard, looking up. A drop landed on her nose. Then another.

She began to spin. Her mother came to the door, wiping her hands, and for a moment seemed about to scold. Instead, she stepped out too, laughing, and lifted her face to the sky.

Neighbours joined them. Children ran barefoot. Old men stood with their eyes closed.

That night the pond began to fill. Banu fell asleep listening to the water still falling on the roof.
Retell the tortoise and the hare, but set it in a bamboo forest.

In a bamboo forest in Assam, a hare named Phurti boasted that he was the fastest animal alive. A slow old tortoise named Kaasim said, "Shall we race to the big stone?"

Phurti laughed, but he agreed. At the signal, he shot ahead. Halfway there, he stopped to chew some tender shoots. Then he nibbled a few more. The afternoon was warm, and the bamboo whispered above him. He dozed.

Kaasim plodded on, step after step, never stopping. By the time the hare woke, the sun was low. He sprinted, but the tortoise was already touching the stone.

Phurti stared. "You won," he said, a little hoarse.

Kaasim only nodded, and the two walked home together as the stars came out.
How about a talking tree and a little boy in a story?

At the end of Lokesh's lane stood a very old peepal tree. One evening, as Lokesh sat under it crying because he had failed his maths test, the tree spoke.

"Why the tears, little one?"

Lokesh jumped. "You can talk?"

"Only to people who sit still for a while," said the tree. "Now tell me."

Lokesh told him everything. The tree listened, leaves rustling. "I once dropped all my leaves in a single night," it said. "I thought I had died. But in spring, new ones came."

Lokesh wiped his nose. He did not feel instantly fine, but his chest felt lighter.

The next day he asked his teacher for help. The tree, he decided, would keep their secret.
Give me a story about a parrot and a cat who become friends, with a title.

Mango and Mr. Whiskers

Mango the parrot lived in a cage by the window, and Mr. Whiskers the cat lived on the sofa. They had eyed each other for months. The cat wanted a feathery snack. The parrot wanted the cat to go away.

One day, the cage door was left open. Mango flapped out, landed on the floor and, to his own shock, did not run. The cat padded over slowly.

"Boo," said Mango.

Mr. Whiskers jumped back so quickly that he knocked over a vase. They both stared at the broken pieces, then at each other.

After that, Mango rode on the cat's back around the room, shouting directions. Mr. Whiskers sighed. He had lost his lunch, but he had gained a very loud friend.
Please use no dialogue in a story about a very patient kingfisher.

Every dawn, a blue kingfisher named Neel sat on the same low branch above the pond. He watched the water without moving. Dragonflies landed near him. A frog croaked and sank away. Neel did not stir.

The young kingfishers dived again and again, splashing loudly, and most days they came up with nothing. Neel only watched. When the sun climbed above the reeds, a small silver fish drifted just beneath the surface.

He dropped like a blue stone. The water barely rippled. A moment later he was back on the branch with the fish flashing in his beak.

A girl named Seema, who came each morning to fetch water, had watched the whole thing. She stood very still herself for a while, then smiled and went home.
Begin with the sentence "The rain came sideways that night." and write a story from there.

The rain came sideways that night, slapping against the shutters of the lighthouse where Keeper Jonas lived with his granddaughter Elsie. The wind howled around the tower like a hungry animal.

Elsie pressed her face to the glass. "Grandpa, there is a light out there!"

Jonas squinted. A tiny flicker bobbed on the black water: a fishing boat, far off its path, heading for the rocks.

He climbed the stairs and turned the great lamp until its beam swept across the waves. Elsie held the lantern and signalled with it. After a tense hour, the small boat veered, found the channel and slid toward the harbour.

In the morning, three tired fishermen climbed the hill to thank them, and Elsie served them hot cocoa.
Street dogs have stories too. Tell me one about a Mumbai dog and his favourite tea stall.

A scruffy brown dog called Bhura lived on a lane in Dadar, and his favourite place in the whole city was Anwar's tea stall. Every morning, Anwar tossed him half a bun, and every morning Bhura wagged his tail and lay beneath the counter while customers came and went.

One rainy night, thieves crept toward the stall to steal the gas cylinder. Bhura woke, growled and then barked so loudly that lights flickered on in the windows above. The thieves ran.

Anwar, who slept on a cot behind the stall, came out in his lungi and saw the empty street and the damp, proud dog.

The next morning Bhura got a whole bun and a saucer of milk tea, and he ate both slowly.
For children, a short story about a worm who wants to see the sky.

Wiggle the worm lived deep in the garden soil, where it was always dark and cool. He loved his tunnel, but sometimes he wondered what was above.

"What is the sky?" he asked the beetle.

"Blue," said the beetle. "And very big."

Wiggle decided to look. He pushed up through the dirt, up and up, until his head popped out. It was a rainy morning. He saw grey clouds, bright green leaves and a fat drop falling toward him. Plop!

"It is wet!" Wiggle gasped. "And lovely!"

He stayed for a while, feeling the rain on his back. When a robin swooped nearby, he scooted back down, giggling, to tell the beetle everything he had seen.
Exactly three paragraphs, please: a story about a girl and a banyan tree.

Asha loved the huge banyan tree behind her school. Its roots hung down like ropes, and during lunch she and her friends swung on them. But one Monday, a notice was pinned to the gate. The tree would be cut for a new road.

Asha did not sleep that night. In the morning she brought her class a big sheet of paper and asked every child to draw something that had happened under the banyan. They drew races, picnics, a birthday and a lost tooth. She took the pages to the headmaster, Mr. Rao.

He looked at them for a long time. Then he made a phone call. Two weeks later, the road was moved a few metres to the left, and the banyan was still there, its roots swinging in the breeze.
My little brother needs a bedtime story about a sleepy kitten.

Pillow was a very small kitten who did not want to go to bed. The moon was out, the house was dark, and her mother had curled up in the basket with a soft purr.

"Come, Pillow," her mother said.

"But I am not tired," said Pillow, and she pounced on a shadow. She chased a sock. She climbed the curtain halfway and slid down.

Soon her legs felt heavy. Her eyes went slow. She yawned, a huge pink yawn, and tumbled into the basket beside her mother.

The warm fur smelled of milk. Pillow tucked her nose under her paw. Outside, a cricket sang a soft song, and the kitten was asleep before it ended.
Two boys build a raft and float it down a stream. Write that as a story.

Rohan and his cousin Faisal spent three days gathering planks, rope and empty plastic bottles from the lane behind their houses. On Sunday, they lashed everything together and carried the raft to the village stream.

"It looks like a pile of rubbish," said Faisal.

"It looks like a ship," said Rohan.

They climbed aboard. The raft wobbled, dipped and floated. Both boys whooped. They drifted past reeds, a startled heron and some washing women who waved. Then they hit a shallow patch and stuck fast on a sandbank.

They had to jump out and push. Mud squelched around their ankles. When the raft finally slid free, they were filthy and laughing so hard they could barely hold the paddles. They agreed to build a better one next summer.
Think up a story about a buffalo calf born during a storm.

Thunder shook the shed the night the buffalo calf was born. Farmer Dilip's wife, Pooja, held a lantern while he helped the mother, Kali, through the long hours. Rain hammered the tin roof, and a leak dripped onto the straw.

At last, a small wet shape slid out and lay still. Dilip's heart sank. He rubbed the calf's side with a sack and spoke to it in a low voice. Nothing. He rubbed harder.

Then the calf sneezed. Her legs jerked. She lifted her head and blinked at the lantern.

Pooja laughed through her tears. By morning, the storm had passed and the calf, whom the children named Bijli, was standing on shaky legs, nuzzling her mother's side for milk.
A little spooky but with a happy end: a boy hears a strange noise in the forest at night.

Karan was camping with his uncle Mohan at the edge of a dark forest. In the middle of the night, a strange sound woke him: a low, wet snuffle, followed by a crunch of leaves.

He grabbed his torch with a shaking hand. "Uncle," he whispered. "Something is out there."

His uncle sat up slowly. The snuffling came closer, right outside the tent. Karan held his breath. Then a pointed nose pushed through the flap, followed by a spiky back. It was a hedgehog, sniffing for crumbs from their dinner.

Karan burst out laughing, and his uncle joined in. They watched the little creature munch a biscuit crumb, then waddle back into the dark. Karan fell asleep smiling.
Under 120 words, write a story about a lonely giraffe who finds a friend.

Gina the giraffe stood taller than every other animal in the savannah, and that made her feel lonely. The zebras were too small to talk to, and the lions never looked up.

One afternoon she noticed a tiny bird, an oxpecker named Pika, riding on her neck. "Excuse me," Gina said.

"Oh, sorry," said Pika. "It is the best view in the savannah."

Gina laughed softly. "Stay as long as you like."

After that, Pika sat on her head each day and told her everything she saw: lions napping, rain coming, a baby elephant lost. Gina was not lonely anymore, only careful when she walked, so her small friend would not fall off.
Write a simple story about an eagle chick afraid of heights.

High on a cliff lived a young eagle named Aaru. He could flap from the nest to the nearest rock, but whenever his cousins soared high above the valley, he stayed low. Looking down from up there made his tummy twist.

One warm afternoon, his cousin Tara landed beside him. "Come and ride the warm air," she said. "You hardly have to flap."

Aaru followed her to a sunny slope. She spread her wings wide and began to circle, rising without a single beat. Aaru copied her. A gentle push of warm air lifted him, round and round, higher and higher.

He was so busy watching Tara's wingtips that he forgot to be afraid. When he finally looked down, the valley was small and green below him, and it looked beautiful.
It is a monsoon night and the power is out. Write a story about a family playing a game.

The lights went out at eight o'clock, right in the middle of the rainstorm. Outside, thunder boomed. The whole building was dark.

"No TV," groaned Dinesh, who was ten. His sister Mallika, seven, started to cry a little.

Their mother lit two candles and put them on the table. Their father looked at the flickering walls. "Shadow animals," he said, holding up his hands. A rabbit appeared, then a dog with a long nose. Mallika giggled.

Soon the children were making their own shadows, an elephant, an eagle, even a very bad giraffe. Mother brought roasted peanuts. They played until nine thirty.

When the lights flicked back on, nobody wanted to switch off the candles right away.
Beach story wanted, with a crab and a sandcastle.

Little Zara spent the whole morning building a sandcastle with a tall tower and a moat. Just as she placed a shell on top, a wave rolled in and flattened half of it. She sat down with a thump, her lip trembling.

A small crab emerged from the foam and crawled over the ruins. He picked up a bit of sand in his claw and began to pile it back, slowly. Zara blinked.

She helped him. Together they dug a deeper moat and built the wall higher. The crab, whom she named Clicky, pushed a piece of seaweed on top as a flag.

When the tide came in at last, the castle fell, but Zara just waved goodbye to the water and carried Clicky's seaweed flag home.
I need a story about an old dog and a puppy sharing a house.

Raja was a fourteen-year-old Labrador who liked sleeping in the sun. Then the family brought home a puppy named Kuku, who bit his tail, stole his bed and barked for no reason.

Raja sighed. He tried ignoring the puppy. He tried leaving the room. Nothing worked. Kuku followed him everywhere.

One afternoon, Kuku fell into the empty fish tank in the garden and howled. Raja rose slowly, stiff in the legs, walked over and leaned down. He grabbed the puppy by the scruff and lifted him out gently.

Kuku licked his face. For the first time, Raja wagged his tail.

From that day, they slept side by side in the sunny spot, the old dog's paw resting over the puppy's back.
Write a story about a river that is sad because it is dirty.

Long ago, the river Veena was clear as glass. Children swam in her, and fish jumped silver in the sunlight. But as the town grew, plastic bags floated in her and the water went grey. Veena felt heavy and sad.

One morning, a girl named Devika walked down to the bank with a sack. She picked up a bottle, then a shoe, then a tangle of plastic. Her friends saw her and joined in. By noon, thirty children were wading and hauling.

A week later, they were joined by their parents. Then by the shopkeepers, who stopped giving out plastic bags.

Slowly, patch by patch, the water cleared. One evening, Devika saw a small silver fish leap near the bank. Veena, she thought, had begun to smile.
Missing prize pumpkin at the village fair: make that a story.

The village fair at Rampur had a prize pumpkin contest, and Mrs. Joshi's pumpkin was the biggest anyone had ever seen. She set it on a table for the judges. When she came back from fetching tea, the pumpkin was gone.

"Thief!" shouted a man. Everyone gathered. A boy named Vikram noticed a trail of seeds and orange scraps leading behind the tent. He followed them. There, snug in the shade, sat a very fat goat, chewing happily, a huge hole eaten out of the pumpkin.

Mrs. Joshi stared. Then, to everyone's surprise, she began to laugh. The judges, who were laughing too, gave the goat a ribbon for the biggest appetite, and Mrs. Joshi won first prize next year.
Is it possible to get a story where a squirrel forgets where he buried his nuts?

Autumn had come, and Sandy the squirrel had buried forty-one nuts around the park. He was proud of himself. Then winter arrived, the ground turned white, and Sandy ran out of food.

He dug under the oak. Nothing. He dug beside the bench. Nothing. He sat in the snow, sad and hungry.

A girl named Noor, walking by with her father, saw him scrabbling. "Poor squirrel," she said, and tossed a handful of nuts from her pocket.

Sandy gobbled them. When spring came, many of the acorns he had buried and lost sprouted into small green oak trees all over the park.

Noor walked there with her father, and Sandy watched from a branch, full and satisfied.
Sweet story about a sunflower that follows the sun, please.

In the corner of Grandma Rosy's garden stood a sunflower named Sunny. She was the tallest flower there, and every morning she turned her face toward the east and waited for the light.

One cloudy week, the sun hid. Sunny drooped. "Where did it go?" she asked the bees.

"It is behind the clouds," said a bee. "It is still there."

Sunny did not believe her. She kept her face turned up, day after day, though the sky stayed grey. Her petals drooped, but she did not give up.

On the eighth morning, a golden ray burst through. Sunny's whole stem seemed to straighten. Grandma Rosy came out with her coffee and smiled, because the flower looked as if she were laughing.
City rooftop, two pigeons: write their story.

Two pigeons, Gutru and Mitu, lived on the roof of a tall building in Pune. They had a favourite spot beside the water tank, where an old man named Mr. Kulkarni scattered rice every evening.

One day, a larger pigeon swooped down and pushed them aside. "This is my spot now," he said, gobbling the rice.

Gutru puffed up, but Mitu pulled him back. "Let him," she whispered. "Come."

She led him to the next building, where a woman was drying grain on a mat. They ate a hearty meal there.

The next evening, Mr. Kulkarni noticed only the big pigeon. He waited, puzzled. When Mitu and Gutru returned for a visit the day after, he put out double rice for them and smiled.
Give a happy ending to a story about a girl and a boy who find a cave while hiking.

Sana and her brother Imran were hiking with their uncle when they spotted a narrow cave behind a waterfall. "Can we look inside?" Sana begged.

"Just the entrance," said their uncle.

They crept in with a torch. The walls sparkled with wet stone. Imran shone the light higher and gasped. Hundreds of small bats hung from the ceiling, wrapped in their wings.

"Do not wake them," whispered Sana. They stood still, hardly breathing, as a chorus of tiny squeaks echoed.

Outside, the sun was bright. They told their uncle what they had seen, and he nodded. "You were gentle guests," he said.

All the way down the hill, the children drew bats in the air with their fingers.
A hamster runs away and comes back. Tell it as a story.

Nibbles the hamster pushed against the loose door of his cage one night and squeezed out. He scurried across the floor, under the sofa and into the wall behind the bookshelf, where he found a warm nest of old paper.

The next morning, nine-year-old Gaurav cried. He searched everywhere. His mother put sunflower seeds in a trail on the carpet, and they waited, quiet.

That evening, Gaurav heard a tiny scratching in the wall. He lay on the floor, very still. A whiskered nose appeared at a hole in the skirting board, sniffed, and followed the seeds one by one to his open palm.

Gaurav carried Nibbles back to the cage and fixed the latch with a clothes peg.
Place a boat race on a Kerala backwater and write a story around it.

In the backwaters near Alappuzha, the boat race was only two days away, and Anil's team needed one more rower. Their best oarsman, Thomas, had sprained his wrist.

"I can do it," said Anil's sister Lekha. The men laughed. She was fifteen, and the boat was long and heavy.

But she was fast. For two days she practised at dawn, her palms blistering, and by the morning of the race she matched the rhythm of the others.

The horn sounded. Twenty oars struck the water together. Mist rose, drums beat, and the crowd on the bank roared. Lekha kept her eyes on the man in front of her and never missed a stroke.

They finished second. Nobody cared. Lekha was carried on shoulders to the tea shop.
Share the tale of a baby goat learning to climb.

Little Gudiya, a baby goat, watched the older goats leap up the rocky hill behind the farm. They seemed to float from stone to stone. She wanted to try.

She stepped on the first rock and slipped. She tried the second and fell on her side with a bleat. Her mother watched but did not help.

"Lean forward," the old billy goat Bheem advised. "Keep your feet under you."

Gudiya tried again. This time, she leaned into the hill, and her small hooves gripped. One step, then another. Soon she was halfway up.

She looked down and wobbled, but a small ledge was near. She jumped, landed and stood proud. From the top, she could see the whole farm, small as a toy.
Could you write a story where a beekeeper and a bear reach an understanding?

Old Mateo kept thirty beehives on the edge of a pine forest, and every night, a brown bear came to steal the honey. Mateo shouted. He banged pots. The bear just waited until he went to sleep.

One evening, instead of shouting, Mateo set a small pot of honey down far from the hives, at the edge of the trees. In the morning, it was empty and clean.

He left another pot the next night, then another. The bear came every time, and the hives remained untouched.

Mateo's neighbour called him a fool. But in the autumn, when the hives were heavy and golden, he harvested forty jars, and the bear was still visiting, sitting at the tree line like a shy guest.
Short and simple: a dolphin rescues a fisherman's net.

A dolphin named Sudo swam near a fishing village each day. Fishermen waved to him. He chirped back and sometimes jumped through the waves.

One windy afternoon, a young fisherman named Pedro lost his net. It had slipped from his hands into the deep water, and without it, he could not fish. He sat on his boat with his face in his hands.

Sudo heard the splash. He dived, found the net drifting on the current and pushed it with his nose, up and up, until it floated at the surface beside the boat.

Pedro stared at the dolphin, then grabbed his net. "Thank you, friend," he said.

Sudo did a happy flip and swam away into the blue.
Please make a story out of a bee and a flower learning to help each other.

A bee named Bela was out of nectar. It had been a dry week, and most flowers had shrivelled. Tired and hungry, she landed on a small yellow marigold.

"I have just a drop," said the marigold. "Please, take it."

Bela sipped. Then, feeling stronger, she shook the pollen from her legs onto the marigold's heart. "Thank you," she buzzed.

A few weeks later, the marigold had made seeds. She dropped them onto the soil, and soon a whole row of yellow flowers stood where there had been one.

Bela returned with her sisters. The garden hummed. A boy named Jai watching from the window said to his mother, "Look, the bees are having a party."
Hopeful, with a little humour: a farmer waiting for rain.

Farmer Gopal looked at the sky every morning, and every morning the sky looked back at him, blue and empty. He had sown his rice, and the seedlings were turning brown.

His wife, Revati, told him to stop staring. "Staring does not make it rain."

"Neither does washing the cow," said Gopal, but he wiped his face and went to look at the field. He wore his oldest hat, for luck.

The next afternoon, a single cloud appeared, then four. The cow lowed. A gust of wind snatched his hat and carried it into the paddy.

The rain came while he was still chasing it. He caught the hat at last. His wife ran out with a pot on her head, and the two of them stood laughing in the downpour while the field drank.
Kindly write a story where a young owl learns to hunt at night.

Ollie the owl was a worried young bird. His brothers hunted well, but he kept missing. Whenever a mouse scampered by, he swooped too early.

"Be patient," his father hooted. "Listen first."

That night, Ollie sat on a branch in the moonlight, closing his eyes. He heard the wind in the grass, a cricket's chirp and, far to the left, the tiny scratch of paws.

He opened his eyes and tilted his head. He waited one more breath. Then he glided down on silent wings and landed softly on a mouse. For the first time, he had caught his own supper.

His father hooted proudly. Ollie did not say anything. He just fluffed his feathers and smiled with his big round eyes.
A tiny island gets a visitor. Can you tell that story?

The island of Cheeru was so small that you could walk around it in ten minutes. Only a few palm trees, some crabs and a family of seagulls lived there. Nobody ever visited.

One stormy morning, a battered rowboat washed up on the sand. In it lay a young man named Joel, dizzy and sunburned. The crabs scuttled away. The gulls stared.

Joel crawled to a palm and cracked open a coconut. He rested for two days, drinking and sleeping. On the third, a gull dropped a fish at his feet, and he laughed weakly.

A passing fishing boat spotted his waving shirt and took him home. Joel promised to come back, and a year later, he did, with a sack of seeds and a small flag.
Gently, please: a girl scared of dogs meets a friendly one.

Tanya crossed the street whenever she saw a dog. When she was little, a big dog had barked at her, and she had never forgotten it.

One afternoon, she walked to the park with her grandmother. A small brown dog with floppy ears trotted up and sat down in front of her, looking up.

Tanya froze. Her heart thumped. "Just stay still," her grandmother said quietly. "Let him sniff your hand."

Tanya held out her fingers, shaking. The dog touched them with his nose, which was cool and damp. Then he licked her wrist and wagged his tail so hard that his whole body wiggled.

Tanya giggled. She touched his ear. It was soft as velvet. She asked his owner his name, and learned it was Peanut.
Let us have a story about a girl sailing a toy boat across a village pond.

Nisha's grandfather had made her a toy boat from a coconut shell and a bamboo mast. Its sail was a piece of an old green saree. She was so proud of it that she took it to the village pond every evening.

One day, a breeze caught the sail and carried the boat toward the middle, away from her reach. She walked around the edge, but the boat kept sailing, further and further.

A water buffalo bathing nearby lifted its head. It waded slowly toward the boat, creating small waves that pushed it back toward the shore.

Nisha watched with her mouth open. When her boat bumped the bank, she scooped it up and patted the buffalo's wet nose. It blew out a big, happy breath.
Funny story time: a donkey carrying a big surprise.

Donkey Dholu carried sacks for the baker every morning. Today, as he plodded up the hill, the load felt heavier than usual. And, oddly, it was moving.

He glanced back. A small cat was sitting on top of the sacks, licking her paw as if she owned them.

"What are you doing up there?" Dholu snorted.

"Free ride," purred the cat.

A moment later, three chickens hopped onto the sacks as well. Then a puppy. By the time Dholu reached the market, he looked like a small, grumpy bus.

The baker threw up his hands. "Dholu, I asked you to carry flour, not passengers!"

Dholu sighed, shook them off one by one and had a long drink at the trough, with the cat watching.
For a seven-year-old, a story about a lion cub who loses his roar.

Tambo was a small lion cub who loved to roar. He roared at the butterflies and roared at the grass. But one morning, when he opened his mouth, only a tiny squeak came out.

"Oh no," said his sister Zuri. "You lost it!"

Tambo looked everywhere. Under a rock. Behind a bush. He even asked a tortoise, who had not seen it.

Finally, his mother licked his ear. "You have a cold," she said. "Rest."

He curled up and slept in the shade for two days. On the third morning, he stood at the top of a rock and took a deep breath. A great, big ROAR rolled across the plain, and every zebra jumped.
An old gardener's flowers keep getting dug up by a stray cat. Story, please.

Mr. Pereira had spent twenty years growing roses, and every morning a grey cat dug in the middle of his best bed. He chased her away with a broom. He put wire around the roses. He sprinkled pepper.

The cat kept coming back.

One day Mr. Pereira stayed and watched. The cat scraped out a soft hollow in the cool earth under the biggest bush. Then she went to the hedge and came back carrying a tiny kitten in her mouth. She fetched another, and another, until three kittens lay curled in the shade.

The old man put down his broom.

That afternoon he set an old basket lined with a towel by the wall, under the jasmine. The next morning, the cat and her kittens were sleeping in it, and the roses were left alone.
Tell it as a story: a rainbow-coloured bird teased by others.

In a mango grove lived a bird with feathers of red, orange, green and blue. The other birds were all brown or grey, and they teased her. "You are too loud," they said. "You look like a kite."

The bird, named Indra, tucked her bright wings tight and tried to look plain. She sat in shade, silent.

One day, a storm came, and the grove grew dark. A baby sparrow got lost in the gloom, crying. None of the brown birds could see it.

Indra spread her wings and flew above the trees. Her feathers glowed in the grey. The sparrow saw the colours and flew to her.

After that, the others stopped teasing. Indra stopped hiding, and the grove looked prettier.
Even a girl who forgets her umbrella can have a story with a happy end. Write one.

Divya had left her umbrella on the school bus again. Now she stood at the gate, watching a wall of rain, with her bag clutched over her head.

"Hey, you can share," said a boy from the class below. His name was Prem, and he held a big black umbrella. She had never spoken to him.

They walked together, splashing through puddles. Prem talked about his pet rabbit, Gajar. Divya told him about her goldfish. By the time they reached her lane, her shoulder was soaked, but she was laughing.

"Thanks," she said.

"See you tomorrow," said Prem.

The next day, he waited at the gate. Divya had her umbrella, but she walked under his anyway, and he did not mind.
Young monkey, tall trees, learning to swing: write that story.

Chiku the young monkey sat on a low branch and watched his cousins leap from tree to tree. They shrieked with joy and never fell.

"Your turn," said his Aunt Bandari.

Chiku gripped the branch. The next tree seemed very far. He took a deep breath, swung once, twice, and let go. His fingers missed. He tumbled down through leaves and landed in a soft bush.

He was not hurt, only embarrassed. The cousins laughed, but Aunt Bandari said, "Again."

He climbed back up. This time, he swung harder, reached longer and caught the branch with both hands.

He hung there, swinging, grinning from ear to ear. By evening, he was racing the others through the canopy, shrieking louder than all of them.
A thirsty traveller finds a magic well in a desert. Can you tell that tale?

Salim had walked all day across the sand dunes of Rajasthan. His water was gone, and the sun burned down on him. At last he spotted an old well beside a dry tree.

He dropped the bucket. It came up empty. He tried again. Empty. A third time. Nothing.

Salim sat down, tired. A thin voice came from the well. "Whoever wants water must first give a kind word."

Salim, surprised, thought a moment. "Well," he said, "thank you for waiting here so many years for travellers like me."

The bucket began to feel heavy. When he pulled it up, it was brimming with cold, sweet water. He drank, filled his flask and bowed to the well before walking on under the long red sunset.
What if a cat wanted to be a dog? Write the story.

Whiskers the cat watched Bruno the dog play in the garden. Bruno fetched sticks, rolled in the mud and got scratched behind the ears by everyone who passed. Whiskers, who mostly sat on a wall, felt left out.

"I want to be a dog," she announced.

So she tried. She wagged her tail. She chased a stick, then looked bored and left it. She barked, which came out as a squeaky meow. Bruno rolled on his back laughing.

"You are a very bad dog," he said.

"I know."

"But you are the best cat I know. You catch the lizards. I never can."

Whiskers thought about this. She jumped back on her wall, licked her paw and watched Bruno chase his tail below.
Two children find a message in a bottle by the river. Write what happens.

Chitra and her cousin Arun were skipping stones on the river when something green glinted in the reeds. It was a small glass bottle with a rolled paper inside.

They pulled the cork with a stick. The note said, in wobbly writing, "My name is Ben. I live in the town upstream. I am seven. Will you be my friend?"

"We have to write back," said Chitra.

She wrote about her village, her dog and the river. Arun drew a picture of a buffalo. They put the paper in the bottle, and Chitra's father, who drove his milk van to the town upstream every Friday, promised to drop it into the river there.

Two weeks later, a different bottle drifted down. Ben had written again, with a drawing of a house. After that, letters passed between them all summer.
When a cow gets stuck in a mud pit, the whole village helps. Write that.

Gauri the cow, the pride of the village of Chandpur, wandered off one afternoon and sank up to her belly in a mud pit behind the temple. The more she struggled, the deeper she went. Her calf cried from the bank.

A boy ran through the lanes shouting. Men came with ropes. Women brought boards. Children carried buckets of water to loosen the mud.

They tied the ropes around Gauri, and a dozen people pulled together while others poked planks beneath her. She bellowed and kicked, and then, with a great wet slurp, she popped free.

The whole crowd cheered and then looked at their muddy clothes and burst out laughing. Gauri, filthy and happy, trotted straight back to her calf and let him drink.
Invite a fox and a stork to dinner in a story of your own making.

One evening, a fox named Rufus invited a stork named Sarus to dinner. He served thin soup on a flat plate. The stork, with her long beak, could barely drink a drop. Rufus lapped his portion happily.

"Delicious," said Sarus politely, and left hungry.

A week later, she invited him back. Dinner was a tasty stew in a tall, narrow jar. Rufus tried to push in his snout. He could not get a bite. Sarus dipped her beak in, one neat bite after another.

Rufus's tummy rumbled. He understood. The next time, he invited her again, and this time he served the soup in two bowls and a tall jar side by side, so that each could choose.
Include the word leaf in a story about a girl who helps a ladybird find its way home.

Mia was eating her lunch on the garden bench when a ladybird landed on her sandwich. It walked in circles around the crust, looking lost.

"What is wrong?" Mia whispered.

She slid a leaf under it and lifted it carefully. The ladybird sat very still, as if it were thinking. Mia carried the leaf from bush to bush, holding it near each plant. At the rose, the ladybird perked up and waved its tiny feelers.

On the stem, a whole red-and-black family waited. The little one marched off the leaf and joined them.

Mia put the leaf back down and finished her sandwich. She wondered whether the ladybird told its family about the giant who had helped.
Hummingbird versus butterfly in a race: write a story about it.

In a flowery meadow, a hummingbird named Zippy boasted that nothing in the world was faster than he was. A butterfly named Lila, floating by, said calmly, "I wonder."

"Race you to the lavender!" Zippy said.

He shot off like a bullet. Lila drifted along on the breeze, wings slowly beating. Zippy reached the lavender in three seconds and swung round, smug. But a gust had caught Lila. She floated by, light as air, and landed on the flower just a breath later.

"A tie?" said Zippy.

"Perhaps," said Lila, smiling.

They drank the nectar together. Zippy zoomed around the meadow, but sometimes he slowed down, just to see how the butterfly flew.
A monsoon cloud falls in love with a mountain. Tell me that story.

Every year, the monsoon cloud Megh drifted over the mountains of the Western Ghats, and every year, he saw one peak that shone above all the others. Its name was Sahyadri, and she was green and tall and wrapped in mist.

Megh wanted to stay with her. But clouds cannot stop, because the wind always blows them on.

He pleaded with the wind, who laughed. So he decided to leave her a gift. He poured out his water on her slopes, filling the streams, the valleys and the waterfalls with silver.

When he left, he felt light and empty. But the next year, as he rose over the ocean again, he saw her green and gleaming below. She had kept every drop of his gift, and she was singing with rivers.
Take a little ant and a leaf bigger than herself, and make a story.

Anu the ant found a big green leaf on the forest floor and decided to carry it home. It was twice her size. The other ants had gone ahead with crumbs.

She pushed. She pulled. She dragged it over a root, up a small stone and down a muddy slope. The leaf kept catching on twigs. A beetle laughed at her. "Leave it," he said.

Anu did not answer. She just kept pulling, one step at a time. When she reached a steep bank, she paused and almost cried.

Then a line of her sisters came marching back. They each took an edge. Together they lifted the leaf over the bank and carried it in a long green parade to the anthill, where everybody cheered.
Starting with "Once upon a time", write a story about a wolf who is afraid of the dark.

Once upon a time, there was a young wolf named Fenris who was afraid of the dark. When the pack howled at the moon, he hid in the den with his paws over his ears.

One night, his little sister Luna padded in. "Come outside," she said.

"No," said Fenris. "Things are out there."

"Only crickets," said Luna. "And stars. Hold my tail."

Fenris took the tip of her tail in his teeth and followed her out. The forest was black, but his sister walked steadily ahead. He heard the crickets. He saw a hundred stars sparkling through the branches. A soft breeze stroked his fur.

He let go of the tail halfway up the hill, and neither of them mentioned it. They howled together at the moon.
There is a crow who learns to talk to a girl. Can you tell it?

A crow named Kallu sat on the wall of Pari's garden every afternoon, and every afternoon, Pari left a few peanuts for him. She talked to him about school and her friends, and Kallu cocked his head and listened.

One day, Pari said, "Hello, Kallu," and the crow, after a long pause, croaked back, "Hullo."

Pari nearly dropped her peanuts. "You talked!"

"Hullo," said Kallu again, very proud.

It was the only word he learned. But he used it every day, and soon, whenever Pari came home, a rough little voice greeted her from the wall.

Her mother heard it from the kitchen once and wondered who the strange guest was. Pari only grinned and went out with a handful of peanuts.
Lost shoe, flooded street, one boy: write the story.

The monsoon had flooded the lane in front of Shiv's house, and the water came up to his knees. He was on his way to school, carrying his bag over his head, when his left shoe stuck in the mud and stayed there.

He reached down. The water was brown, and he could not see the bottom. He felt around, found a stone, a plastic bag, a bit of stick. No shoe.

A man selling vegetables from a cart watched him. "Lost something, beta?"

"My shoe."

The man waded in, poked with a long stick and, on the second try, hooked the shoe by its laces. Shiv grinned and thanked him, and the man gave him a ripe tomato as a reward. Shiv went to school with one muddy foot and a tomato.
A turtle wants to see the ocean; make it a happy story.

Tilly the turtle lived in a small pond far from the sea. A passing gull had told her about the great blue ocean, and she wanted to see it.

One morning she began walking. A girl named Kamala found her crossing the street and picked her up. "Where are you going?" she asked.

"The ocean," said Tilly, though the girl heard only a small turtle squeak.

Kamala's uncle was driving to the coast that afternoon, so she took Tilly along in a basket of wet leaves. On the beach, she set the turtle on a smooth rock above the waves. Tilly watched the water roll in, felt the salty spray on her shell and blinked at the endless blue.

That evening, Kamala carried her back to her pond. Tilly slid into the cool, fresh water, and told the frogs about the ocean for weeks.
Friends who are unlikely: a rose and a weed. Could you write their story?

Among the neat rows of Mrs. Gupta's flower bed grew one tiny weed. The roses looked down on him. "You do not belong," said Rani, the reddest rose. "You are plain."

The weed, named Dhaniya, said nothing. He kept growing, staying near the roots, soaking up sunlight in his small way.

Then a hot, dry month came. The soil cracked. The roses wilted. But Dhaniya's low, wide leaves shaded the ground around Rani's stem and kept the soil from drying out.

When the rains came, Rani looked down and noticed that the weed had kept her soil damp. "Thank you," she said softly.

Mrs. Gupta pulled out the other weeds but left Dhaniya, saying he looked rather sweet beside the roses.
Write a short story for me about a girl who trains her dog to bring her slippers.

Maya was determined to teach her dog, Bolt, one clever trick. Every evening she held up her slippers, said "Fetch!" and tossed them across the room. Bolt chased them, chewed one and brought back a sock.

She tried again the next day. This time, Bolt brought a spoon. The third day, he brought a cushion, which was bigger than he was.

Maya's father laughed so hard he coughed. "He is trying his best."

On the fifth evening, Maya said "Fetch!" very slowly, pointing at the slippers. Bolt sniffed them, picked them up with great care and trotted over, tail wagging, and dropped them at her feet.

Maya cheered and gave him a biscuit. Bolt looked very pleased, though the next day he brought the cushion again.
Fisherman and kingfisher share one river. What is their story?

Every morning at dawn, the fisherman Joseph rowed out on the river with his net, and every morning a blue kingfisher watched him from a post. The bird caught small fish with a splash. Joseph caught bigger ones with patience.

One day, the river was nearly empty. Joseph threw his net again and again and caught nothing. He sighed.

The kingfisher dived and returned to the post with a tiny silver fish. Then it dived again. Joseph watched where the bird dived and rowed to that place. There, near an old log, the water was full of fish.

He cast his net, and it came up shining. Joseph left the smallest fish on the post as a thank-you and rowed home with a full boat.
Tell about a little girl who names every chicken on her farm.

Seven-year-old Esha lived on a small farm in Punjab, and she knew all twenty-three of her chickens by name. There was Pinky, who always pecked first. There was Dabbu, who was afraid of the wheelbarrow. There was Gulab, who laid eggs in the wrong places.

One morning, Gulab was missing. Esha looked everywhere: the coop, the haystack, the well. At last, she heard a muffled cluck from the old tractor tyre in the corner.

She peered in. Gulab sat on a nest of eggs, glaring.

Esha ran to tell her grandmother. They counted eleven eggs under the hen. Three weeks later, eleven fluffy chicks peeped around the yard, and Esha spent a whole afternoon thinking of names, with her chin on her fists.
Let the wind be a character and play a trick on a kite, in a short story.

The wind was bored. All afternoon he had pushed leaves and tickled washing, and nothing was fun. Then he saw a bright red kite fluttering above a field, with a boy named Jai holding the string below.

"Let us play," thought the wind, and he gave the kite a sudden tug. The kite shot higher. Jai laughed. The wind dropped it a little. Jai gasped. The wind lifted it again, and the kite danced in loops.

Jai ran across the field with the string, giggling. The wind raced beside him. For an hour, they played, kite and boy and wind, until the sun went red.

When the wind finally grew tired, he set the kite gently on the grass. Jai wound up the string and thanked the empty air before he went home.
Using simple words, write about a swan who feels ugly but is loved.

A swan named Sita lived with her family on a lake. Her feathers were grey and her neck was too long. The other swans were white and shiny, and they always looked beautiful in the water.

Sita swam alone. She did not like her reflection.

One day, a little duckling named Dodo got caught in some weeds and cried. Sita swam over, tugged him free with her long neck, and he climbed on her back to rest.

"You are so tall!" said Dodo. "I can see the whole lake!"

Sita smiled. She carried him around the lake, and the other ducklings came running, asking for a ride too. By evening, she had six on her back, and nobody was thinking about her feathers at all.
Zoo animals hold a meeting at night. What happens? Make it a story.

After the last visitor left the zoo, the animals gathered in the middle of the lawn. The elephant, Gaj, banged his foot for silence.

"Friends," he said. "There is a problem. The new keeper forgets to give the monkeys their bananas."
