"We have been hungry for two days!" shrieked a monkey.

The parrot, who had learned many words from visitors, said, "I will tell him."

Next morning, when the new keeper, a young man named Arvind, walked by, the parrot yelled, "Bananas! Bananas! Bananas!" Arvind blinked, then checked his list and smacked his forehead.

By noon, the monkeys had a heap of bananas, and that night the animals met again, this time just to say thank you to the parrot.
On a train during a monsoon storm, a family has an adventure. Tell it.

The train from Pune to Mumbai slowed and stopped in the middle of a green valley. Rain lashed the windows. The announcement said there was water on the track.

Ayaan, aged eight, pressed his nose to the glass. Waterfalls poured from every hillside. His grandmother opened her tiffin box and shared her thepla with everyone in the compartment. A man across the aisle started singing an old song, and a girl joined in.

Two hours passed. Strangers swapped stories and fruit. A baby fell asleep on a stranger's shoulder.

When the train finally rolled on, Ayaan was sorry. He had liked the waterfalls, the song and the warm food. He asked his grandmother whether trains could be delayed more often, and she laughed and told him not to push his luck.
Lost in a forest and helped by a firefly: a girl's story, please.

Ritu had followed a rabbit into the woods and now could not find the path. The sun was setting, and the trees grew black around her. She sat down on a log and tried not to cry.

A tiny light blinked beside her. A firefly. It floated ahead, paused and blinked again.

Ritu stood up. The light moved a few steps more. She followed it slowly. More fireflies joined, glowing between the trunks, forming a winding trail of soft gold.

The lights led her over a stream, around a thick bush and then to a gap in the trees, where she saw her father's torch beam swinging.

"Ritu!" he shouted.

She ran to him. When she turned, the fireflies were drifting back into the dark, one at a time.
Hungry stray cat meets a kind shopkeeper; can you write that?

A thin orange cat walked along the market lane one cold evening. Shopkeepers shooed her away from the fish stall, the bakery and the dairy. She crept to the last shop, a small stationery store run by an old woman named Mrs. Alvares.

The cat sat on the step. She did not mew. She just looked.

Mrs. Alvares sighed, went inside and returned with a saucer of warm milk and half a chapati. The cat ate it all in seconds and looked up.

"More?" the woman said, smiling, and gave her the rest of her own lunch.

The cat stayed. She slept among the notebooks and caught the mice that had been chewing the paper. Customers began to call her the shop manager, and Mrs. Alvares did not correct them.
Give me the story of children seeing a rainbow over a waterfall.

The school trip to Jog Falls was almost over. The class stood on a viewing platform, damp with spray, while their teacher, Mr. Iyer, counted heads. Everyone was tired.

A girl named Preeti looked up and gasped. "Look!"

Above the roaring water, a rainbow had formed, a perfect arch of colour glowing in the mist. The children went silent. Even the boys who had been shoving each other stopped.

Mr. Iyer took off his hat. A bird flew through the rainbow and vanished into the white spray.

For a full minute, nobody spoke. Then Preeti whispered, "I will never forget this."

On the bus home, they all slept, and some of them dreamed of colours.
Narrate how a horse who wants to run free gets his chance.

Chetak the horse pulled a cart through the town every day, carrying vegetables for his master, Mohan. He did not mind the work, but each time he passed the open fields at the edge of town, he longed to run.

One afternoon, a strap on his harness broke. The cart tilted. For the first time in years, he was free of the weight. He looked at the grass and then at Mohan.

"Go on," said Mohan, who had seen the look. "I will fix the strap."

Chetak ran. The wind streamed through his mane. He galloped across the field, kicked up his heels and swerved around trees, until he was out of breath and sweating.

Then he trotted back, calm, and stood patiently while Mohan mended the harness.
Penguins cannot fly, but one wants to. Write his story.

Pablo the penguin stood on the ice, watching gulls wheel through the sky. "I want to fly," he told his father.

"Penguins swim," his father replied.

"But I want to fly!"

So Pablo climbed a tall iceberg and jumped, flapping his wings like mad. He fell in the water with a loud splash. He tried again. Splash. The gulls laughed.

Then, in the cold water, something wonderful happened. His wings pushed him forward. He shot through the sea like a dart, twisting and rolling, faster than any gull in the air.

When he popped up on the ice, he said, breathless, "I can fly. Underwater."

His father nodded, and Pablo dived again, and flew for the rest of the afternoon.
Loves gardens, allergic to flowers: write a story about that boy.

Teo loved gardens, but every time he stepped into one, he sneezed. His eyes watered. His nose turned red. His mother said he should stay indoors.

But Teo wanted to see the bees. So he put on a mask, borrowed his uncle's goggles and walked to the community garden. He looked like a very small scientist.

A girl on the next plot burst out laughing. "What are you?"

"A bee watcher," said Teo, dignified.

She grinned and showed him her hives. Together they watched the bees from a bench, with Teo sneezing only twice. The girl, whose name was Una, offered him a jar of honey.

He took it home and decided that a mask and goggles were a small price for such a good afternoon.
Shiny button, sparrow, trouble: story please.

Tuk the sparrow was tidying his nest under the eaves when he spotted something sparkling in the street. It was a round gold button. He grabbed it in his beak and flew home.

He set it in the middle of his nest. It looked wonderful. He sat beside it all morning.

But the button flashed in the sun, and soon a big crow landed on the edge of the nest, poking at it. Twigs fell. Tuk chirped and flapped, and the crow flew off, but he was back after lunch, and again in the evening. By night, the nest had a hole in one side.

At dawn, Tuk carried the button to the crow's tree and dropped it on his branch. The crow cawed with delight and never came near the nest again.

Tuk mended the hole with fresh straw and decided that a plain nest was a quiet nest.
By the sea there is a lighthouse. Write a story about the sea and that lighthouse.

The lighthouse stood on a rock at the mouth of the bay, and the sea had washed around its feet for a hundred years. Every night the lighthouse shone, and every day the sea told it what it had seen: whales, boats with red sails, children building sandcastles.

One spring, the lighthouse grew sad. Its stripes had faded, and salt had crusted its windows. "I look old and tired," it said.

The sea did not answer. Instead, it grew calm for a whole week, so calm that a small boat could row out easily. In it came the keeper, Mr. Bose, with his grandson Kunal and three tins of paint.

They scrubbed the windows and painted bright red and white bands. When they rowed home, the sea rocked them gently.

That night the lighthouse shone its brightest, and the sea sent a long, soft wave to its feet.
Nurse a sick puppy back to health in a short story about a little girl.

Lina found the puppy under a bush near her school. It was small and thin, with dull fur and half-closed eyes. It did not run when she came close.

She wrapped it in her scarf and carried it home. Her mother took them both to the vet, who gave the puppy medicine, and then helped Lina make a bed from an old towel in a box. For three days, Lina gave the puppy sips of water with a spoon and soft rice with milk. She stayed beside him at night.

On the fourth morning, the puppy lifted his head and licked her hand. On the fifth, he stood up on wobbly legs. On the sixth, he chased her shoelace across the floor.

Lina named him Chhotu, and her mother sighed and bought him a proper bowl, and she did not mention getting rid of him at all.
Everybody fears him, and he is tired of it: a crocodile story.

A crocodile named Kroko lived in the river Narmada. Every animal ran from him when he surfaced, and the villagers shouted and threw sticks. Kroko had never eaten anything bigger than a fish, but nobody believed him.

One morning, a boy named Pintu was playing with a little wooden boat on the bank while his grandmother washed pots. The current snatched the boat and carried it toward the middle of the river. Pintu cried, and his grandmother held him back.

Kroko watched. Then he swam out slowly, nudged the boat with his snout and pushed it all the way to the shallows.

Pintu's grandmother fished it out with a stick and looked at the crocodile for a long time. After that, the villagers still kept a safe distance from the water, but nobody threw sticks at Kroko again, and Pintu waved to him every morning from the high bank.
Hill country, a sheepdog, a shepherd: tell their story.

Gabbar was a black-and-white sheepdog who lived in the hills of Himachal with a shepherd called Kishan. Every morning at dawn, Gabbar rounded up the sheep and led them up the slopes to the green pasture.

One afternoon, mist rolled over the hills. Kishan, who was counting, found that one lamb was missing. He called, but the fog swallowed his voice.

Gabbar put his nose to the ground. He trotted off along the path, sniffing, ears alert. Kishan followed his white-tipped tail through the grey.

Below a ledge, they found the lamb, wedged between two rocks, bleating. Kishan lifted it free and tucked it under his coat.

Gabbar led them back to the flock. That night, he got the biggest bone in the village.
A humorous story about a bat who is afraid of the night.

Batty the bat had a secret: he was afraid of the dark. All the other bats flew out at dusk, whooping and swooping. Batty hung upside down in the cave, clutching a small torch he had found in a campsite.

"Come on," said his friend Barry. "The insects are out!"

"I need my torch," said Batty.

"You are a bat. You hear everything. You do not need a torch."

"I like my torch."

Finally, Barry grabbed the torch and flung it into a bush. Batty gasped and flew after it, straight into the night. He swooped, dived, and noticed, with surprise, that every tree and every moth was perfectly clear in his ears.

He forgot his fear and caught six mosquitoes before dinner.
Rooftop vegetable garden at a school: write a story set there.

Ms. Fernandez's class had a rooftop garden. It was not much: ten buckets, some soil and a few seeds. The children took turns watering it before school.

In July, a storm blew over two buckets and ruined the tomato plants. The class was crushed. "We worked so hard," said Rehan.

"Then let us do it again," said Ms. Fernandez.

They replanted, this time tying the buckets together with rope. In September, small green tomatoes appeared on the vines. By October, they were red.

Each child got to pick one. Rehan held his in his palm and sniffed it. It smelled of sunshine and rain. He bit into it right there, and juice ran down his chin, and the whole class laughed and cheered.
A quiet village hears a night bird sing. What is that story?

In the village of Chandanpur, nobody ever heard birdsong at night. Then one summer evening, a sweet, trilling melody drifted from the mango tree beside the well.

People came out on their porches. Old Mr. Ghosh closed his eyes. Children crept out of bed and sat on the steps. The song rose and fell like water.

The bird, a small brown singer the children named Bulbul, had flown a very long way and was lonely. She sang because she had nobody to talk to.

As the villagers listened, a young girl named Rina tiptoed to the tree and placed a small dish of water below it. Bulbul sang louder. The song continued until the moon went down.

She stayed in the mango tree all summer, and the village slept peacefully.
Two ducks and their love of puddles: story, please.

Waddles and Paddles were two young ducks who lived on a farm. Their favourite thing in the world was a puddle. After every rain, they ran across the yard, quacking happily, and jumped right in.

The farm dog watched. "They are silly," he said.

One morning, after a night of heavy rain, the yard was full of puddles. Waddles and Paddles raced from one to the next, splashing everyone nearby. They splashed the dog, the farmer's boots and the cat.

The dog shook himself, grumbling. Then, to his own surprise, he stepped into a small puddle himself. It felt cool on his paws. He splashed once, then twice.

"Told you," quacked Waddles.

Soon three of them were soaked and laughing.
When a storm comes, animals shelter in an old tree. Write that story.

The great banyan stood at the edge of the forest, and when the sky turned black, the animals ran to it. A deer came first, then two monkeys, a squirrel and a family of mice. They crouched among the thick roots.

The wind roared. Branches snapped nearby. Rain came down like pebbles. But the banyan, with its wide arms and hundreds of roots, hardly swayed.

"Will you fall?" whispered the smallest mouse.

"I have stood through a hundred storms," said the tree in its slow, deep voice. "Stay close."

They huddled together. After a long night, the wind died. Dawn broke, pink and gold over the dripping leaves. The animals crept out, shook off their fur and thanked the tree, who only rustled its leaves.
Funny story, please, about a dog who chases his own tail.

Pepper the dog noticed something strange one morning: a tail. It was black and fluffy, and it was right behind him. He turned to look at it. It moved away.

"Hey!" he barked, spinning.

The tail spun too. He lunged. The tail dodged.

Pepper chased it around the kitchen. He chased it round the sofa. He chased it into the garden, where he got dizzy and fell over a flower pot.

His owner, Mrs. Thapa, watched from the doorway, holding her tea. "Pepper, it is yours," she said.

Pepper stopped, panting. He looked at the tail. The tail looked at him, or at least it seemed to.

He lay down with it tucked under his chin and decided it was not worth chasing, but that he would try again tomorrow.
Learning to swim in a village river is hard for one girl. Tell her story.

Fatima was ten and the only girl in her village who could not swim. When her friends ran into the river in summer, she sat on the bank, hugging her knees.

Her cousin Salim, who was twelve, said, "I will teach you."

The first day, she only put her feet in. The second day, she waded up to her waist, clutching his arm. On the third, she let him hold her up as she kicked.

It took two weeks. She swallowed water, coughed and almost quit. But on the fifteenth day, Salim let go, and she did not notice. She paddled three strokes alone before seeing his hands were away.

"I am swimming!" she shrieked, and sank, laughing, and came up spluttering.
Neighbours who are a rabbit and a tortoise: what is their story?

A rabbit named Raju moved into the burrow next to a tortoise named Dhairya. Raju was quick and noisy. Dhairya was slow and quiet. At first, they annoyed each other. Raju stomped around at dawn, and Dhairya hummed boring songs all afternoon.

But then one evening a fox came sniffing near the burrows. Raju froze, his legs shaking. "Quick, into your burrow," Dhairya whispered, and Raju squeezed inside just in time. Then Dhairya, calm as a stone, pulled his head into his shell.

The fox sniffed the burrows and the tortoise and found nothing but hard shell, so he gave up and went away.

After that, the two shared carrots on the front step, and Raju learned to walk quietly while Dhairya learned to enjoy a bit of speed.
Once in a hundred years, a flower blooms. Tell me a story about it.

High on a misty mountain slope grew a plant that the villagers called Shatabdi. It had no flowers, only a ring of green leaves. Grandmothers said that it would bloom once in a hundred years, and no one alive had seen it.

A girl named Hema, aged twelve, walked up to check on it every Sunday. Her friends said she was wasting her time.

One April morning, she found a pale bud. By afternoon, it had swelled. At dusk, with the sky turning rose, it opened into a huge white flower with a faint, sweet scent.

Hema ran down the mountain to fetch the village. By the time they arrived, it was dark, but the flower glowed faintly in the starlight. Everyone stood in silence, and old Mrs. Kamat cried a little.
A family of storks nests on a village rooftop. Write the story.

Each spring, a pair of storks returned to the old school's rooftop in a village in Poland. The children called them Bolek and Lola. They built their nest from sticks, and the whole school watched.

One year, a bad storm blew the nest apart. Sticks lay scattered all over the playground. The storks circled overhead, calling.

The headmaster, Mr. Nowak, sent the students out. They picked up the sticks, and the caretaker climbed a ladder and placed them back on the roof. The storks watched, then landed, and began to weave the nest again.

In May, three small, fluffy chicks poked their heads over the edge. Every child at the school ran to look, and the headmaster, who did not usually allow noise, let them cheer for five whole minutes.
Magic in a watering can: write a story about it.

Grandpa Hari's old tin watering can looked ordinary, but it had a secret. Whatever it watered grew twice as fast. His granddaughter Sneha discovered this by accident when she sprinkled a dry bean seed and, within minutes, a green shoot popped up.

She told nobody. She watered the tomatoes and the chillies, and soon the garden was bursting. The neighbours gawked.

But one evening, she saw Grandpa watering the same plants with a mug, slowly, in the dim light. "Why not use the can?" she asked.

He smiled. "Because the plants need time as well, and so do I. Some things should not grow too fast."

Sneha put the can away on the shelf. She kept the secret, and she watered the garden with a mug beside him.
Rain keeps the animals in the barn on a farm. What do they do? Write it as a story.

Rain hammered the barn roof. Inside, the animals huddled together. The hens sat on the beams. The cows chewed slowly. The pigs squealed at the leaks.

"I am bored," said Rosie the pig.

"Let us tell stories," said the old horse, Bhanu.

One by one, the animals spoke. The hen told of the day she laid a double-yolk egg. The cow told of her trip to a wedding. A sheep told of a dream where the whole world was made of grass.

The stories grew sillier and louder. By the time the rain stopped, everyone had laughed so much that the barn rocked. Farmer Jim opened the doors and found them all asleep in a heap, with smiles on their faces.
A baby kangaroo does not want to leave the pouch. Story, please.

Joey the baby kangaroo liked his mother's pouch. It was warm and safe, and he could see everything from inside without moving.

"It is time to hop," said his mother.

"I like it in here," said Joey.

She tipped him gently out onto the red dirt. He sat there blinking. The world was big and bright. A lizard ran past, and a magpie shrieked in the gum tree. Joey's heart pounded.

He took one shaky hop. Then another. The ground felt springy under his feet. He jumped higher, and a third time, further.

He was still hopping when the sun went down. At last he tumbled back into the pouch, tired, and told his mother about every bush he had seen.
Snowstorm in the mountains, one shepherd boy: write what happens.

Pasang was twelve, and his task was to bring the sheep down from the high pasture before winter. One afternoon, the sky turned white. Snow fell thick and fast, and he could barely see his own feet.

He counted the sheep: forty-two, forty-three. One was missing. He tied a red scarf to a bush as a marker and went back into the snow, calling.

He found the missing sheep curled in a hollow, shivering. He lifted it onto his shoulders and, following the scarf, found the path again.

When he reached the huts, his fingers were numb, and his father was already outside, with a lantern. He did not scold. He wrapped Pasang in a blanket, and the sheep got a place by the stove.
Dadu is a very old, very slow tortoise. Tell me his story.

Dadu the tortoise was a hundred years old and lived in the courtyard of a big house in Lucknow. Four generations of the family had fed him lettuce. He moved so slowly that the kids once used him as a landmark in hide-and-seek.

One day, a new baby arrived in the house, a girl named Ira. As she crawled around the courtyard, she found Dadu and put her small hands on his shell. She laughed.

Dadu stopped chewing. He looked at her, and for the first time in years, he walked forward on purpose, step by step, to keep beside her.

The family watched, wide-eyed. "He is never this fast," said Ira's father.

By evening, the two were asleep in the sun, side by side.
Could you spin a story about a duck who swims upstream?

Dolly the duck was tired of drifting. Every day the river carried her downstream, and every day she paddled back up. The other ducks said, "Why bother? Just float."

But Dolly was curious about the source. She wanted to see where the water came from.

She paddled against the current. Her legs ached. Several times she gave up and drifted back, but she tried again. She passed a mossy bridge, a field of sleepy cows and a noisy waterfall that she had to climb around on foot.

After two days, the river opened into a wide, still lake high in the hills, where lilies floated and a family of grebes was diving for weeds. One of the young grebes swam over and asked where she had come from.

Dolly stayed a whole week. Then she drifted all the way home, with her new friend paddling beside her.
Toddler story wanted: a pig who loves mud.

Pinky the pig loved mud. Squelch, squelch, squelch! She rolled in it in the morning. She rolled in it at noon. She rolled in it at night.

One day, the farmer's little girl, Tina, came to the sty. "Pinky, you are dirty!" she said.

Pinky grunted.

Tina got a bucket of water and a soft brush. Scrub, scrub, scrub! Pinky squealed and wriggled. Soon she was clean and pink, and her skin glowed in the sun.

Tina went to fetch a towel. Pinky looked at her clean self. Then she looked at the mud. Squelch! She jumped right back in.

Tina laughed and shook her head. "Okay, Pinky," she said. "Tomorrow we will wash again."
Stand very still in a paddy field like a heron, and tell the story of what happens.

A grey heron stood in the paddy field near Thanjavur, as still as a post. Boys going to school shouted at it. Bullocks passed. The heron did not move.

A boy named Mani, who was late as usual, stopped to look. "Why does he never move?" he asked an old farmer.

"He is waiting," said the farmer. "A fish will come."

Mani decided to wait too. He stood beside the heron. A minute passed, then two. His legs itched. A bug landed on his nose.

Suddenly, the bird's neck shot forward and came up with a wriggling silver fish. Mani gasped aloud and the heron flew away with its prize.

He arrived at school late, and when the teacher asked why, he said, "I was learning patience," and she let him sit.
Short and sweet, please: a girl named Nora finds a turtle in her garden.

Nora was digging for worms in the garden when her spade hit something hard. It was a small turtle, shell mud-covered, head tucked in.

She stopped. She sat back. "Hello," she whispered.

Nothing happened. She waited. Slowly, a wrinkled face peeped out, and two black eyes blinked at her.

Nora gave him a lettuce leaf. He munched it. She named him Pebble.

For a week, he lived in a box with water and leaves beside her bed. Then her father told her that Pebble belonged outside by the pond. She carried him there and set him down on the grass.

He walked slowly into the reeds. She waved. The next day, a small head popped up near the shore, and Nora knew he was fine.
School roof torn off by a monsoon storm; everyone helps fix it. Write it as a story.

A fierce storm in the night tore a big part of the roof off the village school in Madhubani. In the morning, the children arrived to find water on the floor and books soaked.

Their teacher, Mrs. Jha, stood in the doorway with tears in her eyes. "We cannot teach here," she said.

But a boy named Gopal ran home and returned with his father and a ladder. Then came the blacksmith with sheets of tin. The potter brought clay tiles. Mothers carried tea.

By evening, the roof was patched, and the children had spread the wet books in the sun to dry. The floor was swept, and benches were back in rows.

Next day, class started on time. The new roof was a patchwork of colours, and Mrs. Jha called it the prettiest school in Bihar.
No enemies here: a girl and an old tiger. Write about them.

In a thick jungle in Madhya Pradesh lived an old tiger named Sher Khan. He was thin, his teeth were worn, and he could no longer hunt quickly. A girl named Bina, who collected firewood at the edge of the forest, sometimes saw him from a distance.

One day, she found him lying by a dry stream, panting. He looked at her but did not move. She was very afraid.

She remembered her grandfather's rule: never run from a tiger. So she backed away slowly, walked home and told the forest ranger.

The ranger came with a water tanker and filled the pool by the stream. Within an hour, the tiger drank deeply.

Bina never saw him up close again, but sometimes, she heard a low, rumbling sound from the trees, like a thank-you.
Cheese is a must in a story about a clever mouse who escapes from a cat.

A grey mouse named Pitu lived behind the kitchen cupboard, and every night he sneaked out to nibble cheese. A fat orange cat named Bagheera lived in the same house, and every night he waited by the cupboard.

One evening, Pitu peeked out and saw Bagheera's tail swishing. He thought for a moment. Then he ran back and returned dragging a small ball of wool.

He rolled it across the floor. The cat's ears perked up. He pounced on it, batted it around and chased it under the sofa.

Pitu crept to the cheese, took the biggest piece he could carry and slipped back into his hole.

Bagheera emerged with a tangled ball and no mouse. He sulked all night. The next night, Pitu used a button.
About 120 words, please, on a girl who grows a giant pumpkin for the village fair.

Sia planted one pumpkin seed in April. All summer she watered it, pulled weeds and shooed away squirrels. By August, the pumpkin was the size of a football, then a drum, then a small boat.

She wanted it for the village fair, but it was too heavy to lift. Her father scratched his head.

Then she had an idea. She asked her friends to bring their wheelbarrows, and five children rolled the pumpkin up a plank into the biggest wheelbarrow and took turns pushing it all the way to the fair.

The judge's eyes went wide. "That is the biggest I have ever seen," he said, and pinned a gold ribbon on it.

Sia stood beside her pumpkin, grinning, with her friends around her and dirt on all their knees.
Seal and a lost baby penguin: write the story.

Little Oki was playing near the edge of the ice when a big wave carried him away from his colony. He floated on a chunk of ice, calling for his mother, but the wind swallowed his voice.

A seal named Selma surfaced next to him. Oki trembled, because seals sometimes ate penguins. But Selma only said, "You look lost."

"I am," whispered Oki.

Selma looked around. She knew the waters well. "Hold on," she said, and nudged the ice chunk with her nose, pushing it across the sea for an hour, until the black-and-white crowd of the colony appeared on a distant shore.

Oki's mother rushed into the water. Selma slid under and disappeared with a flick of her tail, and Oki, safe in his mother's feathers, waved goodbye.
Discovering a hidden pool in a river changes a boy's day. Tell it.

Sohail had walked along the river a hundred times, but today he noticed a gap in the reeds. He pushed through, and there was a hidden pool, round and green, shaded by trees, with water so clear he could see every pebble.

He sat on a flat rock. A tiny fish nibbled his toe. A kingfisher dived into the pool and came up with a fish.

He wanted to tell everybody. He wanted to bring his friends, his brother, his whole class. Then he looked at the kingfisher and the quiet water. He decided to bring only his best friend, Jamal.

The next day, the two boys sat on the flat rock, whispering. The pool stayed secret all summer, and the kingfisher ate well.
Different from the flock: a sheep's story, please.

Everyone in Shanti's flock was white. Shanti was black. The other sheep stayed away from her. At night, she slept at the edge of the field, and in the morning, she ate alone.

One evening, thick fog descended. The shepherd, an old man named Akbar, struggled to find his flock in the grey. He could not see white wool against white fog.

But Shanti was easy to spot: a dark shape like a small hill. Akbar found her first. Next to her, huddled for warmth, were the others. He counted them, one by one, and led them all home.

After that, the white sheep started grazing next to Shanti. Akbar, as he lit his lamp, said she was the best marker on the hillside.
Every birthday he plants a tree. Tell me that boy's story.

On his sixth birthday, Rohit asked for a sapling instead of a toy. His grandfather helped him dig a hole behind the house and plant it. A neem, they decided.

Every year after that, on his birthday, he planted another tree. A jamun, a guava, a banyan seedling and a tamarind. By the time he was twelve, there was a small grove behind the house, with birds in every branch.

In the summer of that year, the village was hot and dry. People came to rest under the shade of his trees, and children played on the cool earth. Old women sat in the shadows telling stories.

Rohit sat on a low branch, swinging his legs. His grandfather watched him from a bench and said nothing. He just nodded, slowly, and smiled.
Far from home, a dog finds his way back. Write that.

When the family moved to a new town, nobody noticed that Tiger, their old brown dog, slipped out of the car at the first petrol stop. They drove on for an hour before they realised.

By then, Tiger was alone on a busy highway. He sniffed the air. Then he turned around and started walking back toward the only home he knew.

It took him eleven days. He drank from puddles, ate scraps and slept under bridges. A trucker gave him half a sandwich. A little girl poured water into a bowl for him.

When he reached the old house, it was empty, with strangers inside. But a neighbour recognised him, took him in and called the family.

They drove back that same night, and Tiger wagged his tail so hard his whole body shook.
Make a quiet boy brave on a rainy day, in a story.

Hari never spoke up in class. When the teacher asked a question, he stared at his desk. But one rainy afternoon, as the downpour drummed on the roof, the lights flickered and went out. The class gasped.

"Do not worry," said the teacher, "I will find a candle." She left the room. In the dark, the little ones began to cry.

Hari did not know why, but he stood up. "Let us sing," he said, in a small voice. Nobody heard. He tried again, louder. "Let us sing the rain song."

He started it. One by one, others joined. Soon the whole room was singing in the dark.

When the teacher returned with a candle, she found thirty children singing loudly and Hari at the front.
A cow and a crow argue about who is more useful. How does it end?

A cow and a crow stood together in a village lane. "I give milk," said the cow proudly. "Everyone needs me."

"I give warnings," said the crow. "When trouble comes, I call."

They argued all morning. Neither would give way. A little girl named Pooja, passing by with her school bag, listened for a while. "Why not both?" she asked.

Both animals paused. "Both?"

"The cow gives milk in the morning. The crow wakes everyone up with his call. You each help in a different way."

The cow chewed slowly. The crow ruffled his feathers. They looked at each other and did not speak again about it, but that evening they sat side by side on the wall and watched the sun go down.
Befriend an owl, an old teak forest, a boy: write the story.

Jeevan lived near a teak forest in Kerala and loved to walk there at dusk. One evening, he noticed two big round eyes in a hollow tree. An owl was looking at him.

He sat down quietly. The owl blinked slowly, once.

Every evening after that, Jeevan came to the same spot. He brought no food, only himself. He sat for half an hour and watched. Gradually the owl came out, perched on a branch, and puffed up.

One evening, when Jeevan arrived, the owl flew down and landed on a stump an arm's length away. The two sat there in the dusk, looking at each other, while the forest grew dim.

Jeevan went home feeling that he had been given a secret, and he told only his mother.
Under 120 words, tell a story about a little girl who talks to her plants.

Every morning, Lila stood by her window and talked to her plants. "Good morning, Tulsi," she said. "Good morning, Rose. Good morning, Cactus."

Her brother laughed. "They cannot hear you."

"They like it," said Lila.

That summer, the family went on holiday for a week and forgot to water the pots. When they returned, the cactus was fine, the rose had drooped, and the tulsi looked brown and sad.

Lila watered them quickly, then sat down among them. "I am sorry," she said. "I am back."

By the next morning, the tulsi had perked up. Her brother frowned at it, then, quietly, said, "Good morning, Tulsi," when he thought nobody was listening.
Shy flamingo, one leg: write the story.

Flora the flamingo lived in a pink flock on a salt lake. She always stood on one leg, with her head tucked in and her eyes half shut. The others splashed and honked. Flora just stood, wobbling slightly.

"Why one leg?" asked a young flamingo named Mingo.

"I am afraid of falling," Flora mumbled. "If I stand on two legs, I will have to walk. And everyone will see."

Mingo laughed kindly. "We all fall. Look." He stepped, tripped on his own long toes and splashed face-first into the water. Everyone cackled, including Mingo.

Flora felt a giggle rise. She put down her other leg, took one step, then another. She did not fall. She walked into the shallows, and the flock made room for her at once.
A new bridge is being built over a river and the animals are worried. Write the story.

When the workers arrived at the river bank with trucks and cranes, the animals were frightened. The frogs hid in the mud. The herons flew to a distant tree. Only an old tortoise called Kachua stayed on his rock and watched.

The men built the bridge for a year. They hammered, drilled and shouted. Dust filled the air. The animals peeped from the reeds, whispering.

When it was finished, a few cars rolled across. The noise was loud, but the animals slowly got used to it. Under the bridge, there was shade. Swallows built nests beneath the arches, and the frogs found cool spots to croak in.

Kachua still sat on his rock. He told anyone who asked that the bridge was no worse than a very big log.
Write up how a calf and a boy grow up together.

On the same night that Mohan was born, a calf was born in the shed next door. The villagers said they would be friends. His father named the calf Nandi.

The boy and the calf grew up side by side. When Mohan learned to walk, Nandi was wobbling beside him. When Mohan started school, Nandi stood at the gate every afternoon, waiting. On holidays, they went to the river together, and Mohan splashed while Nandi drank.

When Mohan was twelve, Nandi was a big bullock. A thunderstorm came while they were in the field, and Mohan, frightened, clung to the bullock's neck. Nandi walked slowly home, ignoring the rain and thunder.

Mohan's father saw them from the doorway, and the two came in together, dripping, as always.
Patience is tough for a girl with a new pet fish. Write her story.

For her ninth birthday, Gita got a small blue fish in a glass bowl. She named him Neelu and watched him for hours. But Neelu hid behind a plastic plant, and Gita felt let down. She had wanted a fish who came when called.

She tapped on the glass. Neelu did not move. She dropped in food. He stayed in the corner.

Her mother said, "Give him time."

So Gita sat quietly each evening, feeding him a tiny bit. After a week, he came out for the food. After two, he swam to the front when she came near. After a month, he followed her finger along the glass.

Gita laughed with delight. She told her friends that her fish had learned her name, and none of them argued.
Every kite was ready, then the rain came: kite festival story, please.

All year, the children of Ahmedabad had waited for the kite festival. Tara had made her kite herself, bright yellow with a long tail. On the morning of the festival, she woke early, stuck her head out of the window and groaned. Dark clouds covered the sky.

By ten, rain fell in sheets. The terrace was empty. Tara sat on the stairs with her kite in her lap, miserable.

Her grandfather came and sat next to her. "The kites are resting," he said. "The sky is busy."

Tara sighed. But then the rain thinned, and a patch of blue appeared. Her grandfather winked.

By three, the sky was clear and wet and shining. Tara ran up to the terrace with her kite, and soon, hers was the first one in the sky.
Which is more stubborn, a mule or a girl? Write a story to find out.

A mule named Bhura stood in the middle of the mountain path and would not move. Pema, who was ten, tugged on the rope. "Come on, Bhura. We have to deliver the potatoes."

The mule sat down.

Pema pushed. She pulled. She begged. Bhura chewed a mouthful of grass and looked bored.

Pema sat down too, right in front of him, crossed her arms and glared. "Then we will both stay here."

They sat in silence for an hour. A gentle rain began. Bhura stood up, shook himself and looked at her as if she were being ridiculous.

Pema stood. The mule walked on, step after step, all the way to the village, and she followed, grinning, with the rope hanging loose in her hand.
The sun and the moon never meet. Tell me a story about that.

The sun and the moon lived in the same sky but had never met. The sun worked all day, and the moon worked all night, and between them was only the thin pink hour of dawn and dusk.

"I wonder what he is like," said the moon.

"I wonder what she looks like," said the sun.

One morning, a little girl named Aarohi woke up very early and went onto her roof. She saw the pale moon still hanging in the west and the red sun rising in the east, both in the sky at the same moment.

She waved to both. The sun and the moon, hearing a small voice, looked toward each other for a second and then smiled across the clouds, before the moon slid away and the day began.
A lost child is helped by a parrot. Can you write it?

At the Sunday market in Jaipur, a little boy named Ali let go of his mother's hand to look at a juggler. When he turned back, she was gone. The crowd swirled around him. He began to cry.

A green parrot on a perch outside a tea stall cocked its head. "Ammi! Ammi!" it squawked, in a voice that sounded very much like a child's.

Ali stopped crying and looked. The parrot repeated, "Ammi!" over and over, louder than the market noise.

His mother, who had been searching frantically two stalls away, heard the cry. She followed the sound and found him standing under the perch.

She hugged him tight. The tea seller laughed and said that the parrot had learned the word from a child last month, and that it was very useful today.
Ranger, baby elephant, a ditch: make it a story.

Ranger Kiran was driving through the forest at dawn when he heard a faint, high cry. He stopped the jeep. At the bottom of a deep ditch stood a baby elephant, trumpeting weakly. Its mother paced anxiously at the rim, afraid of the steep edge.

Kiran called two colleagues. They brought spades and began to dig a ramp in the side of the ditch. The mother elephant watched, ears flapping, but did not charge.

After an hour, there was a slope. The baby scrambled, slipped and tried again. Finally, it climbed out to its mother, who wrapped her trunk around it.

The whole herd trumpeted from the trees. Kiran sat down on a log, wiped his forehead, and watched them wander off into the morning mist.
A girl finds a lost anklet in a river; write her story.

Anjali was washing clothes by the river when the water swirled around her foot and she felt something hard. She reached down and pulled out a silver anklet, blackened with age, with tiny bells.

She rubbed it clean with sand. It was beautiful. She wanted to keep it. But on the bank, a grey-haired woman named Savitri was searching along the water's edge, crying.

"I lost it thirty years ago," Savitri said, when Anjali asked. "My mother gave it to me on my wedding day. I came back every year to look."

Anjali looked at the anklet in her hand. She held it out.

Savitri took it with trembling fingers. She fastened it on her ankle, and it chimed. She hugged Anjali and could not speak.
There is a goat who sings very well. Write about her.

Goat Meena lived on a farm outside Jodhpur. Her bleat was not like the others. It rose and fell and trembled in a way that made people stop and listen.

The farmer, Mr. Rathore, noticed the pattern. Whenever Meena bleated at dusk, the neighbours leaned over their walls. He was puzzled.

One evening, a music teacher named Mrs. Bhatt walked by. "That goat is singing a raga," she said, astonished. "Listen. It is perfectly on pitch."

Mr. Rathore laughed. But when he listened, he heard it too, the slow notes.

The next week, the whole street gathered on the wall at dusk, drinking tea, while Meena sang. She did not care. She just chewed hay between verses and bleated whenever she felt like it.
Panda trouble: his bamboo is gone. Write the story.

Pandu the panda sat in the bamboo grove with his lunch beside him. He stood up for a moment to stretch. When he turned around, the bamboo was gone.

He sniffed. He looked behind trees. Not a stalk. His stomach rumbled.

"Who took my lunch?" he cried.

A tiny red panda named Rusty peeked out from behind a rock, her cheeks stuffed. "I did not know it was yours," she mumbled through the bamboo. "It looked like nobody's."

Pandu sighed and sat down. "I am very hungry."

Rusty felt guilty. She led him to a hidden grove with bamboo that was even greener than before, and they shared a long, happy meal. Pandu decided that being surprised was not always bad.
Balcony garden, city flat, a nesting pigeon: story, please.

Revati lived on the sixth floor of a building in Chennai, and her balcony was small. She had four pots: tulsi, jasmine, a chilli plant and a curry leaf.

One morning, she found a pigeon sitting among the pots, with a few twigs piled beside her. A nest. Revati's first thought was to sweep it away. Her mother said it was bad luck to disturb a nest.

So she left it. Every day, she watered her plants carefully, working around the bird. After two weeks, two white eggs appeared. After four weeks, two grey chicks.

Revati watched them grow from her window. When they flew, one flew into the jasmine bush first, and stayed there a while, looking at her. Then the pair soared up over the city and disappeared into the evening.
A cat that sits on a laptop makes for a funny story. Keep it under 120 words.

Misha the cat had one favourite spot in the house: the warm keyboard of Dev's laptop. Every time Dev sat down to work, Misha climbed on top and lay flat.

"Misha, I have an essay due," Dev groaned.

Misha purred.

Dev tried moving her. She flowed back like water. He tried putting a pillow beside the laptop. She ignored it. He tried tempting her with a treat. She ate it and sat back down.

Finally, at midnight, Dev gave up and typed one-handed with Misha stretched across his arm. The essay was finished at two in the morning, with one extra line at the end: "jjjjjjjjjjjjjjjjj."

He deleted it, and Misha, satisfied, curled up and fell asleep.
Follow a tiny drop of water from a cloud to the sea, as a story.

A drop of water named Bindu fell from a grey cloud over the Himalayas. She landed on a leaf, rolled off and joined a trickle. The trickle joined a stream, and the stream joined a river.

Bindu was swept over rocks, through narrow gorges and past villages. She saw children bathing and cows drinking. She passed a temple with bells ringing. She was pulled through a turbine and came out spinning.

She grew tired but kept going. The river widened. Mud and silt swirled round her. Fishermen cast nets. The air smelled of salt.

At last, a great flat blue stretched before her. The river poured into it, and Bindu became part of the sea.

Months later, the sun warmed her, and she rose as vapour, light and free, ready to become a cloud.
Two roosters hate each other and then do not. Write that story.

Two roosters, Raja and Kaalu, lived on neighbouring farms separated by a low stone wall. Each morning at dawn, they crowed at each other across it, trying to be louder. The neighbours covered their ears.

One day, a storm blew a branch across the wall and knocked it down. The roosters stared at each other through the gap. Neither moved.

Then a stray dog bounded into Raja's yard, barking at his hens. Raja puffed up, but he was outnumbered. Kaalu leapt over the fallen stones, flapped his wings and pecked the dog's nose. Together, they chased it away.

Breathing hard, the roosters looked at each other. They did not say anything.

The next morning, they crowed together. It still was not quiet, but it sounded better.
Dream of an ocean, little puddle: tell me that story.

A small puddle sat in the middle of a dusty lane in Hyderabad. Each time a bus rumbled past, it shivered. A bird landed and drank half of it. The puddle felt very small.

"I wish I were an ocean," it sighed.

A boy named Waseem came along, kicking a pebble. He stopped, looked at the puddle and then dropped a paper boat in it. The boat floated, slowly turning.

For a few minutes, the puddle was a vast sea, with a ship sailing across it. The boy knelt and made engine noises. Waves rippled from the boat's hull.

Then he fished the boat out and ran home. The puddle, calm again, reflected a patch of blue sky. It no longer felt small. The sky, it noticed, was in it.
River bank, otters, a family: story please.

The otter family lived in a burrow beneath the roots of a willow tree. Mother Otter, Father Otter and three pups named Pip, Pop and Pup played on the bank every afternoon, sliding down the mud into the river.

One day, Pup, the smallest, swam too far and was caught by the current. She squeaked. The others turned.

Father Otter dived. He swam alongside her, nudging her toward the shallows, while Pip and Pop raced downstream and held out a long, floating branch. Pup grabbed it with her paws.

Together, they towed her to the bank. She lay on the mud, panting.

Mother Otter licked her face. By dusk, Pup was sliding down the bank again, though now she stayed within her brothers' reach.
Hidden well, young farmer, a donkey: write this story.

Young Dilshad had been farming his uncle's dry land for two years. The wells were empty, and the crops were dying. One afternoon, his donkey, Gulu, wandered off and began to paw at the ground beside a rock.

Dilshad scolded him, but Gulu would not stop. He kept pawing, then sniffing, then braying.

Dilshad grabbed a spade, annoyed, and dug beside the donkey's hoof. Half a metre down, the soil grew dark and cold. Another half metre, and it turned to mud. Then water seeped slowly into the hole.

He shouted for joy. His uncle came running. Together they dug it wider, and by evening, they had a small well.

Gulu got the first drink and, for once, nobody complained when he stepped in the bucket.
Kittens plus wool equals chaos; write a story about it.

Two kittens, Tikka and Masala, found a ball of red wool under their owner's armchair. Tikka pounced. Masala pounced harder. The ball shot across the floor, trailing a long red thread.

They chased it round the table leg, then the chair, then the sofa. The thread wrapped around everything. Soon the living room looked like a spider's web, red and tangled.

When Grandma Usha came in with her tea, she stopped. A kitten sat on the sofa, wound up like a parcel. The other was tied to a lamp.

"Oh dear," she said, and sat down to unwind them, laughing. It took half an hour.

When she had finished, the wool was a heap on the floor, and the kittens were asleep inside it, side by side.
Drowning kitten, brave boy, a river: please write it.

A boy named Anwar was fishing when he heard a thin cry. A kitten was struggling in the water, being carried away by the current, its little head bobbing.

He dropped his rod. He could swim, but the river was fast. He ran along the bank, found a long branch and held it out. The kitten missed it. He ran farther and tried again. This time, the kitten clawed at the branch and held on.

He pulled it in slowly. It came onto the grass, soaked and trembling.

Anwar wrapped it in his shirt, rubbed it dry and carried it home. His mother let him keep it. He named the kitten Naddi, after the river, and she slept at the foot of his bed every night.
Write gently about a rabbit who is afraid to leave her burrow.

Bunty the rabbit had never left her burrow. Outside, there were foxes and hawks and strange noises. Her friends hopped in the meadow every morning, but Bunty stayed under the earth with a small lantern of fireflies.

One spring day, her friend Pika came to the burrow's edge. "The clover is in flower," she said. "It is beautiful. I will wait by the entrance."

Bunty took a breath and stepped out. The sun blinded her. She sat still. Pika stayed close.

She nibbled one clover blossom. It was sweet. A butterfly landed on her nose, and she giggled.

By evening, she was hopping through the grass, with Pika beside her. When she went home, she left the door open, and lit the fireflies only for fun.
Climb a mountain with grandfather and use the word summit in a story about it.

Grandfather Anand had climbed the hill behind their village every year of his life. This year, he was eighty, and for the first time, he asked his granddaughter, Veda, to come along.

They set off at dawn. The path was steep. Grandfather walked slowly, leaning on a stick. Veda was impatient, then worried, then proud of him.

They stopped often. He showed her wild flowers, a bird's nest and a stream where he had once caught fish. The sun climbed. At noon, they reached the summit. The whole valley lay below them, green and gold, the village tiny as a toy.

Grandfather sat on a rock and breathed deeply. "Fifty years ago," he said, "I brought my father here."

Veda sat beside him, and they ate boiled eggs in silence.
Dramatic, please: a young eagle faces a thunderstorm.

The sky over the mountain turned the colour of ink. Thunder cracked like a whip. In a nest on a cliff, a young eagle named Garuda clung to the rock, his feathers wet and heavy.

His mother had left to find food and had not returned. Lightning flashed. A wind slammed into the cliff, tearing at the nest. Sticks flew into the abyss.

Garuda spread his wings for the first time. The gale caught them. He flipped, tumbled and plunged. His heart pounded. He tilted a wing, as he had watched his mother do, and the wind turned beneath him, lifting.

He rose through the rain, over the cliff, and into the clear air above the storm. There, in the last golden light, his mother was circling, calling, and he flew to join her.
A lizard in the garden wall and a girl who befriends him: include a small funny moment.

There was a lizard in the garden wall, and nine-year-old Ritika knew it. She called him Chhipkali Chacha, which meant Uncle Lizard. Every afternoon, she put a tiny dish of sugar water by his hole.

Chacha watched her with a bulging eye. He came out only when she had gone.

One day, her aunt arrived on a visit. She was terrified of lizards. When Chacha appeared on the wall, she screamed so loudly that a pot fell over.

"He lives here!" Ritika giggled. "He is my friend."

The aunt said she did not want friends with a tail. But next morning, she went into the garden and, when she thought nobody saw, placed a small dish of sugar water by the hole, then ran back inside very fast.
Rescue puppy, learning to trust. Under 130 words, please.

The puppy had been found in an empty lot, thin and shaking. The shelter named him Cinder. When volunteers came near, he shrank into the corner of his kennel.

A teenager named Diego volunteered every Saturday. He never reached for Cinder. He sat outside the kennel, reading aloud from a comic book in a soft voice.

For three weeks, Cinder watched from the back. In the fourth, he crept to the front. In the fifth, he sniffed Diego's shoe.

On the sixth Saturday, Diego held out his hand, palm up. Cinder sniffed it. Then, trembling, he pressed his head into it.

Diego stayed very still. That night he told his parents about the puppy. Two weeks later, Cinder rode home in their car, asleep on Diego's lap.
No rain for a year in a small town, then it rains. Set the story there.

For a whole year, not a drop of rain fell on Soranpur. Every morning, old Mr. Rao, a retired teacher, walked to the brass rain gauge in the school garden, looked inside and wrote a zero in his notebook. The pages filled with zeros.

His neighbour's son, Kabir, sometimes walked with him. "Why do you still check?" he asked one day.

"Because one day it will not be zero," said Mr. Rao.

That night, Kabir woke to a strange drumming on the tin roof. He ran outside. Water was pouring off the eaves, and the whole street was shining.

At dawn, he found Mr. Rao already at the gauge, his slippers soaked. "Forty-two millimetres," he said, and his voice shook. He wrote the number in large figures, and beside it, for the first time Kabir could remember, he drew a little smiling face.
First snowball fight ever, for a polar bear cub: write it.

Nanu the polar bear cub was three months old when he saw snow properly for the first time. His mother led him from the den, and the world was white and sparkling.

He tasted it. It was cold. He rolled in it. He sneezed.

A second cub, Sila, scooped up a pawful and threw it at him. It landed on his nose, and he blinked in surprise. Then he scooped some himself and flung it back. He missed, hitting his mother.

She turned slowly. The cubs froze. Then she gathered a huge pile and dumped it on both of them, and they vanished in a cloud of white.

When the cloud cleared, two small bears lay giggling, flat on their backs, while their mother licked the snow off their ears.
Lamps on a river each year in one village. Story, please.

Every autumn, the village of Dwar lit lamps on the river. Each family made a small leaf boat, put a clay lamp inside and floated it away in the dusk. The tradition was older than anyone could remember.

This year, ten-year-old Parth had made his boat alone. He had folded the leaf carefully and lit the wick. But when he set it on the water, the wind blew it out.

He tried again. It blew out again. A girl beside him, Sunaina, cupped her hands around his lamp. "Light it now," she said.

The flame caught. It trembled, steadied and glowed. They set the boat down, still shielding it with their hands until it slid away from the bank.

It joined hundreds of other lights, drifting slowly downstream like stars.
Short and funny: a hen afraid of the rain.

Henrietta the hen hated rain. When the first drop fell, she squawked, ran in circles, and tried to hide under a flower pot. The other hens clucked at her.

"It is only water," said Cluck.

"It is wet," said Henrietta.

One morning, the sky grew dark again, and the first drop landed on her head. She yelped and darted for the barn, but the door was shut. She ran to the doghouse, but the dog snarled. She ran to the scarecrow and stood beneath his hat.

But the hat was full of holes. The water poured down on her, cold and hard. She stood there, sopping, blinking.

After a while, she realised she felt fine. Henrietta shook herself out, shrugged, and went back to scratching the mud.
Storm, nest, two children. Make a story of it.

After the storm, Kavita and her brother Neel went into the yard to check for damage. A big branch had fallen from the neem tree. In the leaves lay a small nest, with two small speckled eggs still inside.

Kavita lifted it carefully. "We have to put it back."

Neel fetched a ladder. He climbed, with Kavita holding it steady, and set the nest in a fork of the tree, high up. A bulbul watched them from the next roof, chirping nervously.

They went inside and watched through the window. For an hour, nothing. Then the bulbul fluttered down, hopped over the eggs and settled on top of them.

Kavita and Neel hugged each other quietly. They counted the days on a calendar, and two weeks later, two small beaks poked out.
A crow steals a diamond ring and regrets it. Write the story.

A crow named Karkash loved shiny things. One morning in the market, he spotted a ring on a jeweller's tray, glittering with a clear stone. He snatched it and flew off.

Back in his tree, he tucked it in the nest. It was the finest thing he had ever owned.

But for three days, he heard shouting in the market. A bride was crying, because the ring was her family's. The wedding could not go on.

Karkash felt uneasy. On the fourth morning, he picked the ring up in his beak, flew to the market and dropped it into the jeweller's lap.

The jeweller leapt up. The bride, passing, clapped her hands. Karkash flew away, a little embarrassed, but not as embarrassed as the jeweller, who had not guarded his tray.
Deer that talks and a boy who is lost: tell it.

Pranav had wandered off during a picnic in the forest, and now the trees all looked the same. "I am lost," he whispered.

"No, you are not," said a gentle voice. A spotted deer stepped out from behind a bush. "You are only far from home."

"Can you show me the way?" asked Pranav.

"I do not know where your home is," said the deer. "But you do. Climb that rock and look for something you know."

Pranav scrambled up the big grey rock. Above the treetops, far to his left, he saw a red kite bobbing in the sky. It was his sister's kite.

He climbed down and walked toward it, checking the sky every few steps. Soon he reached the clearing where his sister stood holding the string. He turned to thank the deer, but it was already nibbling grass among the trees.
What a clever crow can teach a dog: write a story.

Jimmy the dog watched a crow crack a walnut by dropping it on the road. A car rolled over it, and the nut split. The crow hopped down and ate happily.

"Neat trick," said Jimmy.

"Try it," said the crow.

Jimmy found a stick and dropped it on the road, and a car crushed it. This was not helpful. He tried a bone. The bone stayed whole, and the driver honked at him.

"Dogs are not good at it," said the crow kindly.

So Jimmy went home, chewed his bone instead and sat on the porch watching the crow. Each afternoon, they shared the road, the crow cracking nuts, and Jimmy lying in the sun, tail thumping, bone between his paws.
Begin your story with "Once upon a time" and make it about a nightingale and a king.

Once upon a time, a king named Harsha ruled a rich land but could not sleep. Doctors came and went. Nothing helped, and he grew pale and cross.

One evening, a small nightingale landed on his window ledge and began to sing. The notes were soft and clear. The king stood still. Slowly, his shoulders dropped.

He listened until the song ended. Then he lay down on his bed, closed his eyes and slept until noon.

The next evening, the bird returned. And the next. The king ordered a golden cage, but his minister, Devika, said, "A caged bird will not sing."

Harsha thought about it and had the window left open instead. Every night, the nightingale came, and the king slept soundly, and his people noticed he was kinder.
A four-year-old needs a bedtime story about a little elephant who cannot sleep.

Ellie the little elephant lay in the long grass, but she could not sleep. The moon was too bright. The crickets were too loud. Her blanket was too warm.

Her mother came and sat beside her. "Count the stars," she whispered.

Ellie looked up. One star. Two stars. Three. They twinkled. She counted twelve before her eyes grew heavy.

A breeze rustled the leaves. A night bird sang one soft note. Her mother's trunk curled gently around her back.

Ellie counted thirteen. Then fourteen. Her trunk drooped. Her ears flopped. She breathed in, slow and deep, and her mother tiptoed away, because the little elephant was fast asleep.
Skip the usual opening; give me a story about a mountain goat that does not start with "once upon a time".

High in the mountains, a young goat named Tenzin could climb any rock and leap any gap. But one morning the herd set off for the summer meadow, and the path crossed a windy pass hung with long lines of coloured prayer flags.

The flags snapped and flapped in the wind. Tenzin stopped dead. To him they looked like a hundred bright birds about to swoop. The rest of the herd trotted under them, but he would not move.

A herder girl named Dolma came back for him. She did not pull his rope. Instead, she reached up, held one fluttering flag still and let him sniff it. It smelled of cloth and dust.

Tenzin sniffed again. Then he took a small bite of its corner.

Dolma laughed and let go. Tenzin trotted under the flags without looking up and was first into the summer meadow.
A boy called Elias and his dog Coco take a long walk and find something surprising. Write their story.

Elias and his dog, Coco, set out on a long walk one Sunday morning. They followed a trail through the fields, past a pond and up a gentle slope. Coco ran ahead, sniffing every stone.

At the top of the slope, she stopped and barked. Elias caught up. In the grass lay a small wooden box, old and damp, with a rusty latch.

He opened it with some effort. Inside were a few marbles, a folded drawing of a boat and a note that said, "For whoever finds this. Play with them."

Elias smiled. He took one marble and left a new item in its place: a pebble from the pond. He closed the box and put it back, and Coco wagged her tail all the way home.
An old man sells umbrellas in a busy market; tell me a story about him.

Mr. Chacko sold umbrellas at the edge of the market in Kochi. He sat on a stool with a hundred of them hanging around him in a rainbow. On sunny days, no one even looked at him.

He did not worry. He had a cup of tea and a small radio. When the clouds gathered, he leaned back and smiled.

One afternoon, a very heavy shower began, and people rushed to his stall. He sold forty umbrellas in an hour. But then he noticed a young girl standing alone in the rain, with no money in her hand, looking at a small red umbrella.

"Take it," he said, handing it over.

She stared. "Really?"

He nodded. She ran off holding it high, and he sat back and watched the downpour with a smile.
Dragonfly in the story, please: a girl follows a river to the sea.

Maya had always wondered where the river went. One summer morning, she packed a bag and began walking along the bank. A blue dragonfly hovered at her shoulder, then zipped ahead, as though showing the way.

She walked past fields, past a mill and a village. She crossed a bridge made of stone. Her feet ached, but the river kept going, widening and slowing, growing browner and bigger.

At sunset, she smelled salt. Then she saw it: a great grey sheet, wrinkling to the horizon. The river poured gently into it without a sound.

Maya sat on the sand with her sore feet in the water. The dragonfly landed on her knee, and they watched the sun go down together. Then she called her father and said she was ready to be picked up.
Heart-shaped patch on a newborn calf: make a story.

When the calf was born at Mehta's farm, everyone gathered round. She was brown, with white legs and, on her side, a perfect white patch shaped like a heart.

"A good omen," said Mrs. Mehta. Her granddaughter Janvi named the calf Priya.

Priya grew up gentle and slow. She let small children sit on her back. She followed Janvi to the pond and waited while she did her homework on the bank.

One year, drought struck. The village had little fodder, and many farmers had to sell their animals. Mr. Mehta came home from the market with a heavy face.

But when he looked at Priya, who was leaning against Janvi, he decided to sell a field instead. Priya stayed, her heart-shaped patch shining in the sun, and so did the family.
Swapping places for a day, a snail and a butterfly: story time.

Sonu the snail looked up at Tara the butterfly. "You are so lucky," he sighed. "You see the whole world. I see only the dirt."

"I envy you," said Tara. "You are never in a hurry."

They agreed to swap for a day. Tara crawled onto a leaf, and Sonu climbed onto her back, trembling. She flapped slowly up and then over the roses. He saw the garden spread below him, a patchwork of green and red.

Meanwhile, Tara slowly inched along the leaf. She noticed a droplet, a tiny spider and a ladybird sleeping. She saw the veins in the leaf, like a map.

By evening, they returned and sat side by side. "I will stay low," said Sonu, smiling. "And I will fly," said Tara, "but I will stop sometimes."
Not the usual jug story, please: a clever crow and a jug, told differently.

Kaka the crow sat on a fence and saw a glass jug on a window ledge. Inside was a little water, but the neck was too narrow for his beak. He knew the old pebble trick, but there were no pebbles anywhere.

Kaka looked around. Below the ledge stood a flowerpot with a wide, empty saucer underneath it. Beside the pot lay a long, bent twig.

He picked up the twig, hooked it through the jug's handle and pulled. The jug wobbled. He pulled again. It tipped, and the water poured over the edge, straight into the saucer below.

Kaka hopped down and drank until the saucer was dry.

A boy named Sandeep had seen it all from the doorway. He laughed and set the jug back. After that, he filled the saucer every morning, and Kaka never needed his twig again.
Set in the jungles of Kerala, write a story about a very small mouse who saves a very big elephant from a trap.

In the jungles of Kerala lived a small field mouse named Pappu. One evening, as he scurried through the grass, he heard a pitiful trumpeting. A big elephant named Kuttan was caught in a hunter's rope net, thrashing.

"Do not struggle," called Pappu. "You will make it tighter."

Kuttan stopped. His eyes were wide. Pappu climbed up the net and began to gnaw at a cord. It took a long time. His teeth ached. But one rope snapped, then another, and another.

Finally, the net sagged open. Kuttan stepped out, trembling with relief.

"How can I thank you?" he rumbled.

"Just keep away from the hunters," said Pappu.

Kuttan lifted him gently onto his head and carried him through the jungle at sunset.
Two paragraphs please, about a lonely lighthouse keeper and a seagull.

Old Mr. Dsouza lived alone in a lighthouse on a rock far from the shore. Months passed without anyone to talk to. One morning, a one-legged seagull landed on his windowsill, squawking for food. He tossed it a crust, and the bird stayed, hopping on the rail and shrieking at the waves.

He called the gull Captain. Each day, Mr. Dsouza shared his breakfast and spoke aloud about the weather. The gull answered with squawks, and the old man understood him perfectly. When the storms came and the lamp had to be tended, Captain perched near the lens and kept him company all night long. One evening, a supply boat arrived and the boatman asked whom he had been talking to. Mr. Dsouza smiled, and pointed up at the roof.
Learning patience from his mother: a hungry young tiger, in a story.

Young Veer was a tiger cub who was always hungry and always impatient. When his mother led him out to hunt, he crashed through the bushes, and every deer ran away.

"You are too loud," she said.

"But I am hungry!"

She led him to a clump of tall grass beside a water hole and crouched. "Wait," she whispered.

Veer waited. His tummy growled. A bird sang. Insects buzzed. Time dragged. Just when he wanted to leap up and complain, a young deer stepped to the water to drink.

His mother nudged him. He crept forward, silently, belly low, one slow paw at a time. At the last moment, he sprang, and he caught it.

His mother watched, her tail flicking. That night, Veer ate well and slept without complaint.
Tell me a story about a new student who is afraid to speak in class.

Meera joined Class 5 in the middle of July, and for three days she said nothing at all. When the teacher, Mrs. Pillai, asked her to read aloud, her voice shrank to a whisper and the back benches giggled. Meera went home and told her mother she wanted to leave. The next morning a boy named Jacob slid his notebook across the desk. On the page he had drawn a tiny cartoon of the giggling boys wearing paper hats. Meera laughed out loud before she could stop herself. During reading hour she stood up again, and when the story reached a grumpy old king, she read his lines in a deep, funny voice. This time the whole class laughed with her, and Meera finished the page.
Old-fashioned village sports day where the prize is a lemon: write that.

In the small village of Sindur, the school had no trophy, so the winner of each race got a lemon. At the sack race, Kamal hopped furiously and came in first. He took his lemon and held it above his head. For the egg-and-spoon race, a girl named Revu won, and the headmaster handed her the second lemon of the day, to cheers. By the end, thirty children each held a lemon. The headmaster's wife brought a large pot of sugar water and the children squeezed their lemons into it. They drank the cool lemonade as the sun dipped behind the field, and nobody remembered who had won which race.
Let a lunch box get mixed up and lead to a new friendship; write the story.

Gayatri's tiffin box and Rehan's looked exactly alike, and when the bell rang for lunch, Gayatri opened the wrong one. Inside was a thick, spicy biryani. She had never tasted anything like it. At the same time, across the room, Rehan stared at Gayatri's neat curd rice with mango pickle. He walked over, embarrassed. "I think I took yours." She grinned and held out the biryani. "It is delicious. Who made it?" "My mother," said Rehan. "She would be pleased to know you liked it." They agreed to trade a spoonful every Friday, and a month later, their mothers met at a parent-teacher meeting and were already friends.
Give me a story with a talking parrot that lives in a school office.

A green parrot named Tiku lived in the school office, and he knew every teacher's voice. One morning, the Class 3 girl Ananya came in crying, because she had lost her house key and her mother was away. Tiku cocked his head. "Key, key!" he squawked, copying the clerk, who said it every time he locked a cupboard. Then he hopped to the ledge and tapped something shiny with his beak. It was a key hanging from a nail, with a tag that said Ananya Rao. She had dropped it the day before and a cleaner had hung it there. She thanked Tiku with half a biscuit.
Take a story about a boy who wants to be a magician and performs at the class party.

Hemant had been practising card tricks for months and finally got a chance to perform at the Class 6 party. He stood on a chair, held up the pack and asked a girl named Daisy to choose a card. She picked the seven of hearts and showed everyone. Hemant shuffled, closed his eyes, murmured a rhyme and pulled out the card. It was the three of spades. The class stared. His face turned red. Daisy, giggling, said, "Sorry, I did not tell you. I changed it." Hemant burst out laughing, then bowed. He tried again, and this time, the seven of hearts popped out of her own pocket, and Daisy gasped in amazement.
Provide a story about a class that goes silent when the teacher cries.

Mrs. Mehra had always been calm, so when she stopped in the middle of the lesson and wiped her eyes, Class 7 froze. Nobody knew what to do. Boys looked at their desks. Girls glanced at each other. At last, Anita, who sat in the front, stood up and handed her a tissue. "Miss, would you like some water?" Mrs. Mehra nodded, and a boy ran to fetch a glass. She sipped it and said in a low voice that her mother was unwell and she had not slept. Then she smiled slightly. "Thank you, children." The class finished the day with unusual quiet, and the next morning a card sat on her desk, signed by everyone.
Pottery class, a pot that cracks: could you turn that into a story?

In art class, Wasim spent an hour shaping a clay pot, pressing the sides thin and smooth. When the teacher put it in the kiln, he was proud. But the next morning, a long crack ran down its belly. He stared at it, and the girl beside him, Gita, said, "It looks like a river." Wasim hesitated. He asked the teacher for some gold paint and filled the crack with a thin shining line, like a river running through brown land. The class gathered to look. The teacher said that she had seen potters in Japan do the very same thing. Wasim set the pot on the window sill, where the morning light caught the golden river.
Deliver a story about a boy who fixes the school clock.

For weeks, the big clock in the school hall had been stuck at ten past four, and nobody bothered to fix it. Then Jatin, a quiet boy in Class 8, noticed a small screw sitting on the floor beneath it. He told the caretaker, who rolled his eyes. "It has been broken for ages." Jatin asked for a ladder and a screwdriver. The caretaker gave them to him mostly to make him stop asking. Jatin climbed up, tightened the loose part, twisted the hands and gave the pendulum a push. It began to tick. The staff stood in the doorway, astonished. Jatin was thanked at assembly, and the caretaker started calling him "Engineer" for the rest of the year.
Two girls find out they have the same birthday. Tell me their story.

On the first day of Class 5, the teacher asked everyone to say their birthday aloud. Ananya said, "The ninth of August." From the back, a girl named Linda gasped. "Mine too!" They looked at each other across the room, suspicious at first, as if one of them had copied. At lunch, Linda marched over with her tiffin. "Which year?" Both were born in the same year. They compared everything: favourite colour, favourite fruit, which side they slept on. Different on every point, except the date. Still, from that day, they declared themselves twins, though one was tall and the other short. On the ninth of August, they shared a single cake, and each insisted the other should cut the first slice.
Two best friends must compete for the same prize. What does the story look like?

Naveen and Joby both wanted the Class 9 art prize, which was a box of real oil paints. They had drawn side by side for years, but now each hid his canvas. On the day of the judging, Naveen sneaked a look at Joby's painting of a fishing boat and felt his heart drop, because it was much better. He thought about turning in his own work unchanged. Instead, he went over to Joby and said, "Your boat is amazing." Joby blushed. When the results were announced, Joby won. Naveen, though disappointed, was the first to clap. A week later, Joby arrived at school with a small tube of blue paint and said, "For your sea."
A story for a six-year-old: a boy is afraid of the dark and a friend lends him a night light.

Little Nikhil was afraid of the dark, and he told his friend Rubi at school. She listened carefully. The next day, she brought a small glowing star made of plastic. "My grandma gave me this," she said. "It shines all night. You can have it for a week." Nikhil took it home and put it near his bed. That night, the room did not feel so big or black. He fell asleep before the star dimmed. In the morning, he drew a picture of it and gave it to Rubi. On the last day, he gave the star back, and Rubi laughed. "Keep it," she said. "I have lots at home."
Can I get a happy story about a boy who is teased for his accent and finds a friend?

Jaspreet moved from Punjab to a school in Chennai, and the boys in Class 6 copied his accent every time he answered. He stopped putting up his hand and ate his lunch alone behind the library. One afternoon, a boy named Karthik sat down beside him with a cricket ball. "They laughed at my accent last year, when I came from Kerala," he said. "It stopped. Do you bowl?" Jaspreet did. He bowled fast, the way his uncle had taught him on the farm. Karthik's eyes went wide after the third ball whizzed past him. The next week, Karthik made sure Jaspreet was picked for the class match. He took four wickets, and when he shouted for a catch, the whole team shouted with him. After that, the two boys ate lunch together every day.
Weave a story about two boys who build a go-cart for the school fair and fail the first test.

Mihir and Nelson spent a month building a go-cart out of old wheels, planks and a rusted steering rod. On the morning of the school fair, they pushed it to the top of the slope behind the school. Mihir climbed in. Nelson gave a shove, and the cart rolled for three metres before one wheel dropped off and sent Mihir tumbling into the grass. The watching children cheered. Mihir sat up, spitting grass. "It works!" he shouted. They fixed the wheel with a bolt from the caretaker and tried again. This time, the cart rolled all the way to the gate. Nelson ran after it, waving his cap.
Caught in a sudden downpour, two friends shelter in a bus stop. Write what happens.

Sunil and Ravi had just left school when the sky went black and the rain began to pour. They dashed to a bus shelter, where an old woman was selling roasted corn from a cart. They squeezed in next to her, dripping. For half an hour, rain drummed on the tin roof, and the boys had nothing to do. Sunil had a rubber ball in his pocket, and they invented a game of tossing it against the wall without letting it hit the puddle. The old woman laughed at their score-keeping and gave them each a free cob. When the rain stopped, the road shone, and they walked home, chewing, with wet feet and light hearts.
I would like a tale about a girl who is picked last for a team and then saves the game.

Ishita was always picked last for kho-kho in Class 8, and on Friday it happened again. The captain, Rahul, sighed and put her at the end of the line. The other team chased hard, and one by one her teammates were tagged out. With two minutes left, only Ishita was still in the game. If she was not tagged before the whistle, her side would win. She was small, and she had spent years dodging her little brothers in a crowded house. She ducked, turned sharply and slipped past every outstretched hand. The chasers grew tired and clumsy. When the whistle blew, she was still running, breathless and laughing. Her whole team rushed onto the field to lift her up. The next week, Rahul picked her first.
Sketch out a story about an Independence Day programme where the microphone stops working.

At the Independence Day programme, Class 6 had practised a speech for a month, and the lead speaker, Farida, stepped up to the microphone. Nothing came out. The mike was dead. The audience shifted.
