Farida looked toward the teachers, then the back of the field. She took a breath, stepped forward and began to speak as loud as she could. Her voice carried only to the front rows. At once, her classmates repeated each sentence in a chorus behind her, so that the words rolled down the field like a wave. By the end of the speech, the headmaster was smiling, and nobody noticed that a technician had been fixing the wires all along.
Please give me a tale about a boy who is the school's worst archer and hits the target once.

For a whole term, Quentin had missed the archery target by a mile. His arrows landed in bushes, on the roof and once in the headmaster's flowerpot. The coach, Ms. Roy, never scolded him, but his friends giggled. On the day of the school contest, he stood in line, bow in hand, and took a long breath. He pictured the flowerpot. He let go. The arrow hummed through the air and struck the red circle in the middle with a loud thud. The field went silent, then burst into cheering. Quentin looked at his bow in bewilderment. He never hit the target that well again, but nobody ever forgot it.
Children decorate the school for Ganesh Chaturthi and a clay idol falls. Tell what happens next.

For the festival, the children of Class 7 were modelling a small clay Ganesha for the school hall. After a week of work, it stood on the table with a golden crown and a round belly. On the day of the celebration, Siddhi pushed the door open too fast, and the table shook. The idol toppled and its trunk snapped off. Gasps filled the room. Siddhi's eyes filled with tears. Her friend Murali picked up the broken piece and said, "He has a new look." They took a little wet clay, pressed the trunk back on and curved it slightly upward. The idol looked even more cheerful than before. The teacher said it was the happiest Ganesha she had seen.
My cousin wants a story where a boy's nickname causes trouble and then helps him.

Everyone in Class 7 called Raghav "Tortoise" because he walked slowly and always arrived last. He pretended to laugh, but it stung. On the school trip to the fort, the teacher gave out a hunt for clues hidden along a long winding path. The fast boys sprinted up the stairs and missed the small signs painted on the lower steps. Raghav, walking slowly, noticed every one of them. By the time he reached the top, he had the full list of clues in his notebook. The others gathered around, copying from him. That evening, the teacher announced the winners, and when somebody called him "Tortoise," it sounded different.
Write a tale of a boy who gets to school early and finds the building strangely quiet.

Aman arrived at six-thirty, because his father had a shift and dropped him off before sunrise. The school gate was open, but the corridors were empty and silent. His footsteps echoed on the tiles. He peered into the Class 5 room, where the chairs stood on the desks in neat rows. A strange scratching came from the library. Aman tiptoed over and pushed open the door. The caretaker, old Mr. Pillai, was sitting on the floor, mending a torn book with tape and a ruler, humming. "Come in, come in," he said without looking up. "You can hold this page for me." Aman held it down, and they worked together until the first bell.
Put together a story about a girl who brings a plant to school and it gets damaged.

Sera carried a small tulsi plant to school for the Class 3 nature display, holding it carefully in both arms. In the corridor, a rushing boy bumped her, and the pot slipped and cracked on the floor. Soil sprayed over her shoes. She stared at the broken pot, close to tears. The boy, Danny, stopped, white-faced. Without a word, he ran to the garden shed and came back with a plastic bucket. They scooped the tulsi and its soil into it, patting it down with their hands. At the display table, the bucket looked rough but sturdy. Sera wrote on its label, "Tulsi, in a hurry." Danny wrote under it, "Sorry. It was me."
Set at a school swimming gala, tell a story about a nervous boy who finds courage.

Ajay stood at the edge of the pool with goosebumps on his arms, because he had only learnt to swim two months earlier. The gala crowd buzzed above him. His coach, Ms. Fernandes, knelt beside him. "You do not need to win. You only need to finish." The whistle blew, and Ajay dived in with a splash that was more of a belly flop. He swam hard, arms flailing, with the others far ahead. By the last length, he was alone in the water, and the whole stand began to cheer his name. He touched the wall, gasping, last by a long way, and the lifeguard hauled him up. He grinned at the sky.
Boy and girl swap places for a day in class and learn something: can you make that into a story?

Rani and Naveed made a bet: she would sit in his desk and act like him, and he would act like her, for a whole day. Rani slouched, doodled and answered questions with a shrug. Naveed sat up straight, raised his hand, and wrote notes in perfect handwriting. By noon, they were both exhausted. At lunch, they sat on the stairs, sagging. "I did not know you worked so hard," said Rani. "I did not know you were so funny," said Naveed. They agreed to end the bet. From then on, Naveed doodled a little and Rani raised her hand a little more, and the teacher never found out why.
Can you make up a story about a boy who forgets his lines in the school play?

Rohit was playing the king in the Class 6 annual play, and he had practised his speech for two weeks. On the night itself, he stepped onto the stage, saw the rows of parents and felt his mind turn blank. The hall went silent. Behind the curtain, his friend Zoya, who was the queen, whispered the first word. It was not enough. So she walked out, curtsied and said loudly, "My lord, you look troubled. Have the enemy soldiers come again?" Rohit grinned. The line came flooding back and he answered with a thundering speech about the border. The audience clapped so hard that the curtain shook. Afterwards, Zoya asked for a samosa as her payment.
Please write a short story about a rainy day at school when the power went out.

The rain started during maths, and by noon the lights in the whole building flickered and died. Class 7 sat in a grey dim room with the thunder rolling overhead. Sana, who was scared of the dark, gripped her desk. Mr. Thomas cleared his throat and said, "Anyone know a story that can be told without light?" Nobody spoke. Then Sana's friend Lakshmi stood up and began telling the tale of a monkey who stole a mango from a king's garden. She added funny voices for each character, and Sana forgot her fear. When the lights came back an hour later, the class groaned, because Lakshmi had stopped just before the monkey was caught.
A school bag goes missing on the bus and comes back with a surprise inside. Tell me the story.

Lakshman left his blue school bag on the bus seat and realised it only when he was halfway down the road. He ran back, but the bus had gone. That night, he could not eat. The next morning, the conductor stopped him at the gate and handed him the bag. "Found it under the seat." Lakshman opened it and gasped. Inside, on top of his books, lay a neatly folded paper with a drawing of a smiling bus. Underneath, in pencil, the driver's daughter had written, "We took good care of it." He turned to wave at the bus, and the driver honked twice, grinning behind the wheel.
Make up a bedtime story for my little brother about a brave pencil sharpener in a classroom.

In Class 1, on the third desk, lived a small silver sharpener named Shiv. Every day he sharpened pencils, and every night he fell asleep inside a pencil box. One evening, a storm blew the classroom window open, and a gust swept him off the desk and into a dark corner. He was afraid. He heard a tiny rustle. It was a family of ants carrying a crumb. "Do not worry," said the biggest ant. "We will carry you." Together, the ants pushed and lifted him, step by step, across the floor and back to the desk. Shiv thanked them with a shower of pencil shavings, which the ants thought were the finest curls they had ever seen.
Chess final between best friends: what is the story?

Hari and Tejas had played chess together since Class 3, but this was the first time they faced each other in the school final. Both sat very still, thinking, while the audience watched in silence. Hari was ahead until he made a careless move with his queen, and Tejas pounced and trapped it. Hari's ears went red. Tejas looked up, then down at the board, then up again. "You can take it back," he said quietly. Hari shook his head. "No. That is how it is played." He tipped over his king, shook Tejas's hand and went to buy two cups of tea. Tejas said afterwards that he almost wished he had lost.
Mention in a story something about a girl who takes the blame for a friend and what happens next.

When a cricket ball cracked the staffroom window during games, Ritu knew it had come from her friend Sunil's bat. Sunil had already been in trouble twice that month, and he stood frozen, his face white. Before the teacher could ask, Ritu stepped forward. "It was me, ma'am." The teacher looked at her for a long moment and told her to help the caretaker sweep up the glass after school. Ritu swept every piece without complaining. Sunil could not sleep that night. The next morning, he went to the staffroom before assembly and told the teacher the truth. She listened, then said they could both help the caretaker fit the new pane on Saturday. They held the glass together while he fixed it, and afterwards Sunil bought Ritu a cone of roasted peanuts.
Paint a story about a boy whose flute makes a strange sound at the school concert.

Madan was to play the flute at the school concert, and he had practised the folk tune until his lips were sore. When his turn came, he blew into the flute and out came a terrible squeak, like a cat that had stepped on a nail. The hall went silent. A few children snickered. Madan's eyes filled with tears. From the front row, his friend Teja stood up and, instead of laughing, began to clap in a slow, steady rhythm. Others joined. Madan wiped his eyes, took a breath and played again. This time the music rose smoothly, and when he finished, the clapping that Teja started had grown into a roar that shook the hall.
Describe, as a story, a shy girl who dances at the annual day.

Sunita loved to dance in her bedroom but never in front of anyone. When her teacher announced the annual day, Sunita hid behind her desk. Her friend Esha, however, had seen her dance in the corridor once and kept nagging her to try. On the evening of the show, Sunita peeked through the curtain, saw a full hall and felt dizzy. "I will do it only if you stand at the side where I can see you," she said. Esha stood by the wings and made silly faces. Sunita burst into a grin and danced the whole folk number without a single missed step. Her mother cried in the third row and clapped louder than anyone.
Produce a story about a boy who gets a surprise on his first day of school when he finds his older sister in his class.

Little Keshav walked into Class 1 holding his mother's hand, then dropped it at the door, determined to look brave. He stared at the rows of benches. Then he spotted a familiar face. It was his big sister, Sita, who was helping the teacher as a student volunteer. She waved. "Over here, you!" He ran and hugged her legs. The teacher laughed. She settled him next to a boy named Tipu, who was crying quietly. Keshav, now feeling large, patted Tipu on the back and said, "It is fine. My sister is here." He spent the day proudly showing Tipu where the toilets and the water tap were, as if he owned the school.
A substitute teacher turns out to be a former student of the school. Write that as a short story.

When Mrs. Kulkarni fell ill, a young man named Mr. Aziz arrived as the substitute for Class 6. He looked around at the old brown benches and smiled. "Who sits at the third desk on the left?" he asked. A boy named Vivek raised his hand. "There is a carving under the top of it. Look." Vivek bent down and found tiny letters scratched into the wood: "A.Z. was here, 2009." The class erupted. Mr. Aziz explained he had sat at that desk fifteen years before, and he had been caught carving it by the same headmaster. "I got a week of cleaning the blackboard," he said, laughing. That day, he taught the whole lesson from memory, standing on the old platform.
Two girls hold a contest about who can stay silent the longest. Tell me how it ends.

At lunch, Rupa dared her friend Safina to a silent contest, and the loser had to buy a samosa. Neither spoke for the entire afternoon. When the teacher asked Rupa a question, she wrote the answer on a slate. When Safina's mother came to the gate, Safina waved and smiled without a word. By evening, both were bursting. They walked home in the same direction, side by side, glaring and giggling. At the corner, a cow stopped in the middle of the road and let out a tremendous moo. They both screamed at once, then collapsed in laughter. "We both lost!" cried Safina. They bought two samosas and ate one each, talking at the same time.
Cook up a story about a girl who is shy about her village accent and is encouraged by friends at a city school.

When Kalpana joined a city school after leaving her village, she barely spoke because her accent sounded different. In the first week, a girl laughed gently at the way she said "school." Kalpana went quiet. Then one afternoon, the teacher asked who could recite a poem from memory. Kalpana raised her hand and recited a folk rhyme from her village, the words rolling and rhythmic. When she finished, there was a pause, and then Hema, who had laughed, clapped. "Teach us," she said. By the end of the month, a small crowd followed Kalpana at break, chanting the rhyme, and Kalpana had started enjoying her own voice.
Give me a short story with a talking frog about a rainy day at a village school.

When the monsoon started, a green frog named Tukku climbed through the window of the village school and sat on the teacher's desk. The children were reciting a poem about rain. Tukku listened, then croaked loudly, "Wrong rhyme!" The children screamed with delight. The teacher, Mrs. Joseph, put her hand to her mouth. "Which line?" she asked. "Fifth," croaked Tukku. They checked, and he was right: the poem's last words did not rhyme. A girl named Ladli took out her pencil and changed one word. The poem now sounded perfect. Tukku gave a deep croak of approval and hopped out into the downpour, trailing a few tiny wet footprints across the floor.
How does a boy get the whole class quiet by whistling a tune? Tell it as a story.

The Class 7 room was as noisy as a market. The substitute teacher, Mr. Kishore, tried shouting, but it only made things worse. At the back of the room, a boy named Prasad cleared his throat and began to whistle a slow, gentle tune, the kind his grandfather played on the fields. One by one, the chatter faded. A few heads turned. By the time he reached the second line, every face was calm, and the whole room had gone quiet. Mr. Kishore, astonished, waited until the tune ended. "Thank you," he said. "Please do that again every time I need you." Prasad grinned. He whistled for the rest of the year.
Could you make up a story about two friends who run a small stall at the school fair and quarrel over the money?

At the school fair, Manish and Oscar set up a stall selling lemonade, and by noon they had a heap of coins. They had agreed to split it equally, but Manish wanted extra for the lemons he had paid for. Oscar felt that was unfair. Their voices rose, and customers drifted away. A teacher, Mr. Kapoor, walked past and lifted an eyebrow. The boys fell silent. Oscar picked up a pencil and wrote the costs in a notebook, line by line. Manish read it, and his shoulders dropped. Together, they counted the coins, took out the lemon money and divided the rest. They sold their last glass at four and shook hands over the empty jug.
Give us a story about a boy whose birthday is forgotten and a friend who remembers.

Nobody wished Rizwan at school on his birthday, not even his teachers. At break, he sat on the steps and tried to tell himself that it did not matter. His mother had said she would bake a cake in the evening, but the long day felt grey. As the final bell rang, his friend Tej ran up, panting. "Wait!" From his bag, he pulled a small crumpled card and a half-melted chocolate. "I wrote it in maths class," he said. "I did not forget. I was waiting until the end so that no one would see." Rizwan laughed, wiped his eyes and ate the chocolate in two bites. It was the best birthday present ever.
Present a story about a girl who brings a new girl to her group and the group is unwelcoming at first.

Shalini led the lunchtime group in Class 6, and when Ananya, a newcomer, hovered at the edge of the circle, she patted the ground and said, "Sit with us." The other girls exchanged looks. One of them, Fiona, said, "We do not have room." Shalini shifted over and made space. "We do now." Ananya sat. For the next few days, the group spoke in clipped sentences to her. On the fourth day, Ananya brought out a tin of sweets from her grandmother, and the circle softened. By the end of the week, Fiona was asking for the recipe and Shalini had stopped needing to defend her.
Narrate a relay race where the baton is dropped.

The Class 7 relay team was in the lead when Pranav, the third runner, fumbled the baton and it clattered onto the track. Gasps came from the stands. Pranav froze, then bent down, picked it up and kept running as fast as he could, though two teams had already passed him. His friend Aditi, the last runner, took the baton with a firm hand and ran as if the track were on fire. She caught one team, then another, and crossed the line second. Pranav sat on the grass afterwards with his head down. Aditi dropped beside him, wiped her forehead and said she had almost dropped it herself in the practice last week.
Write about a girl and a boy who start a newspaper in the school with a funny first headline.

Chitra and Moin were tired of the dull school notice board, so they started their own newspaper, written by hand on a single sheet. Their first headline read: "Mystery of the Missing Chalk Solved: It Was in Mr. Rao's Pocket." Half the school read it in the lunch queue, laughing. Mr. Rao himself, seeing the crowd, pushed forward to read it. He stood frozen for a moment, then pulled a stub of chalk from his shirt pocket, held it up and bowed. The whole queue cheered. By the end of the week, the newspaper had a long waiting list of readers and a tiny staff of six, all writing in a corner of the library.
Tell me about a student who is afraid of the school science lab, in story form.

Everyone else loved the science lab, but Ritu froze at the door because of the strong smell and the rows of glass bottles. She told her partner, Yash, that she felt dizzy, and he did not tease her. Instead, he moved their table next to the open window and gave her the job of writing the results. She wrote neatly while he poured the liquids, calling out each step. When the red liquid turned blue as the teacher had said it would, Ritu gasped and forgot her fear for a moment. She stayed for the whole lesson, and by the end of the month she was the one holding the test tubes and reading out the labels.
Say a story about a girl who finds out she needs glasses and sees the blackboard clearly for the first time.

Samira squinted at the blackboard for two years and assumed everyone else did the same. She copied from her neighbour and guessed at the sums. In Class 4, the school nurse tested everyone's eyes with a chart on the wall, and Samira read only the biggest letter. A week later, her father took her to a shop, and she came out with round pink glasses. The next morning, she walked into school and looked up. The board was sharp and crisp, every word clear. She turned around and could see the faces at the back, the clock, the tree. "Everything has edges!" she announced, and the whole class laughed along with her.
I want a story about a boy embarrassed by his lunch and a friend who makes it right.

Rakesh hid his tiffin box under his desk every day because his mother always packed boiled eggs, and the smell made the others wrinkle their noses. One afternoon, a boy named Chirag opened his own box and revealed a thick, steaming egg curry. "My grandmother makes this," he said proudly. "Anyone want a bite?" Rakesh stared. Then he slowly took out his own boiled egg and cut it in half, offering one to Chirag. Chirag ate it with a big grin and said it was the best egg he had ever eaten. Others leaned in, curious. From that day, Rakesh set his tiffin on top of the desk with no embarrassment at all.
Begin with the words "Once upon a time" and tell a story about a school for birds.

Once upon a time, in a tall banyan tree, there was a school for young birds, and the teacher was an old owl named Mr. Hoot. Every morning, the chicks learned to flap, glide and sing. One small sparrow, Pip, could not fly higher than a branch, and the others chirped about it. Pip hid behind a leaf. On the day of the great flying test, a storm cloud rolled in, and the wind tossed the bigger birds about. Pip, who was small and light, slipped under the gusts, zigzagged through the leaves and reached the highest branch first. He sat there panting, wings trembling. Mr. Hoot nodded his head and said the lesson would be about wind next.
Story please: a slow runner surprises everyone on sports day.

Everyone knew Dev was the slowest runner in Class 4. On Sports Day he stood at the end of the line for the hundred-metre race, tying his shoelace twice. When the whistle blew, the others raced ahead and he trotted behind with a red face. Halfway down, the fastest girl, Naina, tripped on a loose stone and fell with a cry. Dev stopped. He pulled her up and checked her knee. "Can you walk?" he asked. She nodded, and they crossed the line together, last of all, while the whole school laughed and clapped. Later that afternoon the sports teacher gave both of them a ribbon for finishing, and Dev wore his all the way home.
Write about two friends who stop talking after a quarrel and then make up.

Kavya and Imran had shared a desk for three years, but on Monday they argued over a borrowed pencil box. Kavya said Imran had broken it. Imran said it was already cracked. By lunchtime neither had spoken, and they sat at opposite ends of the bench. For two days they pretended the other was invisible. On Wednesday, Kavya found a small packet on her desk. Inside was a new pencil box, a little crooked, with a note: "I tried to fix yours but I made a new one out of cardboard. Sorry." She ran to Imran and hugged him so tightly that his glasses slipped. They laughed about the crooked lid for the rest of the term.
Spin a tale about a heavy school bag and a classmate who helps carry it.

Every day, Neel dragged his bag up the stairs to the third floor, wheezing at the landing. It held eleven books, a water bottle and a steel tiffin box. One Wednesday, he stopped halfway and sat down with his head on his knees. A tall boy named Gautam from Class 10 passed by and asked, "Why so heavy?" Neel shrugged. Gautam unzipped the bag, looked at the pile and said, "Today is Wednesday. You only need five of these." He took out the extra books, and together they carried them back to the locker. Neel's bag felt light as a feather. He nodded politely, though he had never spoken to a senior before.
Invent a story about a girl who becomes class monitor and has to tell her best friend to be quiet.

When Pooja was chosen as class monitor, she felt proud for exactly one day. On the second day, the teacher left for a meeting and told her to write the names of those who talked. The loudest talker was her best friend, Revati, who was telling a long joke to half the room. Pooja's hands shook. She said, "Revati, please stop," and Revati stared at her with wide eyes. "Are you really going to write my name?" Pooja swallowed. "I have to." She wrote it. Revati did not speak to her for the whole afternoon. But at the end of the day, she dropped a folded paper on Pooja's desk. It said, in capital letters: "Good monitor. Still my friend."
Kindly write a story about a girl who joins the school athletics team and is scared of the starting gun.

Padmini loved to run, but the sound of the starting gun made her heart jump. At every trial, she flinched and lost a second. The coach, Mr. Dutta, noticed. At the next practice, he fired a cap gun right behind her, again and again, until she stopped jumping. Then he let her fire it herself. She held the little pistol with both hands, shut her eyes and pulled the trigger. Pop. She laughed. On the day of the meet, when the starter's gun went off, she was already in motion, sprinting down the track like a gazelle. She won the heat by half a stride and hugged Mr. Dutta at the finish.
Tell me a short story about a strict teacher who surprises her class.

Mrs. Dsouza was the strictest teacher in school, and no one in Class 8 dared to chew gum or whisper in her lesson. On the day before the holidays, the whole class walked in nervously, expecting a surprise test. Instead, she wrote one sentence on the board: "Tell me your worst failure." Nobody moved. Then she told them about the time she had failed her own maths exam and cried in the bus. A boy named Henry laughed, then another girl shared her own story. By the end, half the class had spoken, and the bell rang without anyone noticing. Mrs. Dsouza simply collected her papers and said, "Happy holidays," with a tiny smile.
Surprise me with a story about a girl whose best friend moves away and sends a letter.

When Reema's best friend Nalini moved to another city, the desk beside her stayed empty for weeks. Reema looked at it each morning and tried not to cry. At home, she wrote a long letter about her day at school: the teacher's broken glasses, the new puppy at the gate, the maths test. She posted it with a stamp she had saved. A week later, a letter came from Nalini, with a drawing of her new school's playground and a line: "I sit alone, but I tell the empty seat all your jokes." Reema laughed through tears. They wrote every week for years, and each letter ended with a joke written upside down for the other to puzzle over.
Write a story about a boy who tells a secret and loses a friend, then tries to fix it.

Sameer promised his friend Dhruv that he would never tell anyone about the poem Dhruv had written for the school magazine. But during games period, Sameer blurted it out to a group of boys, and they teased Dhruv all afternoon. Dhruv stopped speaking to him. That night, Sameer could not sleep. The next morning he walked into the classroom early, stood on a bench and read his own awful poem about a goat, which he had written secretly last year, in front of the whole class. Laughter filled the room. Dhruv, watching from the door, laughed too, and he walked over and shook Sameer's hand. The teasing about Dhruv's poem faded by lunchtime.
Left out of a group, a girl starts her own. Show me that story.

When Ila asked to join the group that played skipping at lunch, the leader, Sheena, said the game was full. Ila walked away, face stinging. She sat under the neem tree and picked at the grass. A small girl from Class 3 asked what she was doing. "Nothing," said Ila. "Can we do nothing together?" said the girl. Ila laughed. She took a stick and drew a big circle in the dust for a new game of marbles. More children came to watch. By the end of the week, her group had twelve members and a long rulebook with silly rules. Sheena, passing by, watched them for a while and asked quietly, "Can I play?"
Tell me one about a school trip to a farm where a city boy meets a cow.

Class 4 went on a trip to a farm, and Arvind, who had grown up in a city flat, had never seen a cow up close. He kept his distance, hiding behind his friend Shobha. A large brown cow named Lakshmi turned her head and blinked at him. He yelped. The farmer laughed and showed him how to hold out a handful of grass. Arvind stretched out a trembling hand, and Lakshmi's rough, warm tongue wrapped around the grass. He giggled and jumped back, then stepped forward and tried again. By the end of the visit, he was patting her side and asking whether he could milk her, and the farmer let him try.
Make a story about a girl who is shy about her drawing until a classmate asks to see it.

Nilufar drew in the back pages of her maths notebook, tiny birds and trees and cats with long tails, and she never showed anyone. One Friday, her desk-mate Pradeep saw a page by accident. "Whoa. Who drew this?" Her ears turned red. "Nobody." He grinned. "It looks like somebody." He asked her to draw a bird for the class chart on migrating birds, which he had been struggling to make. She hesitated and then took the pencil. By Monday, the chart was covered in graceful sketches, each with its tiny label. The teacher pinned it on the board and asked who had drawn them. Nilufar slowly raised her hand, and Pradeep clapped first.
Write about a boy who always wins and learns to enjoy a game with a loser who becomes a friend.

Dhruv won every carrom game in Class 6, and the others had stopped playing with him. At lunch one day, he saw a new boy named Neville sitting alone with a board and no partner. "Play?" said Dhruv. Neville nodded and lost badly. Dhruv grinned. They played again the next day, and Neville lost again but laughed and asked for tips about the angle of the strike. Dhruv, who had never taught anyone, explained slowly. By the end of the month, Neville won one game by a single piece. Dhruv threw up his hands and hollered with delight, louder than the winner. Other boys, hearing the commotion, came over to ask whether there was space at the board.
Could you tell me, as a bedtime story, about a little girl who played a tree in the school play?

Little Mina was only six, and in the school play she had to be a tree. She did not mind, but her friend Rina, who played the princess, wore a sparkling crown. Mina stood still in her brown sack with green paper leaves on her arms. During the second act, Rina's crown slipped and fell on the floor, and the music kept playing. Mina quietly bent her branch, scooped the crown with her paper leaves and held it up. Rina took it, put it on and smiled, and the princess walked on as if nothing had happened. After the play, the teacher said the tree was the bravest actor on stage. Mina fell asleep that night with a leaf still in her hand.
Two classmates pass the same test with different results and still stay friends. Tell it.

Mehul scored ninety-two in the maths test, while his friend Sharon scored fifty-one. When the papers came back, Mehul was happy but kept quiet, because he saw Sharon's face. At lunch, she sat staring at her tiffin. He sat beside her and said nothing for a while. Finally, she spoke. "I studied all weekend." He nodded. "Which sums did you miss?" She showed him. He looked, then smiled. "These are the ones I missed on the last test." They worked through them together on the back of a notebook. The next test, Sharon scored seventy-eight, and she bought him a gulab jamun from the canteen as a thank-you.
Outline in story form something about a boy who gets a bad nickname and decides to turn it into something good.

The boys called Faisal "Pencil" because he was thin and tall. It stung, but he said nothing. At the school art fair, he decided to use it. He drew a series of comic strips about a hero called Captain Pencil, a thin, tall man who solved crimes using only a ruler and an eraser. The strips went up on the notice board, and children crowded to read each new episode. The same boys who had teased him began to ask when the next one would come. They started calling him "Captain." He did not mind. At the end of the year, the school magazine printed a full collection of his adventures.
Once upon a time, there were two girls at a school in the hills. Tell me their story.

Once upon a time, in a school high in the hills, there lived two girls named Pema and Rukmini. Pema was bold and loud, and Rukmini was quiet and careful. They shared a desk but little else. One winter, heavy snow blocked the road, and they were stuck in the school overnight with ten other children and a single teacher. In the dark, the lamps flickered. Pema, scared and pretending not to be, started to shiver. Rukmini quietly handed over her own blanket and began to tell a story about a snow leopard. By dawn, they were both asleep against each other, and when the snow cleared, they walked down the mountain hand in hand.
Bedtime story needed: a little elephant goes to school and dances at lunch.

In a green forest, there was a school for young animals, and the newest student was a small elephant named Chintu. He was shy and kept his trunk curled under him. At lunch, all the animals tapped their feet to the beat of a drum that the monkey played. Chintu watched, then stamped one big foot on the ground. Thud! The animals turned. He stamped again, then swung his trunk from side to side. The monkey drummed faster, and the little elephant swayed and twirled. The parrots whistled, the deer clapped their hooves, and the tortoise nodded slowly. When the bell rang, Chintu followed the others back to class with a swing in his walk.
Please write a happy story, in about 100 words, about a girl who finds her lost best friend on the first day back.

After the summer holidays, Alisha walked into school and could not find Pooja anywhere. The desk they shared was empty. She waited by the gate through two bells, and then a taxi pulled up. Out stepped Pooja, tanned and breathless, her bag half unzipped. "My train was late!" she cried. Alisha ran across the yard and hugged her so hard that her bag fell. They sat together in the front row, whispering about the holidays, until the teacher said, "Girls, the lesson." Neither could stop smiling. By lunch, they had told each other every story, and then they started to tell them again from the beginning.
Fashion a story about a boy who was mean to his friend and finds a kind way to say sorry.

Bipin laughed when his friend Ashok tripped over his own bag and everyone looked. Ashok did not laugh. He picked up his things and walked off without a word. Bipin felt a stone settle in his chest. The next day, Ashok avoided him in class. Bipin thought hard about what to do. At lunch, he walked up to Ashok's desk and quietly put down a small paper boat. Inside it, he had written, "I should not have laughed. Can you forgive me?" Ashok read the note, folded the boat into a pocket and said, "Next time, help me pick up the books." Bipin nodded and promised.
What happens when a boy forgets his lunch and his friends each give him a small bite? Tell me in a story.

On Wednesday, Hardik arrived at school and discovered his tiffin was still on the kitchen table. At noon, his stomach rumbled so loud that the boy beside him turned. "Where is yours?" "Forgot." Without a word, the boy, Ali, broke a piece of his paratha and gave it to him. Then Meera passed a slice of cucumber, and a boy at the back sent over a piece of cake. By the end of the break, Hardik had a little heap of food from six different homes: paratha, cucumber, cake, a pickle, a single dosa and a sweet. He ate it slowly, tasting each, and said it was the most interesting lunch of his life.
Frame a short story about a boy who is bad at sports but great at keeping score.

Mukund could not catch, throw or run, and he stood at the edge of every game, hands in pockets. On Sports Day, the scorer for the long jump fell ill, and the PT teacher shouted for a volunteer. Mukund raised his hand, partly out of boredom. He sat at the table with a notebook and a measuring tape. He measured each jump to the millimetre and wrote it in a neat column. When two girls argued about who had won, he showed the numbers calmly. "Priya, 3.42. Sumi, 3.41." They looked at each other and shrugged. The teacher patted his shoulder. Next year, he was made the official scorer, and he wore a badge with great pride.
Write me a talking-cat story about a class that cannot find its pet goldfish.

The Class 3 goldfish, Bubbles, had vanished from his bowl, and the children were close to tears. Their teacher, Mr. Pinto, turned the room upside down. Under the window sat the school cat, Tigdi, washing her face with a long, slow paw. A girl named Fiza knelt in front of her. "Tigdi, where did Bubbles go?" The cat blinked and said lazily, "Not in my stomach. Look behind the tank." Fiza ran to the tank and found a small plastic cup that someone had used for cleaning. Bubbles was swimming happily inside it, forgotten. Mr. Pinto carried him back to the bowl with great care, and the children cheered loud enough to wake the teachers next door.
Make for me a story about two friends who disagree about a movie and nearly lose their friendship.

Both Anil and Sapna had seen the same film, but Anil called it the best of the year and Sapna called it boring. At first, they argued over lunch. The next day, they argued before the bell. By Friday, they sat on opposite sides of the room, each telling other friends why the other was wrong. Soon, the class was split. A teacher, overhearing, asked them to write a short review each. They did so, grudgingly, and she read both aloud. The class listened. "Both of these are well argued," she said. "And neither of them has changed the film." Anil and Sapna looked at each other, and a laugh escaped them both.
Why not a story about a boy and a girl who walk to school together every day and one day take a different road.

Every day, Ravi and Mala walked to school by the same road, past the tea stall and the temple. On Thursday, a pile of sand blocked the path because of road work. "Let us go through the lane," said Mala. They took a narrow path they had never used and found a hidden courtyard with a single old well and a tree full of parrots. They stopped to look. The parrots shrieked and flew in a green cloud. They arrived at school ten minutes late and were scolded, but they did not care. The next morning, they left early on purpose, and from then on, they visited the parrots every day.
Dream up a story about a boy who lies to impress a new friend and then tells the truth.

When a new boy named Dominic asked who the fastest runner in class was, Vinay said, "Me, of course. I won the district race." That was not true. Dominic's eyes lit up, and he asked Vinay to race him at lunch. Vinay's stomach knotted. At the field, he ran as fast as he could and was beaten by ten metres. Dominic looked puzzled. Vinay looked at his shoes. "I did not win the district race," he said. "I lied." There was a long silence. Dominic shrugged. "You were still fast." They sat on the grass, panting, and Dominic confessed he was afraid of the dark. Vinay swore to keep the secret.
Food goes missing at a school picnic and a classmate solves it. Make up that story.

On the Class 6 picnic to the lake, the teacher put all the lunch packets in a large bag under a tree. When it was time to eat, the bag was open, and half the packets had vanished. The children looked at each other in alarm. A girl named Tina, who liked detective books, studied the ground. There were small paw prints in the dust leading toward the bushes. She followed them with three others and found, behind a bush, a stray dog gnawing a chapati. Hungry himself, the dog looked guilty. Tina went back and told the teacher. They shared what remained, and each child gave one piece of bread to the dog, who wagged his tail all through the picnic.
Offer me a story about a girl who forgets her friend's name on the first day of the new year.

Over the long holidays, Priti lost track of a few things, and on the first day back, she saw a girl who had been her best friend since Class 3. She was smiling, and Priti could not remember her name. It started with an M. She spent the whole morning trying to guess. At lunch, she said, "Hi, you," and the girl looked hurt. In a panic, Priti confessed. "I forgot your name. I am so sorry." The girl burst out laughing. "It is Madhu. I forgot yours too. Priti, is it?" They giggled until their tiffins spilled. After that, they wrote their names on their hands every Monday as a joke.
Within 110 words, write a story about a boy who is late to the first day of Class 6.

Dilip ran into the school gate on the first morning of Class 6, only to find the assembly already over and the corridor empty. He read the new timetable on the board twice before finding his room. Everyone turned to look as he opened the door. His face burned. A girl named Kamala patted the seat beside her. "I saved you this one," she whispered, "because I was late too, last year." Dilip sat down, and the teacher, Mr. Rao, simply handed him a notebook with his name already written on the cover. He opened it, took out his pencil and felt his heartbeat slow.
Please tell me about a girl who finds a lost wallet in the school corridor.

On the way to the canteen, Nandini found a brown leather wallet near the water cooler. Inside were a few notes, a photo of a family and a school identity card of a boy named Zubin from Class 9. Her friends said they should split the money for a treat. Nandini hesitated, thinking about how worried Zubin might be. She walked to the office and handed it to the clerk. After lunch, the announcement crackled over the speaker, and Zubin came to collect it with shaking hands. He counted the notes, then found Nandini in the corridor and gave her a small packet of peanuts. She was glad to have missed the treat.
Think up a story about a new teacher who is nervous and is helped by a student.

Mr. Anand stood outside the Class 9 door for a full minute, gripping his folder. It was his first day as a teacher, and he could hear forty teenagers shouting inside. His hands were damp. A girl named Tanya came up behind him, carrying a bag. "Sir, are you the new maths teacher?" He nodded miserably. "Do not worry. They go quiet if you write a hard problem on the board before you turn around." He took a breath, walked in, wrote a tricky equation and turned. The class stared at it, silent. By the time they solved it, he had forgotten to be afraid. He thanked Tanya at the end of the day, and she shrugged.
I would love a story about a girl who runs the last leg of a relay with a torn shoe.

In the final leg of the relay, Ritika felt her shoe sole flap open as she ran, and every step slapped against the track. She kept going, because the baton was in her hand and her team was in second place. The flapping grew worse. At the last turn, her shoe came off completely, and she ran the final stretch in one sock, gasping. The crowd gasped too. She crossed the line just behind the leader and fell onto the grass. Her teammate Lubna rushed over, holding the lost shoe like a trophy. "Second place with one shoe is better than first place with two," she said. Ritika laughed so hard her sides ached.
Why does a boy always sleep in class, and what finally wakes him? Tell it as a story.

Dinesh slept through most of Class 6, his head on his arms, snoring softly. The teachers sighed and let him be, because he never disturbed anyone. His friend Alfred wondered why. One afternoon, he asked. Dinesh admitted that he woke at four every morning to help his father deliver milk, so he was always tired. Alfred was quiet. The next day, he turned up at four, yawning, and helped carry the milk cans. He did it every morning for a week. By the end, Dinesh was talking and laughing at school, awake for the first time in months, and the teachers sat him in the front row, where he stayed alert, though still a little proud of his milk route.
How about a story about a stray puppy that wanders into a school ground?

A thin brown puppy wandered into the school ground during the games period, and Class 5 forgot about the cricket match at once. Teacher Mrs. Rego told them not to touch it, because it might be sick. Arun, though, noticed that the puppy kept licking an empty steel plate someone had left near the tap. He ran to the canteen and came back with a small bowl of water. The puppy drank it all. By the end of the week, the children had asked the watchman to build a little shelter near the gate. Mrs. Rego called a kind neighbour, who agreed to take the puppy home, and Arun was allowed to visit every Saturday.
Read me a story about a girl who gets a bad mark and hides her report card until a friend helps her tell her mother.

Padma got a poor mark in science and hid her report card at the bottom of her bag. At home, she smiled brightly and said nothing, but her stomach hurt for two days. Her friend Esther noticed at lunch. "You look ill," she said. Padma whispered the truth. "Show your mother," said Esther. "She will be upset for five minutes, and then she will help. My mother was." Padma shook her head. Esther took her hand and walked her to the gate, waiting until Padma's mother arrived. Padma handed over the report card with trembling fingers. Her mother read it, sighed and said, "Come, we will look at the chapters together tonight." Padma sagged with relief.
Tell me of a sack race on sports day in which a girl wins by accident.

Sunaina had never won anything, and she joined the sack race only because her friend begged her to. She hopped slowly at the back, wobbling. Just ahead, three runners bumped into each other at the halfway mark, and all tumbled in a heap of sacks and elbows. Sunaina was too far behind to avoid them. She hopped around the pile, lost her balance, but held her sack up and kept going. In a surprise, she crossed the line first, flapping her arms in a panic. The crowd roared. She stood with the ribbon in her hand, flushed and breathless. "I think I won by luck," she whispered to her friend. "Luck needs legs," her friend said.
Disagreement over where to sit, then a compromise: can you tell it with two friends?

Hema wanted to sit near the window, and Alpa wanted to sit near the door. Each said the other was being stubborn. The teacher, tired of the squabbling, moved them to separate benches. Both pouted. After three days, Hema noticed that the window seat was too bright and made her head ache. Alpa found the door seat too noisy because of the corridor. At lunch, they met by the water tap. "I miss you," Hema said. "I miss you," said Alpa. They asked the teacher to put them in the middle of the row, where it was neither bright nor noisy. The teacher agreed, shaking her head, and the seat swap was never mentioned again.
About 120 words, please: a boy loses his school shoe in the mud.

During the rainy season, Anwar's left shoe came off in the mud outside the school gate, and no amount of pulling brought it back. He hopped around on one foot, soaking his sock. A group of Class 6 girls came by and laughed, and he turned red. A girl named Jaya, however, found a long stick and began poking the mud near his foot. Another girl found a second stick, and together they dug until the sole appeared. Anwar pulled out the shoe, covered in brown sludge, and shook it triumphantly. They washed it under the tap. He walked into class with one very clean shoe, one muddy sock and a loud, happy squelch with each step.
Prepare a story about a boy who wakes up late on exam day and still arrives on time.

Murali opened his eyes and saw that the clock said seven-thirty. His exam began at eight and school was fifteen minutes away. He threw on his uniform, stuffed his pen into his pocket and ran down the stairs. His mother pushed a banana into his hand. He ran to the corner and flagged down an auto, which stopped only because the driver felt sorry for him. The auto rattled through traffic, and the driver took a shortcut through a lane full of chickens. He leapt out at the gate with two minutes to spare, gasped his name to the invigilator and found his seat. Only then did he realise he had put on odd socks.
Write a story with no dialogue about two friends who stop being angry at each other.

Anu and Bela had not spoken for six days. Each walked into the classroom with her chin up and looked past the other. On the seventh day, it rained, and Bela arrived without an umbrella, soaked to the knees. Anu saw her shivering at the gate. She took out her spare umbrella, walked across the yard and held it above Bela's head. Bela looked up in surprise, then looked at her own wet shoes. A small smile pulled at her mouth. They walked into school under the same umbrella, shoulders touching, water dripping off its edges. At lunch, Bela unwrapped her sandwich and set half beside Anu's plate without a glance.
Some people are too proud to ask for help. Tell a story about a boy like that with a school project.

Karan insisted that he could finish the model of the solar system alone, though the planets kept rolling off the table and the glue had made a mess of his fingers. The deadline was Friday. On Thursday night, he sat at his kitchen table with half a Saturn and no Mars. His friend Dilip, who lived next door, knocked and held up a bag of coloured paper. "Need a hand?" Karan wanted to say no. Instead, he said, "Yes." They worked until midnight, cutting and sticking. In the morning, Karan carried the finished model to school, and told the teacher, truthfully, that two people had made it.
Is there a story in a boy who wants to join the football team but is told he is too short?

Zain was the shortest boy in Class 7 and the best dribbler. At football trials, the coach looked down at him and said, "Maybe next year." Zain walked home with his shoulders sagging. For the next month, he practised every morning on the empty lane near his house, weaving the ball between water bottles. When the school had a practice match, one of the players got hurt and the coach, scratching his head, called Zain to fill in. Zain slipped between the taller boys like a fish and passed the ball to the striker for an easy goal. The coach blew the whistle at the end of the match and said quietly, "Trials again on Thursday. Be there at seven."
Write a story in which a class pet rabbit is the cause of a school mystery.

Every morning, the Class 2 lettuce vanished from the rabbit's cage. The children suspected the caretaker. Then they suspected the cat. A girl named Preeti decided to stay behind and watch. She hid under the teacher's desk with a flashlight. At dusk, the cage door opened from the inside. Snowy the rabbit hopped out, nibbled a leaf from a plant on the windowsill and went back, pulling the latch closed with her teeth. Preeti nearly cried out. The next day, the class fixed the latch with a clothespin, and the lettuce stayed in the cage. Snowy gave them an offended look, and for a week, she sulked in the corner of her bed.
Build a story around a boy and a friend whose model breaks in front of the class.

Edwin and Faiz spent two weeks building a model bridge from ice cream sticks for the Class 8 science test. The day arrived. They carried it carefully to the class, and Edwin set it on the table. The teacher placed a small weight in the middle, and the bridge groaned, then cracked in two. Sticks scattered across the floor. Faiz covered his face. Edwin, though, picked up a stick and examined the break. "Look, the glue failed here, at the joint," he said to the teacher. She raised an eyebrow. "That is a correct observation." They got half the marks for the model and full marks for their explanation, and they rebuilt it that weekend, twice as strong.
Make up two friends who meet outside the exam hall and exchange good luck charms.

Outside the Class 10 exam hall, Rasheed and Ketaki stood in the queue, both pale. Rasheed was holding a small green pencil he used for luck. Ketaki had a tiny brass elephant in her pocket. They spotted each other and burst into nervous laughter. "Swap?" said Rasheed. She nodded, and they traded. He took the elephant with a bow, and she tucked the pencil behind her ear. Inside, the paper was hard, and both of them felt the funny weight of the other's charm in their hands. Afterwards, they met on the steps and compared notes. "Elephants do not forget," Rasheed said, holding up the answer sheet. They exchanged the charms back and agreed to repeat it next time.
Badminton at school, a girl who never loses, then loses: show me the story.

Meenal had never lost a badminton match, so when Nandita beat her in the final, she stormed off the court and threw her racket under a bench. Her friends stared. She sat alone in the corridor, red and furious, for ten minutes. Then she heard the sound of a racket bouncing. Nandita was practising alone against the wall. Meenal wanted to say something sharp, but she saw Nandita's tired arm and heard her mutter a count. She walked over, picked up the other racket and said, "Again?" Nandita grinned. They played until the shadow of the wall reached the middle of the court, and Meenal lost three games, laughing each time.
Please write a story where a class pet hamster escapes and the whole school helps find it.

On Monday morning, the cage door of Class 4's hamster, Pepper, was open, and Pepper was gone. The class split into search parties. Some looked in cupboards, others under desks, and a few climbed on chairs to check the shelves. The news spread, and soon, children from other classes joined, whispering in the corridors. The librarian went through her stacks. The peon peered into every dustbin. At last, near the staffroom, a girl named Maya heard a faint scratching in a pile of cardboard boxes. She called softly, and a small brown nose poked out. Pepper had made a nest from shredded paper and was fast asleep. Maya carried him back, and the school applauded all the way down the hall.
Describe in story form something about a school cleanliness drive where the class finds a lost object.

For the cleanliness week, Class 8 was assigned the playground. Each child carried a bag and a stick for picking up litter. Joel found paper cups, wrappers and plastic bottles. Near the old drain, his stick hit something hard. He pulled out a small, rusty tin box. Inside was a folded note and a marble: "To the person who finds this: the Class of 1998 was here. Hope the school is still fun." The class gathered around. They wrote their own note, added a bright new marble and sealed the box with tape. The teacher dug a hole by the same drain, and they buried the box and drew a small map to be found years later.
Two best friends are put in different sections and miss each other. Write their story.

When the new term began, Yasmin discovered she was in Section B and her best friend Roopa was in Section D. They could not sit together, could not share lunch at their old bench and hardly met except at assembly. Yasmin ate alone and felt sorry for herself. One day, she tore a page from her notebook and wrote a short note: "The maths teacher here sings when he explains. You would like it." She slipped it under Roopa's door during break. The next day, a note came back: "Our science teacher keeps a frog in a jar." They wrote every day, and soon the notes became a long, funny newspaper that both sections quietly read.
Walk me through a story about a class birthday where the cake falls.

For Anika's birthday, her mother sent a big chocolate cake to school in a box. The class lined up in the corridor to sing. As the monitor carried it in, his foot caught the edge of the mat and the cake slid out of the box and landed upside down on the floor. A horrified silence followed. Anika's lip began to wobble. Then her friend Joseph picked up a spoon, scraped the top layer off the floor paper and said, "The bottom is still fine." He cut it into small squares from the middle, where the cream was still clean. Everyone got a piece, and Anika blew out the candle on a tiny square that was still perfect.
A boy shares his umbrella with a girl he barely knows. Tell me what happens.

When the final bell rang, rain was crashing down, and Manav stood at the gate with his one umbrella. A girl from his class, Heer, stood at the other pillar, holding her bag over her head. He had never spoken to her, but he could tell she lived the same way. "Would you like to share?" he said, stepping forward stiffly. She smiled and ducked under it. They walked together through the puddles, their shoes squelching, in a polite silence. At the corner, she turned and said, "This is where I go. Thank you." The next day, she handed him a small chocolate wrapped in paper, and from then on they argued about everything on the way home.
Find me a story about a lost friendship bracelet and what happens when it is found.

Priya made friendship bracelets for her three best friends from bits of coloured thread, each in a different pattern. By Wednesday, hers was gone. She searched every corner of the room, and then she stopped speaking to her friend Neeta, whom she suspected of taking it as a joke. Neeta's eyes went wide. "I would not do that!" she said, hurt. The day ended in silence. On Thursday, the cleaner found the bracelet under a bench and returned it. Priya felt a hot flush of shame. At lunch, she knelt in front of Neeta and tied the pink bracelet on her friend's wrist. "I am sorry," she said. "Keep it. I will make another."
Write for a 6-year-old: a pencil gets lost and found at school.

Pinky the pencil lived in Tara's pencil box, and she was bright red with a pink eraser. One day, Tara was colouring a big flower, and Pinky rolled off the desk and under the cupboard. It was dark and dusty there. Pinky heard a tiny voice. "Hello, who are you?" It was a lost button named Bo. They sat together and waited. Soon, Tara got down on her knees and shone a small torch. "There you are!" She picked up Pinky and also found Bo, who belonged to her friend Meena's school shirt. Tara gave Bo back to Meena, and Pinky went into the box again, a little dusty but very happy to be home.
Come up with a story about a Christmas nativity in which the donkey costume rips.

In Mrs. D'Souza's Class 3, the nativity play had a donkey, played by two boys inside one brown costume. Moments before the show, the back half, a boy named Tarun, sat on a bench and heard a loud rip. The seam had split from tail to waist. He turned pale. His partner, Edwin, who played the front legs, held up the cloth. "Pins?" Nobody had any. A girl named Sheela ran off and returned with two hair clips and a spare green ribbon from her costume. They clipped the tear and tied the ribbon in a bow around the donkey's middle. On stage, it looked like part of the plan. Even Mary smiled when the donkey bowed, ribbon swinging.
Try writing a story about a boy who wakes up early to meet his friend before school and gets a surprise.

Shyam had promised to meet his friend Imtiaz at the park at six, before school, to practise cricket. He dragged himself out of bed in the dark, tiptoed past his sleeping family and ran through the cold lanes. At the park, nobody was there. He sat on the bench, hugging himself. Then he heard a shout. Imtiaz and six other classmates jumped out from behind the bushes, holding a banner that read "Happy Birthday Shyam!" He had completely forgotten. They had a small cake, a bat wrapped in newspaper and a pack of balls. They played until the sun rose, and then everyone rushed to school, shirt-tails flying, laughing and out of breath.
Somebody gets picked as goalkeeper because nobody else wants to and becomes a star. Tell that as a story about a boy.

Nobody wanted to be goalkeeper in the Class 5 match, so the captain, Rishi, pointed at the nearest boy. It was Jaydev, who preferred drawing. "Stand there and try to stop the ball," said Rishi. Jaydev stood between the posts, trembling, convinced he would be hit. The first shot came in like a rocket, and he threw his arms up in fright. The ball bounced off his hands and out of play. The team cheered. Over the next ten minutes, he made four more saves, mostly by accident. By the whistle, they had won one-nil, and Jaydev was carried around the ground by boys who had never spoken to him before.
Let me hear a story about a boy who is scared of the school's tall slide.

Everybody in Class 2 loved the tall red slide, except Lalit. He stood at the bottom every break, watching the others whoosh down. His friend Gudiya noticed and climbed down the ladder. "Do you want to go together?" she asked. Lalit shook his head. "Then I will hold the rail with you." She went up first, step by step, with him right behind, and stopped at the top. "Look at the view first." Lalit peeked at the whole school ground, the green field and the tiny teachers. Slowly, he sat down, closed his eyes and pushed. The slide was over in two seconds, and Lalit landed on the sand laughing so hard that he asked to go again, immediately.
Two friends are afraid to tell the teacher about a mistake. Write the story.

Tanuj and Boris had accidentally smudged paint on the school's new notice board while carrying a poster. They each stared at the stain, then at each other. "Say nothing," said Tanuj. But all afternoon, the stain seemed to shine like a lamp. By evening, Boris was sweating. "I cannot keep this in." They went together to the teacher, Mrs. Verma, and stood at her desk shuffling their feet. "We made a mess," said Tanuj. "It was both of us," said Boris. She walked over, looked at the stain and said, "A damp cloth should do it." She handed them each a sponge, and they scrubbed until it was clean.
A boy is scared of the librarian but learns she is kind. Tell me that story.

The school librarian, Mrs. Gomes, wore thick spectacles and always said "Shh" in a voice like a closing door. Prem avoided the library because of her. One day, he needed a book on volcanoes for homework and had no choice. He tiptoed in, found it on the top shelf and could not reach. Mrs. Gomes appeared at his elbow, and he nearly jumped out of his shoes. She pulled down the book and said, "You will like page forty. There is a picture of lava." Prem blinked. He read page forty at a table while she quietly dusted the shelves. When he left, she said, "Come back soon," and he did, with a growing list of questions.
The lead role in the class play goes to a boy who cannot sing. Write that short story.

When the teacher read out the cast, Gaurav's name was first, for the part of the singing shepherd. His heart sank, because he could only croak. He practised in secret in the cupboard, and each time the song came out worse. Two days before the show, his friend Nina found him sitting on the stairs with his head in his hands. "Teach me the melody," she said. He hummed it, and she hummed the harmony. On the night of the play, Gaurav stepped forward and began, and Nina, hidden behind a painted bush, sang along softly. The audience heard one clear voice, and no one ever knew that the shepherd had some help.
Write a short piece about a boy who misses the school bus and gets help from a classmate.

Vikram woke up late and ran to the bus stop, but the yellow bus was already turning the corner. His heart sank. The school was five kilometres away and he had no money for an auto. He stood on the pavement, close to tears, when he heard a bicycle bell behind him. It was Farah from his class, who lived two lanes away and rode to school every day. "Sit on the back," she said. Vikram climbed on the carrier and held the seat. They wobbled, laughed, and made it just as the assembly bell rang. The teacher, Mr. Das, only raised an eyebrow and let them walk in quietly.
A girl has to share her best friend with a new student. Tell that story.

Aarti and Smita had been best friends since Class 1, so when a new girl, Grace, joined, Aarti felt a pinch in her chest. Smita invited Grace to sit with them at lunch, and Aarti ate her roti in silence. Over the week, she watched the two of them laugh at a joke she had not heard. On Friday, Aarti sat alone in the corner and drew in her notebook. Grace came over with a plate of cookies. "Smita says you draw the best horses," she said. "Would you draw one for me?" Aarti hesitated, then drew a galloping horse with a long mane. By Monday, she had drawn a horse for each of them.
Tell of a classroom argument over whether a tomato is a fruit or a vegetable.

In Mrs. Alvares's biology class, the topic of the day was fruits. A boy named Ketan said a tomato was a vegetable, because his mother cooked it in curry. A girl, Sofia, argued that it was a fruit because it had seeds. The class split into two sides and shouted until the teacher raised her hand. "Settle this with evidence," she said. They opened books, searched the library and quizzed the canteen cook. By the end of the period, the class had a long table of arguments on the board. Sofia was right, scientifically, but Ketan kept the cook on his side. Mrs. Alvares ended the debate by serving tomato sandwiches, and nobody could decide how to describe them.
Pen a story about a girl who is nervous before her first board-style exam.

Shreya sat outside the exam hall with her hands cold as ice. Her friend Mohan, who had passed the same fear last year, sat down next to her and said nothing at first. He opened his pencil box and took out a small smooth pebble. "I found this on the way to my exam," he said. "Hold it. It is heavy enough to remind you to breathe." Shreya took it, felt its weight and drew a long breath. When the bell rang, she walked in and placed the pebble on her desk, next to the pen. The paper was hard, but she wrote steadily to the end. Afterwards, she gave the pebble back, and Mohan put it in his pocket for the next friend.
A boy's grandmother packs too much food and it saves the day. Tell me that story.

Every morning, Hari's grandmother packed enough lunch for four, and every morning he groaned. "Ajji, it is too much." She just smiled. On the day of the school trip to the hills, the bus broke down at noon, and the canteen at the stop was closed. Forty hungry children sat sulking by the roadside. Hari opened his enormous tiffin, three layers of rice, curry and sweets, and the teacher stared. "Share," she said, and Hari divided it among his friends. There was enough for ten children, and the rest ate biscuits. When the bus finally arrived, Hari was surrounded by grateful faces. That night, he told his grandmother, and she only said, "I know."
Write me a story about a cricket match where the youngest player scores the winning run.

The Class 5 cricket match was tied, and one run was needed from the last ball. The youngest player, eight-year-old Faisal, walked out holding a bat nearly as tall as himself. The bowler, a bigger boy, scowled. Faisal's hands trembled as he gripped the handle. The ball came slowly and bounced short. Faisal closed his eyes and swung. There was a soft tock, and the ball rolled lazily past the fielder's foot toward the boundary rope. Faisal ran as fast as he could and made it to the other end just as the ball crossed the rope. His teammates carried him around the field on their shoulders, and the bat fell from his hands.
Funny story wanted: two friends get stuck in a school lift.

The school had a lift that nobody ever used, but Gaurang and Shabana got in one afternoon to see what it was like. The doors closed, the lift rose a few feet, shuddered and stopped. A small light flickered. They stared at the buttons, pressed all of them, and heard nothing. Shabana started to sing to pass the time. Gaurang joined, loudly and off-key. After ten minutes, the caretaker, hearing the noise, thought a ghost was trapped in the wall and ran to fetch the headmaster. When the doors finally opened, a crowd of teachers saw the two children singing a film song at the top of their voices, and nobody spoke for a long moment.
Compose a story about a class preparing Diwali decorations when the rangoli goes wrong.

Class 6 spent the whole morning making a rangoli in front of the school entrance, pouring coloured powder into a peacock pattern. Then a gust of wind swept across the compound and blew a pile of the blue powder over the peacock's head. The children groaned. Kiran, the shortest in the class, crouched down and looked closely. "It looks like the peacock is wearing a crown," she said. The others tilted their heads. With a spoon and a steady hand, Kiran widened the blue patch into a crown shape and added yellow dots like jewels. The headmaster, passing by, stopped for a long time and told them it was the best rangoli the school had ever seen.
Keep it under 120 words and tell me about a school choir that lost its best singer the day before a contest.

The day before the district contest, Mr. Fernandes announced that Pooja had lost her voice to a cold. The choir gasped, because she sang the opening solo. Everyone looked at Tanvir, who sat at the back and only hummed. "Me?" he squeaked. That night he practised in the bathroom with the tap running so nobody would hear. On the stage the next day, his knees shook as the lights came up. He took a breath and sang the first line low and shaky. Then the other voices joined behind him, steady as a wall, and his voice found its place. They placed second, and Pooja, who watched from the front row, waved her scarf the whole time.
One more story, about a girl who brings a snake skin to school and causes excitement.

On Monday, Revathi brought a long, dry snake skin to school, folded in a plastic bag. The kids crowded around her desk, gasping, while a few of the braver boys poked it. A rumour spread that she had brought a live snake, and by recess, the story had grown into a cobra. The headmaster, hearing this, hurried in. "Where is the snake?" Revathi held up the thin, papery skin. "It left this behind in our garden, sir." The headmaster blinked, then inspected it carefully. "Marvellous," he said. He asked her to show it to the whole school at assembly, and she stood beaming while the little ones lined up to touch it.
Entertain me with a story about a girl who finds out her school is going to close and what the students do.

The notice on the board said that the village school would close by April because there were too few children. Hasina read it three times. She ran home and told her grandmother, who sighed. The next morning, Hasina went from door to door in the village, asking neighbours to send their children, even the little ones. By Friday, she had added seven names to the list. Her friend Mohan helped by painting a sign, and the class held a small fair, selling sweets to raise money for books. When the officer came to inspect in April, he counted twenty-three pupils and a garden full of paper flowers. The school stayed open, and Hasina became its first head girl.
A new student from another country makes a friend in Class 4. Write that story.

Lucas arrived from Brazil in the middle of term, and he knew only a few words of English. At lunch, he sat alone with a sandwich while the others played tag. A small girl called Diya noticed him. She did not know Portuguese, so she picked up a stick and drew a football in the dust, pointing at him. Lucas lit up. He took off his shoes, set down two bags as goalposts, and the two of them kicked a crumpled paper ball until the bell rang. The next day Diya brought a list of English words on a card, and Lucas taught her how to say "goal" in his language. By Friday, half the class could say it too.
Let us hear a story about a boy who hides his fear of failing and a friend who notices.

Nikhil laughed and joked before every test, so nobody guessed how frightened he was. The night before the big exam, he stood in front of the mirror, rehearsing a smile. The next morning, his friend Fatima saw him standing by the gate, tugging at his sleeves. "You do the same thing with your sleeves when you are afraid," she said. "I have seen it." He stared at her. "I do not want to fail." "Neither do I," she said. "Come, let us go in together." They walked in side by side. During the paper, whenever his hand began to tremble, he remembered her saying it, and he put his pen down for a second to breathe.
Write a story set in a boarding school in the hills about two girls who share a torch after lights out.

At the hill school in Mussoorie, lights went out at nine, and Kamini and Tsering shared a dormitory with twelve other girls. They had only one torch. Every night, they crept under a blanket and read a thick adventure book, taking turns to hold the light. One night, the matron's footsteps echoed in the corridor, and Tsering switched off the torch in a panic. They lay frozen, hearts pounding. The door creaked open, a beam of light swept the room, and the matron stood a long minute. Then she shut the door softly and went away. In the morning, a tiny new torch sat on each girl's pillow, with a note in neat writing: "Reading is permitted."
Two classmates cheat on a test but one confesses; I want that as a story.

During the Class 8 history test, Ritvik leaned over and peeked at Dalip's answers for question four. He copied it and felt a cold lump in his stomach for the rest of the paper. Dalip noticed but said nothing. That afternoon, Ritvik walked slowly to the teacher's desk and spoke in a low voice. "Sir, I looked at a classmate's paper. I did not know the answer." Mr. Sharma put down his pen. "Thank you for telling me. You will redo question four tomorrow, in my room." Ritvik nodded. On the way out, Dalip was waiting in the corridor. "I was not going to tell on you," he said. "But I am glad you did it yourself." They walked to the bus together.
Dictate a story about a girl who finds a friend by sharing an umbrella at the school gate.

On the first morning of the monsoon, Mehek arrived early with her father's enormous black umbrella. At the school gate, she saw a girl in a Class 3 uniform standing under the guard's tiny roof, staring at the long, open path to the building. She had no raincoat. "Come under," said Mehek. "There is room for three people in here." The girl ducked in. Her name was Jasleen, and she had joined the school only the week before. Halfway along the path, a gust turned the umbrella inside out, and both girls shrieked as the rain soaked their hair. They wrestled it back into shape, laughing so hard that they could barely hold it. In the classroom, they sat dripping side by side, and the teacher handed them one towel to share.
Unfold a story about a boy who is picked to ring the school bell for the first time.

For years, Ravindra had watched the peon ring the big brass bell and dreamed of doing it himself. On the last day of term, the headmaster surprised him. "Would you like to ring it today?" Ravindra's hands shook as he took the hammer. He aimed, swung and hit it dead centre. The bell boomed so loud that birds flew out of the trees. He grinned, then rang it again, and again, until the headmaster coughed. "That is enough, thank you." The children cheered as they streamed out, and the peon winked and pointed at his own ears, which were ringing for the next hour.
A tiffin box goes missing and turns up somewhere surprising: tell me that story.

Gauri was certain she had put her tiffin box into her bag that morning, but at lunch the bag held only books. She asked three classmates, checked the classroom and went down to the lost-and-found shelf. No box. She sat on the steps feeling hollow, until the school cat, a small orange creature named Biscuit, trotted past with something in her mouth. It was a plastic sandwich bag, torn and empty. Gauri followed her around the corner of the building and found, under a bush, the missing box, lid chewed and food gone. She sighed, then laughed. The cat sat beside her, licking a paw, looking very pleased. Gauri bought a samosa from the canteen instead.
My niece is six. Could you write her a story about a class that plants a seed and waits?

Miss Anita gave each child in Class 1 a small cup of soil and one bean seed. Tia pressed hers in with her thumb and put a sticker on the cup. Every morning she ran to the window and looked. Nothing happened for a week. Her friend Sam said, "Mine is dead." Tia felt sad, but she kept watering hers a little each day. On Monday of the second week, a tiny green curl poked out of the soil. Tia squealed so loudly that the whole class rushed over. Sam's cup had a green curl too, hiding behind a small clump of mud. They stood in a row and gave each plant a name.
Tell a story about a boy who gets lost on his first day in a big new school.

The new school building had four floors and about a hundred identical doors, and Ishaan was lost by 8:15. He had a paper with his classroom number, but the numbers made no sense to him. He walked up and down the same corridor three times, feeling smaller each time. A girl carrying a pile of notebooks stopped. "Are you new? Which room?" He showed her the paper. She turned it upside down and laughed. "You were reading the six as a nine." She walked him to the right door on the second floor, handed him a notebook from her pile and said her name was Ria. He entered the classroom just as the roll call began.
Make up a story about a drawing competition and a broken colour pencil.

Before the drawing competition, Ayaan's yellow pencil snapped in half. He needed it for the big sun in his picture, and he had only five minutes left to start. His neighbour, a girl named Rhea, looked at his sad face and slid her own yellow pencil across without a word. Ayaan began to colour the sun. Then he noticed Rhea had no yellow now, and she was drawing a lemon tree. He took a deep breath and broke his half pencil again, handing her the longer piece. They shared the stub for the whole hour. Neither of them won a prize, but their sun and lemon tree hung side by side on the notice board.
Mind telling me a story about a ghost in the school library that turns out to be the wind.

Whispers went around that the old school library was haunted. Chairs scraped at night, pages rustled, and a low moan came from the top shelf. Three brave boys, Piyush, Lenny and Kabir, stayed behind one evening with a torch and a bag of biscuits. At seven o'clock, they heard it: a long, hollow moan. They clutched each other. Piyush shone the torch toward the sound and saw a loose window in the corner, its latch broken, rattling in the wind. Each time the breeze passed through the gap, it made the moaning noise. They closed the window and the library fell silent. In the morning, they told no one, to keep the legend alive.
Could you tell a story where two classmates swap lunch boxes by mistake?

Nisha and Kabir both had round steel tiffin boxes, and one Monday Kabir carried the wrong one home. His mother washed it before she noticed the name scratched on the lid. She did not like to send back an empty box, so she filled it with coconut laddoos. On Tuesday, Kabir handed it to Nisha, who blushed and gave him back his own box, unwashed. That evening, Nisha's grandmother saw the laddoo crumbs and decided her family would not be outdone. On Wednesday, Kabir's box came back full of sweet pongal. After that, the boxes went back and forth all term, each time with a new dish inside. By December, the two families had never met, but they had swapped twenty recipes, and Nisha and Kabir sat together at lunch every day.
Narrate how a girl writes to the headmaster asking for a swing in the playground.

Zarina was tired of waiting in the long line for the one slide, so she wrote a polite letter to the headmaster, Mr. Roy. "Dear Sir, we need a swing. Many children wait long and get angry.
