A swing would make break time happy. Yours sincerely, Zarina." She slipped it under his door. Nothing happened for a week. She sighed and told her friend Boman, who shrugged. Then, on a Monday morning, a team of workers arrived with long poles and chains. By afternoon, a bright blue swing hung from the old tree. Mr. Roy, standing beside it, held up her letter and called her up to cut the ribbon. She swung for the entire break.
Where a girl apologises to a friend with a handmade card, write that story.

Jyoti had said something unkind to her friend Hamida at lunch, something about her stitched shoes. Hamida's face had closed like a book, and she left the table. Jyoti spent the afternoon feeling more and more ashamed. At home, she took a sheet of paper and drew a pair of shoes with large, happy faces. Underneath, she wrote, "I am sorry. Your shoes are brave." She slid it into Hamida's bag the next morning before the first bell. At recess, Hamida read it twice, then burst into a smile that she tried to hide behind her hand. She walked across and said, "I am keeping this." They shared a plate of puffed rice.
Try a story where a boy mistakes a girl's kindness for a prank, and they sort it out.

In Class 7, a girl named Bhumi left a note on Pratik's desk that said, "Look in your bag." Pratik was sure it was a prank, because the boys had pulled a few already. He looked in the bag with a stick, expecting a frog. Nothing. He found only a small packet of his favourite biscuits. Puzzled, he looked up and caught Bhumi watching. He frowned and marched over. "What is this?" he said. She blinked. "You looked sad yesterday." Pratik's ears burned. "I thought it was a trick." She laughed. "I would never bring a frog. I am afraid of them." They shared the biscuits in the corridor, and he apologised twice.
Write up a tale about a class that welcomes a new boy who uses a wheelchair.

When a boy named Rustom joined Class 7 in a wheelchair, the class went quiet and stared. The first morning, he struggled to reach his desk, because the ramp ended before the door. A girl named Pallavi marched to the headmaster's office and came back with the caretaker and a wooden plank. Together, the class worked for the break, fixing the plank over the step. Rustom rolled in, grinning. At lunch, the boys asked him which cricket team he supported, and he said, "Mumbai," and they argued happily for the entire break. By Friday, Rustom had a seat in the middle of the class and had been invited to a birthday party at the weekend.
Class play, narrator with a cold: what would the story be?

The narrator for the class play, Vandana, woke up on the big day with a blocked nose and a voice like a croaking frog. She almost stayed home but dragged herself to school. Backstage, her words came out as "Wuns upon a tibe." Her classmates stared. Then the boy playing the prince, Samar, grinned and said, "We could make that funny on purpose." He walked onstage and, in a loud voice, translated each of her sentences for the audience, adding a silly gesture. The audience roared. Vandana, honking through her handkerchief, kept going. At the end, the two bowed together, and she blew her nose with a loud trumpet.
Write the story of a student who forgot his homework and how he handled it.

Kunal opened his bag at the start of the English period and realised his homework notebook was still on the kitchen table. He thought of making up a story, but when Ms. Bhatt called his name he stood up and said, "I did the work, but I left the notebook at home. I can redo it in the break, if you will allow me." Ms. Bhatt looked at him for a moment. "Do it now, at the back, and show me before lunch," she said. Kunal wrote the answers quickly and handed her the page. She read it, nodded and put a tick in her book. He walked out with a dry throat and a lighter heart.
Select a story about a boy who studies all night before a test and falls asleep during it.

Chetan stayed up until two in the morning with his science notes, drinking cold tea from a steel glass. At school, he sat down for the test with burning eyes and a fuzzy head. The first page went fine. By the third question, the words started to swim. His chin dropped, and the pencil rolled out of his hand and clattered on the floor. The teacher, Mr. Abraham, walked over quietly, picked it up and tapped the desk. Chetan woke with a jerk, red-faced. Mr. Abraham whispered, "Wash your face. I will stop the clock for five minutes." Chetan splashed cold water on his cheeks in the corridor and came back awake. He finished the paper with ten minutes to spare.
Make up a short story about a girl who finds a hidden message in a school desk and writes a reply.

When Zoe got a new desk in Class 7, she found a message scratched under the lid: "If you read this, you are now my friend. I sat here in 2016. Tell me about school." Zoe stared at it for a long minute, then took out her compass point and carefully scratched underneath: "Hello. The canteen now sells noodles. The maths teacher still wears a green tie. I am your friend." She closed the lid, feeling strangely connected. The next year, a new student might find it. She smiled at the thought. Each month, she added another line about the school, because she wanted the next person to have plenty to read.
Create a story with a talking squirrel about two children who share their lunch under a tree.

Under a big tree near the playground, Reena and Chetan ate their lunch every day, tossing crumbs to a squirrel named Nutmeg. One day, Nutmeg hopped onto Chetan's knee and said in a tiny voice, "You always give me the crust." The children jumped. "You can talk?" Reena whispered. "Only to those who share," said Nutmeg. She told them about a hidden pile of acorns that she could not carry alone. They followed her to the roots of the tree and helped her move the pile into a hollow. In return, Nutmeg promised to guard their lunch from the crows. From then on, she sat on their bench like a very small teacher.
What about a story where a school bus breaks down on the way to a field trip?

Halfway to the science museum, the Class 6 bus coughed, shuddered and rolled to a stop on a quiet road. The driver, Mr. Salim, lifted the bonnet and shook his head. The teachers looked worried, and the children began to groan. A boy named Kiran spotted a mango orchard by the road and a farmer waving. The farmer invited them to sit in the shade while a mechanic came. For two hours, the class ate ripe mangoes, climbed the trees and listened to the farmer explain how fruit grows. When the bus finally started, the children begged to stay. The teacher admitted afterwards that it had been a better lesson than the museum could have given.
Write a story where a girl teaches a friend a skipping game and a bully joins in.

Shanti was jumping rope in the corner of the yard when her friend Perin asked how to do the double jump. Shanti showed her, counting aloud. Perin tangled her feet and fell. A boy named Bunty, known as the class bully, came over to laugh. He loomed over them. Shanti held out the rope. "Try it." Bunty snorted and said it was a girls' game. "Then you will not be able to do it," said Shanti. His jaw tightened. He took the rope and managed a single jump, then fell flat on his back. The girls laughed, and for once, Bunty laughed too. After that, he stood at the end of the line every day, swinging the rope.
Do you have a story about two boys who fall out over a game of marbles and make up over a broken window.

Zubair accused Anand of cheating at marbles, and they stopped talking. Two days later, a stray marble flew out of the game and shattered a classroom window. Both boys jumped. Anand looked at Zubair. "Yours?" "No, yours!" Their eyes met, and a grin crept over both faces. They went to the headmaster together and took the blame, shoulder to shoulder, and were told to wash the windows on Saturday. They scrubbed side by side, splashing water at each other. When they finished, the glass was cleaner than it had ever been. They sat on the step and counted their remaining marbles, and neither said another word about cheating.
Two girls write secret messages in their notebooks and get caught. Tell it as a story.

Rekha and Manju wrote notes to each other in a code made of numbers, passing them back and forth during Hindi class. They thought nobody could ever decode them. One day, the teacher, Mrs. Nambiar, picked up a crumpled paper that had fallen and read it silently. Then she raised an eyebrow. "Seven, twelve, three," she said. "That is G, L, C, if A is one." The girls went pale. "Good code," Mrs. Nambiar went on, "but not a secret one. I used the very same code at your age." The class tittered. She handed back the paper and told them they could keep the code, as long as they used it after the bell.
His friends plan a goodbye for a boy who is moving schools. Tell that story.

When Jeevan told his class that he was moving to another city, the room went quiet. For a week, his friends whispered at the back. On his last day, they led him to the school ground, where a long banner hung between two trees. On it were drawings and messages in a dozen different pens. Each friend had also brought something small: a pencil, a marble, a bookmark, an old coin from a grandfather's collection. They put it all in a small box. Jeevan took the box and tried to speak, but his voice cracked. They hugged him, all at once, in a heap. On the train, he opened the box again and again.
A lunchtime misunderstanding leads to a new friendship for a girl; write it as a short story.

Leela thought the girl at the next bench, Priya, was laughing at her new haircut. All lunch she kept her head down and ate nothing. Priya kept looking at her and smiling, and finally she walked over. "I wanted to say I like your clips," she said. Leela blinked. "I thought you were making fun of me." Priya laughed so hard that the whole bench shook. "I was trying to work up the courage to talk to you." They sat together and shared Leela's idli, which Priya declared the softest she had ever eaten. From then on, they swapped clips every Friday and wore each other's colours.
Write a short story about a lost tiffin box.

On Tuesday, Arjun opened his bag and found no tiffin box. His stomach growled as the bell for lunch rang. He searched under the bench, behind the cupboard and even in the dustbin corner. Nothing. His friend Salma offered half a chapati, but Arjun shook his head because his mother had packed his favourite aloo paratha. After school he walked back along the corridor, feeling heavy. Then he heard a faint clang from the water cooler room. The steel box had slid behind the pipe when he filled his bottle that morning. He crawled in, grabbed it and found the paratha cold but whole. He sat on the stairs and ate it happily, sharing a corner with Salma.
Story idea: a girl forgets her dance steps on stage and a friend improvises.

On the night of the school annual function, Janaki and her best friend Ayesha stood on the stage in matching blue costumes. The music began. Janaki's mind went blank, and she froze for four beats. Ayesha, without turning her head, whispered, "Follow me." She spun, added a clap that was not in the routine and swept her arm toward Janaki. Janaki copied it and suddenly remembered the whole sequence. The audience took the sudden clap for part of the dance and cheered. When the music ended, they bowed together, breathing fast. Backstage, the dance teacher said she had not choreographed the clap but she wanted to keep it, so they practised it the next week.
Stitch together a story about a school garden where the vegetables vanish overnight.

Class 4 had planted tomatoes, chillies and spinach in a small plot behind the school, and each child watered a row. One Monday, three of the tomato plants lay flattened, and the red tomatoes were gone. The children stood in a worried circle. "Someone stole them," said Pavan. "Let us watch tonight," said Abha, and she brought a torch. At dusk, they hid behind the wall and saw a family of monkeys sliding down from the tree and snatching tomatoes. The children laughed in spite of themselves. The next day, they covered the plants with old fishing net from the caretaker, and left a small pile of bananas near the wall as a peace offering. The monkeys took the bananas.
For bedtime, tell me about a boy who plays the sun in a school play.

Little Kabir was chosen to be the sun in the school play, and he wore a big yellow cardboard circle with rays all around. He stood in the middle of the stage and did nothing but shine. The other children played clouds, birds and flowers, and they danced around him. In the middle of the song, one of the rays fell off and rolled across the floor. Kabir did not know what to do. A little flower girl named Rani picked it up and tucked it back into his costume with a clip. The audience clapped as though it were part of the dance. At home that night, Kabir slept with his sun hanging beside his bed, glowing in the dark.
Carry me through a story about the school bell that rings at the wrong time.

On Wednesday, the school bell rang at ten o'clock instead of eleven, and the whole building emptied into the yard. Teachers stood confused, children cheered and the headmaster hurried out from his office with a half-eaten sandwich. The peon, old Shankar, stood at the bell with a sheepish look, blaming the new watch his son had given him. For ten minutes, children raced and shouted. Then Shankar rang the bell again, properly, and everyone trooped back inside. In the Class 7 room, a girl named Neha asked her teacher, "Can we tell this story to the school magazine?" The teacher, with a tiny smile, agreed. The headline was "The Bell Who Took a Holiday."
Could you write a story about a girl who forgets the words to the school song at assembly.

Everyone knew the school song, but on the Monday that Geeta was asked to lead it, her mind went white. She stood at the front with a microphone in her hand, and the first line would not come. Hundreds of faces looked at her. She opened her mouth and nothing happened. In the second row, her friend Jenny mouthed the words slowly, one at a time. Geeta watched her lips, then began, hesitant, and the whole school joined her halfway through the first verse. By the end of the song, her voice had steadied. The headmaster thanked her, and she walked off with her cheeks burning. Jenny was waiting by the stairs with a bag of peanuts.
Imagine two friends who study together before a big exam, and tell their story.

Before the Class 9 science exam, Omar and Preeti sat on the stairs of the library with a stack of notes. Omar knew biology by heart but could not remember a single physics formula. Preeti knew every formula but fell asleep at the sight of diagrams. They struck a deal. For one hour Preeti explained force and motion using a toy car, and for the next hour Omar drew the heart on a napkin and made her colour it. By evening both of them were tired and hungry, so they shared a packet of biscuits. At the exam, Omar wrote the formulas carefully, and Preeti labelled the heart without a single mistake.
Teachers forget things too. Tell me about one who forgets his glasses and a class that helps.

Mr. Thakur lost his glasses on the morning of a spelling test, and without them, the words on the board were a blur. The class waited. "I will have to postpone this," he said. A boy named Quincy raised his hand. "Sir, we can read the words out for each other." Mr. Thakur considered it, then agreed. One by one, the children took turns reading words aloud, and others wrote them down. The class became unusually quiet and careful. At the end, the papers were marked by swapping, and everyone scored well. Late in the afternoon, the caretaker found the glasses in the staffroom fridge, inside a carton of milk, and Mr. Thakur took them with a sigh.
Can I have a story about a boy who wins the school quiz and shares the prize with the team.

Bhaskar answered the last question correctly, and the headmaster handed him a large shiny trophy. Applause rolled through the hall. Bhaskar took it in both hands, then froze. Behind him stood Teena, who had answered three questions, and little Osman, who had stayed up all night to learn the capitals. He turned toward the audience and said into the microphone, "This belongs to the whole team." The headmaster raised an eyebrow, then nodded. The team gathered on the stage for a photograph, passing the trophy from hand to hand. Later, Bhaskar placed it on the shelf in the staffroom, and the three of them sneaked in each Friday to polish it.
Describe a class that makes Holi colours from flowers and the colours run, as a story.

The Class 5 teacher had asked each child to make natural Holi colours from flower petals and turmeric, and they dried them on trays in the sun. Overnight, a sudden shower hit the school roof. In the morning, the trays held a pool of swirling orange, pink and yellow. The children stood staring, silent. A girl named Mehr dipped her finger in and drew a line on a sheet of paper. It made a lovely blend, soft as a sunset. "We can paint with it," she said. They spent the morning painting their hands and faces and covering a long sheet of paper with a wild picture of a rainbow. The teacher hung it on the wall.
What would happen if a girl found a mysterious note inside a library book? Tell it as a story.

While searching the school library for a book on dinosaurs, Hana opened a thick green volume and a folded paper fell out. It said, in a careful hand: "Meet me by the mango tree at lunch. Bring a friend." She told her best friend Joel, and at lunch they crept to the mango tree, giggling. Under it sat the librarian, Mr. Gupta, holding a tray of mango slices. "I hide notes in books every year," he said. "Only the children who read the whole shelf find them." Hana and Joel looked at each other in surprise, then accepted the slices. Then they asked if they could write the next note themselves.
Lay out a story about a girl who finds out that her teacher is afraid of lizards.

Ms. Pandey never showed fear, until the day a small green lizard fell from the ceiling onto her desk. She shrieked and leapt on to a chair, clutching her sari. The class went silent, then a few boys began to snigger. A girl named Vidya, who had kept lizards in jars at home, walked calmly to the desk, cupped the lizard in her hands and carried it outside, setting it gently on a bush. When she returned, Ms. Pandey was still on the chair, pale. "It is gone, Miss," Vidya said. Ms. Pandey climbed down, smoothed her sari and said, "Thank you. Let us never discuss this." For the rest of term, she called Vidya "Lizard Catcher" in a kind voice.
Everything goes wrong in a school play and the audience loves it. Make up that story.

In the Class 5 production of "Robin Hood," the paper arrows fell off the walls, the tree wobbled, and the sheriff lost his hat. The narrator mixed up the scenes and read the ending first. Robin tripped on his cloak and landed on Little John, who burst out laughing. Both fell over. The audience started giggling, then roaring. The teacher in the wings buried her face in her hands. Still, the children carried on, improvising, with Robin shouting, "I meant to do that!" At the end, the whole hall stood and applauded for five minutes. The headmaster later told the teacher it had been the funniest play in the history of the school.
Hand me a story about a girl who moves to a new school and finds out her old friend is there.

When Dhwani began Class 6 at the new school, she walked down the corridor with her eyes on her shoes. At the end of the hall, a girl was fixing a poster on the wall and, without turning, said, "Dhwani? Is that you?" Dhwani looked up. It was Annie, her friend from kindergarten, whom she had not seen for five years. They both shrieked. Teachers peeked out of classrooms. They stood hugging and talking over each other, asking and answering all at once. "You still have the same laugh," said Annie. At lunch, they sat together, and Dhwani found that the new school was suddenly much smaller and friendlier than before.
Tell me how a girl writes a story for the school magazine and her friend helps her edit it.

Soumya spent a whole weekend writing a story about a dragon who was afraid of fire. She typed it, printed it and handed it proudly to her friend Cyril. He read it twice and went quiet. "The ending is rushed," he said. Her face fell. "I worked so hard." "I know," he said. "But the best part is the middle, when the dragon hides from the candle. What if the ending stayed there longer?" Soumya grumbled, then took the pages home. On Monday, she returned with a longer ending in which the dragon befriended a small boy with a lantern. Cyril read it and wiped his glasses. It was printed in the magazine on page three.
Create a story about a class mural that two friends disagree about.

Class 7 was painting a mural on the long wall of the library corridor. Divya wanted a forest of green trees and Mohit wanted a rocket ship flying across the night sky. They argued so loudly that the art teacher, Ms. Jones, banished them to opposite ends of the wall. For three days, Divya painted trees on the left and Mohit painted stars on the right, and the middle stayed blank. On Friday, both stood in the middle, each with a brush, not looking at each other. Finally, Divya painted a tall tree reaching upward, and Mohit added a rocket launching from its tallest branch. They stepped back, grinning. The mural became the school's favourite, and little children stopped to point at the rocket tree.
Write a boy's story: he is injured before the big match and has to be the team's cheerleader.

Sidharth sprained his ankle in practice, the day before the big inter-school football match, and the doctor told him to rest for two weeks. He watched from the bench with a crutch beside him, angry and miserable. Before the match, the team looked glum. He thought about what he could do, then stood up on one leg and began a chant they had made up last year. It was silly and loud and the players began to grin. When the second half started, the team was one goal behind, but the stands now echoed with Sidharth's chant. They won three to two. In the huddle afterwards, the captain lifted Sidharth's crutch like a trophy.
Set in a village school in a hot summer, write a story where the well dries up.

In the village of Rampur, the school well dried up in the hottest week of May, and the children had to carry pots of water from the river. Teacher Sharda watched them trudge in with their small buckets. Little Bhavna looked at the empty well and said, "Maybe the rain forgot it." Sharda smiled and organised the class into a line. Each child carried water from the river and poured it into the school tank, one cupful at a time, singing a counting song. After three days the tank was full. That night a short, heavy shower fell, and by morning a thin pool of water shone again at the bottom of the well. Bhavna insisted the song had called the rain back.
Two children save a classmate from being teased by a clever trick. Write the story.

At lunch, a group of older boys surrounded a small boy named Waseem and snatched his cap, tossing it around while he begged. Two Class 6 girls, Alka and Beth, saw it from a distance. They walked over, calm as anything, and Beth held up a tennis ball. "We bet none of you can catch this from the far wall," said Alka loudly. The boys could never resist a challenge. They dropped the cap and ran to the wall, pushing each other to be first. Beth threw the ball high, and while they jostled and argued over who had caught it, Alka picked up the cap and handed it to Waseem. By the time the boys remembered it, Waseem was sitting with the girls on the steps, and Beth was asking for her ball back.
For my little sister, write a bedtime story about a puddle in the school yard.

After the big rain, a large brown puddle sat in the school yard, and every child ran around it. A small girl named Pari looked at the puddle and thought it looked lonely. She tiptoed up and dropped in a paper boat she had folded from her rough notebook. The boat floated! Her friends gathered round and folded boats of their own, red, blue and yellow, and soon the puddle was full of tiny sails. A gentle wind pushed them across to the far side. When the sun came out, the puddle began to shrink, but the boats stayed, dry and bright on the pavement. Pari tucked hers in her bag and carried it home as a treasure.
Quarrel over hopscotch, then a settling: write two girls' story.

Mallika and Sneha were playing hopscotch near the school gate when Sneha stepped on a line. "Out!" cried Mallika. "It was not on the line," said Sneha, hands on hips. They argued for five minutes, their voices rising, until a small crowd gathered. Both stomped off in opposite directions and sat on different walls. After a while, Mallika noticed a younger girl trying to play alone and failing to balance. She walked over to show her how, hopping on one foot. Sneha, watching from her wall, came across and drew a new set of squares with chalk. Without a word, the three of them started a fresh game, and nobody checked the lines again.
Let me read a story about a girl who volunteers to read to younger children and finds a surprising friend.

Every Friday, Seema, a Class 9 student, read picture books to the Class 1 children. One boy, Aryan, sat at the back, silent, never smiling. One Friday, she asked what he liked. He mumbled that he liked trucks, but nobody read about trucks. The next week, she brought a book about road-building machines. Aryan sat at the front and watched every page with big eyes. He asked the names of each truck. She did not know them all, so she looked them up and told him the following Friday. By the end of the term, he was standing on a chair, explaining excavators to the entire class, while Seema sat, quietly proud, taking notes.
Write a story titled 'The Seat Beside Me' about a boy who saves a seat for a new classmate.

The Seat Beside Me

Sachin always sat alone in the last row, and he preferred it that way. On Monday, a boy named Idris walked in with a heavy bag and stood at the front, looking nervously at the crowded benches. Nobody moved over. Sachin watched him for a moment, then pulled his own bag off the empty seat and tapped it twice. Idris saw the gesture and hurried down the aisle. "Thanks," he whispered. During the maths test, Idris slid a spare eraser across without being asked. Sachin glanced at it, then pushed his own ruler back in return. By the end of the week, the two of them were sharing one long conversation about trains.
Mix-up at the school canteen: a girl orders the wrong thing and likes it. Tell the story.

Rina was in a hurry and told the canteen man, "One sandwich," but he heard "sundae" and handed her a cup of ice cream with chocolate sauce. She did not have time to argue. She sat on the bench with the cup, feeling foolish. Her friend Dolly stared at her. "Ice cream at lunch?" "Mistake," Rina muttered. She took a spoonful, and her eyes widened. It was cold, sweet and exactly right for the hot day. She ate it all. The next day, she went back and asked for a sandwich, correctly, then added a sundae to the order. The canteen man winked and gave her an extra spoon of sauce.
Jealous of his best friend's new bicycle, a boy learns to ride it. Write his story.

When Tarun's best friend Alok showed up at school with a shiny red bicycle, Tarun said he did not like red and looked away. Inside, he burned with envy because his own family could not afford one. Alok noticed the silence. After school, he wheeled the bike over. "I cannot ride it properly. Can you hold the seat?" Tarun, who had been waiting for just such a chance, held it as Alok wobbled and fell into a bush. They laughed. Then Alok said, "You try." Tarun climbed on, and after three falls, he glided the length of the lane. That evening, he came home with a scraped elbow and a glowing face.
Let's have a story about a girl who discovers a secret garden behind the school building.

Behind the old science block, where nobody ever went, Hetal found a gap in the wall and squeezed through. On the other side lay a tiny garden, overgrown with marigolds, tall grass and one crooked mango tree. She stood stunned, as if she had walked into another world. At lunch, she told her friend Sana, who did not believe her. Hetal took her through the gap. Sana's mouth dropped open. They sat under the mango tree, whispering. Over the next weeks, they cleared the weeds and set up a tiny sign. The caretaker found them and, instead of scolding, brought a spade. The garden became the school's favourite spot, though only the oldest children knew how to get in.
Write about a school marathon where a boy stops to help another runner.

The whole school lined up for the three-kilometre fun run, and Kunal was in the lead. At the halfway mark, he spotted a boy from Class 4, Imran, sitting on the roadside holding his knee. Tears ran down his face. Kunal hesitated, looking ahead at the empty road, and then turned around. He helped Imran up and let him lean on his shoulder. They walked, slowly, side by side, while the other runners streamed past. The last teacher waited at the finish line and clapped for each of them. Kunal came in twenty-fourth. Imran's mother, who had been watching, hugged him and thanked him in Gujarati, and he understood every word.
Craft a story about a girl who helps a friend who cannot read well and keeps it a secret.

Divya noticed that her friend Karthik always asked her to read aloud the instructions for the science experiment. He said his eyes hurt. After a week, she guessed the truth: the letters swam on the page for him. She did not tell anyone. Instead, during recess, she suggested they read together on the steps, taking turns on a page. She read slowly, tracing the words with her finger, and asked him to say each one after her. He stumbled, then got faster. By the end of the month, he could read a full paragraph, and he told her a secret in return: he wanted to read his father's old letters.
Two girls must work together to carry a heavy school banner. How does it go?

For the Republic Day parade, Class 8 had to carry a long cloth banner down the main road. Only two girls were assigned the front poles, Lata and Vandana, who had never been friends. The banner was heavy, and the wind kept tugging it sideways. Halfway down the road, Lata's pole slipped, and the banner sagged. "Hold on!" cried Vandana. She shifted her grip and moved closer, matching her pace to Lata's. "Count your steps," Lata said. They counted aloud, left, right, left, right, and the banner steadied. At the end of the parade, their arms ached, but they stood proudly next to each other, and the teacher took their photo.
Jot down a story about a boy who wants to dance in the school show when his friends think it is silly.

Abir loved classical dance, but he kept it secret from his friends in Class 8. When the annual day auditions were announced, he stood outside the hall for ten minutes, unsure. His friend Chandan found him there. "What are you doing?" Abir confessed. Chandan looked surprised, then said, "Do it. I'll clap loudest." Abir went in and danced for the panel, spinning and stamping with perfect rhythm. The teacher chose him for the main role. On the day of the show, a few boys in the audience started to snicker, and Chandan stood up on his chair and shouted, "That is my friend!" The snickering died down. When Abir finished, the whole hall stood up.
How do a girl's friends react to her new haircut? Tell it as a story.

Over the weekend, Lavanya cut her long hair short, and on Monday she walked into school feeling light and a little frightened. Her friends turned to look. Nobody said a word. Her stomach dropped, and she sat down. After a long pause, Gita burst out, "You look like a film star!" The others agreed loudly, and soon everyone wanted to touch it. A boy at the back said, "It looks like a helmet," but Lavanya just shrugged. She spent the whole day swinging her head to feel the breeze on her neck. By the afternoon, two of her friends had asked whether she would take them to the same barber on Saturday.
Two friends fall out over a shared secret clubhouse in the school playground. What happens?

Behind the big banyan tree, Sanjay and Mehul had built a clubhouse out of cardboard and old bricks. They had one rule: only two members. Then Sanjay invited a third boy, Aman, without asking, and Mehul exploded. "You broke the rule!" They stopped speaking, and the clubhouse stood empty. After a week, rain collapsed the cardboard roof, and the whole thing sagged in the mud. Mehul came by and found Sanjay and Aman already trying to fix it. He stood there with arms crossed for a minute, then picked up a brick. "Three members," he mumbled. "But I stay the leader." Sanjay shrugged and agreed. By evening, they had a stronger roof than before and a new sign.
Does a dog really eat a boy's homework? Write a story where it does.

Nobody believed Tomas when he said the dog ate his homework. Mr. Kelkar smiled thinly and held out his hand for the notebook. Tomas, red in the face, reached into his bag and pulled out a few chewed scraps of paper with the corner of a maths sum still visible. The class gasped. Mr. Kelkar took the soggy pieces and read them as if they were a rare manuscript. "This is a first," he said. He asked Tomas to bring the dog to school the next day, and Tomas, trembling, did. The dog, a fat spotted terrier named Bruno, wagged and slobbered over the teacher's shoes. Mr. Kelkar let Tomas redo the sums and gave Bruno a biscuit.
Tell me a tale about a class getting ready for Republic Day in a small town.

In a small town school, Class 5 practised the flag march for two weeks, and everyone wanted to carry the flag. Mrs. Nair chose a girl named Sakina, who stood tallest. On the morning of the parade, Sakina woke with a high fever and could not stand up. Mrs. Nair looked around at the disappointed faces. Then Palash, a quiet boy who had been the shortest in the line, said, "I know all the steps. I watched every day." He took the flagpole and stood straight, though it wobbled in his hands. The parade went smoothly, and Palash held it high through the whole march. Sakina watched from a chair under the tree and clapped with all her strength.
I am looking for a story about a girl who plays a villain in the class play and is teased afterwards.

Roshni was cast as the wicked witch in the Class 6 play, and she threw herself into it, cackling and stirring a plastic cauldron. The audience hissed in delight. The next day, however, some children in the corridor started calling her "witchy" in a nasty voice, and one pulled at her braid. Roshni's face crumpled. At lunch, she sat alone with her plate. The boy who had played the hero, Anup, slid in beside her. "You were the best part of the show," he said. "No one would have been afraid of the hero without you." He stood up on the bench and announced it loudly to the canteen. Within minutes, the teasing turned into requests for her cackle.
Share a tale set in a village school, with a talking buffalo.

In the village of Kothur, the school stood next to a pond where a big black buffalo named Kaali loved to rest. One day, the teacher, Master Venkat, realised that the school bell had gone missing. The children searched everywhere. Little Anbu sat beside the pond, almost in tears, when Kaali turned her head and said in a slow voice, "The crow took it to the neem tree." Anbu gasped, then ran to the tree and spotted the brass bell wedged between two branches. He climbed carefully, with two friends holding his legs, and pulled it free. When the bell rang that afternoon, Kaali flicked her tail as if she had known all along.
Two sisters on opposite teams in a school match: tell their story.

Amna and Hira were sisters, but in the school netball match, they were captains of rival houses. Their mother sat in the stands, unsure whom to cheer for. The game was tight, and in the last minute, Amna passed the ball to a teammate, who missed. Hira scooped it up and shot, scoring the winning point. Amna's jaw tightened. For a moment, the sisters stared at each other across the court. Then Hira ran over, and they hugged, rocking from side to side. "Mummy is crying," Amna said, pointing at the stand. They walked off arm in arm, and their mother handed each of them a sweet, one in each hand.
Imagine a boy who cannot afford a canteen snack and a friend who offers to share; make it a story.

Every day at the break, the canteen smelled of fried potato, and every day Manoj felt his empty pocket. His father had lost his job that month and there was no pocket money. He pretended that he was not hungry and stayed in the classroom with a book. A boy named Colin noticed. The next day, Colin bought two vada pavs and said, "They gave me one free. Can you help me finish them?" Manoj looked at him closely, then took one. They sat on the steps and ate. Colin asked him to keep a seat at their cricket game and mentioned, without any fuss, that he would be getting "free ones" often. Manoj understood, and thanked him with a quiet nod.
Whip up a story about sports day, in which it rains halfway through.

The morning of Sports Day was bright, and the whole school lined up in white shirts. By the time of the sack race, thick clouds rolled in, and then the rain poured over the field. The teachers shouted for everyone to run for shelter. But Ruhi, who had trained for the sack race for weeks, stayed standing on the muddy track. Her friend Sam stood beside her, then a few others joined, laughing as the rain soaked them through. The headmaster looked at them from under the verandah and sighed. Then he blew the whistle. The race went on in the downpour, with sacks sliding and children toppling into the puddles. Ruhi finished last, covered in mud, and cheered the loudest of all.
Please make up a story for a 7-year-old about a mouse who gets the biggest role in the class play.

In Class 2, the teacher asked who wanted to be the mouse in the play. A small boy called Tito raised his hand so slowly that nobody noticed. "I want to be the lion," said Rohan loudly, and the teacher agreed. Tito became the mouse, with grey ears made of felt. In the story, the lion got stuck in a net, and the mouse had to chew through it. On the big day, Rohan roared so hard that he forgot the next line and stood there with his mouth open. Tito stepped forward, squeaked the line for him, then pretended to nibble the net. The audience laughed and clapped for both. Afterwards, Rohan gave Tito a big hug and a biscuit.
On her last day at a school, a girl brings sweets for the class. Tell that story.

It was Chandni's last day in Class 6, because her family was moving to Pune. She carried a big box of laddus into the classroom. Everyone gathered around, and she passed them out one by one. When she came to Fareed, who had sat next to her for two years, she stopped. They had quarrelled the week before about a lost ruler, and neither had apologised. Fareed looked at the floor. Chandni held the box out to him and said, "This one is the biggest." He took it and said quietly, "Sorry about the ruler. It was in my bag all along." She laughed. He ate half of the laddu and wrapped the rest in his handkerchief to keep.
A school loses electricity and the class holds a lesson under a tree. Tell me the story.

When the generator stopped working on a hot afternoon, Mrs. Thomas led Class 4 under the neem tree in the yard, where a cool breeze blew. She had no blackboard, so she asked each child to find a stick and scratch letters in the dirt. Little Girish wrote the longest word he knew, "elephant," and misspelled it. The others giggled but helped him correct it. A squirrel scampered down the trunk and watched. Soon, every child was drawing animals and spelling their names in the dust. When the bell rang at three o'clock, nobody wanted to leave. The next day, the electricity was back, but they all asked to go back outside.
Plot idea: a girl is nervous because she is the new teacher's first student.

In the first week of the term, Kritika was the only student who arrived early, and the new young teacher, Ms. Fatima, was standing alone at the board. She looked as nervous as Kritika felt. Her hands trembled when she picked up the chalk. Kritika, thinking quickly, sat up straight and said, "Good morning, Miss. I like your handwriting." Ms. Fatima smiled and let out a long breath. As other children filled the room, she began the lesson, and her voice grew steadier with each line. At the end of the day, she stopped Kritika at the door and said, "Thank you for being first." Kritika walked home feeling taller than she had all year.
Our class needs a story about a girl who volunteers to be class monitor for a week and finds it harder than expected.

Lopa put her hand up for class monitor because she thought it meant standing at the front and being important. By Tuesday, she had been shouted at by two boys, ignored by three girls and scolded by the teacher for the noise. She wrote names on the board and rubbed them out when somebody pleaded. By Thursday, she had a headache. She stayed behind after school to clean the blackboard, tired and cross. Her friend Marcus came in with a duster. "It is a lot," he said. "You are doing fine." She sniffed. On Friday, she handed over the chalk and thanked the next monitor in advance for being brave.
A girl gets stage fright and learns to look at one face in the crowd. Tell me her story.

Zeenat was the lead in the Class 9 play, and on the night of the show, her palms were slippery with sweat. She peeked through the curtain at the sea of faces and felt faint. Her drama teacher, Mrs. Almeida, put a hand on her shoulder. "Pick one face and speak only to that person." Zeenat chose her little cousin, who was sitting near the front, holding a toy. When the curtain rose, she looked at him and said her first line. He grinned and waved. She said the next line to him, and the next. By the end of the play, she had forgotten the other hundred faces completely.
Under 120 words, please: a boy loses his library book and finds it again.

Gopal borrowed a book about sharks from the school library and lost it somewhere between home and school. For three days, he checked his bag, his bed and the bus. On Thursday, the librarian looked up and said, "Your book is due tomorrow." His face fell. After school, he walked back along his route, scanning the pavement. By the pond, he saw the corner of a blue cover under a bench. A stranger had set it there, and it was damp but whole. He dried it with his shirt, carried it back and slid it across the counter. The librarian opened it, sniffed and smiled. "Sharks do get wet," she said.
Share a story about a school football match in the mud where both teams end up laughing.

A heavy rain the night before had turned the school football field into a brown swamp. Despite this, the teams lined up, and the referee blew his whistle. The ball stuck in the mud, and the players slid, tripped and splashed. Within minutes, nobody could tell which team was which, because everyone was the same brown colour. The goalkeeper, Sandeep, lost both shoes. A player slid fifteen feet on his stomach. The referee, trying to stand upright, fell into a puddle himself. By half time, the score was nil-nil and everybody was laughing too hard to run. They finished the match as a draw and lined up to be hosed down by the groundsman.
Imagine and write a story about a boy who accidentally walks into the wrong classroom and stays.

On the first day of Class 8, Rohan walked into the wrong room, sat down at the back and opened his notebook. The teacher began a lesson on the French Revolution, and Rohan nodded along, thinking this was a new history syllabus. After twenty minutes, a boy in front turned and whispered, "Are you in this class?" Rohan looked at the faces. All strangers. His own class, Class 8B, was down the hall. He stood up in a flush, and the teacher paused. "Stay," she said kindly, "if you wish, until the bell. You seem interested." He stayed. The next day, he sat in the right room, still thinking about the crowds in Paris.
Two rival kabaddi teams end up helping each other. Can you tell it as a story?

Class 9 and Class 10 had been rivals since the first term, and the kabaddi match was a fierce one. In the second half, the Class 10 raider, Harshad, crossed the line and fell with a cry, clutching his ankle. The whistle blew. Both teams crowded around. The Class 9 captain, Bilal, who had been shouting insults a minute earlier, knelt down and loosened Harshad's shoe. Others fetched water and ice from the canteen. A teacher carried Harshad to the sick room while the teams stood in silence. When the match resumed, nobody played as roughly as before. Class 9 won narrowly, but afterwards, Bilal walked to the sick room with the winner's sweets and offered Harshad the first piece.
Open a story about a boy who plants a mango seed at school and sees it grow over the years.

In Class 2, Dev ate a mango at lunch and pushed the seed into a corner of the school garden with his thumb. He told no one. Every Monday, he checked, and after a month, a thin green stalk appeared. He watered it daily with his water bottle. By Class 5, it stood as high as his shoulder, and the gardener asked who had planted it. Dev raised his hand. By Class 8, it was taller than he was. At the end of Class 10, on his last day, Dev stood under the young tree for a long time. A small green fruit hung from a branch. He touched it gently and walked out of the gate smiling.
A student's project falls apart on the morning of the science fair; write that.

At eight o'clock on the morning of the science fair, Yusuf's model volcano collapsed in the bag on the bus. Clay, paper and a broken paint bottle lay in a soggy heap. He walked into the hall dragging his bag, close to tears. His classmate Bela saw the mess and said, "Do you have the instructions?" He nodded. She found two paper cups, borrowed a roll of tape from the teacher and held the pieces while he stuck them together. It was crooked and had no paint, but it worked. When it was his turn, the baking soda fizzed and the red foam poured out of the side. The judges laughed with surprise and wrote a long comment.
A girl who cannot run still wins on sports day, through the quiz. Tell that story.

Anjali had a broken ankle and could not join any race on Sports Day, so she sat in the shade holding a crutch, watching her friends sprint. A teacher noticed her glum face and invited her to join the quiz team in the hall, where no running was needed. Her team had four members, and the questions were on geography and history. Anjali knew the capital of every country, because she loved her atlas. When the final question asked for the longest river in Africa, her team looked at her at once. "The Nile," she said calmly. The judges announced that her team had won, and her friends, still sweaty from the track, ran into the hall and carried her chair.
I need a story about a girl named Beena who is the new student and brings a strange lunch.

Beena's first day at the new school began well, until lunchtime. She opened her box and the whole bench leaned back. Her grandmother had packed fermented rice with a pickle so sharp that it made two boys sneeze. "What is that?" asked a girl named Carol, holding her nose. Beena's cheeks burned and she closed the lid. She spent the break in the washroom, staring at the tap. When she came out, Carol was waiting by the door with her own sandwich cut in half. "Mine is boring," Carol said. "Can I try a bit of yours?" Beena hesitated, then opened the box again. Carol tasted a tiny spoon, gasped, coughed and reached for water, laughing until she cried.
Could you write about a boy who does not like reading until a friend finds him the right book?

Pankaj thought reading was punishment, and he hid in the back of the library every Thursday. His friend Zara noticed that he loved fixing broken things at home. One Thursday, she slid a thick book across the table. It was about how clocks work, with detailed drawings of springs and gears. Pankaj scowled at it, opened it for two pages and kept reading until the bell rang. He borrowed it that evening and carried it everywhere for a week. At the next library period, he asked the librarian whether there was a book on bicycles. Zara, passing by, pretended to be very busy shelving a row of dictionaries, though her face glowed.
Give a short tale about two former enemies who must share a project.

Tara and Nikhil had not spoken since Class 6, when Nikhil had laughed at her stammer. In Class 8, the teacher paired them for a science project on the solar system, and both groaned. They worked in separate corners of Tara's balcony for a day, cutting paper planets without exchanging a word. When Nikhil's glue ran out, Tara handed hers over silently. When her ladder slipped, he held it steady. By evening, the planets hung in the correct order on a string, and Nikhil said, "I am sorry about the stammer thing. It was a stupid joke." Tara shrugged and nodded. Their project won first prize, and they celebrated with warm samosas from her mother.
School tug of war, a rope that snaps: tell me that story.

The Class 8 and Class 9 teams grabbed the thick rope, dug in their heels and pulled with all their might. Neither side gained an inch. The crowd shouted. Then, with a loud crack, the rope snapped in the middle, and both teams fell backward in a tangle of arms and legs. For a second, nobody moved. Then the captains, Ramesh and Joseph, sat up, covered in dust, and began to laugh. The whole field joined them. The PT teacher scratched his head and declared the match a draw. The two teams walked together to the tap and splashed water on their faces, and later, they carried the broken rope as a trophy to the staffroom.
Set on sports day, write about a boy who is afraid of the long jump.

The long jump pit looked enormous to Abhay, a wide brown strip of sand that he had to cross in a single leap. His name was called, and he did not move. His friend Selvi, who was waiting for her turn in the line, walked over. "Pretend it is the puddle outside your house," she said. Abhay smiled weakly. He backed up, ran with small steps, and then jumped, landing in the sand with a thump and a cloud of dust. The judge measured it and said, "Not bad." It was not the longest, but Abhay stood up and brushed himself off with the biggest grin. He took three more jumps, each a little longer than the last.
Sketch a simple story about a grandmother who teaches her grandson to make rotis.

Dadi Kamala woke Aarav before sunrise on Saturday. "Today you learn rotis," she said. Aarav yawned, but he washed his hands and stood on a little stool beside the stove. His first dough stuck to his fingers like glue. His second roti came out shaped like a map of Africa. Dadi only laughed and added a pinch more flour. By the sixth try, Aarav pressed the dough thin and flipped it with a quick flick of his wrist. It puffed up like a golden balloon. He carried it to the table, still hot, and Grandfather tore off the first piece. "Better than mine," Grandfather said, and Aarav grinned all through breakfast.
Dream up a tale set on market day in a village, with a clever goat in it.

On Thursday, the village of Haldipur filled with sellers, and old Ramesh brought his goat Moti to carry his vegetable baskets. Moti always watched the crowd with sharp yellow eyes. While Ramesh argued over the price of onions, Moti slipped her rope and trotted straight to the sweet stall. Halwai Sunder shouted, and soon half the market was chasing her. Moti ran past the cloth sellers, ducked under a cart, and stopped in front of Ramesh. Her mouth was full of jaggery. Everyone laughed so hard that the angry stall owner forgot to scold. Ramesh paid for the sweet, and Moti got one small piece more, which she ate very slowly.
My little sister needs a bedtime story about a lamp that would not light on Diwali.

Tiny Mira had one clay lamp, and she had painted it blue herself. On Diwali evening, all the lamps on the balcony glowed except hers. Mira poured in more oil, but the flame would not catch. She sat down and sniffed, feeling very small. Her older cousin Rohan knelt beside her and looked closely. "The wick is wet," he said. They dried it near the warm stove, and Rohan lit it with a long match. This time a little flame stood up straight and bright. Mira set the blue lamp at the very front of the balcony, where everyone on the street could see it shining. Then she went to sleep, smiling.
Draft a tale about a girl who travels alone on a train for the first time.

Neha was twelve when her mother let her ride the night train from Pune to her aunt's house. Her bag was packed, her ticket was safe in her pocket, and her stomach felt full of butterflies. At the second station, a big family climbed in with baskets and a baby. The baby kept staring at Neha until she made a funny face, and then he laughed loudly. The grandmother shared a steel box of puris with her. Neha slept well, rocked by the wheels. In the morning, her aunt waved from the platform. Neha stepped down, tall and proud, with an empty puri box to return.
Tell us a made-up story where a boy helps an old neighbour carry her shopping.

Mrs. Dsouza lived on the third floor of Sunrise Apartments, and the lift had been broken for a week. On Sunday, ten-year-old Kabir saw her stop on the second landing with two heavy bags. Her knees were shaking. "Let me take those, Aunty," he said. The bags were heavier than he expected, and a bottle of oil clanked against his leg. Step by step, they climbed together, stopping twice to rest. At her door, Mrs. Dsouza searched her purse and handed him a warm coconut biscuit. Kabir ate it on the stairs going down. The next day, he knocked on her door again before school and asked if she needed anything.
I'd like a short story about a family during a power cut in the city.

At eight o'clock on a hot evening, every light in the Menon flat went out at once. The fan stopped, the television went dark, and little Anu began to cry. Her father, Suresh, found a candle in the kitchen drawer. They carried it to the balcony, where the whole street was black and the stars looked brighter than usual. Grandfather told a story about his own childhood, when there had been no electricity at all in his village. Anu's crying turned to giggles as he described a goat that ate a lantern. When the lights returned an hour later, nobody cheered. Anu asked if they could blow out the bulbs again.
Write a short story for a six-year-old about a grandfather and a lost umbrella.

Grandpa Joseph had a big black umbrella, and he loved it very much. One rainy morning, he walked to the bakery with his granddaughter Lily and left the umbrella by the door. When they came out, it was gone. Grandpa looked sad. Lily held his hand and said, "Let's find it." They walked down the wet street and looked under benches and behind flower pots. At last, Lily saw a black shape outside the post office. A kind lady was holding it carefully. "I wanted to keep it safe for the owner," she said. Grandpa thanked her and opened it wide. Lily stood under it with him all the way home.
I would love a small story about a boy who gets lost in a busy Mumbai street and finds his way home.

Nine-year-old Imran lost his mother's hand in the crowd outside Dadar station. People rushed past, and every face looked strange. His heart pounded, but he remembered what his father had taught him: stay in one place and look for someone in uniform. He walked to the ticket window and told the clerk his name and his mother's phone number. The clerk called, and within five minutes his mother came running, her dupatta flying behind her. She hugged him so tightly that his glasses slipped. Later, on the train, Imran held her sleeve and recited her number again and again, until he was sure he would never forget it.
I want to hear a story set in a village about two sisters who dig a well together.

In the dry month of May, the well in Sundarpur village gave only mud. Sisters Pooja and Geeta, aged eleven and nine, had to walk three kilometres to fetch water every day. "We could dig a new one," Geeta said, half joking. Pooja did not laugh. With the village elders and a hired digger, the girls helped for two weeks, carrying stones and bringing tea to the workers. Their arms ached, and their palms blistered. On the fifteenth day, a dark patch appeared at the bottom, and then water bubbled up, cold and clear. Geeta poured the first bucket over her own head and laughed. The whole village came to drink.
Give me a quick story about a wedding feast where the sweets disappear.

At the Sharma wedding, the sweets table was the most important place in the hall. Uncle Dinesh guarded it with a stern face and a ladle. But after the ceremony, a hundred guests rushed in, and in ten minutes the gulab jamun bowl was empty. Uncle Dinesh searched for the thief. Under the table, he found five-year-old Bunty with syrup on his chin and a happy smile. "I was only helping," Bunty said. Uncle Dinesh tried to look angry, but the bride's grandmother laughed first. The caterer quickly brought more from the kitchen, and Bunty got to hand out the first plate himself.
Can you invent a story about a girl whose father cannot read, and how she helps him.

Savita noticed that her father always asked her to read the bus numbers. At first she thought he simply liked her voice. One evening, he held a letter from the bank and looked worried. "Read it to me, beta," he whispered, and she understood. Mr. Rao had never been to school because he had worked in the fields since he was seven. Savita read the letter slowly, word by word. Afterwards, she brought out her old primer. "Let me teach you," she said. Every night after dinner, they practised one letter. By the winter, he could read the name of their town on the station sign.
Please craft a small story about a boy who builds a kite for Makar Sankranti.

Dev wanted the tallest kite on the terrace for Sankranti, but he had no money to buy one. So he gathered thin bamboo sticks, a sheet of red paper, and a ball of thread from his mother's sewing box. His hands trembled while he glued the paper on. The kite looked a little crooked. On the festival morning, his friends laughed softly when they saw it. Dev tied the string and ran into the wind. The crooked kite rose, wobbled, and then climbed higher than every shop-bought one on the street. His friend Aman, who had laughed the loudest, asked Dev to show him how to make one.
Please give me a little story about a family driving to the hills when the car breaks down.

The Kapoor family was halfway up the mountain road when the car coughed twice and stopped. Father lifted the bonnet and frowned at the smoke. Mother checked her phone and found no signal. Twelve-year-old Ishaan and his little brother Rohit sat on a rock and looked at the valley below. A truck driver named Gurmeet soon stopped, and with a rope and a bottle of water, he fixed the pipe that had come loose. He refused any money. "Just drive carefully," he said. The family reached the guesthouse after dark, tired but laughing. That night, Rohit drew the truck driver in his notebook and wrote "Hero" beneath it.
Imagine a made-up story where a girl returns a lost wallet to a neighbour.

On her way to school, Tanvi found a brown leather wallet near the gate of building B. Inside were some notes, a bus pass, and a photo of an old man with a white moustache. She recognised him at once. He was Mr. Pillai from the fourth floor, who always waved from his window. After school, she knocked on his door and held out the wallet with both hands. His eyes grew wide. "I searched everywhere," he said. He asked her to wait a moment. He came back with a jar of homemade mango pickle. Tanvi carried it home, and her mother said it was the best pickle she had ever tasted.
Narrate a little story about two brothers who argue over the last piece of cake.

Rahul and Sameer both stared at the last slice of chocolate cake. "I'm older, so it's mine," said Rahul. "I'm hungrier," said Sameer. Their voices rose until Mother walked in and took the plate away. "Neither of you will have it," she said and put it on the high shelf. For an hour, the boys sat silently in separate corners. Then Sameer came to the kitchen with a knife and a plate. "Let's cut it exactly," he said. They measured the slice with a ruler and cut it into two even halves. It tasted much better than it would have alone.
Create a gentle story about an old well in a village, and a girl who lowers a bucket.

Granny Bhagya always said that the old well behind the temple was cursed, so no one in Rampur went near it. But eight-year-old Chinni was thirsty on a hot afternoon, and the tap had run dry. She tied a rope to a bucket and lowered it carefully. The bucket splashed and came up full of clear, cool water. Chinni drank until her stomach hurt. She ran home and told everyone. Granny Bhagya doubted her until she tasted a cup herself. "Well, I was wrong," she admitted, and that evening the entire lane lined up with pots, laughing and talking together.
Please create a little story about a bus conductor and a schoolgirl who forgets her bus fare.

Every morning, conductor Raghav stood at the door of bus number 42 and called out the stops in a singing voice. One rainy Monday, a schoolgirl named Fatima stepped on and searched her bag in a panic. Her purse was missing. Her cheeks went red. Raghav smiled and said, "Sit down, beta. Pay me tomorrow." The next morning, she held out two coins, but he waved them away. "Give them to someone who needs it," he said. A week later, a younger boy boarded without a ticket, and Fatima quietly paid his fare. Raghav saw it in the mirror and said nothing, but his song grew louder.
Give me a happy story about a village that prepares for Holi.

In the village of Nandgaon, children began collecting dry wood for the Holi bonfire a week early. Little Sanjay, who was seven, felt left out because he was too small to lift the big logs. He found a handful of twigs and placed them in a pile. Bigger boys laughed at first. Then they noticed that his twigs lit up quickly and helped start the bigger fire. On Holi morning, everyone covered each other in pink and yellow powder. Sanjay's face was bright orange. His grandmother hugged him tightly and said, "You started the fire, my brave boy," and he danced all day long.
Try to write a gentle story about a grandmother who tells her granddaughter about the day she first saw a train.

Sitting on the veranda one evening, Granny Leela said to her granddaughter Asha, "When I was your age, I had never seen a train." Asha listened closely. A whole village had walked to the station to watch the first engine arrive. Leela's mother held her hand tightly. When the iron giant roared in, white smoke rolled over the crowd, and Leela hid behind a pillar. But then the driver waved at the children, and she waved back. That night, she dreamt of wheels. Asha laughed and asked to hear it again. So Granny Leela told it once more, adding a pigeon this time, which made Asha giggle.
Share a little story about a boy who sells flowers outside a temple and meets a kind customer.

Every morning, eleven-year-old Jayant sat outside the temple with a basket of marigolds and jasmine garlands. Business was slow on rainy days. One grey Tuesday, only a single customer came, a tall woman with a silver umbrella. She bought three garlands and asked his name. "Jayant," he replied. She asked why he was not in school, and he explained that his mother was ill and needed the money. Her eyes softened. She was the new headmistress, and she arranged an evening class for him. Jayant ran home with an empty basket and a full heart. Afterwards, he sold flowers in the morning and went to class every evening.
Please compose a story about a family reunion where the youngest cousin gets lost in a mango orchard.

The cousins met every June at their grandfather's mango orchard near Nashik. This year, four-year-old Piya wandered off while everyone was busy eating. The adults called her name, and the older children ran between the trees. Eleven-year-old Veer climbed a big branch to look further. He saw a small yellow frock under a tree, near a pile of fallen fruit. Piya was sitting on the ground, sticky with juice, eating a mango with both hands. "I was hungry," she said calmly. Veer carried her back on his shoulders while she sang. Grandfather picked her the biggest mango and told her never to walk alone again.
Offer me a made-up story set in a village during a storm and a power cut, where neighbours share candles.

The storm hit Kalyanpur at dusk, and by seven o'clock every house was dark. Old Mrs. Verma lived alone, and she had only one stub of candle left. She sat in the shadows, listening to the rain. Suddenly, a knock came at her door. It was her neighbour's son, Tarun, holding a lantern. "My mother says you should come to our house," he said. Soon, four families sat in one room, sharing tea and stories by the light of three flames. Mrs. Verma taught the children a rain song. When the rain stopped at midnight, Tarun walked her home with the lantern, and she hummed the song all the way.
How about a tale about a boy who misses his train and meets someone helpful at the station.

Arjun ran onto the platform just as the Chennai Express pulled away, its tail lights slipping into the dark. His lunchbox was in his bag, but his ticket was in his shirt, and his uncle was waiting at the other end. He sat on a bench and rubbed his eyes. A porter named Subbu noticed and asked what had happened. He listened and then took Arjun to the stationmaster. The stationmaster phoned his uncle and found him a seat on the next train, an hour later. Subbu even brought him a cup of tea. When the train came, Arjun waved to Subbu until the platform was only a speck.
Invent a story where a girl and her neighbour share a mango tree.

A big mango tree grew right on the wall between the houses of Ruchi and old Mr. Khan. Its branches hung on both sides, and every summer they argued about who owned the fruit. One day, a storm shook the tree, and the mangoes fell everywhere, some in each garden. Ruchi gathered the ones in her yard and stopped. Mr. Khan's knees were bad, and he struggled to bend. She picked up his fruit as well and carried a basketful to his door. He smiled, took two mangoes, and handed the rest back. "They are for both of us," he said. After that, they never argued again.
I'm hoping for a story about a street musician in a big city and a small girl who listens every day.

Outside the metro station, a man named Joseph played an old violin every morning. Most people rushed past with their ears closed, but a girl named Ada stopped every day on her way to school. She stood quietly with her backpack and watched his fingers. One morning, it began to rain, and Joseph covered his violin with his coat. Ada took out her small umbrella and held it over him. He played one more song, just for her. The next day, he brought a second chair, and Ada sat with him for ten minutes before school. Soon, a crowd gathered around the two of them.
Please share a quick story about a boy who is nervous before his first day at a new school in the city.

Mohan had grown up in a village, and the school in Delhi looked as big as a palace. On the first morning, he stood at the gate and gripped his bag. Hundreds of students were shouting and running. A boy with glasses came up to him and asked, "Are you new? I'm Dhruv." Mohan could barely whisper his name. Dhruv showed him the classroom and the water tap, and shared a pencil because Mohan had forgotten his own. At lunch, they sat together under a tree and talked about cricket. By the afternoon, Mohan had forgotten to be afraid. At home, he told his mother, "The school is not so big."
Imagine and tell me a gentle story about a girl who makes tea for her grandfather for the first time.

Six-year-old Sia watched her grandfather sip his morning tea every day and decided she would make it herself. She asked her mother to light the stove and stand beside her, then climbed onto a stool at the kitchen counter. She poured milk, water, and sugar into a pan and stirred slowly. Her hands shook as she added the tea leaves. The tea turned brown, then nearly black, and it smelled strange. She poured it into his favourite cup, carried it outside, and held her breath. Grandfather took a sip and paused. Then he smiled widely. "Perfect," he said, and drank every drop. Later, he secretly added more sugar.
Spin me a tale about a boy and his father who build a Ganesh idol from clay.

Each year before Ganesh Chaturthi, Vikram and his father shaped a small idol from river clay in their courtyard. This year, Vikram was ten and wanted to make the trunk by himself. His father stepped back and watched. The first trunk drooped and fell. The second one cracked. Vikram sighed and almost quit, but his father quietly showed him how to keep the clay damp. On the third try, the trunk curled just right. They painted the idol together and carried it into the house. That evening, neighbours came to see it. Vikram stood quietly beside the idol and pretended he did not hear their praise.
Imagine a little story about a family on a ferry ride that goes wrong when the engine stops.

Halfway across the river, the old ferry shuddered and went silent. Thirty passengers looked at each other. The boatman, Bhola, scratched his head and checked the engine. Seven-year-old Naina and her mother sat near the rail, watching the water drift by. "Don't worry," said her mother, though her hands were cold. Bhola called the shore on his radio, and twenty minutes later a small motorboat arrived with a rope. Slowly, they were towed to the bank. Naina clapped as soon as her feet touched the sand. Bhola bowed shyly, and her mother bought everyone on the ferry a glass of hot tea from the stall.
Craft a tale about a village school teacher who walks to class across a river.

Every morning, Master Haridas crossed the shallow Gomti river to reach his school in Pipli. In the rainy months, the water rose to his waist, and he carried his books on his head. One day, the river was too high, and he stood on the bank for a long time. Then he heard shouting. The children of Pipli had tied ropes between two trees and stood in a line across the water, holding hands. "Come, sir!" they called. He crossed carefully, step by step, and arrived at class soaked but laughing. That day, he taught the lesson with wet shoes, and nobody complained about the puddles.
Could you tell me a small story where a girl bakes a birthday cake for her mother in secret.

Tara decided to bake a cake for her mother's birthday while Mother was at work. She found a recipe in an old notebook and gathered eggs, flour, and sugar. By noon, her kitchen looked like a battlefield. Flour covered the floor, and a bowl was stuck on the shelf. She poured the batter into a tin and slid it into the oven. Forty minutes later, a flat, dark cake came out. Tara almost cried. Then her brother Ishan spread whipped cream over the top and added strawberries. It looked much better. When Mother came home, she cut a slice slowly, chewed, and said it was the best she had ever eaten.
Surprise me with a quick story about a grandfather who plants a neem tree with his grandchild.

Grandfather Hari was seventy when he took little Neel to the back of the house with a spade and a tiny neem sapling. "This tree will be taller than the roof one day," he said. They dug a hole together, and Neel patted down the soil with his hands. Every morning before school, Neel poured a mug of water on the roots. Years passed. When Neel was twenty, he came home for the holidays and found the neem standing taller than the house. He sat beneath it and thought of Grandfather. Then he took the spade and planted another sapling beside it.
Please compose a gentle story about a woman who sells bangles at a fair, and a girl who cannot afford a pair.

At the Kartik fair, Salma spread her bangles on a blue cloth under a banyan tree. Glass in red, green, and gold flashed in the sunlight. A girl of about ten stood watching them for a long time. She touched a pair of green ones gently and then pulled her hand back. "I have only two rupees," she whispered. Salma looked at her thin wrists and thought of her own daughter. She slipped the green bangles onto the girl's arm. "These are two rupees today," she said. The girl paid her two coins and ran off, jingling happily.
I'm in the mood for a gentle story about a boy who helps a neighbour whose cat is stuck on a roof.

Mrs. Ghosh stood in her yard calling, "Biscuit! Biscuit!" Her orange cat sat on the roof of the shed and refused to come down. She was too old to climb. Eleven-year-old Samir saw her from the lane and brought a ladder from his garage. His arms shook as he climbed, and the ladder creaked. Biscuit hissed at him first. Samir waited, then offered a piece of dried fish from his pocket. The cat sniffed, stepped closer, and jumped into his arms. Down on the ground, Mrs. Ghosh wiped her eyes. Samir was invited for tea every afternoon that week, and Biscuit sat on his lap.
Put together a quick story about a girl who rides a rickshaw to school every day with a kind driver.

Every morning, Zoya climbed into the cycle rickshaw of Bablu Bhai, who always rang his bell three times at her gate. He knew every shortcut in the old city. One morning, there was a procession on the main road, and the lane was blocked. Zoya worried about being late for her exam. Bablu Bhai pedalled through narrow alleys, between dosa stalls and sleeping dogs, and arrived with five minutes to spare. Zoya jumped down and promised to pay him extra on Friday. He shook his head. "Study well, that is my payment," he said. She passed her exam with good marks and told him first.
Pen a short story about a girl who lights her first sparkler on Diwali.

Prisha had watched her older cousins light sparklers for three years, and now she was finally allowed to try. Her mother handed her one with a bucket of water nearby. Prisha's hand shook as the tip touched the flame. It hissed, spat, and burst into silver stars. She yelped and nearly dropped it. But then she waved it in a slow circle and drew a glowing ring in the dark. Everyone clapped. She lit another one, and wrote her name in the air with it. By the end of the night, she had used twelve and wanted twelve more. Her mother laughed and said, "Tomorrow, beta."
Share a short story where the lights go out in an apartment block during exams and a girl helps others study.

The lights went out in Green Park Apartments the night before the board exams. Twelve students sat in the dark, holding their books. Sana lived on the ground floor and had a small solar lamp that her uncle had sent from abroad. She knocked on neighbours' doors and invited them to study together in the courtyard. Soon, nine students gathered around the lamp, reading in turns and quizzing each other. Someone brought biscuits, and someone else brought a mat. When the power returned at eleven, they were already on the last chapter. In the morning, they all agreed that they had learned more together than alone.
Could you share a simple story about an old man and a boy who share a window seat on a long train journey.

The train from Kolkata to Delhi was packed, and young Sohan found himself pressed between a window and a sleeping stranger. Across from him sat an old man with a walking stick and a long white beard. "Would you like the window?" Sohan asked politely. The old man shook his head and smiled. Instead, he pointed to the fields passing by and named every bird. Heron, kingfisher, drongo. Sohan wrote them down in his notebook. By the time they reached Kanpur, the old man was asleep, and Sohan had filled four pages. When he left the train, he left the notebook open on the seat, with a drawing of a kingfisher for his friend.
Draft a small story where a boy teaches his father how to use a phone to video call his sister abroad.

Mr. Iyer had never touched a smartphone, and his daughter Latha was working in Canada. His son Karthik handed him a phone one Sunday morning. "Press here, Appa, then here," he said. Mr. Iyer pressed the wrong button, and the screen went dark. He frowned. Karthik showed him again, slowly. This time, a face appeared, and Latha said, "Appa!" Mr. Iyer jumped, then held the phone very close to his nose. "Why are you so small?" he said. Everyone laughed, even Latha. After thirty minutes, he understood how to hold it properly. That night, he practised calling Karthik from the other room, five times, just to make sure.
Please spin me a fresh story about a village boy who finds a lost calf in the rain and brings it home.

Rain poured over Madhopur, and Bittu was running home from school when he heard a thin cry near the pond. A small brown calf stood in the mud, shaking. He looked around, but no cow or farmer was in sight. Bittu took off his jacket and wrapped it around the calf. He pulled gently on its rope until it followed him. At the tea shop, he asked if anyone knew the owner. An old woman recognised the calf. It belonged to her neighbour, Gopal, who had been searching since noon. Gopal arrived panting, and thanked Bittu with a glass of warm milk.
Imagine a story about a girl who bargains for a toy at a night market.

At the night market in Hyderabad, Sana held a red wooden top in her hand. The seller wanted fifty rupees, but she had only thirty. Her mother whispered, "Try bargaining." Sana took a deep breath. "It has a small crack," she said, pointing. The seller looked and shrugged. "Forty," he offered. "Thirty-five, and I'll buy a second one for my cousin," said Sana. The seller laughed and agreed. Sana spun the top on the pavement, and it hummed in a bright circle. Her mother bought tea, and they walked home through the lit lanes, with two spinning tops in the bag.
There was once a village with a singing rooster. Can you tell that story?

Once upon a time, in the village of Chandanpur, a rooster named Kallu sang so loudly that nobody could sleep past four in the morning. The farmers grumbled. The washerwoman Leela put cotton in her ears. "Someone should teach that bird to be quiet," said the baker. But one dark morning, Kallu did not sing. Everyone woke late, and the bus to the market left without them. Kallu had a sore throat. The children brought him warm water with honey, and after two days, his voice came back, a little rough. This time, the farmers rose with a smile, and the washerwoman threw her cotton away.
Can you write me a story, with a title, about a spice seller and a sneezing customer?

The Sneeze at Spice Lane

Old Mr. Qureshi sold chilli powder, turmeric, and cumin in the oldest corner of the Jaipur market. One noon, a tall tourist named Mr. Brown leaned over a sack of red chillies and sneezed so hard that his hat flew off. The powder flew too, and soon the whole lane was coughing and laughing. A boy carried the hat back, covered in red dust. Mr. Qureshi gave Mr. Brown a glass of cold water and a small bag of cardamom as a gift. Mr. Brown bought three kilos of chilli, though he could hardly eat one spoonful.
