On Vedant's first day at the new school in Gurgaon, he went to the washroom and could not find his way back to his class. The corridors all looked the same. A boy with a green bag was walking the other way. "Are you lost?" he asked. Vedant nodded. "Me too," said the boy, whose name was Neel. They laughed. Together, they walked around, peered into doors, and finally found the right room, where the teacher stood waiting with a frown that melted when she saw them. From that day, the two boys were always seen together, and they never needed a map.
Compose a quick story about a woman who gets on the wrong train and ends up at a lovely village.

Sumitra boarded what she thought was the train to Pune, but it was going the other way. By the time she realised, the train was already far from the city. She stepped off at a small station called Wadi, with one tea stall and a goat on the platform. The tea seller, Mr. Pawar, laughed kindly and told her the next train would come in three hours. He took her to the river, where children were bathing and women were washing clothes. Sumitra sat on a stone and watched. When the train finally came, she was almost sad. She promised to return on a holiday.
Pen a tale about a sugar cane juice seller and a hot afternoon.

Ganesh pressed sugar cane through his old iron machine and filled glasses with green juice and a squeeze of lime. It was a very hot afternoon, and the line was long. A delivery boy on a bike pulled up, sweating. He had no money left, only a few coins. Ganesh looked at his flushed face. "Take a glass," he said. The boy drank it in one go. "I'll pay tomorrow," he said. The next day, he came back and not only paid but also brought two friends. By evening, Ganesh had sold three hundred glasses and could not feel his arm.
Offer me a tale where a girl and her mother have a small quarrel and make up by baking together.

Anjum slammed her door after her mother refused to let her go to a friend's party. She sat on her bed, angry. For an hour, no one came. Then she smelled something sweet from the kitchen. Her mother was baking biscuits. Anjum crept down and stood at the doorway. Her mother did not turn around. "Pass me the flour, will you?" she said. Anjum did. They rolled the dough in silence, then Anjum said, "I'm sorry I shouted." Her mother nodded. "Me too. Maybe next week for the party." They ate warm biscuits at the table, and the quarrel was over.
Dream up a gentle story about a village that gets electricity for the first time.

When the poles went up in Kothapalli, the villagers thought they were only for show. But one September evening, a man from the electricity board flicked a switch, and the street lamp at the temple gate glowed. The children shrieked. Old Mr. Reddy touched the glass and pulled his hand back. "It's warm," he said, amazed. In every house, a single bulb was lit. Mothers cooked in the new light, and children did their homework late. For the first time, people sat outside after dark without fear. That night, nobody wanted to sleep, and the lights burned until the early hours.
Put together a story about a girl who gets a new pair of glasses and sees the city differently.

Nilam, nine, had squinted at the blackboard for months. When the optician gave her glasses, she put them on and walked out of the shop. Everything looked sharp. She gasped at the leaves on the trees, each one clear. She read the signs on shops that had always been a blur. She noticed that her brother had a mole on his cheek. "Look at the bird!" she cried, pointing at a tiny sparrow on a wire. All the way home, she kept stopping to look at new things. That night, she wrote a list of everything she had never seen before, and it ran to three pages.
Show me a story about a girl in a village who plays on a swing during Teej.

Each year, when the monsoon came, the women of Rampur hung swings from the mango trees for Teej. Seema, twelve, waited all year for it. This time, the best swing hung from the highest branch. Her friends pushed her, and she flew up, up, her green dupatta flapping. She sang a Teej song, and her cousin joined from the ground. The wind smelled of wet earth. When she came down, her head was spinning, and she laughed. Her grandmother, sitting on a mat, handed her a plate of ghevar and said the sweet tasted better after a swing.
Invent a made-up story about a girl who finds out her grandfather used to be a wrestler.

Whenever Sakshi asked about Grandpa Ranbir's thick arms, he laughed and said it was from carrying vegetables. One afternoon, she found a dusty photo in a drawer. It showed a young man in a loincloth, holding a silver cup, with a crowd around him. "That's you!" she cried. Grandpa blushed. He told her about the akhara, the mud, and the early morning exercises. Sakshi asked him to show her a move. He grunted, bent, and lifted her onto his shoulders in one motion. She squealed, and her grandmother called from the kitchen to be careful. That night, Sakshi told everyone at school.
Please share a made-up story about two friends who go to the beach for the first time and meet a crab.

Hari and Ameena, both ten, had never seen the sea. When their school bus stopped in Goa, they ran to the shore, shoes in hand. The waves rolled in with a roar and tickled their toes. Ameena laughed and splashed. Hari spotted a tiny crab on the sand, running sideways. "Look!" he shouted. They followed it to a rock pool, where it disappeared under a stone. They crouched and waited, patient. After a long minute, the crab peeked out again and waved a claw. They cheered and dug a small pond for it. At sunset, they said goodbye and promised to come back.
Please craft a simple story about a family that is new in the city and a neighbour who brings them dinner.

The Rahmans moved to the city on a Tuesday, and by evening they had no groceries and no gas. The children were hungry. Someone knocked on the door, and Mrs. Thomas from next door stood there holding a covered dish. "I thought you might be tired," she said. Inside were hot rice and fish curry. The Rahmans sat on the floor and ate every grain. The youngest, Sana, asked Mrs. Thomas if she could have more. Mrs. Thomas laughed and promised more tomorrow. A week later, Mrs. Rahman returned the favour with her own biryani, and the two families ate together every Sunday after that.
Share a gentle story about a boy who rides his cycle to fetch candles during a power cut.

When the lights failed at seven, Manoj's mother realised that they had no candles. The nearest shop was a kilometre away. "I'll go," said Manoj, thirteen. He took his cycle, and the dark road felt strange without street lamps. Fireflies hovered above the hedges. He passed houses lit by lanterns. At the shop, the owner was selling the last few candles by torchlight. Manoj bought six and rode home carefully, holding them in a bag on the handlebar. The wind blew against him. At home, his mother lit the first one and set it in the window. "Well done," she said, and the flame bobbed.
Put together a simple story about a girl and her mother who take a rickshaw ride through the old city and see their old school.

On a Sunday, Reena took her mother to see the old city where she had grown up. In a cycle rickshaw, they wound through narrow lanes with sweet shops and balconies. "That's my school," her mother said suddenly, pointing at a yellow building with a green gate. Reena, twelve, stared. It looked smaller than she had expected. Her mother asked the rickshaw driver to stop, and they stood by the gate. A watchman recognised her mother's face and smiled. Inside, a tree still grew in the courtyard where she had once carved her name. They found it, faint, and Reena traced the letters with her finger.
Please craft a short story where a boy tries to cook his first egg and gets it wrong.

Armaan, eleven, woke early on Sunday and decided to surprise his parents with fried eggs. He found the pan and the oil and turned on the gas. The oil spat, and he jumped. He cracked an egg into the pan, and half the shell fell in too. He tried to fish it out with a spoon. The egg stuck and burned. The second egg came out raw in the middle. By the third, he had learned to lower the flame. When his parents woke up, the kitchen smelled of smoke, but a plate of three imperfect eggs sat on the table. They ate every one.
Share a made-up story about a class trip to a vegetable market in a village school.

Teacher Mrs. Pillai took her class to the Tuesday market to learn about weights and prices. Each child was given ten rupees and a list. Dinesh, nine, was told to buy tomatoes. He asked the seller for a quarter kilo and watched the scale. "How much?" he said. The seller told him the price, and Dinesh counted out his coins carefully. He got a little change back. All around him, his friends were doing the same, giggling and comparing. At the end, they returned to class with bags of vegetables, which Mrs. Pillai cooked in a big pot for lunch, and everyone said the maths tasted good.
Create a quick story about a girl whose brother is away in the army and what happens when he returns on leave.

Seema counted the days on the kitchen calendar, and at last, it was the morning her brother Major Vikram was due home. She stood at the gate for an hour. A taxi finally pulled up, and a tall man in a green uniform stepped out. He knelt and opened his arms. Seema ran into them, and he lifted her high. Their mother cried in the doorway. That evening, Vikram told stories of mountains and snow. Seema, ten, listened until she fell asleep on his lap. When he left for his post, she gave him a card she had made, and he put it in his pocket.
Share a quick story about a village girl who saves her goat from a snake.

Little Jaya's goat, Chameli, grazed near the haystack every afternoon. One day, Jaya heard her bleat in fear. A long brown snake was coiled near Chameli's legs. Jaya's heart pounded. She knew not to go near it, so she stayed back, called for her father, and banged a steel plate loudly. The snake raised its head, hissed, and slid slowly into the bushes. Jaya led the goat away and shut the pen. Her father heard the story and praised her calm head. That night, Jaya made sure the pen door was latched, and Chameli licked her hand through the bars.
Time for a small story about a girl who helps her father sell mats at a market and finds a new customer.

Pooja and her father wove reed mats at home and sold them at the Saturday market. Business was slow that week, and the pile of mats grew. Pooja, twelve, took a mat and sat on it in front of the stall. She read her schoolbook and looked comfortable. Passers-by stopped. "Is it soft?" one asked. "Try it," she said. A woman sat on it and smiled. She bought three. Others followed. By afternoon, the pile was half gone. Her father looked at her, amazed. "Who taught you to sell?" he asked. Pooja only shrugged and went back to her book.
Compose a made-up story where a girl and her grandfather watch the moon and make a wish.

Aisha's grandfather often sat on the roof after dinner, looking at the sky. One night, she joined him with a blanket. A full moon hung over the water tank. "Make a wish," he said. Aisha closed her eyes and thought hard. "I wish that you never get old," she said. Grandfather laughed gently. He told her that the moon had watched him since he was a boy and he had made many wishes to it. Most had come true in odd ways. They sat for a long time, the cool air on their faces. Before she went to bed, Aisha made one more wish, in silence.
Spin me a quick story about a man who fixes the neighbourhood generator during a power cut and wins a surprise.

When the power failed in Anand Colony, the old generator in the compound stuttered and died. Residents gathered, frowning. A young man named Sanjay, who worked as a mechanic, rolled up his sleeves and opened the casing. He worked for an hour by torchlight, with oil on his hands. The generator coughed, then roared, and the lights flickered back on. The residents cheered. The secretary, Mrs. Murthy, handed him the first plate. "Dinner is on us," she said. The whole colony ate together in the courtyard, and Sanjay was given the seat of honour, and the biggest piece of cake.
Let's have a short story about a girl who rides the double-decker bus for the first time in Mumbai and sits on the top deck.

Tanisha, eight, had always wanted to sit on the top deck of the red double-decker bus. On her birthday, her father took her. They climbed the narrow stairs, and she chose the front seat. The bus rolled along the sea road, and the wind blew her hair. She waved at people below, who looked small. She saw the old stone buildings and the glittering sea. At the traffic light, a boy on a bicycle looked up and waved back. Tanisha squealed. When they got off, her father asked what she liked best. "Everything," she said, and wanted to go again.
Time for a story about a family that prepares for a Bengali wedding feast in a city flat.

Two days before the wedding, the Mukherjee flat in Kolkata was a storm of activity. Aunties argued about sweets, uncles carried baskets of fish, and the children darted under tables. Debjani, twelve, was told to tie flowers on the gate. She was nervous but she worked carefully, twisting marigolds into a long garland. When her mother saw it, she smiled and nodded. On the wedding day, the guests admired the gate and asked who had made it. Debjani's grandmother pointed to her. The girl turned red and bowed. She spent the rest of the evening handing out sweets and answering questions.
Tell us a story about a boy and his grandfather who always travel in the same train compartment.

Every summer, Rohan travelled with his grandfather to the hills in the same compartment of the same train, the one with the creaky fan. Grandfather said it was lucky. Rohan, ten, thought it was silly, but he never argued. One year, a new rule moved them to another coach. Grandfather's face fell. Rohan thought hard. At the next station, he asked the guard if they could swap seats with someone. The guard laughed and found a family willing to switch. Soon, they were back in their old spot, with the creaky fan. Grandfather clapped Rohan on the back, and the fan creaked louder.
Kindly write a quick story about a girl who writes a letter to her new neighbour.

When a new family moved into the flat next door, Jyoti was curious. She wrote a short note on pink paper: "Hello, I'm Jyoti. I live next door. Do you like cats?" She slipped it under the door. The next morning, a reply was pinned to her door: "Hello Jyoti, I'm Shreya. I love cats. Do you want to meet mine?" Jyoti knocked, and a girl her age opened the door with a fluffy orange cat in her arms. They sat on the floor and played with string. The two families began to share a bench in the evenings, and the girls shared everything.
Create a small story about a village boy who finds a hidden treasure of old coins.

Banti was digging a pit for a new post behind his house when his spade clinked on metal. He brushed away the soil and found a clay pot full of old, dark coins. His heart raced. He ran to his father, who took the coins to the village teacher. The teacher said they were very old and should go to a museum. Banti was disappointed for a moment. Then the museum sent a letter of thanks and a small reward. Banti used the money to buy books for his school library, and the headmaster put up a sign that said, "Donated by Banti."
Please share a fresh story about a girl who gets lost in a shopping mall and uses a map to find her mother.

Aditi was looking at a toy shop window when she realised her mother was gone. The mall was huge, with four floors and many shops. Aditi, nine, took a breath. She remembered that her mother had said they would visit the bookshop. She looked for a map on the wall and found one with a red dot that said, "You are here." She traced the bookshop's location with her finger and walked to the escalator. On the second floor, she saw her mother standing in front of the bookshop, looking worried. They hugged, and her mother said she had done well.
Invent a fresh story about a family that keeps a pet tortoise and a funny escape.

The Mathew family kept a tortoise named Kuttan in the back garden. He was old and slow, and no one worried about him. One morning, the gate was left open, and Kuttan was gone. The children searched all day. At dusk, Joel noticed a line of tiny tracks leading across the road. They followed it to the neighbour's house, where Kuttan sat in the middle of a bed of lettuce. The neighbour was laughing so hard she could barely speak. Kuttan chewed a leaf calmly. Joel carried him home in both arms, and his father fixed the gate with extra wire.
How about a short story about two children who help their grandmother sell homemade snacks outside a school.

Grandmother Kamla made crisp murukku and spicy peanuts and sold them at the school gate. Her grandchildren, Hari and Sita, helped on weekends. Hari handled the money, and Sita wrapped the packets in paper cones. One day, a big boy tried to take a packet without paying. Hari stood up straight. "Two rupees, please," he said in a firm voice. The big boy paused, then paid. Grandmother pretended to be busy, but she smiled. That evening, she gave each child a coin and a handful of peanuts. They shared them on the bus home, feeling like real shopkeepers.
Imagine a short story about a city where the whole power grid goes out and the people come together on the street.

At nine o'clock on a hot Friday, the entire city of Nagpur went dark. Traffic lights failed, shops closed, and a thousand people spilled into the streets. At first, they were annoyed. Then a man with a guitar sat on a kerb and began to play. A woman handed out cups of cold water from her doorstep. A teenager named Rizwan walked old people home with his torch. By ten, the street looked like a fair. People shared stories and food. When the power returned at midnight, the crowd cheered. Many lingered, saying it was the best night out they'd had in years.
Long ago a boy in a village found a flute. Please tell the story.

Once upon a time, a boy named Dilip found a bamboo flute beside the pond in his village. He blew into it, and only a squeak came out. Day after day, he practised under the banyan tree. The older boys teased him and called his music a sick crow. Dilip kept going. One evening, a lost cow wandered into the village, and no one could catch her. Dilip played a soft tune, and the cow stopped and turned her head. She followed him slowly, all the way to her owner's gate. The teasing stopped, and that night, the whole street asked him to play again.
Would you mind telling me the story of a rickshaw puller in Kolkata who found a ring?

Once upon a time, a rickshaw puller named Bimal found a gold ring on the seat after a rainy evening. He turned it over in his hand. It was engraved with the letters S and R. Bimal could have sold it for a month's pay, but he thought of the person who must be worrying. The next day, he asked every customer if they had lost a ring. At noon, a young woman burst into tears as she described it. Bimal gave it back. She tried to give him money, but he shook his head and asked only that she tell people he was honest.
Time for a fresh story in which a girl and her father repair a broken radio together.

Ira found an old radio in the storeroom, covered in dust. Her father, Mr. Chopra, said it had not worked in twenty years. Ira, eleven, begged to open it. They placed it on the table and unscrewed the back. Inside were tiny coloured wires and a cracked part. Her father taught her how to solder, and she held the iron carefully. After two Sundays, they tightened the last screw. Ira turned the knob, and a crackle came, then a song from an old film. Her father closed his eyes and hummed. He said it was his mother's favourite song. Ira turned the volume up.
Craft a made-up story about a girl who shares her umbrella with a neighbour during heavy rain.

Heavy rain began just as Gita left school. She opened her yellow umbrella and walked down the lane. Near the corner, she saw Mr. Fernandes from the next building, carrying a bag of groceries and getting soaked. He did not have an umbrella. Gita ran after him. "Please, uncle, come under," she said. He smiled and bent a little. They walked together, side by side, with the rain drumming on the cloth. At his gate, he said she was very kind. Gita, twelve, replied that it was nothing. When she got home, her left shoulder was wet, but she was happy.
Let's have a fresh story about a boy who sells newspapers in a city market and finds a stray kitten.

Jeevan, thirteen, sold newspapers at the market every dawn before school. One misty morning, he heard a mewing sound from behind a pile of crates. A tiny grey kitten sat there, shivering. He took it into his shirt and kept selling. At noon, a woman at the tea stall gave him a saucer of milk. Jeevan carried the kitten home and showed his mother, who sighed but allowed it. He named it Akhbar. Every morning, the kitten sat in his newspaper basket and watched the customers, and soon people started to buy papers just to stroke it.
Let's have a small story about a girl who gets a new frock for Easter and wears it to church.

Nina, eight, had been waiting for Easter for weeks. Her aunt had sent a frock from the city, pale yellow with white lace. On Easter morning, she put it on and twirled before the mirror. At church, she sat in the front row, trying not to move. After the service, the priest's dog ran in and jumped on her lap with muddy paws. The frock was smeared with brown. Nina stared in horror. Then she began to laugh, and her mother laughed too. Her grandmother washed the frock that afternoon, and by evening, it was drying on the line, yellow again.
How about a story about a grandmother who joins her granddaughter's school sports day and runs a race.

At the school sports day, a race for grandparents was announced. Nine-year-old Kiara looked at her Nani and shook her head. "No, Nani, you'll fall." But Nani Usha had already tied her sari tight. Six grandparents lined up. At the whistle, they all hobbled forward. Nani Usha, who had walked ten kilometres a day in her youth, soon pulled ahead. Kiara screamed from the stand. Nani crossed the line first, gasping and laughing, and held the cup high. Kiara ran onto the field and hugged her. That evening, Nani Usha rubbed her knees with oil and said she would defend the title next year.
Please narrate a little story about a man and his daughter on a boat ride across a lake in the hills.

Mr. Bhatt took his daughter Rhea to the lake on the last day of the holiday. The boatman, an old man in a woollen cap, rowed them out as mist rose from the water. Rhea, seven, dipped her fingers in. It was freezing. A bird with a long neck stood on a rock and watched them. "A heron," said her father. They drifted for a long time, saying nothing. Then the boatman began to sing, and his voice carried over the water. Rhea leaned her head on her father's arm. On the shore, she told him it was the best day of the trip.
Two neighbours play cards during a power cut. Tell it in 120 words or fewer.

When the lights went out in Tower B, Mr. Bose took his lantern to the landing and found Mrs. Kaul standing in her doorway, bored. "Cards?" he asked. She nodded and brought a pack. They sat on the stairs and played rummy by the yellow light. Mr. Bose, who always claimed to be an expert, lost three hands in a row. Mrs. Kaul cackled. Soon, other neighbours drifted out of their flats, and a small crowd gathered to watch. When the power returned two hours later, Mr. Bose demanded a rematch. Mrs. Kaul agreed for the next power cut.
Tell me a story about a kite that could talk.

Meera found the kite folded under her cousin's bed in Jaipur. When she tied it to a string in the park, it said, "Finally! Do you know how long I have waited?" Meera dropped the spool in surprise.

"I only fly when someone asks nicely," said the kite. "And I like to go high, above the water tanks."

Meera asked nicely. Up they went, past the pigeons and the clotheslines. But the string was short, and the kite began to sulk.

So Meera tied three spools together, and her cousin helped let out the line. The kite climbed until the whole city looked like a spilled box of buttons, and it laughed all the way down.
A girl finds a magic paintbrush in her grandmother's button tin; can you turn that into a short story?

Tanvi found the brush in her grandmother's old tin of buttons. It was thin and silver, and when she dipped it in water, a blue line stayed in the air.

She painted a small door on the kitchen wall. It opened with a creak, and behind it was a garden where the tomatoes were as big as pumpkins. She picked one and carried it back.

Her grandmother laughed so hard she had to sit down. "My mother had that brush," she said. "She painted me a swing once."

Tanvi painted a swing now, and a second one beside it. They sat together, kicking their feet, while the tomato soup bubbled on the stove.
Make up a bedtime story for my little brother about a shy dragon.

Deep in a green valley lived a small dragon named Pico. Pico was very shy. When anyone came near, he hid behind a big rock and blew tiny puffs of smoke.

One evening, a village boy named Arun lost his lantern on the hill. It was getting dark, and he could not see the path home.

Pico peeked out from behind his rock. He took a slow, deep breath and blew a soft, warm glow into the air. It lit the path like a row of little stars.

Arun followed the glow all the way to his door. At the gate he turned and waved. Pico waved back with one claw, and for the first time, he did not hide.
My little sister wants a robot who loves to dance. Can you write a story for her?

Bolt was a delivery robot in a big Mumbai building. All day he carried parcels in the lift, and all day he heard music from the flat on the fourth floor, where a girl named Zoya practised dance.

One night he stopped at her door. "Excuse me," he said in his flat voice. "May I learn?"

Zoya showed him a step. Bolt's wheels slid the wrong way, and he bumped the wall. He tried again. He spun too fast and knocked over a plant.

Zoya laughed and put some tape on the floor to mark the steps. Slowly, Bolt learned to glide in a circle. By the end of the month, the whole building clapped when he spun in the lobby.
Please keep it gentle: a story about a treasure map found in the attic.

Kabir and his sister Isha were cleaning the attic when a yellow paper slid out of an old suitcase. It showed a mango tree, a well, and a big red cross.

"Our grandfather drew this," said Isha, pointing to the tiny signature in the corner.

They followed the map across the back garden. They counted twelve steps from the mango tree and found the well. Beside it, under a flat stone, was a small tin box.

Inside lay a handful of marbles, a folded note, and a photograph of two children grinning. The note said, "For whoever finds this. Play with them." Kabir and Isha sat down on the grass and started a game right there.
Can you write a story set in a village, where a talking buffalo helps a child?

Nandu was eight, and his family's buffalo, Kamli, was the slowest walker in the village. Every morning she ambled to the pond while Nandu ran ahead to school.

One day, Nandu could not find his school bag. He looked under the cot, behind the door and in the cowshed. The bell would ring soon.

"Look in the hay," said a deep voice.

Nandu dropped his slate. "Kamli, did you just speak?"

"Only when something matters," said Kamli, chewing slowly. "Yesterday you left your bag on the haystack, and I lay down beside it."

Nandu dug into the hay and pulled out his bag, a little squashed but safe. He reached school just as the bell rang. That evening, he brought Kamli the greenest grass from the canal bank and told her all about his day.
I'd like a happy story about a cloud that was afraid of rain.

A little cloud named Wisp floated over a dry farm in Punjab. Every other cloud around him let go of its rain and grew thin and light. Wisp held on tight, because he was afraid that if he rained, there would be nothing left of him.

Below, a farmer called Harpreet looked up each morning. "Please," she whispered, "just a little."

One afternoon, Wisp felt a single drop slip away. It fell on the farmer's nose. She laughed out loud. Wisp felt a tickle of joy and let go of another.

By evening he was small and pale, but the wheat shone green below him. The next morning, the wind carried him over the sea, and he filled up again.
My cousin is six, so could you write her a story about a tiny drum that could not stop dancing?

Tom had a tiny red drum. It was the kind of drum that did not wait for a stick. When music played, it jumped up and bounced across the floor.

One day Tom's mother was making soup, and the drum bounced into the kitchen. It hopped on the table. It rolled under a chair. It knocked a spoon off the counter, and the spoon went clang.

"Drum, stop!" said Tom. But the drum only went faster.

Then Tom had an idea. He sang a slow, quiet song. The drum slowed down. It slid to a stop in his lap and made one soft sound.

That night, Tom sang it the same slow song, and the drum went to sleep.
Story time: a boy, a talking crab, and a sandcastle, in no more than 100 words.

Rohan was digging a sandcastle on a beach in Goa when a small crab marched out of the moat. "You are building on my doorstep," said the crab.

"Sorry," said Rohan. "Where is your house?"

"Under the third rock. The tide took my front step."

Rohan built a new step beside the rock, round and smooth. The crab tested it with a claw.

"Acceptable," said the crab. Then it gave Rohan a shiny white shell and scuttled inside.

At night, Rohan held the shell to his ear and heard a small voice say, "Goodnight, neighbour."
What happens when the moon falls asleep and forgets to rise? Tell it as a story.

One evening, the Moon was so tired that she dozed off behind a hill. The sky stayed dark, and in a small town in Kerala, the fireflies could not find their way.

A girl named Anitha noticed first. She went out to the courtyard with a torch. "Moon, are you there?" she called.

A far-off yawn answered her. Anitha thought hard. She took a steel plate from the kitchen and polished it until it shone like silver. She held it up and waved it back and forth.

The Moon woke up and saw the light. "Oh!" she said, and rose in a hurry. The fireflies cheered, and Anitha went back to bed with a warm cup of milk.
A giant who is scared of mice finds a friend; write that story.

Big Gopal was the tallest man in the valley, but he was afraid of mice. When one ran across his kitchen floor, he jumped on a chair and the chair broke.

A little mouse named Tikki watched from the corner. She was afraid of him, too, because his boots were the size of boats.

One rainy night, Gopal sat in the dark, because his candle had blown out. Tikki crept out, carrying a matchstick almost as long as herself. She could not light it, but she dragged it to his foot.

Gopal looked down and smiled. He struck the match gently and lit the candle. After that, he left a crumb of bread by the door every evening.
A magic seed story, please, with a title at the top.

The Seed in the Teacup

Nina found a round, silver seed in her teacup after a family picnic. She planted it in a pot on the balcony and watered it every morning.

On the fifth day, a tiny green shoot appeared. On the sixth, it was as tall as her hand. On the seventh, it opened a flower, and out of the flower came a very small voice.

"Good morning," said the voice. "I am the garden's first alarm clock. Nobody has ever listened to me."

Nina laughed and set the pot on her windowsill. Every morning after that, the flower sang her awake, and Nina was never late for school again.
Could you do a story about a lantern that was afraid of the dark?

Lalit's lantern had a secret. It was afraid of the dark. Every evening, when the boy carried it down to the river to fetch water, the lantern shook so hard that its light jiggled.

"Why are you shaking?" asked Lalit one night.

"The dark is so big," said the lantern, in a small voice.

Lalit thought for a moment. Then he held the lantern up high. "Look," he said. "The dark has stars in it."

The lantern looked up. Hundreds of tiny lights twinkled over the river. They looked like many small lanterns, far away.

The lantern stopped shaking. It glowed steady and gold all the way home, and it never jiggled again.
Tell a story for kids around seven about a school bus that learned to fly.

Bus Number Five took the children of Sundar Nagar to school every day. It was old and yellow, and its engine always coughed on the hill.

One foggy morning, the hill was very steep, and the bus gave a big cough. Then it did something strange. Its wheels lifted off the road!

"Whoa!" cried the children. The bus floated over the fog, over the temple, over the green fields. The driver, Mr. Dinesh, held the wheel tightly and laughed.

They landed softly in the school yard, exactly on time. The children climbed out with wide eyes.

"Same time tomorrow?" the bus seemed to say, as its engine rumbled. The next day, all the children brought extra scarves, just in case.
Write about a snowman who wants to see summer, as a story.

Fred the snowman stood in a garden in Shimla and wondered what summer was. All the children talked about it, but he had never seen it.

"If I stay cold," he said to a sparrow, "I can hold on until it comes."

The sparrow, called Pip, helped. She brought him a bit of ice from the shady side of the house. A girl named Charu put an old umbrella over his head.

Spring came, and the snow grew thin. Fred got smaller and smaller. In the end, Charu scooped what was left into a bucket and put it in the back of the freezer.

In June she carried it outside. "Look, Fred," she said, "summer!" The bucket glistened in the sun.
Here is an idea: a kite that is scared of the wind. Can you write it up?

Ravi's blue kite hated the wind. Every time a breeze came, it squeezed its paper eyes shut and tugged downward.

"A kite who won't fly is just a piece of paper," said Ravi's grandfather, who was sitting on a cot nearby.

"But the wind is rough," said the kite.

Ravi's grandfather smiled. "Try a very small wind first."

The next morning, there was only a whisper of air. Ravi lifted the kite, and it rose a little, as high as a doorframe, and stayed there, wobbling.

Day by day, the winds grew stronger and the kite climbed higher. By the festival of Makar Sankranti, it flew above every roof on the street, and its tail danced.
Narrate a story in which a boy's drawings come to life for exactly one minute.

Dev drew a green frog on the back of his maths notebook. At exactly four o'clock, the frog blinked, jumped off the page, and landed on his desk.

"One minute," the frog croaked. "Make it count."

Dev had so many ideas. He wanted to ask the frog about ponds, and about flies, and about swimming. He talked so fast that his words tumbled together.

The frog listened patiently and croaked answers. Then the minute ended, and the frog flattened back into lines on the page.

Dev sat quietly. Then he picked up his pencil and drew a second frog, beside the first. Tomorrow, he decided, he would ask just one good question.
Something funny, please: a dragon who can only breathe out bubbles.

Dragon Dolly was ashamed. Every other dragon in Cloud Mountain could breathe fire. When Dolly opened her mouth, out floated a stream of shiny soap bubbles.

"Hot enough to roast a goat!" bragged old Brahm, blasting a boulder black.

Dolly sneezed. Pop-pop-pop went a hundred bubbles over his head. They floated onto his nose and stuck there.

"Hey!" Brahm sputtered. "I can't see!"

Then a very big wind blew in, and all the dragons' fires went out at once. They were cold and cross, until Dolly breathed a giant bubble and invited them inside it. It was warm and quiet in there.

After that, the dragons took turns riding in Dolly's bubbles.
A robot is learning to cook in a small Indian kitchen. What happens?

The robot was called Gudu, and it lived in Savita Aunty's kitchen in Pune. It could chop onions, but it did not know how to make anything taste good.

"Today we make dal," said Savita Aunty. "Listen, don't just measure."

Gudu listened to the cooker whistle. It watched the mustard seeds pop. It leaned in and sniffed the steam from the pot.

"Too flat," said Gudu. "It needs something sharp."

Savita Aunty nodded and handed it a lemon. Gudu squeezed one careful drop into the dal.

They ate the dal together with hot rice. Savita Aunty took a second helping, and Gudu's little lights flashed green.
Two friends find an old map inside a library book; what happens next? Write the story.

Sam and Priya were returning a library book when a folded map slipped out from between the pages. It showed their own town, with a dotted line from the library steps to a star near the river.

"Someone used it as a bookmark," said Sam.

They showed it to the librarian, Mrs. Thomas. She put on her glasses and smiled. "I drew this forty years ago," she said. "It shows the way to the best reading spot in town. I lost the map, and I never found the spot again."

That Saturday, the three of them followed the dotted line together. It led past the post office, along the river path, and up to a wide neem tree with a flat stone seat beneath it.

Mrs. Thomas sat down and sighed happily. Every Saturday after that, she, Sam and Priya read there together.
Hedgehog, hot-air balloon: could you tell me a story?

Hetty the hedgehog had always wanted to see the top of the oak tree. One morning, a red hot-air balloon came down gently in her meadow, and out climbed a pilot named Mr. Okoye.

"My rope is caught," he said. "It's tangled in that thorn bush, and my hands are too big to reach in."

Hetty was small, and thorns did not bother her. She wriggled into the bush and pulled the rope free, loop by loop.

"Would you like a ride?" he asked.

Hetty climbed in. They rose above the oak tree, above the river, above the chimney smoke. She saw her meadow as a small green patch.

When they landed, she was giggling too hard to speak.
In a village, the well sings every morning. Write the story of it.

In the village of Chandanpur, the old well sang. Nobody knew why. Every morning at dawn, a soft hum rose from the water, and the women who came to fill their pots hummed along.

One year, the well went quiet. The villagers shook their heads. A girl named Sunita looked carefully from behind the low wall and saw a round stone stuck in a little hole in the well's side, just below the rim.

"The song comes out of that hole," she said, "and the stone is blocking it."

She ran to fetch her uncle Mohan. He reached in with a long bamboo hook and eased the stone out, while Sunita pointed to the exact spot.

The next morning, the well sang louder than ever. The whole village stood around it, humming together, and the pots clinked in rhythm.
Under 90 words, please: a paper boat that wanted to reach the sea.

Paper boat Pinku floated down the street after the rain. A boy named Manoj ran beside him.

"The sea is far," said a frog on a leaf.

"I'll get there," said Pinku.

He bobbed past a puddle and spun in a whirl. At a big stone, he nearly tipped over, but Manoj nudged him free with a stick.

By evening, Pinku reached the big river. It was not the sea, but it flowed that way.

Manoj set him down gently, and Pinku sailed off into the gold light.
A story about a girl whose flute made flowers grow, please.

Asha's flute was made of bamboo, and it was nothing special, until the day she played it beside her mother's dry flower bed. The notes drifted down, and a tiny green shoot pushed up through the soil.

She played another tune, and the shoot grew taller. By the third song, a marigold was in bloom.

Soon the neighbours came to listen. A boy named Kiran asked if she could help his grandmother's garden, which had not bloomed in years.

Asha went over with her flute. She played a slow tune by the fence, and a row of jasmine buds opened one by one. Kiran's grandmother wept happy tears and gave Asha a warm laddu.
For a four-year-old, make up a story about a teddy bear lost at the market.

Teddy was very small and very brown. One busy Sunday, he fell out of Meena's bag at the vegetable market.

"Oh no," whispered Teddy. A cabbage rolled past him. A basket of tomatoes tipped over. People's feet went by like tall trees.

A friendly cat named Mishti sniffed him. "Are you lost?" she asked.

"I think so," said Teddy.

"I know everyone here," said Mishti. She picked Teddy up gently in her mouth and trotted from stall to stall until she found a girl with red ribbons, who was crying beside the potato seller.

"Teddy!" cried Meena. She hugged him tightly. Mishti purred and got a fish from the fish seller as a thank-you.
A little star wants to visit Earth. Could you write that as a story?

A little star named Tara lived at the edge of the sky. Each night she looked down at the twinkling lights of a town in Assam and wished she could visit.

"Stars can't leave the sky," said her big brother.

But one night, a meteor shower began. Tara hopped onto a passing streak of light and slid down, down, down, with her tiny arms stretched out.

She landed in a field, where a boy named Jimmy was lying on the grass. "A star!" he whispered. He gently cupped his hands around her.

Tara glowed between his fingers for a while. Then another streak of light came by, and Jimmy lifted his hands and let her go home.
Keep it light and silly: a talking jalebi.

A jalebi named Jilu sat at the top of a tall pile in Mohan Uncle's sweet shop. "I'm the curliest jalebi in town," he told the others. "Twelve curls. Count them."

The trouble was that Jilu had curled himself so tightly that he was stuck to the jalebi below him. When a girl named Pari pointed and said, "That one, please," Mohan Uncle tugged, and the whole pile came up together like a sticky ladder.

"Oops," said Jilu.

Pari giggled so much that she had to sit down. Mohan Uncle giggled too. Then Pari had an idea. "Can I have all of them?" she asked. "It's my class party today."

So the sticky ladder of jalebis went into one big box, with Jilu proudly on top, and thirty children shared them that afternoon.
I want a story about a fox cub who could not whistle.

Fennel the fox cub could not whistle. Everyone in the forest could, even the squirrels, and Fennel was tired of being the only one who just blew air.

"Round your lips," said Owl, from her branch. "Not so tight."

Fennel tried. Whoosh. He tried again. Wheeze.

All week he practised by the stream, while the leaves fell around him. His cheeks ached.

On Saturday, a baby rabbit named Lulu got stuck in a bramble bush. She was too far away to hear him shout. So Fennel puckered his lips, one more time, and a clear, high whistle rang through the trees.

Mother Rabbit came running at once. Fennel was so proud, he whistled all the way home.
Write a tale of a house that hummed lullabies at night.

Nobody in the town of Rampur knew that the blue house at the end of the lane could hum. It only did so late at night, very softly, when the lights were out.

A boy named Imran, who had just moved in, lay awake one evening. He was missing his old school and his old friends. Then he heard it, a low hum coming from the walls, like a lullaby his grandmother used to sing.

He pressed his ear to the pillow and listened. The tune went up and down like waves.

Imran fell asleep before it finished. In the morning, he wrote a thank-you note and left it on the windowsill.
Write a Diwali story about a diya that refused to light.

On Diwali evening, Roshni set out thirty diyas along the steps. One by one, her father lit them with a taper. Twenty-nine glowed bright. But the thirtieth diya, a small, chipped one, would not catch.

"Maybe it's broken," said Roshni's father.

"No," said Roshni. She looked closer and found a little bit of dust in the wick. She blew it away, then dipped the wick in oil.

Her father touched the flame to it again. The little diya sputtered, then burned with a steady, golden light.

All thirty diyas shone in a row. Roshni sat on the top step and watched them until the stars came out.
Imagine a boy who borrowed the wind for an afternoon, and write it as a story.

Joshua wanted to fly his kite, but the air was still. He stood in the field with the string in his hand, and the kite lay flat on the grass.

"Wind," he called, "could you lend me a little breeze?"

To his surprise, a voice replied. "I can give you one afternoon," said the wind. "Take care of me."

A cool gust swept up. Joshua's kite rose, spun, and soared. All afternoon he ran and laughed, and he never once pulled the string too hard.

When the sun set, the wind said, "Thank you for being gentle." And it slipped away, leaving the kite floating down, light as a leaf, into his hands.
A message in a bottle washes up for a girl; write what happens.

Zainab was collecting shells on the beach near Kochi when she spotted a green bottle in the foam. Inside was a rolled-up note.

She unscrewed the cap with trembling fingers. The note said, in careful handwriting, "Hello! My name is Luca. I live in a very small town near the sea. Do you like cats?"

There was a postal address at the bottom, and a drawing of an orange cat.

Zainab sat on a rock and wrote back. "Hello Luca! I love cats. I have two." She added a drawing of her own.

Her mother helped her post the letter the next morning. Three weeks later, a reply arrived, with a photo of Luca's cat wearing a tiny hat.
Can you invent a library where the books whisper at night?

At Mrs. Dsouza's tiny library, the books whispered when the lights went out. They traded stories, argued about endings, and sometimes shuffled themselves into new order.

One night, a brand-new book arrived. It had a bright cover and no words inside. All the old books gathered around it.

"It's blank," said a thick dictionary. "What a shame."

"Maybe not," said a small poetry book. "Maybe it's waiting."

The next morning, a boy named Vikram came in with a pencil. He sat down and began to write. The blank pages filled slowly, one word at a time.

That night, the books leaned close and read his story together, and they all agreed it was good.
Tell the story of a train that took a wrong turn and found a secret station.

The little blue train from Ooty was supposed to go straight to the plains. But one misty morning, the driver, Mr. Selvam, turned his lever the wrong way, and the train glided onto a track nobody had seen before.

It ended at a tiny station with a wooden sign that said, "Cloud Halt." There was one bench, a flowerpot, and a stationmaster named Aunty Lakshmi, who was surprised to see them.

"No train has come here in ten years," she said, and she served everyone hot tea and steamed idlis.

The passengers drank tea in the cool air. When the mist cleared, Mr. Selvam found the right turn, and the train rolled on, with every window waving.
Please write a story about a girl and her talking cricket bat.

Divya's cricket bat was old and had a crack down the middle. She almost threw it away. But one afternoon, before the school match, it spoke up.

"Don't swing so hard," it said, in a creaky voice. "Watch the ball, then let me do the work."

Divya was nervous. The other team's bowler was fast. In the first over, she missed twice and heard the others sigh.

"Watch the ball," whispered the bat.

On the third ball, she kept her eyes steady and tapped it lightly. It rolled past the fielders and to the boundary.

The team cheered. Divya patted the bat. It did not say anything else, but she was sure it was smiling.
A new dragon is too shy to greet his neighbour. Write that as a story.

A small green dragon named Ember had just moved into a cave next to a snail named Gus. Ember wanted to say hello, but each time she opened her mouth, only a little cough came out.

She wrote "Hello" on a leaf and left it by his door. The wind blew it away.

She baked a tiny pie and set it outside. A beetle ate it.

At last, Ember stood on the path with her heart pounding. Gus slid slowly over. "You're the one who keeps leaving things," he said.

"Yes," whispered Ember.

"I like that," said Gus. "Come in for tea. It takes me a while to make it, though."

Ember grinned and sat down to wait.
Make a happy story about a lonely robot in a toy shop.

In the corner of Mr. Banerjee's toy shop sat a tin robot called Clink. Children picked up the teddy bears and the cars, but nobody picked Clink, because his key was missing.

One rainy day, a girl named Esha wandered in. She saw Clink in the corner and held him gently. "You're sad," she said.

She searched the whole shop for a key. At last, in a drawer of pencils, she found a little brass one.

She turned it three times, and Clink's arms began to swing. His eyes lit up. "Hello," he said, in a clanky voice.

Mr. Banerjee smiled and wrapped Clink in paper. Esha carried him home in her arms, under her umbrella.
Write a bedtime story about a pirate map that a child drew.

Leo had drawn a pirate map on the back of a cereal box. It had a skull, an island shaped like a banana, and a big X marked "treasure."

He hid it under his pillow and fell asleep. In the night, the map glowed softly. Leo opened his eyes and found himself standing on the banana island, with sand between his toes.

A friendly parrot flew over. "Follow me," it said.

They walked past a palm tree and a pond. At the X, Leo dug with a shell and found a wooden chest. Inside were seventeen shiny buttons and a note: "Go back to bed."

Leo woke up in his room, smiling, with a button in his hand.
An old painter gets a brush that paints how he feels; story please.

Old Mr. Fernandes lived above a bakery in Goa. His hands shook now, and he had not painted in years. But one day, a student gave him a new brush, and he idly touched it to the wall.

A warm orange streak appeared, like a sunset. He felt happy, and that was exactly what the brush had painted.

He tried again, while thinking of his late wife. A soft blue wave rolled across the wall.

Every day, he sat with the brush and let his feelings spill out in colour. The bakery girl, Jenny, stopped to look.

"It's beautiful," she said.

Mr. Fernandes smiled. He painted a small yellow square for her, and she hung it in the shop.
A talking kite helps a boy find his lost dog, can you write that?

Arjun's dog, Bruno, had slipped out of the gate, and the boy could not find him anywhere. He sat on the steps with his head in his hands.

"Hey," said a voice. It was the old red kite, which he had left leaning against the wall. "I can see farther than you can. Let me up."

Arjun tied the string and let it fly. The kite swooped high over the market, the temple, and the bus stand.

"There!" the kite called. "Behind the tea stall, near the green gate."

Arjun ran. Bruno was there, wagging his tail, with a biscuit in his mouth.

Arjun hugged him, then thanked the kite, which swayed proudly in the air.
What if a puddle showed you other places? Write a story about it.

After the monsoon, a round puddle appeared outside Sana's school. When she looked down, she did not see her own face. She saw a snowy mountain, with a small red cabin.

"Hello," said a tiny girl in the puddle. She waved. "I'm Ingrid. It's snowing here."

Sana waved back. "It's hot and wet here," she said.

They talked for a long time about hats and cocoa and mud. Ingrid showed Sana a snow dog. Sana showed Ingrid a very wet crow.

The bell rang. "Come back tomorrow?" asked Ingrid.

But the sun came out and dried the puddle. Sana was sad, until the next big rain, when the puddle returned and Ingrid was still waving.
Write a story about a snail who wanted to win a race, ending happily.

Sonu the snail wanted to win the garden race. All the other creatures laughed. "You'll finish tomorrow," said the grasshopper.

On race day, they lined up beside the rose bush. The grasshopper leaped ahead. The ladybird zipped off. The ants marched in a line.

Sonu moved a tiny bit at a time. Soon, the others stopped to rest in the shade. The grasshopper fell asleep. The ladybird went to chat with a bee.

Sonu never stopped. Slowly, steadily, he crossed the finish line by the watering can.

The garden was quiet. Then the creatures woke up and clapped. Sonu blushed inside his shell, and the grasshopper gave him a clover to eat.
My grandmother has an old trunk; make up a story where it holds a new surprise every day.

Every Sunday, Nani opened her old wooden trunk. It was a funny trunk. Each time, it held something different.

One week, it held a tiny set of silver bells. The next, it held a map of a faraway river. The week after, a single feather as blue as the sky.

Her granddaughter, Pooja, always asked, "Where do they come from?"

"The trunk decides," said Nani. "It knows what we need."

One Sunday, Pooja was feeling down because she had lost a school game. The trunk opened to show a small gold medal, with her name carved on it.

Pooja gasped. Nani winked, and they shared warm halwa at the table.
A very small dragon lives in a girl's teapot. Tell me that story.

When Kavya poured her morning tea, a tiny dragon the size of a thumb crawled out of the spout. "Excuse me," he squeaked. "I'm Spark. This is my house."

"Oh!" said Kavya. "I didn't know."

"It gets very hot in here when you pour," said Spark, fanning himself with a wing.

Kavya felt sorry. She found a small bowl, filled it with cool water, and set it by the teapot as a bath. Spark splashed in with a happy cry.

After that, she poured her tea very slowly and always said, "Coming through!" And Spark would wave from his bowl and sometimes warm her chai with a gentle puff.
I'd like to hear about a boy who built a cardboard rocket and flew to the moon.

Omar built a rocket from a refrigerator box. He painted it silver and wrote "MOON" on the side. Then he climbed inside with a flask of juice and a torch.

"Three, two, one," he whispered.

The box shivered. Then, softly, it lifted. Omar peeked through the window and saw his street shrinking.

He landed on the Moon with a gentle bump. The ground was soft and grey. A small moon rabbit, wearing a tiny cap, hopped over.

"Welcome," it said. "Would you like some rice cake?"

Omar sat and ate rice cake with the rabbit, and they watched the blue Earth turn. When his torch dimmed, the rocket gently floated him home, just in time for dinner.
Set a story in a Rajasthan village with a camel who loved to sing.

In a desert village in Rajasthan lived a camel named Shahu, who loved to sing. His songs sounded like a rusty gate. The villagers covered their ears.

"Please, Shahu," said little Gita, "maybe hum quietly."

Shahu was sad. He plodded to the dunes alone and sang at the sky.

One evening, the villagers stayed late at the far well, and the dark came down fast. There was no moon, and the dunes all looked alike. From the gate, Gita heard them calling to each other.

"Sing, Shahu!" she cried. "Loud!"

Shahu sang with all his might. The rusty sound carried across the dunes, and the villagers followed it home, one by one.

Everyone cheered. From then on, nobody covered their ears, at least not completely.
The lighthouse keeper's daughter makes friends with a whale; write that story.

Mina lived in a white lighthouse on a rocky island. Her father tended the big lamp, and she watched the sea. One morning, she saw a huge grey back rise beside the rocks.

It was a whale, and it looked sad. She ran down to the shore. "What's wrong?" she called, not expecting an answer.

The whale lifted her eye. "My song is lost," she said.

"Sing me what you remember," said Mina.

The whale hummed a few notes. Mina found her flute and played them back. They tried again and again, adding a note each time, until the whole song came together.

The whale sang it out loud, and from far away, other whales answered.
A girl learns to make rotis with the help of a magic rolling pin; tell it as a story.

Nisha's rotis always came out shaped like maps of strange countries. Her mother laughed, but Nisha felt embarrassed.

One day, in the back of a cupboard, she found a rolling pin with a little brass ring on one end. It felt warm in her hands.

She set the dough down and began to roll. To her surprise, the pin rolled by itself, making a perfect round circle. It hummed as it went.

"Now you try," it whispered.

Nisha placed her hands on top. Together they rolled and turned. Slowly, she felt the right pressure.

By the end of the week, she made a perfectly round roti all alone. She put it on her mother's plate.
Write the story of an old violin that missed its owner.

The old violin lay in a dusty case in a shop in Kolkata. Its owner, a music teacher named Mr. Sen, had stopped coming. The violin missed him.

One day, a girl named Rupa wandered in. She picked up the violin and drew the bow across the strings. A screech came out.

"Gently," said the violin, very quietly.

Rupa's eyes went wide. She tried again, slower. A soft, round note rang out.

She came every afternoon to practise. The violin taught her how to hold it and how to listen.

Months later, Mr. Sen passed by and heard music. He stepped inside and found Rupa playing his old violin. He sat down to listen, and after that he came every afternoon to teach her.
A sparrow guides a girl home through the fog. Can you tell it?

A thick white fog rolled into the hill town. Tashi was walking home from the shop with a bag of rice when she realised that she could not see the road.

"Which way?" she murmured. She turned in a circle.

A small sparrow landed on her shoulder. "Chirp," it said, and then, "Follow me."

Tashi blinked. "You can talk?"

"Only in fog," said the sparrow.

It hopped ahead, always a few steps in front, calling in a tiny voice. Tashi followed the sound past the prayer flags and the stone wall, until she saw the glow of her own kitchen window.

She scattered a handful of rice on the step. The sparrow ate happily and flew away.
Write a story for children aged 8 about a talking pencil case.

Aditi's pencil case was zipped shut, but it was never quiet. "Ahem," it said, one Monday morning in class. "Don't forget your homework."

Aditi nearly dropped her book. Nobody else heard.

"You can talk?" she whispered.

"Only to you," said the pencil case. "And I do hate it when you leave me on the bus."

Aditi felt a pang of guilt. She had left it on the bus twice that month.

At lunchtime, she opened it and found the ruler, pencil, and sharpener all giggling. They made a deal: she would always put it in her bag, and in exchange, it would remind her of her homework.

It worked, and her teacher was surprised.
I need a calm bedtime story about a firefly who lost her light.

Flicker the firefly woke one evening and found that her light would not switch on. She tried blinking, wiggling, and humming, but her tail stayed dark.

"I can't go to the party," she sighed. All the other fireflies were gathering by the lotus pond.

A frog named Bhim heard her sniffle. "Come and sit with me," he said. "Maybe you're just tired."

So Flicker sat on a lily pad. She watched the water ripple and the moon rise. Soon she felt her wings relax. Her tail gave a small glow, and then a bigger one.

She floated to the pond, where the others welcomed her. Her light twinkled in the night, steady and calm.
Make up a tale about a suitcase that wanted to see the world.

Mr. Rao's brown suitcase had never been anywhere. It lay under his bed for years, hearing him talk about trips he never took.

"I want to see the sea," the suitcase muttered. "I want to see mountains."

One day, Mr. Rao's granddaughter, Leela, came to stay. She pulled the suitcase out and said, "Grandpa, let's go somewhere."

They packed it with sandwiches and a map. They took a bus to the coast. The suitcase sat on the sand while Mr. Rao paddled in the waves.

"Ah," said the suitcase happily. The wind blew through its latch.

Mr. Rao came back with wet feet and a big smile and promised another trip next year.
A wind-up mouse wants to run a marathon; could you tell his story?

Marlo was a wind-up mouse who lived on a shelf in a children's room. He had a tiny key in his back, and every time someone turned it, he ran forty steps, and then he stopped.

One day, he watched a marathon on the television. "I could do that," he said.

His friend, a plastic giraffe, laughed. "Forty steps, Marlo."

But Marlo thought of a plan. He asked the dolls to take turns winding him. One by one, they twisted the key.

Marlo ran across the room, down the hall, and out onto the balcony, where a ribbon was tied between two chairs.

He broke through it. The toys cheered, and he took a long rest.
Describe in story form a tree that wanted to walk.

A banyan tree stood at the edge of a village in Tamil Nadu. For two hundred years, it had watched people come and go. It wanted, more than anything, to walk to the river.

One night, it spoke to a girl named Janani, who was sitting in its shade. "I am so thirsty," it said.

Janani knew a tree could not walk. But she could carry water. Every day, she filled two buckets at the river and poured them around the roots.

The banyan drank deeply. In return, its leaves rustled stories to her about the old days, about kings and monsoon floods.

She did this every dry season, and the banyan stayed green.
Two clouds become best friends. Write it as a short tale.

Puff and Fluff were two clouds in a big blue sky. Puff was fat and round, and Fluff was long and thin. They drifted near each other every day.

One afternoon, a strong wind blew them apart. Puff floated west, over the hills. Fluff drifted east, over the sea.

They called to each other, but the wind swallowed their voices. Puff felt lonely, and so did Fluff.

Then the wind turned. Slowly, gently, it carried both clouds back toward the middle of the sky. Puff stretched out a wisp, and Fluff took it.

They joined together and became a big white cloud shaped like a heart, and the children below pointed up and laughed.
Rangoli that changed colour every morning; write a story around it.

Every morning, Latha drew a rangoli at her door with rice flour. One day, when she came out in the half-light, she saw that the pattern had changed on its own. The white petals had turned pink.

She blinked. The next morning, the petals were gold. The following day, they were deep blue.

Her neighbours came to see. "How is this possible?" they whispered.

Latha knelt down and touched a petal. It glowed softly. "I think it likes being looked at," she said.

So she drew bigger designs, with spirals and stars, and every dawn the colours glowed a little differently.

Children came from three streets away, just to see what the door would show.
There was an umbrella that was tired of being left behind; tell its story.

Mr. Kapoor's umbrella spent most sunny days in a stand by the door. It watched the clouds through the window and sighed.

"I'm only useful when it rains," it muttered, one bright morning.

Mr. Kapoor's daughter, Tia, heard it. "That's not true," she said, and took it to school. In the playground, the umbrella opened wide and gave shade to a boy named Faiz, who had forgotten his hat.

After that, it went along every day. It became a tent for a doll picnic, a sail for a toy boat, a roof for a sleepy cat.

When the monsoon finally came, the umbrella kept Tia dry, humming, because it had never felt more useful.
A girl paints a door on a brick wall and something answers. Write the story.

Rhea loved to paint, but her family's flat was small, and she had no canvas. So one Sunday, with her mother's permission, she painted a tall yellow door on the empty brick wall of the courtyard. She added a round brass knob and a tiny window.

Just for fun, she knocked. Knock, knock.

From the tiny window came a chirp. A painted sparrow looked out. "Thank you for the door," it said. "But we have a problem. There is no sky in here, and my family cannot fly."

Rhea thought about it. Then she painted a wide blue sky above the door, with soft white clouds.

At once, four little painted sparrows flew out of the window and swooped across the blue. They circled and settled on the clouds, singing.

Every morning after that, Rhea stood in the courtyard and listened to them.
Under 120 words, a story about a dragon who learns to knit.

Dragon Moss lived in a cold cave in the north. His claws were too big for gloves, and his tail was always freezing.

One day, he found a ball of wool and a pair of needles that a traveller had left behind. He picked them up. The needles snapped like twigs in his claws.

He tried a gentler grip, and slowly, a stitch appeared. Then another.

By spring, he had knitted a very long, very thick scarf, which wrapped three times around his tail. It was lumpy and uneven, but warm.

A village girl named Hema saw it and clapped. "Could you make one for my goat?"

Moss nodded happily and started a new row.
Our robot gardener needs to learn patience, so write that story.

Robot Sprig was built to tend the rooftop garden of an apartment block in Chennai. He watered the plants, pulled weeds, and measured the soil. But he was always impatient. Every morning he checked the tomato seeds and said, "Nothing."

"They grow slowly," said an old lady named Mrs. Nair, who lived on the floor below.

"I want results," said Sprig.

Mrs. Nair sat beside him on a bench with her tea. "Look at the sky instead," she said.

Sprig looked at the sky for a while. Then at the clouds. Then at a sparrow.

When he turned back to the tomatoes, a tiny green shoot had pushed through, and he blinked his lights in wonder.
Children follow a map drawn on a banana leaf; write it as a story.

During the harvest festival in a village in Kerala, Adil and his cousin Remya found a banana leaf pinned to the door of the old granary. Someone had scratched a map into it, with a coconut tree, a pond, and a big arrow.

They followed it along the edge of the paddy fields and past the coconut tree. But then the arrow pointed straight into thick bushes, and there was no path at all.

"Maybe the map is wrong," said Adil.

Remya turned the leaf round. "No. We were holding it upside down."

They laughed and followed it the right way. It led them back through the village to their own grandmother's courtyard. There, under a string of lights, the whole family was waiting with plates of payasam and a new swing tied to the jackfruit tree.

"You found it," said their grandmother. "That was this year's festival game."
Write a happy story about a kite festival and a kid who couldn't get his kite up.

Ishaan stood in the field with his kite while everyone else's kites danced above him. His own flopped on the ground, again and again.

"Run faster!" shouted his cousin.

He ran, and the kite crashed.

An old woman named Dadi sat on a bench nearby. "May I?" she asked. She felt the kite's frame and pointed to the string. "The knot is too far down."

She retied it, with fingers that moved quickly. "Now wait for a breeze."

Ishaan stood still. He felt a cool wind on his cheek. He let go, and the kite leaped up.

It rose slowly, then steadily, until it was just a bright dot. Dadi clapped, and so did Ishaan.
Bedtime story needed: a sleepy elephant who cannot find his pillow.

Ellu the elephant was very sleepy, but he could not find his pillow anywhere. It was a big, round pillow, stuffed with soft moss.

He looked under the banyan tree. He looked by the river. He asked the monkeys, who were swinging in the branches. "We haven't seen it," they chirped.

At last, Ellu looked behind his own ear. A small mouse named Chintu was curled there, fast asleep, with the pillow beneath his head.

"Oh," whispered Ellu. He did not want to wake him.

So he lay down very gently, leaving the pillow where it was, and rested his big head on a pile of leaves. In moments, both of them were snoring.
How about a scarecrow who wants to be useful in a different way?

A scarecrow named Bhola stood in a field of corn. His job was to scare crows. But the crows were not afraid of him, and they had no trouble at all. They sat on his hat and told him jokes.

"I'm not good at this," he said to a girl named Nila, who was bringing lunch to her father.

"Maybe you're good at something else," said Nila.

That evening, rain started. Nila's little brother was caught outside. Bhola could not walk, but his arms were stretched wide, with an old raincoat hanging from them. "Over here!" he called, and the boy ran to him and crouched underneath it.

Bhola kept him dry until his father came. The crows were quiet that night.
Tell a story about a seashell that remembers every song it has heard.

On a quiet beach in Odisha, a girl named Bini picked up a pink seashell and held it to her ear. She expected to hear the sea. Instead, she heard a lullaby.

"What song is that?" she asked.

The shell hummed. "A fisherman sang it to his baby, long ago, on this very shore. I never forgot."

Bini listened to it again. Then she hummed along.

Day after day, she came back to the shell. She learned the lullaby, the fisherman's boat song, and a sailor's whistle.

When her little cousin was born, Bini sat beside the cradle and sang the old lullaby. The baby fell asleep with a tiny smile.
A stray cat and a girl share a secret; story, please.

A scrawny, orange cat started following Padma home from school. She named him Laddoo and fed him bits of her lunch behind the water tank.

But Padma's mother did not allow animals in the flat. Padma kept the secret for a week, then two. Laddoo waited for her every afternoon, purring.

One rainy evening, he wasn't there. Padma searched the lane, calling his name. She found him curled in a cardboard box, shivering.

She picked him up and carried him straight home. Her mother opened the door, ready to scold, and then saw the wet cat.

"Hmm," she said, and fetched a towel. Laddoo stayed, curled on a cushion, for good.
A boy climbs a ladder to the moon. Write that.

Teddy could not fall asleep. He had counted sheep and turned his pillow over twice, but his eyes stayed wide open.

At last he drifted into a dream. In the dream, a silver ladder stood beside his bed. It went up through the ceiling, past the clouds, and ended at a small, round door.

Teddy climbed, rung by rung, and knocked. A woman with a round, glowing face opened it. "Come in," said the Moon. "Mind the craters."

She showed him her kitchen, where moonbeams were kept in jars. She poured one into a cup. "This is what I drink when I can't sleep," she said.

Teddy sipped. It tasted like warm vanilla milk. He gave a great big yawn, and the dream grew soft and quiet. In the morning, he woke up late, feeling wonderfully rested.
At a market, a vendor sells dreams. Write the story of a bargain there.

In the Sunday market, between the vegetable stall and the bangle shop, there was a tiny stall that sold dreams. A sign read: "Dreams, two rupees each."

Nikhil, who was ten, had only one rupee. He wanted the flying dream in the blue jar for his little sister, Riya, who had been in bed with a cold all week and was very bored.

"One rupee buys half a dream," said the old seller, Mr. Das.

Nikhil thought. "What if I sweep your stall as well?"

Mr. Das looked at the dusty ground and laughed. "That is a fair bargain."

Nikhil swept until the stall was spotless. Mr. Das handed him the blue jar, and that night Riya dreamt that she flew over the market with a kite for wings.

The next morning, she sat up in bed and asked, "Can we go to the market on Sunday?"
Story idea: a girl who talks to her vegetable garden and it talks back.

Anjali had a small vegetable garden on the roof. She was shy at school, but out there, among the beans and brinjals, she chatted away.

"Good morning, tomatoes," she said. "Did you sleep well?"

One day, a very small voice answered, "Not really. It was windy."

She stared at the tomato plant. It rustled its leaves.

"Thank you for asking," said the plant. "No one ever does."

After that, Anjali asked each plant how it felt, and she moved the pots out of the wind, and watered the thirsty ones first. The vegetables grew fat and glossy.

At school, she found it was easier to ask classmates how they were, too.
Write about a rag doll that dreams of being a ballerina.

Ragna the rag doll lived in a basket of old toys. She had button eyes and floppy arms, and every night, when the house was quiet, she practised ballet in the moonlight.

She spun and wobbled. She fell over a lot. The other toys giggled kindly.

One evening, a small girl named Ila tiptoed in and saw her. She did not scream or run. She sat very still and watched.

Ragna took a breath, rose on tiptoes, and turned slowly, three times, without falling.

Ila clapped softly. In the morning, she sewed a tiny pink tutu from an old scarf and slipped it onto Ragna, who wore it proudly.
A little bus conductor finds a golden ticket; make up that story.

Sunil was twelve and spent his holidays helping his uncle Mahesh, who drove a city bus. Sunil rang the bell and called out the stops. His uncle worked every day and had not had a holiday in years.

One evening, while sweeping the floor, Sunil found a shiny gold ticket under a seat. It said, "One free ride to anywhere, for the driver."

"It's for you, Uncle," said Sunil.

His uncle laughed. But the next evening, after the last passenger got off, the bus did not turn at the bridge. It rolled onto a road neither of them knew, between fields of sunflowers and over a rainbow bridge, into a town made of toffee.

Uncle Mahesh sat by a lemonade fountain with his feet up and laughed all afternoon. At sunset, the bus drove them home. The ticket had faded to plain paper, but Sunil kept it in his pocket.
There is a parrot who knows just one word. Can you write a story about him?

Gopi's parrot, Mitthu, knew only one word: "Namaste." He said it to the postman, to the milkman, and to the grumpy neighbour next door.

"Is that all you can say?" asked Gopi.

"Namaste," said Mitthu, cheerfully.

One evening, the neighbour, Mr. Verma, came by looking sad. His wife was away, and the house was too quiet.

Mitthu hopped onto the fence. "Namaste!" he called.

Mr. Verma jumped. Then he laughed. "Namaste to you, too," he replied.

Every evening after that, Mr. Verma stopped by the fence and chatted with the bird for a while. Gopi noticed that he hardly looked grumpy anymore.
A lost river needs help finding the sea. Write it.

A little river called Rani flowed through a forest in the Western Ghats. One spring, a landslide blocked her path, and she spread out in a muddy pool, confused.

"Which way is the sea?" she asked the trees.

"We don't know," said the trees. "We stay in one place."

A young goat herder named Suresh heard her. He was only thirteen, but he knew the hills. He climbed up the bank and cleared away a few stones with his stick. A thin trickle slipped through.

Rani followed the trickle, which grew into a stream. She wound through fields and villages. At last, she tumbled into the wide, blue sea, and sparkled all the way.
For seven-year-olds, please, a story about a chalk that drew by itself.

In Class Three, there was a piece of white chalk on the teacher's desk. When everyone had gone home, it stood up and began to draw on the blackboard.

First, a small house. Then a tree. Then a sun with a smiling face.

In the morning, Miss Rekha came in and gasped. "Who did this?"

The children giggled. They thought she had done it herself.

The next night, the chalk drew a river and a boat. Then it drew a whale.

Miss Rekha stayed late to watch. She saw the chalk working in the dim light, humming.

"Well," she said, "I'll leave the board clean for you."

So she did, every night, and the chalk was glad.
What did a tiffin box do when it went travelling on its own? Tell me.

Kunal's tiffin box was tired of being carried. One morning, when Kunal left it on the bench, it grew two little legs and hopped off the platform and into a train.

It rode all the way to the end of the line, nibbling at its own chapati. At each station, it watched people hurry by.

When it reached the last stop, it looked around. A kind vendor named Abdul noticed a lonely little box standing there. "Whose are you?" he asked.

He read the name inside the lid, which said "Kunal, Class 5, Sunrise School." He phoned the school.

Kunal came running, and the tiffin box hopped into his arms, pleased with the adventure.
A boy's drumbeat brings the rain; write the story.

The farmers of a dry village in Gujarat waited for rain. It had not come in months, and the fields were cracked.

A boy named Hari had an old tabla. He liked to tap it on the doorstep. One afternoon, he beat out a slow, steady rhythm, thinking of nothing.

A grey cloud drifted above him. Then another. He kept drumming, soft and low.

The first drop landed on the tabla. Then more fell, tapping on rooftops and leaves, keeping time with him.

The villagers ran outside, laughing, holding out their hands. Hari kept playing as long as he could, until the whole village was shining and wet.
The smallest elephant and the tallest giraffe help each other. Please write a tale.

Pinto was the smallest elephant in the herd, and Gigi was the tallest giraffe on the plain. They often walked together, but they could never reach the same things.

Gigi could reach the highest leaves, but she could not drink at the low pond without bending down very far. Pinto could drink easily, but he could never reach the sweet leaves.

One hot day, they both felt cranky. Then Pinto had an idea. "I'll pull the low branches down for you," he said, "if you'll pass the high leaves to me."

Gigi nodded. They worked as a team. Pinto's trunk bent the branches, and Gigi's long neck lifted the leaves.

They both had a very good lunch.
Holi story, please, in which a girl invents a new colour.

On the morning of Holi, Shruti mixed her pots of colour on the terrace. She had red, yellow, blue, and green. She poured a little yellow into the blue, and then, to her surprise, the water turned a shimmering turquoise she had never seen.

"Look!" she called to her brother Rahul.

He peered at it. "It's like a peacock's neck."

They named it "mor." They mixed a whole bucket and ran downstairs to show the neighbours.

Soon, every child on the street wanted some. Shruti poured scoops into their palms, and each person left a bright blue-green handprint on the white wall of the building.

By evening, the wall looked like a painting of peacocks.
Could there be a story about a girl who collects stars in a jar?

Pia wanted a star for her bedroom, so one night she went out into the garden with an empty jam jar. She held it up toward the sky and waited.

A small, shiny star dropped in, as light as a moth. Pia screwed on the lid and carried it inside.

The star glowed softly on her shelf. But soon, it began to dim. It looked very sad.

"What's the matter?" whispered Pia.

"I miss the sky," said the star.

Pia nodded. She carried the jar back out to the garden and unscrewed the lid. The star floated out and rose, brighter and brighter, until it joined its friends.

Pia kept the empty jar, and each night she waved to it.
Aliens get lost near my town and ask for directions. What a story that would be.

A small silver spaceship landed behind the bus stand in a town in Madhya Pradesh. Two round, green aliens, Zib and Zab, stepped out, looking confused.
