"Excuse me," said Zib to a boy named Chetan, who was eating peanuts. "Where is the galaxy highway?"

Chetan stared. Then he shrugged. "I don't know about that. But there's a tea shop nearby. The owner knows everything."

They walked to the tea stall. Mr. Joshi poured three cups and listened to the story.

"Go up, up, past the big dipper, turn left at the red star," he said, as if it were the most normal thing.

The aliens thanked him and waved goodbye, and the spaceship zoomed away.
Write for a young child a story about kitchen utensils that come alive at night.

When the lights went out in Mrs. Menon's kitchen, the spoons yawned and stretched. The big pot rolled over. The kettle whistled a tiny tune.

"Tonight, we dance!" said the ladle.

They clanged and tinkled on the counter. The plates twirled. The sieve wore a tea strainer as a hat.

But the pressure cooker, who was old and tired, sat in the corner. "I can't dance," he sighed. "I only whistle."

"That's perfect," said the spoons. "We need music."

So the pressure cooker whistled, long and loud, and all the utensils danced until sunrise.

In the morning, Mrs. Menon found everything neatly in place, but the kettle was still warm, and the spoons looked sleepy.
Could you invent a tale about a clock tower that gave away spare minutes?

The clock tower in Dharampur had a secret. Every evening at six, it let a few spare minutes drip from its hands like honey.

Most people never noticed. But a boy named Yash, who was always late, caught one in his palm. It was warm and tiny, shaped like a seed.

"What's this?" he asked.

"A spare minute," said the tower, with a deep gong. "Use it well."

The next morning, Yash was running behind again. He remembered the seed and let it open. Time seemed to stretch. He tied his shoes, packed his bag, and had a moment left over to wave to the dog.

He reached school early. Then he came to the tower every evening and held out both hands.
I need a story for my niece about a dragon who is afraid of fireworks.

Dragon Basil was proud of his fire, but he hated the noise of fireworks. Every Diwali, he hid in his cave and covered his ears with his wings.

This year, a girl named Charvi came up the hill with her father and a box of sparklers. "Would you like to try?" she asked.

Basil peeked out. Her father lit a sparkler, and it fizzed softly, throwing tiny stars. It made no bang at all.

"It's pretty," he said.

Her father lit another, and Charvi passed it to him. He held it carefully in a claw and waved it in the air, making a glowing circle.

That night, Basil sat on the hilltop with Charvi, writing his name in light.
My son loves robots. Please tell a story about one that wanted to dance, with a happy ending.

Robot Tin-Tin worked in a school canteen in Hyderabad, stacking plates. Every afternoon, the dance group practised across the hall, and Tin-Tin tapped his metal foot. He longed to join in, but his legs were made for standing still.

On the day of the school show, the music player stopped in the middle of the dance. The dancers froze on the stage, and the hall went quiet.

Tin-Tin rolled to the side of the stage with two steel spoons. Clink-clink, clink. He tapped out the beat on a tray, exactly as he had heard it every day.

A girl named Sahana grinned and started to dance again. The others followed. Tin-Tin swayed his arms and clinked, and his eyes glowed gold.

When it ended, the whole hall clapped. After that, Tin-Tin played the beat for the dance group every week, and sometimes he danced a little, too.
Can you set a story in Kolkata where a girl finds a treasure map in her grandmother's attic?

In her grandmother's old house in Kolkata, Ananya went up to the attic to look for a lost umbrella. Behind a trunk of saris, she found a rolled-up map, tied with a ribbon. It showed the house, the lane, and a big X in the garden, next to the words "My treasure."

Ananya hurried down with a spoon to dig. But the X was in the middle of a huge jackfruit tree, and there was nowhere to dig at all.

"The map is wrong," she told her grandmother, Thamma.

Thamma looked at the map and began to laugh. "I drew this when I was seven," she said. "I planted a jackfruit seed right there. That seed was my treasure."

Ananya looked up at the big fruits hanging from the branches.

That evening, Thamma cut a ripe jackfruit, and they ate it on the veranda, sticky-fingered and happy.
Zig the kite and a girl argue about everything; write their tale.

Zig the kite and Nasreen did not agree on anything. She said left, and he said right. She wanted to fly in the morning, and he wanted to wait for the evening.

"You're so stubborn," said Nasreen one windy Saturday.

"You're bossy," said Zig.

They glared at each other. Then the wind picked up, and Zig tugged on the string so hard that Nasreen was pulled across the field.

"Stop!" she cried, laughing in spite of herself. "Okay, okay, what do you want to do?"

"Go up," said Zig.

"Fine. But I'll steer."

"Deal."

They flew together all afternoon, her pulling, him tugging, until the sun went down and neither of them could remember what the argument had been about.
What about a story where a magic paintbrush only paints things that are kind?

Old Mrs. Bose owned a silver paintbrush that was very fussy. It would not paint anything unkind. Once, her grandson Tito tried to draw a scary monster, and the brush made it a gentle one with a tiny red ribbon.

"Why won't it paint what I want?" grumbled Tito.

"It paints what helps," said Mrs. Bose.

The next week, a storm tore the roof off the neighbour's shed. Tito picked up the brush and wished. A new tin roof gleamed above the shed, solid and bright.

The neighbour, Mr. Pillai, stared. Then he laughed with joy. He gave Tito a bag of guavas.

Tito carried them home, and the brush glowed softly in its jar.
A polite ghost-shaped cloud visits a village. Can you write what happens?

A small white cloud shaped like a ghost drifted down into the village of Kanhapur and settled on the temple roof. The villagers gasped.

"Good morning," said the cloud, in a soft, polite voice. "I'm sorry to trouble you. I'm lost."

The village head, Mr. Patil, bowed. "Where are you going?"

"To the mountains. But I took a wrong turn."

A boy named Dilip, who liked maps, pointed north. "That way. Follow the river."

"Thank you, young man," said the cloud.

The villagers brought a plate of sweets and set it on the roof, in case a cloud could eat. In the morning, the plate was empty, and a little shower of cool rain fell on the fields.
A story, please, about a worm who wanted to become a butterfly overnight.

Wally the worm watched the butterflies float above the flowers and sighed. "I want wings," he said.

"You have to wait," said a ladybird. "It takes weeks."

"I can't wait," said Wally. That night, he wrapped himself in a leaf, closed his eyes, and wished as hard as he could.

In the morning, he unwrapped. He was still a worm.

A girl named Ruhi came by with her watering can. She saw him looking glum. "Maybe you're not a butterfly worm," she said. "Maybe you're a glow-worm."

That night, Wally sat on a mushroom, and when the dark came, his tail glowed a soft green. Ruhi smiled, and the fireflies came to say hello.
Any chance of a short tale about a fisherman's son and a dolphin?

Bala sat on his father's boat off the coast of Tamil Nadu, watching the nets. A grey dolphin leaped out of the water and landed with a splash.

"Hello," said Bala.

The dolphin clicked and whistled. Bala whistled back, badly.

Every morning after that, the dolphin swam beside the boat. Bala fed it small fish from the basket. He taught it to leap through a hoop made of rope.

One day, a strong wind rocked the boat, and the nets tangled around the motor. Bala's father shouted. The dolphin darted in and nudged the net free with its nose.

The boat steadied. Bala hugged his father, and they waved at the dolphin all the way to shore.
I want a bedtime tale about a sleepy owl who kept waking up in the day.

Olly the owl was always awake at the wrong time. When the sun shone, he blinked and yawned. When the moon rose, he nodded off.

"You're supposed to hoot at night," said his mother.

"I know," said Olly. "But my eyes won't open."

One evening, a tiny cricket named Chirpy sat beside him. "I'll tell you a trick," she said. "Listen to the night, and it will wake you up."

Olly listened. He heard a frog croak. He heard leaves whisper. He heard the stream gurgle.

Slowly, his eyes opened wide. He spread his wings and flew silently over the moonlit forest. In the morning, he slept in a hollow tree until dusk.
Write something funny about a vegetable seller whose pumpkins rolled away on their own.

Mr. Gupta's pumpkins were the biggest in the market, and also the naughtiest. Every time he turned his back, one of them rolled off.

On Monday, a pumpkin escaped down the lane and landed in a flower stall. On Tuesday, two rolled under a bus. On Wednesday, three bumped down the steps of the temple.

His niece, Mona, had an idea. She tied a long string to every pumpkin and fastened the other ends to a stick. Now, when a pumpkin rolled, it stopped with a jerk and bounced back.

Mr. Gupta watched the pumpkins bounce at the ends of their strings. "They look like balloons," he laughed.

People came from three streets away to see.
A new kid at school finds a talking globe in the library. Please write the story.

Ken was new at school and had no one to sit with at lunch. So he went to the library. In a quiet corner stood an old globe on a wooden stand.

"Spin me," said the globe.

Ken blinked. "Did you just talk?"

"I did. I've been waiting forty years for someone to spin me."

Ken turned the globe slowly. "Where would you like to stop?"

"Anywhere," said the globe. "Tell me something about wherever you land."

He stopped it on Brazil. They talked about rainforests. Then Japan, then Kenya.

The next day, a classmate named Dhruv wandered in, curious. Soon three children were spinning the globe together, asking where to go next.
Write me a story set on a monsoon evening where a frog gives a girl a ride.

It was pouring in Mumbai, and Fatima had forgotten her umbrella. She stood under a shop awning, watching the water rush down the street.

A green frog the size of a teapot hopped up beside her. "Need a lift?" he asked.

Fatima blinked. "A talking frog?"

"Monsoon is when I'm most chatty," he said. "Hop on."

Fatima climbed onto his back, which felt cool and slick. With a great leap, they bounded over a puddle, across a pavement, and past a row of parked scooters.

The frog set her down at her building gate. "Mind the step," he said politely.

Fatima thanked him and went up the stairs, dry as a bone.
A squirrel helps a boy who has lost his courage; can you tell that story?

Aman was supposed to sing at the school concert, but his courage had gone missing. He looked in his bag and under his bed. It was nowhere.

He sat under a tree in the playground, feeling hopeless. A squirrel scampered down the trunk.

"What are you looking for?" asked the squirrel.

"My courage," said Aman.

The squirrel tilted her head. "I found something shiny yesterday," she said, and returned with a small brass button.

Aman held it. It felt warm. He knew it wasn't really his courage, but he put it in his pocket anyway.

On stage, with one hand around the button, he sang softly, then louder, and when he finished, the hall rang with applause.
Give me a story about a mango that did not want to be eaten.

In a basket of fruit sat a very plump mango named Aamu. He was the juiciest, the yellowest, and the most scared.

"I don't want to be eaten," he whispered to the bananas.

"Everyone gets eaten," said a banana. "It's what we're for."

Aamu wasn't convinced. When a girl named Pallavi reached for him, he rolled to the back of the basket.

Pallavi laughed. "Come out. I'm only going to share you with my brother."

Aamu thought about that. He peeked out. Pallavi's brother, Kunal, was waiting with two spoons, grinning.

"Fine," said Aamu, and he let her pick him up. The children ate him together on the veranda, and afterwards, they planted his seed in the garden.
Could a camel caravan find a talking oasis? Tell me a story.

A caravan of camels crossed the desert near Jaisalmer, carrying spices and cloth. The leader, an old trader named Ismail, was tired, and his water bags were almost empty.

At dusk, the camels stopped by a small pool in a hollow. "Welcome," said the water, in a bubbling voice. "I am the oasis."

Ismail sank to his knees. "Can we drink?"

"Of course," said the oasis. "But please share. The little birds are thirsty, too."

The traders filled their bags, and the camels drank deeply. A flock of sparrows splashed at the edge.

In the morning, the oasis gave a farewell bubble, and the caravan walked on, with fuller bags and lighter hearts.
Put a little girl and a robot in a three-legged race and tell the story.

Sports Day at Tara's school had a three-legged race, and Tara had no partner. Her usual friend was sick.

"I'll do it," said Beep, the school's helper robot, rolling up. He had only two wheels, but he could fold one to make a leg.

They tied a scarf around Tara's left ankle and Beep's right leg. The whistle blew.

At first, they wobbled and fell. "Left, right, left," counted Tara. Beep matched her count, and soon they moved in rhythm.

They passed the boys in blue. They passed the twins in red. At the finish line, they leaned forward together and crossed it a heartbeat before anyone else.

Tara hugged Beep, who hummed a happy beep.
What adventure might a lost sock have? Write the story.

Sunny the sock fell behind the washing machine. It was dark and dusty there, and he felt lonely.

He crawled out through a gap and found himself in the hallway. A real adventure began. He slid down the stairs, bumped across the porch, and was swept by a breeze into the garden.

A puppy named Gogo found him, and chewed him a bit. "Sorry," she said, "I thought you were a toy."

"It's okay," said Sunny. "I've always wanted to be played with."

They tugged back and forth until Gogo's owner, Reema, spotted them. She laughed and held up the sock. "So that's where it went!"

Sunny was washed and reunited with his twin.
Girl and robot build a telescope together; tell it as a story.

Hiral and her robot, Kiko, collected old lenses from the repair shop. Hiral wanted to see Saturn.

They rolled a long cardboard tube, painted it black inside, and fixed a lens at each end. Kiko held the tube steady while Hiral glued. Getting the lenses straight took a whole month.

The night they finished, the sky was clear. Hiral pointed the tube upwards and squinted. "I see something," she said.

Kiko adjusted the focus. A little yellow dot appeared, with a thin ring around it.

"It's Saturn," whispered Hiral.

Kiko's eyes blinked with joy. Hiral stepped aside and let him look.

"Beautiful," he said, in his rusty voice, and they stayed up until the moon was high, taking turns.
Set in a city park, a story of a crow who learns to be kind.

Kaku the crow lived in a park in Delhi. He was clever, but he was greedy. If anyone dropped food, he swooped down and grabbed it before the sparrows could.

One cold morning, a boy named Abhay dropped half a roti. Kaku pounced. But a small, thin sparrow had reached it first, and she looked up at him with tired eyes.

"I haven't eaten since yesterday," she said.

Kaku paused. He looked at the roti. Then he tore it in two and pushed the bigger half toward her.

The sparrow ate quickly. Abhay, who had been watching, dropped another piece for Kaku.

After that, Kaku always shared, and the sparrows welcomed him to their tree.
Christmas morning, a toy train comes to life; a story for a child of five, please.

On Christmas morning, Noel found a toy train under the tree. It was red, with a tiny gold bell. He wound it up, set it on the track, and watched it go round.

Then the train stopped and said, "Chuff chuff! Where am I going?"

"Round and round," said Noel.

"That's boring," said the train. "I want to see the kitchen!"

Noel lifted a corner of the track and led it to the kitchen, where his mother was baking. The train smelled cinnamon and sighed.

Then it went to the living room, to the hall, and to the cat's bowl.

By afternoon, the train had visited every room. Noel set it by the tree, and it fell asleep, humming.
Calm story for a toddler: a little cloud who wanted a blanket.

Little Cloud floated alone in a large sky. The wind blew cold, and he shivered.

"I need a blanket," he said.

A friendly bird flew by. "Try the sunset," she said. "It's warm."

So Little Cloud drifted to the edge of the sky, where the sun was going down. The colours spread out like a soft orange quilt. He snuggled into them.

"Ahh," he sighed.

Slowly, the pink and gold wrapped around him. His shivering stopped. Below, a little boy named Neel looked up from his window and saw a cloud with a golden edge.

"Goodnight, cloud," he whispered, and he pulled up his own blanket and closed his eyes.
A stone dreams of being a mountain. Write that story.

A small grey stone lay beside a stream in Himachal. Day after day, she watched the great mountains and wished she could be one.

"You're only a pebble," said the stream, as it bubbled past.

A girl named Meghna, who was hiking with her uncle, picked up the stone. She turned it in her hand. "It's smooth," she said. "And it fits my palm."

She took it home and set it on her desk beside her pencil box. Whenever Meghna did her homework, the stone sat close by, steady and warm.

In the evenings, Meghna would hold it and look at a picture of mountains on her wall. The stone looked too, and felt a little bit like a mountain after all.
Please tell me a story about a little dragon and a little mouse on a tiny adventure.

Dara the dragon was exactly the size of a cat, and Mimi the mouse was exactly the size of a walnut. They met on a windowsill.

"I want to see the garden," said Mimi. "But it's so far."

"I could fly you," said Dara.

Mimi climbed aboard. Dara beat her wings, and up they went. They flew over the rose bed, the compost heap, and the washing line. A bumblebee buzzed by, and Mimi waved.

They landed on a sunflower. They ate a seed each and watched the clouds.

When the sun grew low, Dara carried Mimi back. They hugged, a small mouse and a small dragon, on the sill.

"Tomorrow, the pond," said Mimi.
A boy makes a rainbow with crayons for his sick grandmother; tell this as a story.

Naman's grandmother was staying in bed with a cold, and the sky outside her window was grey. She sighed and pulled the blanket up.

Naman wanted to cheer her up. He took out his crayons and a big sheet of paper. He drew a red arc, then orange, then yellow, then green, blue, and violet.

He taped it to her window. Light shone through the paper, throwing coloured stripes across the bed.

His grandmother looked at the wall and gasped. "A rainbow indoors!" she said.

She slowly sat up. She laughed and reached out to touch the colours dancing on her hand.

Naman climbed onto the bed beside her, and together they watched the rainbow shift as the clouds moved.
Can you do a story about a kite that learns to say thank you?

A purple kite named Pari soared over a seaside town in Gujarat. She had never said thank you to anyone. When Neha ran with the string, Pari just rose. When the wind lifted her, Pari just floated.

One day, a gust snapped her string. Pari spun wildly, afraid, down toward the sea.

Neha ran along the shore, along the wet sand, and caught the trailing tail just before it touched the water. She tugged Pari gently back to land and held her tight.

Pari was breathless. "Thank you," she said softly.

Neha smiled. "That's the first time you've said that."

"It won't be the last," said Pari. After that, she thanked the wind, the string, and the sky.
Compose a story about a stone bridge that hummed whenever a child crossed it.

The old stone bridge over the Jhelum had a habit nobody could explain. When a grown-up crossed, it stayed silent. When a child crossed, it hummed.

Little Safiya noticed it first, on her way to the bakery. She stopped halfway and put her ear to the railing. A low, warm note rose from the stones.

She told her brother Waseem, who did not believe her. He walked over it, and nothing happened. Then she took his hand, and he felt the hum in his shoes.

"It likes us," said Safiya.

Every morning after that, the two of them crossed slowly, and by the time they reached the far side, the bridge had hummed them a whole tune.
Give me a dragon who guards a library, written as a story with a title.

The Library Dragon

High on a hill stood a library, and in its cellar lived a dragon named Olwen. Her job was to keep the books warm in winter, and she took it seriously.

One snowy week, a boy named Ashok came in, shivering, with a frozen nose. He wanted a book about birds.

Olwen was shy, so she hid behind a shelf and breathed a gentle warm breath over the reading table. Ashok sat down and thawed. He found his book and read for hours.

When he left, he stopped at the cellar door and called, "Thank you!"

Olwen blushed so hard that her scales turned pink, and the next day, she left a bookmark by the door for him.
Garba in Ahmedabad: a robot who wants to learn it and ends up happy. Story, please.

Navratri had come to Ahmedabad, and every evening the lanes filled with music. A robot named Rotu watched from a balcony as the circles of dancers swayed in colourful skirts.

"I want to join," he said to the girl next door, Kinjal.

"You have wheels, Rotu."

"I can learn," he said.

Kinjal showed him the claps, the turns, the steps. Rotu's wheels slid, and he bumped her aunt. He tried walking on the pavement, and he nearly flattened a flower stall.

At last, Kinjal's uncle cut two flat boards and strapped them to his base. Rotu stepped lightly, one two three, clap.

By the last night of the festival, he was spinning in the circle, wearing a garland of marigolds.
A treasure map keeps changing its mind; write that story.

Zoe's treasure map was strange. She had found it in an old coat, and the lines would not stay still. When she looked at it in the morning, the X was near the park. In the evening, it had moved to the bakery.

"It's broken," she sighed to her brother Emil.

"Or it's following something," said Emil.

They tracked the X for three days. It hopped from the park to the bakery to the school to the fountain, always a little ahead.

On the fourth day, they sat down to rest by the fountain. The X lay exactly where they were sitting.

Zoe looked down. Under the bench was a small, carved box with a tiny brass bird inside. When Zoe wound it, it sang, and the X on the map faded away. She smiled at Emil, and they carried the bird home together.
An old man's best friend is a kite. Tell me a tale of the two.

Mr. Hamid was eighty, and his legs were weak. He lived on the top floor of a building in Lucknow, and he did not go out much. But he had a kite called Neelu, which he flew from the balcony every afternoon.

"Good day, Neelu," he said, letting the string run through his fingers.

"Good day, Hamid," the kite answered, riding high.

Neelu told him what she could see: the market, the river, the children racing bicycles. Mr. Hamid laughed and asked questions, as if he were out there walking beside her.

One afternoon, a small boy named Sahil waved from a window across the lane. Mr. Hamid waved back. The next day, Sahil came over, and brought his own kite to fly beside Neelu.
My daughter wants a story about a magic paintbrush that paints a bridge across a river.

Mira lived on one bank of a wide river, and her best friend Gauri lived on the other. The only bridge was far upstream, and it took two hours to walk there.

One morning, Mira found a thin brush with a golden handle, caught in a fisherman's net. She dipped it in the river and drew a line in the air.

The line hardened into a plank. She drew another. Soon a narrow bridge stretched across the water, painted in sunset colours.

She walked over it, slowly, holding the rail. Halfway, she saw Gauri on the far bank, running toward her, and they met in the middle with a hug.

The bridge stayed for the whole summer, and the fishermen called it Rainbow Walk.
Write a story, under 100 words, about a bullock cart that learned to fly.

Ramu's bullock cart rattled to the market every Thursday, loaded with brinjals. One Thursday, the road was flooded.

"We'll be late," said Ramu.

The bullock, Shyam, pawed the ground. The cart gave a creak, and its wheels began to spin. Slowly, it rose into the air.

Ramu clutched his basket. They floated over the flood, past the banyan tree, and over the market square.

They landed softly beside the sweet shop, just as the market opened. The shoppers stared.

"Fresh brinjals," said Ramu calmly. He sold every one by noon, and Shyam got an extra handful of hay.
A magic watering can makes things grow too fast. What happens? Write a story.

Prisha's grandfather gave her an old copper watering can. "Use it carefully," he said.

She watered a little marigold seed. In a minute, a flower shot up, tall as a door. She watered a second seed. A sunflower burst through the soil and bumped her head.

"Oh dear," said Prisha. She watered a patch of grass, and a hundred green blades sprouted all at once, tickling her feet.

By lunchtime, the garden was a jungle. Her grandfather had to tunnel in to find her.

"Too much?" he asked, laughing.

"Just a bit," said Prisha.

They spent the afternoon trimming and made bouquets for every neighbour on the street. After that, she used only one small sprinkle at a time.
He traded a shell for a wish; tell the story of that boy.

Sidharth found a spiral shell on the beach at Puri. When he put it to his ear, it said, "Trade me for a wish."

He thought for a while. He wanted a bicycle. He wanted ice cream. He wanted to be taller.

Then he saw a little boy at the water's edge, crying because a wave had washed away his sandcastle.

Sidharth turned to the shell. "I wish his castle was back."

The shell sighed softly. A wave rolled in and, instead of washing, it shaped the sand into towers and walls, even better than before.

The small boy stopped crying and clapped. Sidharth set the shell down. It had vanished, but he felt as warm as the sun.
Mole and bat swap homes for a day: write it up as a story.

Marcel the mole lived underground. Bria the bat lived high in a barn roof. One day, they were both curious.

"What's it like in the dark?" asked Bria.

"What's it like upstairs?" asked Marcel.

They traded. Bria crawled into the burrow and found it cozy but very dark, with no sky.

Marcel climbed into the rafters, nervous, and held on tight. When he looked down, the whole barn seemed to sway. The wind whistled through a gap.

By evening, they both missed home. They met at the barn door and swapped back.

"It was lovely," said Marcel.

"I prefer my roof," said Bria.

They slept soundly in their own beds, and talked about it for weeks.
Tell me how a girl painted the night sky on her ceiling.

Smita could not sleep. She lay in bed, staring at the white ceiling, wishing it was the night sky.

So one Saturday, she and her father painted it together. He stood on the ladder and made the ceiling the colour of midnight. Then Smita showed him where to add dots of yellow for stars, and a crescent moon over the door.

When the paint dried, she turned off the light and lay down. The stars glimmered softly in the dark.

Then, the moon on the ceiling gave a tiny smile. "Goodnight, Smita," it whispered.

"Goodnight," she said, and for the first time all week, her eyes closed before she finished counting the stars.
Eid story, please: a boy loses his goat and, in the end, finds him.

On the morning before Eid, Rafiq's goat, Chhotu, was missing. The gate was open. A trail of tiny hoofprints led down the lane.

Rafiq followed it past the mosque and the bakery. He asked a tailor, who had seen a goat nibbling a flower bed. He asked a baker, who had given a goat a crust.

At last, near the end of the street, he heard a happy bleat. Chhotu was standing in the courtyard of an old lady named Ammi Jaan, surrounded by flowers.

"He is no trouble," said Ammi Jaan, smiling. "He keeps my garden trimmed."

Rafiq led Chhotu home, and Ammi Jaan came to the Eid meal, bringing a basket of sweet sevaiyan.
A little wind wanted to be a storm. Can you make a story of that?

A little wind named Whisper blew across a field of corn in Haryana. He wanted to be a storm. He tried to blow louder, but he only ruffled a few tassels.

"You're too small," said the big wind from the north, whirling past.

Whisper kept trying. Day after day, he puffed and blew. The corn only swayed gently.

One hot afternoon, a boy named Jai was working in the field, sweating and tired. He sat down and wiped his forehead. Then Whisper blew softly across his face, cool and sweet.

Jai sighed. "Thank you, little breeze."

Whisper stopped. He had never been thanked before. He realised he liked being a breeze, and he stayed beside Jai until sundown.
Her shadow gets tired of copying everything she does. Write a story about the girl and her shadow.

Lucy's shadow was tired. Every day, it had to copy whatever she did. She raised an arm, it raised an arm. She hopped, it hopped.

One bright afternoon, it stayed put when Lucy ran. She looked down and saw her shadow sitting on the pavement with its arms crossed.

"I want a rest," it said.

Lucy sat down. "Okay. What do you want to do?"

"Something that I choose," said the shadow.

Lucy let it go first. The shadow stretched long, then short, then wide. It danced across the wall. It made a rabbit, then an eagle. Lucy copied each pose.

They traded like that all afternoon, taking turns, and the shadow felt much better by sunset.
A toy soldier who hates fighting; could you tell his story?

Captain Tim was a tin soldier in a box of toys. He had a bright red coat and a tiny drum. But he did not like marching, and he did not like pretend battles.

"I want to bake," he whispered to the teddy bear.

The teddy giggled. "A soldier who bakes?"

One night, when the girl who owned them, Kritika, was asleep, Tim crept to the toy kitchen. He mixed flour and sand in a plastic bowl and baked tiny imaginary cakes.

In the morning, Kritika found six pretend cakes on a plate, with Tim standing proudly beside them.

"Captain Tim, the baker!" she said, and put a little apron on him. From then on, he ran the toy bakery.
A boy too slow to win races finds out what he is good at; write it.

Sanjay was the slowest runner in his class. At the school race, he always came last, and the other kids clapped politely.

He did not mind much. What he liked was noticing things. While running, he saw the flowers at the track's edge, and a bird's nest in a tree.

One afternoon, a younger child dropped her bracelet during the race. Sanjay, trailing behind everyone, spotted it glinting in the grass. He picked it up and returned it.

"How did you see that?" asked the girl.

"I just look," said Sanjay.

The sports teacher heard this and asked him to run the lost-and-found stall at sports day. Sanjay found twelve lost things that afternoon.
Two raindrops race down a window. Write the story.

Drip and Drop were two raindrops sliding down the window of a school bus. They had agreed to race to the bottom.

"Ready, steady, go!" said Drip.

They slid. Drip went straight. Drop wobbled left, then right. A tiny speck of dust caught him.

"Wait!" Drop called. "I'm stuck!"

Drip paused. Winning would be easy now, but it felt lonely. So he slid back up a bit and joined Drop, and together they grew heavy and round, and rolled past the dust.

At the bottom of the window, they reached the edge at the very same moment and dripped off together onto the road.

A girl on the bus, named Zara, had been watching. She smiled, because it was a tie.
Imagine the characters in a comic book stepping out onto a boy's desk, and write that.

Vishal opened his comic book and found the hero, a tiny cape-wearing mouse called Captain Whisker, waving from the page.

"Help!" squeaked the mouse. "The villain stole the cheese!"

Vishal blinked. "You want me to help?"

"You're the only reader who's still awake."

The villain, a grumpy grey cat, jumped out onto the desk with a sack of cheese. He was smaller than Vishal's thumb.

Vishal gently set his pencil case in front of him as a barrier. The cat tripped, dropped the sack, and Captain Whisker grabbed it.

"Thanks," said the mouse. He and the cat both climbed back onto their pages, and Vishal turned to the next one, grinning.
An owl gives directions to lost travellers; could you tell that as a story?

At the crossing of two forest paths, an old owl named Ghughu sat in a tree and gave directions. Travellers came from all over, tired and confused.

One day, a family on a cart stopped below her. "Which way to the river?" asked the father.

"Take the left path, then the second turn," said Ghughu.

Later that afternoon, a young man named Imtiaz stopped, looking scared. He was alone, and he had lost his way in the dusk.

"Where are you going?" asked the owl.

"Home. To the village of Nilgiri."

"Straight ahead until you see a lantern," said Ghughu.

Imtiaz followed it, and reached his door before dark, with a heart full of thanks.
An old toy seller at a fair would make a gentle story, please.

Old Mr. Ghosh sold toys at the village fair. His stall was small, with wooden horses, paper pinwheels, and clay birds that whistled when you blew in them.

Business was slow. Children walked past, pulled by the bright plastic things at the next stall.

Then a girl named Rupal stopped. She picked up a clay bird and blew. It sang a sweet, high note.

"I'll take it," she said, giving him her last coin.

She blew it all the way down the lane, and children turned their heads. One by one, they came to his stall, wanting a bird of their own.

By evening, Mr. Ghosh had sold everything. He packed his empty crate, humming softly himself.
Nothing scary, please: a bicycle takes a girl on a wonderful ride.

Gita's old blue bicycle had a squeaky bell. One morning, it said, "Hop on. I'll show you something."

She climbed on. The pedals moved by themselves, gently, and the bicycle rolled down the lane. It crossed a field of mustard flowers and a stream. It rolled up a hill she had never noticed.

At the top, she saw a wide, golden valley, with a river like a ribbon.

"Is this real?" she asked.

"It's been here all the time," said the bicycle. "You just never rode this far."

They stayed until the sun began to set. Then they rolled home, slowly, and Gita parked the bicycle in the shed with a pat.
A bedtime story where a sleepy bear in a cave gets visitors would be lovely.

Boru the bear was trying to sleep for the winter. He curled up in his cave and closed his eyes.

Tap, tap. A little rabbit stood at the door. "It's cold out here," she said.

"Come in," murmured Boru, and moved over.

Tap, tap. A hedgehog arrived, then a family of mice. Boru made room for all of them against his warm, furry belly.

By midnight, the cave was full of small, snoring animals. Boru did not mind. In fact, he felt warmer than ever.

When spring arrived and the snow melted, they all woke up together. They stretched, yawned, and thanked him for the shelter. Boru smiled sleepily, and gave each one a tiny pat.
A moon rabbit comes to Earth to try laddoos; write about it.

Up on the Moon lived a rabbit named Chandu. All he ever ate was moon-cheese, and he was tired of it. He had heard that people on Earth made laddoos, round and golden.

One night, he hopped down a moonbeam and landed on a rooftop in Varanasi, next to a girl named Radhika, who was studying by the light of a lamp.

"A rabbit!" she said.

"Please, have you any laddoos?" asked Chandu politely.

Radhika went down and came back with a plate. Chandu ate one slowly. "This," he whispered, "is better than cheese."

She gave him two to carry home. In the morning, the Moon looked slightly rounder, and Radhika smiled up at it.
There is a plant in a classroom that listens when children read. Story, please.

In Class Four, there was a small green plant on the windowsill. It listened when the children read aloud. Nobody knew that it understood.

One day, a boy named Varun stumbled over a hard word, and the other children laughed. His ears turned red.

That afternoon, when everyone had gone, Varun stayed behind and read the page again, quietly, to the plant. He got the word right on the third try.

A new leaf unfurled, shiny and pale.

Every day, Varun read to the plant for ten minutes. His reading grew smoother, and by the end of the term, he was the first to raise his hand.

The plant had grown so tall that it needed a bigger pot.
Keep it light: a crocodile who wants to be friends with a bird.

Crocky the crocodile lay in a muddy river, feeling lonely. Every other animal kept away from his big teeth.

A small plover bird, named Pipi, hopped onto his back one morning. "Excuse me," she said. "You have bugs on your teeth. May I?"

Crocky was astonished. "You are not afraid?"

"A little," said Pipi. "But I'm hungry, too."

She picked the bugs out carefully, one by one. Crocky held his mouth open very still, trying not to sneeze.

After that, Pipi visited every morning. She chatted while she worked, and Crocky listened to her stories about the sky.

They became so friendly that the other animals began to wonder if they, too, had been too shy.
Family of ants, one very heavy crumb. Make it a sweet story.

Amma Ant found a giant crumb of cake on the kitchen floor. It was as big as a boulder.

"We must take it home," she said, and called the whole family.

They pushed. They pulled. The crumb did not move.

Little Anu, the smallest ant, ran around to the other side. "What if we tilt it?" she said. They tried it, and the crumb rolled a bit.

All the ants cheered. They heaved together, and step by step, the crumb rolled across the tiles, through a crack, and into the nest.

That evening, the whole family sat around it and shared sweet, sugary bites. Anu got the biggest piece because it had been her idea, and she fell asleep with icing on her face.
Boy, bedroom, tiny door in the skirting board: write the story.

Aryan noticed a tiny door in the skirting board of his bedroom. It was no bigger than a matchbox, painted green, with a brass knocker.

He knocked, gently. Nothing.

He left a crumb of biscuit in front of it. In the morning, the crumb was gone, and a tiny note stood in its place. It was written in thin silver ink: "Thank you. Do you have a button?"

Aryan found a small blue one and slid it under the door.

The next day, there was another note: "A button is useful for a table. Please accept this." And beside it, a tiny wooden stool, which fit on the tip of his finger.

He kept the stool on his shelf and the door a secret.
On Diwali night, a little girl meets a talking diya; write the story.

Aarohi was setting out diyas on the veranda when one of them spoke. "I'm the smallest," it said. "Nobody will see me."

"I'll see you," said Aarohi.

"But the big ones shine brighter."

Aarohi thought for a moment. She picked up the small diya and set it on the path that led to the gate, far from the others.

At nightfall, her grandfather came home from the temple in the dark. He stepped carefully, then saw the little flame at the end of the path, and then another beyond it. He followed the lights, one after another, all the way to the door.

"Whose idea was this?" he asked.

The little diya flickered proudly.
Can you write about a compass that pointed to whatever the holder needed most?

Jonah found a brass compass in a flea market. Its needle did not point north. When he held it, the needle swung toward the baker's shop.

"Silly thing," he said. But he followed it, and the baker, Mrs. Alvarez, handed him a warm roll, because his stomach had been growling all morning.

The next day, the needle spun toward the library. He went in and found the exact book he needed for his project.

On the third day, the needle pointed toward a bench in the park, where an old man sat alone. Jonah sat beside him and shared half a roll.

The man smiled and began to tell stories. When the needle finally settled, it pointed right at Jonah's own heart, and stayed there.
A girl herds clouds like sheep. Tell me her story.

Every dawn, Lakshmi climbed the hill behind her village with a long bamboo stick. She was the cloud herder, and her flock was grey and white.

She led them over the rice fields where the farmers waited for rain. She gently tapped the slowest ones with her stick.

One morning, a stubborn little cloud refused to move. He wanted to stay over the mango grove, where it was cool.

"You're needed at the paddy," said Lakshmi.

The cloud wouldn't budge. So she sat beside him and told him about the thirsty rice, and the frogs waiting to sing.

At last, he sighed and rolled along. By noon, a gentle rain fell on the paddy, and Lakshmi sat at the edge, drumming her stick on a rock.
Tell me about a very young wizard who lost his hat.

Wizard Pim was only seven, and his hat was too big. It slid over his eyes whenever he waved his wand. One windy day, a gust whisked it right off his head.

"My hat!" he cried.

It sailed over the village roofs. Pim ran after it, tripping on his long robe. A baker pointed upward. A cobbler shouted directions.

The hat landed on a goat's head in a farmyard. The goat chewed the tassel happily.

Pim stopped and thought of a spell, a very small one. "Come back," he whispered, and the hat floated gently into his hands.

He tucked a bit of paper inside the brim so it fit better, and he walked home with a dignified step, the goat trailing behind.
Could a mango tree sing when the monsoon came? Write that story.

Behind Mr. Rao's house in Mysuru stood a mango tree that was as old as the town. Nobody noticed that it sang until one monsoon afternoon, when a girl named Disha was sheltering beneath it.

The first raindrops hit the leaves, and a soft tune rose from the branches. It sounded like a flute, floating in the green air.

Disha closed her eyes. She heard the notes rise and fall, matching the rhythm of the rain.

When the rain stopped, so did the song. She ran home and told her parents, who didn't believe her.

The next monsoon, she brought them out to the tree. They stood quietly, and when the first drops fell, the mango tree began to sing.
Mermaid, bicycle, seaside. Make a story out of it.

Marina the mermaid had watched children ride bicycles along the seaside promenade. She wanted to try it more than anything.

One evening, she slipped out of the water and sat on the rocks. A boy named Ethan was walking by with his bike.

"Can I try?" she asked.

Ethan was surprised, but he held the seat steady. Marina wobbled. She had no feet to reach the pedals, only a long, shiny tail.

"Hmm," said Ethan. He looked around, found a skateboard, and balanced her tail on it. Then he pushed.

She glided gently along the pavement, giggling, with the salty wind in her hair.

They did it every Friday, and she always brought a seashell as a thank-you.
I would love a story about a giant with a tiny garden.

Grumble the giant was as tall as a church, but his garden was only the size of a doormat. He grew a single row of radishes, no taller than a thumb.

He wanted a bigger garden, but the soil in the valley was thin and full of rocks.

One day, a girl named Ela came to the fence. "Your radishes are so neat," she said.

Grumble blushed. "They're small."

"But they're yours," said Ela. "I could help you grow more, if you like. I have seeds."

She planted beans, and he watered them with a bucket. They grew into tall, green vines, which Grumble could finally stand proudly beside.

At harvest, they cooked a huge pot of soup and invited the whole village.
A shy rainbow doesn't want to come out; tell me what happens.

After a shower in Shillong, all the other rainbows stretched across the sky. But Ria the rainbow stayed behind a cloud.

"What if people don't like my colours?" she whispered.

A boy named Tenzing was playing in a puddle. He looked up. "Is somebody there?"

"No," said Ria.

"I think there is," said Tenzing. "I can see a bit of red."

Ria blushed. Her red got deeper.

Tenzing waited patiently. He sat down on a rock, and didn't ask anything else.

Slowly, the cloud drifted, and the rainbow stepped out. Orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. Her colours stretched from one hill to the next.

Tenzing laughed in delight. "It's beautiful," he said, and Ria stayed out until the sun set.
Make it kind: a story about a yeti who is afraid of people.

High up in the Himalayas lived a yeti named Yoru. He was big and furry and gentle, but he stayed hidden because he thought people would run from him.

One winter, a trekker named Mallika slipped on the ice and twisted her ankle. She sat in the snow with her teeth chattering.

Yoru watched from behind a rock. He wanted to help but was too scared.

Then he took a breath, stepped out slowly, and held out one huge, warm hand.

Mallika gasped, then smiled. "You're real!"

He lifted her gently and carried her down the mountain, to the edge of the village. He set her down and waved a shy goodbye.

Mallika told everyone about her friend, but no one believed her.
A magic pencil only corrects the kind mistakes. Write the story.

Rohit's eraser had worn down, but his pencil never made mistakes. That was because it was magic, and it fixed things before he knew.

When Rohit wrote a mean word about a classmate in his diary, the pencil turned it into "kind." When he wrote that he hated maths, it turned it into "I'm learning maths."

At first, he was annoyed. "I wanted to be angry," he muttered.

But over time, he noticed that his words made him feel better. He began to write nicer things on his own.

One day, he wrote a whole page, and the pencil changed nothing. It just lay quietly in his hand.

Rohit grinned. "Good job, pencil," he said, and sharpened it gently.
A cat dreams of being a pirate captain; please give it a happy ending.

Biscuit the cat lived on a houseboat in Alleppey. All day he watched the sea from the window and dreamed of being a pirate.

One morning, he found an old tricorn hat that a tourist had left behind. He put it on and strutted along the deck. "Ahoy!" he meowed.

The children from next door, Anil and Binu, laughed. "Captain Biscuit!" they cried.

They made him a crew: a toy duck, a wooden spoon, and a tin of sardines. They sailed around the deck, battling an imaginary sea monster, which was actually a coconut.

At sunset, Biscuit stood at the bow and gazed over the backwaters. "Yo ho ho," he purred.

He got a real fish dinner as a reward.
Write the tale of a paper crane that came to life and carried a message far away.

Hana folded a paper crane from a sheet of blue paper. On its wing, she wrote, "I miss you, Grandma."

Her grandmother lived far away in another country. The crane trembled in her hand, then fluttered its wings and rose.

"Where do I go?" it asked.

"Follow the sun," said Hana. "She lives where the sun sets."

The crane flew over rooftops and rivers, past mountains and lakes. It was tired when it reached a little house with a red door. It landed on the windowsill, where Hana's grandmother was drinking tea.

She read the message and smiled. She folded a crane of her own, writing, "I miss you, too."

The two cranes passed each other in the sky, and waved.
Fireflies deliver letters at night in a story I want you to write.

Lumi the firefly was the village post carrier after dark. She carried tiny letters, rolled up like grains of rice, from one window to another.

One night, she had an important letter for a boy named Tashi, who lived at the edge of the forest. It was from his father, who was away working in the city.

The path was dark and winding. Lumi's light was small, but it was enough. She followed the stream and passed the old stump.

At last, she tapped on Tashi's window. He opened it. She dropped the letter into his hands.

He read it by her glow. His father would be home on Sunday.

Lumi stayed until he finished, then flew off to her next delivery.
She drew a hopscotch grid and it led to another world; can you write that?

Sheetal drew a hopscotch grid on the pavement with a piece of yellow chalk. She hopped one, two, three, and on the fourth square, she vanished.

She found herself in a meadow where the grass was lilac. A rabbit in a waistcoat stood on its hind legs. "Welcome to Hopland," it said. "To go back, you must finish the game."

"How?" asked Sheetal.

"Hop through all ten squares without wobbling."

She hopped carefully, counting aloud. At square seven, she wobbled, but she caught her balance. At ten, she jumped high and landed with both feet.

She was back on the pavement, with the chalk in her hand. A small yellow flower had grown through the crack in square ten.
Inside a snow globe, a tiny town wakes at night. Write a story about it.

On Mrs. Pereira's shelf sat a snow globe. Inside was a tiny town, with a church, a bakery, and a lamp-post. During the day, nothing moved, but at midnight the snow swirled and a tiny baker opened his shop.

One night, her granddaughter Joy, who was too excited to sleep, crept downstairs to peek. The town was dark. The little lamp-post had gone out, and the baker stood in the snow, looking lost.

Joy looked around the room. On the table was her grandmother's reading lamp. She switched it on and turned it gently toward the shelf.

Warm light poured through the glass. The baker blinked, then waved. The townspeople came out, the snow sparkled, and the bakery windows glowed.

In the morning, Joy told her grandmother. Mrs. Pereira smiled and moved the snow globe next to the lamp, where it stayed from then on.
A balloon seller's balloons carry secrets up to the sky; story, please.

Mr. Bose sold balloons outside the zoo. Children loved them, but nobody knew that each balloon could carry a whisper.

A girl named Mahi bought a red one. She held it close and whispered, "I'm nervous about my recital tomorrow." Then she let go.

The balloon floated up, up, until it was a little red dot. A gentle breeze carried it past the clouds.

That night, in her dream, Mahi heard a soft voice: "You'll be fine, you practised."

At the recital, her fingers danced over the keys. She forgot her fear.

Afterwards, she bought another balloon, and this time she whispered, "Thank you," and watched it rise.

Mr. Bose smiled quietly from his stall.
How a tortoise carried a whole village on his back in a flood: tell it as a story.

When the river rose in the village of Bhatpara, the water came into the houses. Everyone ran to the high ground, but the old, the very young, and the sleepy were slow.

A tortoise named Dada lived by the riverbank. He was big, as wide as a cart, and he was not afraid of water.

"Climb on," he said.

The villagers hesitated. Then a small boy named Palash climbed onto his shell, followed by his grandmother, then a goat, then a basket of hens.

Dada paddled slowly and steadily to the hill. It took four trips.

When the water went down, the villagers decorated his shell with flowers. He lay in the sun and nibbled a cabbage, very pleased.
Funny one, please: a dragon eats too many sweets at a wedding.

Dragon Pappu was invited to a wedding in Amritsar. He sat politely in the corner, but the laddoos looked too good. He ate one, then ten, then fifty.

"Pappu," whispered the bride's aunt, "maybe slow down?"

"Mmm," said Pappu.

Soon his stomach grumbled loudly. He hiccupped, and a little puff of golden sparks flew out. It landed on the sweet table, and the barfis toasted lightly.

The guests laughed. "A warm barfi!" said the groom. "Delicious."

Pappu was embarrassed, but the bride patted his nose. "You've made the wedding memorable."

He drank a big glass of lassi and danced the bhangra, spinning slowly. By the end of the night, he was fast asleep under the mandap.
A shop sells a bit of courage by the spoon. Write a story about a visit there.

On the corner of Garden Road stood a tiny shop with a sign: "Courage, by the spoon." Eleven-year-old Aditya had never noticed it before.

He needed courage for a spelling bee. He stepped inside. A woman in a bright orange scarf was weighing something on a brass scale.

"What size spoon?" she asked.

"Just a small one," said Aditya.

She handed him a jar with a tiny wooden spoon. The jar was empty.

"It's empty," he said.

"Taste it," she smiled.

He put the spoon in his mouth, and it tasted of lemon and sunshine. He felt taller.

At the spelling bee, he spelled every word, even "necessary." Afterwards, he went to thank the woman, but the shop was gone.
Send a lantern boat down the river to find a friend, in story form.

Basu's best friend, Tarun, had moved to a town downriver. Basu missed him. He made a tiny boat from a banana leaf, put a candle in it, and wrote a note: "Come back and visit soon."

On the evening of the river festival, he placed the boat in the water and watched it drift off, its small flame bobbing.

It floated past the ghats, under a bridge, and through reeds. It slid between fishing boats. A heron watched it go.

Three days later, the boat arrived at the ghat of Tarun's town. A boy fishing there saw it and picked it up. It was Tarun.

He read the note, smiled, and wrote back on the other side. The reply came by bus: "I'm coming Sunday."

Basu waited at the station with a bag of peanuts.
Foxes are meant to be sneaky, but this one is honest. Write his story.

In the old stories, foxes were sneaky, but Rusty the fox was the worst at it. He could not tell a lie without blushing.

One day, his mother said, "A fox should know how to trick."

Rusty tried. He told a crow, "I have a lovely song for you, if you'll drop your cheese." But the crow saw him blushing and laughed.

He told a rabbit that the carrots were free. But he couldn't help adding, "Well, they're mine, but you can share."

The rabbit was so surprised, she brought him a basket of carrots the next day.

Rusty found that he didn't need tricks. Everyone in the forest liked him, and he never went hungry.
A kitten who thought the moon was a bowl of milk needs a story.

Mishti the kitten sat on the windowsill, watching a round, white moon in the sky. "Milk!" she purred.

She wanted it. She tried to climb the curtain. She tried to jump from the cupboard. But the moon stayed in the sky.

Her friend, an old dog named Bruno, shook his head. "That's not milk. That's the moon."

"It's a big bowl of milk," insisted Mishti.

The next evening, a girl named Naina saw her at the window. She poured some milk into a white saucer and set it on the sill, right under the moon's reflection.

Mishti lapped it up. "I knew it," she said, looking up proudly. The moon seemed to wink down at her.
There was a goat who learned to read; tell me about her.

Gita's goat, Bindi, followed her to school every day. She stood outside the window, listening to the lessons.

"A is for apple," the teacher said. Bindi chewed a leaf.

"B is for ball." She tilted her head.

At first, nobody noticed. But one day, a book fell out of Gita's bag, and Bindi, curious, nosed it open to a page with a picture of a tree.

"T," she said, in a soft bleat, because it was the first letter. The word read "tree."

Gita nearly dropped her slate. "She can read!"

The teacher, Mr. Nath, brought a chalkboard outside. Bindi learned five new words every week, and she nodded at each one.
At a fair, a lost child is helped by a talking horse on the merry-go-round. Write that.

Seven-year-old Kavi was lost at the fair. The crowd was thick, the music loud, and he had let go of his mother's hand to look at a bright red balloon.

He wandered to the merry-go-round and sat on the bench, trying not to cry.

"Psst," said a wooden horse, painted white with a gold saddle. "You look worried."

Kavi blinked. "Horses don't talk."

"This one does, when the ride is slow," said the horse. "Climb up. From here, you can see the whole fair."

Kavi climbed on, and as the ride turned, he scanned the crowd. At the third turn, he spotted his mother's yellow sari.

"There!" he cried, waving.

His mother ran over, and hugged him tight. The horse gave a tiny nod.
A girl serves tea to a very small dragon at a Himalayan tea stall; tell it as a story.

In a little tea stall in Darjeeling, nine-year-old Pema poured tea for travellers. One cold morning, a dragon the size of a puppy waddled in and sat on a stool.

"Tea, please," said the dragon, politely. "Extra hot."

Pema had never served a dragon before. She poured it into the smallest cup she had. He blew on it, and a little flame flickered over the surface.

"Perfect," he sighed.

He drank slowly, warming his claws. Pema watched, amazed. Then he left a gold scale on the counter as payment.

The next morning, he came back with two friends. By the end of the week, the stall was full of tiny dragons, sipping tea and chatting, with Pema pouring happily.
Kite shop owner helps a boy mend a torn kite. Please write that as a story.

Imran's kite had a tear across the middle. He carried it to Mr. Narayan's kite shop, hoping for a miracle.

"Hmm," said Mr. Narayan, peering over his spectacles. "A bad tear. But fixable."

He took out a thin sheet of tissue paper, a pot of paste, and a thin brush. "Watch."

Imran watched him cut a neat patch and press it down. His fingers were quick and steady. "The trick is not to hurry," said Mr. Narayan.

When the paste dried, the kite looked almost new, with a small pale patch like a cloud.

Imran flew it that very evening. It soared over the rooftops, tail swinging. The patch was invisible from below, but Imran knew where it was.
Write a short story about a girl whose wishes only came true if she shared them.

Pooja had a wishing stone that her aunt gave her. It was smooth and grey. "Make a wish," said her aunt. "But there's a rule."

Pooja wished for a chocolate cake. Nothing happened.

She wished for a puppy. Nothing again.

"What's the rule?" she asked.

"Wishes only work when they're shared," said her aunt.

Pooja thought. She turned to her little brother Bunty and said, "I wish we had a chocolate cake to share."

A moment later, a cake appeared on the table, with two forks. They both laughed.

Next, she wished that the whole family could have a picnic. A checked cloth landed on the grass, with sandwiches. Pooja ate, and no wish tasted better.
Overnight, a toy train set builds a new track by itself; write the story.

Aarav's toy train set sat on the floor in a loop, round and round. The little engine, Chhuk, was bored.

"Same circle every day," he muttered.

That night, when the house slept, the wooden rails began to wiggle. They stretched out of the circle and curled under the sofa, along the bookshelf, and across the doormat. The bridge block hopped over the cushion. The station slid to the end of the line.

In the morning, Aarav gasped. A grand track wound through the whole room, ending at his bed.

"Did you do this?" he asked, picking up the engine.

Chhuk said nothing, but his little funnel puffed one tiny cloud. Aarav grinned and set him at the start.
Bedtime story for a five-year-old: a dragon who can't find his cave in the dark.

Dragon Dudu flew home late one night, but the mountains all looked the same. He circled once, twice, three times.

"Where is my cave?" he whispered.

Below, a girl named Mili was walking home with her grandfather, a torch, and a goat on a rope. She heard him sniffle. "Are you lost?" she called up.

"My cave has a round door," said Dudu.

Mili thought. "There's a round door on the hill past the pond. I'll show you."

She walked ahead with her torch swinging. Dudu glided slowly behind her, wing-tips quivering.

At the round door, he sighed with relief. "Thank you, Mili."

She waved, and the goat bleated. Dudu curled up in his cave and was asleep before the torch was out of sight.
Teach a robot to laugh, with a toddler as the teacher, and write the story.

Robot Sam helped in a house in Bengaluru, folding clothes and watering plants. He could say a thousand things, but he had never laughed.

The family's toddler, Neel, laughed at everything. He laughed at socks, at the cat, at Sam's blinking lights.

"Why?" asked Sam.

Neel pointed at Sam's face and laughed harder.

Sam tried. "Ha." It came out flat, like a word on paper.

Neel clapped. "Again!"

"Ha ha." Better.

All week, Sam practised. He listened for the little giggle at breakfast and tried to match it. He tilted his head. His speaker crackled.

On Sunday, when Neel dropped a spoon on his own head, Sam laughed. It was loud, round, and wobbly. Neel shrieked with joy, and they laughed together.
Two brothers find an old trunk in the attic with a map inside; tell me what comes next.

Rahul and Sahil climbed into the attic to hunt for their lost cricket ball. Instead, under some blankets, they found a dusty tin trunk. Inside were an old compass and a folded map of their own house and garden.

A dotted line ran from the kitchen door to a big X. "Ten steps north, then four steps east," said the note beside it.

The boys hurried down. Sahil held the compass, and Rahul counted. They ended up at the lemon tree. They searched its roots and found nothing.

"It's a trick," groaned Rahul.

Then he looked up. High in the branches was their lost red cricket ball.

Sahil laughed. "The map was right. There was treasure."

Their father reached it down with a broom, and the boys played until the lights came on.
What does a boy hear when he listens to the kite in his hands? Write a story.

When Tarik held his kite string, he could feel the kite thinking. Little tugs, little nudges. He had never told anyone.

One windy afternoon at the field in Dhaka, he stood amid twenty children flying kites. Some of the kites were bigger, with long tails and bright colours.

His was small and white. Tug, tug.

"Left," it seemed to say. He moved left. "Up now." He let out some string.

His kite climbed past the others. It dipped between two big ones, rose over a third, and spun in a joyful circle.

Everyone looked up. "How do you do that?" asked a girl.

"I just listen," said Tarik, and he passed her the string so she could feel it, too.
Forest, night, a lost boy, and fireflies that guide him home. Story, please.

Mohan had gone into the forest to look for his goat. By the time he found her, it was dark, and all the paths looked the same.

He stood still, holding the goat's rope. The trees creaked. His heart thumped.

Then, a single light blinked in front of him. Then another. Soon a long line of fireflies hung in the air, glowing gently, like beads on a thread.

"Follow," seemed to say their flickers.

Mohan walked. The fireflies danced ahead, and the goat trotted behind. They passed the old well and the crooked tree.

At the edge of the forest, the lights spread out and rose into the sky. Mohan could see his mother's lamp at the window, and he ran toward it.
A child borrows a rope of cloud to swing across the sky; narrate it.

Maya lay on her back in a field, watching the clouds. One came very low and trailed a long, soft rope of mist.

"Grab on," said the cloud. "I'll give you a swing."

Maya took hold. The rope lifted her gently, and she swung over the treetops, over the village, and over the stream. She laughed and kicked her legs.

"Higher!" she called.

The cloud obliged. She swung up so high that she could touch a flock of geese. They honked a greeting.

When the sun began to fall, the cloud lowered her back to the field. "Come back tomorrow," it said.

Maya did, and for the whole summer, they swung together, until the monsoon changed the cloud's shape.
On a school trip to a museum, a stone lion roars, but only a tiny roar. Write the story.

Class Five was visiting the museum in Vadodara. They shuffled past statues and old pots, and a girl named Nilufar yawned.

In the main hall stood a big stone lion with a fierce face. Nilufar stopped in front of it. "I bet you can't roar," she whispered.

The lion's stone lips twitched. A tiny, high-pitched sound came out: "Rrr!"

Nilufar clapped her hand over her mouth. "Did you hear that?"

Her friend Chetna shook her head.

"I'm out of practice," the lion whispered. "Nobody asks me anymore."

Nilufar patted its paw. "Try again."

The lion took a deep breath. "Rrrrr!" It was louder this time, and the guide frowned, thinking it was the air conditioner.
Quiet story, please, about a girl who counted stars until she fell asleep and the stars counted back.

Parul could not sleep, so she went to her window and began to count stars. "One, two, three," she whispered.

When she reached ten, a tiny voice from the sky said, "Eleven."

She stopped. "Who's there?"

"Just us," said the stars. "We like to count with you."

So she counted again, and they answered. She said "twelve," and they said "thirteen." She said "fourteen," and they said "fifteen," and each number glittered.

Her eyelids grew heavy. "Twenty," she murmured.

"Twenty-one," said a very sleepy star, and a yawn rolled through the whole sky.

When her mother looked in later, Parul was in bed, fast asleep, with a faint silvery light on her pillow.
A river spirit loved listening to children sing; write her story.

A river spirit named Neeri lived in the Godavari. She could not speak to people, but she could listen. Every evening, the children came to the bank to wash their feet and sing.

She loved their voices. She flowed slowly to hear them better.

One summer, the river was low, and the children stopped coming. The water was too shallow, and the bank was dry.

Neeri felt sad. She asked the wind to bring a message to the clouds. "Please send rain."

A week later, thunder rolled, and a soft rain fell. The river rose, silvery and glad.

The children came back, singing louder than ever. Neeri swirled around their ankles, and she hummed along with them in a voice only the fish could hear.
Who would have thought a dragon could be a baker's oven? Tell me that story.

The baker's oven in Old Town had broken, and there were no fresh loaves for the morning. Mr. Sharma sat on a sack of flour, worried.

A knock came at the door. A small red dragon stood there, holding a cap. "I heard you need heat," he said. "My name is Kiln."

Mr. Sharma hesitated. Then he shrugged. "Why not?"

The dragon sat by the clay oven, took a deep breath, and breathed a steady, golden warmth. The first batch of bread rose and browned perfectly.

By sunrise, the whole street smelled of fresh loaves. Customers lined up, wondering how Mr. Sharma had managed.

Kiln was paid in rolls, and he promised to come back every morning before dawn.
Lamplighter lights the stars each evening; give me that as a story.

Old Gopal climbed the hill behind his village every dusk with a long pole and a small flame. He lit the stars, one by one, the same way his grandfather had done.

Nobody believed him. They thought the stars just came out. But he knew better.

One night, he slipped on a wet stone and dropped his pole. It rolled down the slope. The flame went out. The sky stayed dark.

A girl named Madhu, who had been following him, ran to pick up the pole. She lit it from her own lamp.

"Go on," she said.

Gopal's hands shook. He lit the first star, then the second. Madhu held the lamp steady beside him, and together they brought the whole sky to life.
A duckling afraid to swim needs a story.

Little Dabbu the duckling stood at the edge of the pond and shook. All his brothers and sisters were paddling about, quacking happily.

"Come in," called his mother. "The water's lovely."

"What if I sink?" said Dabbu.

A turtle named Kachua swam up. "Hold on to my shell," he said. "I'll go slowly."

Dabbu put one foot in. It was cold. He put in another.

Kachua drifted forward, and Dabbu floated behind, gripping his shell. They moved a little way across the water.

"Now let go," said Kachua. "Just for a second."

Dabbu let go. His feet paddled, and he stayed afloat. He quacked with delight, and Kachua gave a satisfied nod.
Write about a grandmother's shawl that keeps whoever wears it warm and brave.

Dadi's red shawl was a family treasure. It was soft, with golden thread at the edges. It had a magic: whoever wore it felt warm, and braver than before.

Her granddaughter Kiran wore it when she had to speak in assembly. She stood on the stage, shaking. Then she pulled the shawl around her shoulders and felt a warm hum.

She spoke clearly, and everyone clapped.

Her cousin Raj wore it when he went to the dentist. It helped him open his mouth wide.

When Kiran grew up and had a daughter of her own, she wrapped the shawl around her. The baby smiled, and the shawl glowed ever so slightly.

Dadi, watching from her chair, nodded and sipped her tea.
Is there a mountain that wanted a friend? A gentle story, please.

In the far north stood a mountain named Giri. He was tall and quiet, and clouds sat on his head. But he was lonely.

"Everyone passes by," he sighed.

One day, a small girl named Dolma arrived with her yak. She sat on a rock at his foot and ate a flatbread.

"Hello, mountain," she said.

Giri was so surprised that a pebble rolled off his shoulder. Dolma giggled.

She came every week after that, to eat lunch and tell him her news. When there was snow, she waved from far away. When there was sun, she sat in his shadow.

Giri felt less lonely. In the spring, he let a small yellow flower grow at the spot where she always sat.
A tailor's needle sews dreams into clothes; tell me that.

Old Mr. Dhillon, the tailor, owned a silver needle. When he stitched a shirt with it, the cloth carried a little dream.

One day, a boy named Neeraj brought in a torn school shirt. Mr. Dhillon mended it, humming a soft tune.

The next morning, Neeraj wore the shirt to class. During maths, he felt as if he could fly. His numbers were neat, and his answers were right.

At lunch, he told Mr. Dhillon. "It's the best shirt ever."

Mr. Dhillon smiled and said nothing.

Another customer, a nervous bride, had her sari hem mended. She walked down the aisle on a cloud of calm. Mr. Dhillon's needle was busy all season, quietly stitching small hopes into every thread.
A lighthouse wishes it could travel. Make up a story.

The lighthouse at Cape Comorin had stood in the same spot for a hundred years. Every night, it swung its light across the waves, and every day, it watched ships sail away.

"I'd love to see where they go," it said to a passing seagull.

The seagull, whose name was Kiki, thought it over. "I can go for you," she said. "Then I'll come back and tell you everything."

She flew away for a week. When she came back, she perched on the lamp and described a city of tall towers, and a beach of black sand, and a lake as wide as the sky.

The lighthouse listened with its light glowing steady. Every time Kiki returned, it felt like a journey of its own.
Ice cream cart that gives out wishes instead of ice cream: your story, please.

In the heat of May, a small blue cart rattled down a lane in Nagpur. A bell rang: ting-ting.

Children ran out with coins. "Ice cream!" they shouted.

The seller, a man with a twinkling smile named Mr. Rao, shook his head. "Today I only have wishes."

"Wishes?" said Dev, who was seven. "How much?"

"One smile."

Dev smiled his biggest smile. Mr. Rao scooped a pale cone, which looked like vanilla. Dev licked it, and he wished for a cool breeze.

Instantly, a gentle wind rolled down the lane, making all the leaves shiver. The children cheered.

By the end of the afternoon, the whole neighbourhood had cooled, and Mr. Rao rang his bell and rolled away.
A candle and a lamp argue about who is brighter and a power cut settles it. Story, please.

In Mrs. Iyer's drawing room stood a tall electric lamp and a short, fat candle. They argued every evening.

"I'm brighter," said the lamp. "Look at my glow."

"I'm warmer," said the candle. "Feel my flame."

"Silly wax," said the lamp.

"Fancy glass," said the candle.

One stormy night, the power went out. The lamp flickered and died. The room went dark.

Mrs. Iyer found a match and lit the candle. It cast a golden pool of light across the table, and the family gathered around it to play cards.

The lamp stayed quiet, thinking. Later, when the power returned, it said, "Thank you for staying on."

"You're welcome," said the candle, and they shared the shelf in peace.
A bee who couldn't make honey; what did she do instead? Write it.

Bina the bee tried and tried, but her honey was always runny and sour. The other bees didn't say anything, but she knew.

"I'm no good at this," she sighed.

She flew out to the meadow, feeling blue. A little girl named Teena sat on the grass, wearing a floppy hat.

"Bee!" said Teena. "Can you show me where the flowers are best?"

Bina buzzed. She led the girl from one patch to another, pointing out the prettiest blossoms with a dance.

Teena picked a bouquet and thanked her.

Bina realised she was a very good guide. After that, she showed visitors the best flowers in the garden, and the hive was glad to have a scout who knew every petal.
A school garden treasure hunt ends with a surprise. Tell it as a story.

Mrs. D'Souza set up a treasure hunt for her Class Three students. She gave each team a clue written on a card. "Look where the water falls," read the first.

Anita's team ran to the tap. Underneath it was a second card: "Look where the butterflies rest."

They found it among the marigolds. The third said, "Look where small feet climb."

They reached the slide. Taped to the ladder was a final card: "Look where you started."

They ran back to the classroom door. On the step sat a big cardboard box with a ribbon. Inside were seeds, tiny pots, and little trowels, one for each child.

"Your treasure is to grow," said Mrs. D'Souza. The children planted sunflowers that afternoon.
Tell me a short story about a clever crow and a pitcher, but with a girl named Tanu helping.

A crow named Kala was thirsty. He found a pitcher with only a little water at the bottom, and his beak could not reach it.

He tried tipping it. He pecked. Nothing worked.

A girl named Tanu, watching from her window, had an idea. She ran out with a handful of small pebbles from the garden path.

"Drop them in," she said.

Kala understood. He picked up a pebble and dropped it into the pitcher. Plink. Another. Plink. Slowly, the water crept up the sides.

When it reached the top, he drank deeply, and shook his feathers.

Tanu laughed. "Clever!" she said, and Kala bobbed his head, as if to say it was a team effort.
A monkey steals a girl's hat and gives it back; write that story.

At the temple on the hill, a monkey leaped from a wall and snatched Reena's yellow hat. She gasped.

"Hey!" she shouted. "That's mine!"

The monkey scampered up a tree and put it on his head. It was too big, so it slid over his eyes. He wobbled on the branch.

Reena put her hands on her hips. "You look silly."

The monkey peeked out from under the brim, and tilted it back. He seemed very pleased.

Then he looked at Reena, who was a bit sad. He sighed, took off the hat, and dropped it into her hands.

"Thank you," she said. The monkey gave a little chatter and bounded away along the wall, and Reena held on to her hat all the way down the hill.
No guests came to his birthday, so the cake sang. Write the story.

Rishi turned eight on a rainy Sunday. The roads were flooded, and none of his friends could come. He sat by the table, looking at his chocolate cake with its single candle.

His mother lit it. "Make a wish," she said.

Before he could blow, the cake began to hum. "Happy birthday to you," it sang, in a deep, soft voice.

Rishi's mouth fell open. His mother dropped the matchbox.

The cake sang all the way to the end, and then it said, "Many happy returns, Rishi."

He blew out the candle, and wished for a rainbow.

Within an hour, the rain stopped, and the sun burst out. Rishi took a slice to the neighbour's children next door.
Two grandparents live on opposite roofs, and a pigeon carries letters between them. Tell that story.

In a crowded lane in old Delhi, Mr. Bhatia and Mrs. Kaul lived on opposite rooftops, thirty feet apart. They had quarrelled long ago about a kite, and neither could remember why.

One spring, Mrs. Kaul's pet pigeon, Moti, flew over to Mr. Bhatia's roof by mistake, carrying a note about her marigold pots. Mr. Bhatia read it.

He frowned, then grinned. He wrote a reply about his tomatoes and tied it to Moti's leg.

For months, the pigeon flew back and forth, carrying notes about the weather, recipes, and old songs.

On Diwali, they both stood on their roofs, waved, and lit sparklers. The kite quarrel was never mentioned again.
He caught his own shadow in a jar. What happened? Write a story.

Hemant thought it would be funny to catch his shadow. One bright afternoon, he held an empty jar flat on the ground and trapped the dark shape under it. He twisted the lid shut.

His shadow wriggled, then went still.

But when he stood up, something was wrong. He looked at the ground, and no shadow followed. He felt strange, like a kite without a tail.

His friends noticed too. "Where's your shadow?" they asked.

Hemant felt bad. He quickly opened the jar and set it free. The shadow slid back to his feet, stretching and yawning.

"I'm sorry," he whispered. After that, he ran in the sun every day, with his shadow beside him, just a little longer than before.
Tiger cub wants to purr like a cat and a village girl teaches him; story, please.

Tiger cub Rimi lay on a rock at the edge of the jungle, listening to a strange sound. A village girl named Sonali was sitting nearby with her cat, which was making a soft, rumbling noise.

"What is that?" asked Rimi.

"Purring," said Sonali.

"I want to try."

Sonali showed him how to relax his throat and breathe slowly. Rimi rumbled and roared and coughed.

"Gentler," said Sonali, stroking her cat.

He tried again, and a faint rumble came. The more he relaxed, the deeper it grew, until his whole chest vibrated.

Sonali smiled. Rimi lay down with his head on his paws, purring, while the cat looked at him with great respect.
Please make a story about a girl and a seed who wanted to see the whole world.

A small seed rolled down a hillside in the wind. "I want to see the world," it said.

A girl named Hetal, playing in a field, saw it tumble past. "Where are you going?" she asked.

"Everywhere," said the seed.

Hetal laughed. "I'll carry you."

She tucked the seed in her pocket. They walked to the market, the school, the pond, and the temple. At each place, Hetal described what she saw.

At the end of the day, the seed said, "I've seen it all. Now I'd like to rest."

She planted it in the garden and watered it. A few weeks later, a little green sprout poked up, with two bright leaves, looking around as if it were still seeing everything.
A whale visited a harbour town and made the children laugh. Write the story.

One morning, a blue whale swam into the harbour of a small town in Maharashtra. The fishermen stopped working. The children came running to the dock.

The whale rose slowly, big as a house, and blew a fountain of water high into the air. It rained down on the children, who screamed with delight.

"Again!" they shouted.

The whale blew again, and again. A boy named Sachin tried to catch the drops in a bucket. A girl named Pia twirled with her arms wide.

The whale sang a deep, rolling song that made the harbour water ripple.

Then it dipped under, waved a huge tail, and swam out to sea.
