The children talked about it for weeks and drew whales on every wall.
Street dog walks a blind man home each evening. Can you write it as a story?

Every evening, Mr. Pillai walked home from the tea shop. His eyes had grown weak, and the lane was full of puddles and bicycles.

A thin brown street dog, whom the children called Sheru, began to walk beside him one monsoon evening. He nudged Mr. Pillai's knee when a puddle came, and stopped when a bicycle passed.

"Good dog," said Mr. Pillai, surprised.

After that, Sheru waited outside the tea shop each day. He led Mr. Pillai round the pothole, past the temple, and to the gate.

Mr. Pillai started leaving a bowl of rice and milk on his step. Sheru ate it, wagged his tail, and curled up on the doormat for the night.
A cooking pot that told the best stories in the village; narrate one of its evenings.

In Amma Lakshmi's kitchen, there was a big copper pot. When the dal simmered, the pot told stories, in a soft bubbling voice.

Only the children could hear it. They sat around the stove after school, wide-eyed.

"Today," said the pot, "I'll tell you about a prince and a magic mango."

The story went on for as long as the dal cooked. At the best part, the dal began to boil over, and the pot said, "To be continued."

"No!" cried the children.

But Amma Lakshmi lifted the lid, and the story paused. The next day, the dal went on, and so did the tale.

When the stories ended, the children ate the dal in happy silence, and they still remembered every word.
An island floats across the sea to visit the coast. Tell that tale.

Out in the Arabian Sea floated a small green island called Hari. She was tired of seeing nothing but water. One morning, she drifted slowly toward the mainland.

The people of a fishing village woke up to find the island beside their beach. They rubbed their eyes. A small girl named Fiza waded out and climbed onto the island's soft grass.

"Hello," said Hari, in a sandy voice. "May I stay a day?"

"Of course!" said Fiza.

The villagers brought food and mats. They held a picnic on her shore, and children chased crabs.

By evening, Hari felt happy. She rose with the tide and floated gently back to sea. Fiza waved, and the island's coconut trees waved back.
A puppet wants to cut its strings and be free; write what happens.

Pinak the puppet danced on the stage of a travelling puppet show. His strings were tied to a wooden cross held by an old puppeteer named Bhaskar.

"I want to be free," he whispered one night.

A tiny mouse heard him and gnawed through a string. Pinak wobbled. He took a step, and then another.

He walked off the stage, past the wagon, and into the dark. But without his strings, he could not climb steps or open doors. He sat down by a hedge, feeling lost.

In the morning, Bhaskar found him and gently tied a new string, but this time on only one hand. "You can lead," he said.

Pinak did, and he and Bhaskar worked the stage together.
Gentle jungle adventure, please: a little elephant looks for the end of the rainbow.

Eeku the baby elephant saw a rainbow over the jungle. "I'll find the end of it," he said.

He trundled through the tall grass. A monkey swung down. "Where are you going?"

"To the end of the rainbow."

"I'll come," said the monkey, whose name was Chintu.

They waded through a stream and climbed a gentle slope. A parrot flew along and cheered them on.

At the top of the hill, the rainbow was fading. They stood together, looking at the colours dissolve into the sky.

"We missed it," said Eeku, sadly.

"But look," said Chintu. Below them, in a clearing, a hundred wildflowers glowed in all the rainbow colours.

They ran down and rolled in the petals until dusk.
What if the sun was sleepy and needed a child to wake him? Write it as a story.

The Sun was always late on Mondays. He liked his cloud-pillow too much. One Monday, he slept so long that the sky stayed dark and the roosters didn't know when to crow.

In a village in Bihar, a girl named Champa woke up and found it was still night. She looked out and saw the stars. "It's too long," she said.

She ran out to the courtyard and called, "Good morning, Sun!"

The Sun snored.

She fetched her grandmother's brass prayer bell and rang it three times. Ding, ding, ding.

The Sun opened one eye. "Is it that time already?" He yawned and stretched.

A golden light spilled over the hills. The roosters crowed. Champa gave the bell a final cheerful ring.
I'd like a story about a bathtub boat that sailed to a faraway island, with a happy ending.

Ishita's plastic bathtub boat, Captain Quack, was a bright yellow duck. One evening, when the tap ran too long, the tub overflowed, and a gentle stream carried the duck across the bathroom floor, under the door, and down the hall.

It floated into the garden, where the rain had made a wide puddle. It sailed on, past a flowerpot and around a stone, to a small mound of earth in the middle.

"Land ahoy," said Captain Quack, who was fond of saying things like that.

An ant crawled out and waved. "Welcome to Mud Island."

The duck stayed for tea in a thimble. When Ishita came looking, she found him resting, and carried him home with a very big smile.
Write about a goatherd and a talking hill that shows him a safe path in the mist.

Hari was a goatherd in the hills of Uttarakhand. One morning, a thick mist rolled in while his goats were grazing high on the slope. He could not see his own hands.

"Where are you, little ones?" he called. The goats bleated, but the sound seemed to come from every side.

"Walk straight," said a low voice beneath his feet. It was the hill itself. "Left a little. Now straight again."

Hari trusted it. He stepped slowly, following the voice, and found each goat one by one. Their bells tinkled in the fog.

When the mist cleared, they were all standing together near a stone hut. Hari patted the ground. "Thank you," he said, and the hill gave a faint, mossy rumble.
In 100 words or fewer, tell me about a boy who opened a door in his dream and met a friendly dragon.

Nikhil dreamed of a long blue corridor with one white door at the end. He pushed it open. Behind it sat a small orange dragon, reading a comic.

"Oh!" said the dragon. "I wasn't expecting anyone."

"Sorry," said Nikhil.

"No, no, come in. Do you like jam sandwiches?"

They sat on the floor and ate sandwiches, and the dragon let Nikhil read the comic over his shoulder. When the corridor began to fade, the dragon said, "Same time tomorrow?"

Nikhil woke up smiling. That night, the door was open, and two jam sandwiches waited on the floor.
